protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Airway
protocols.subtitle: The CICO decision tree, why "wake the patient" was removed from the emergency pathway, scalpel cricothyrotomy technique, and the assessment tools that predict trouble before you ever pick up a blade.

sections.title: Emergency Management — The Failed Airway Sequence
sections.tagline: The decision that matters most is made before the laryngoscope goes in. Once you're in trouble, the goal shifts from "get the tube" to "keep oxygenating" — the tube can wait.

steps.title: Declare it and call for help
steps.html: The moment you recognize a failed attempt or failed oxygenation, say so out loud. Most airway deaths occur after the third attempt — task fixation and the "ego tube" (pushing repeated attempts instead of pivoting) are the actual killers, not anatomy.

steps.title: Optimize and reattempt once, with a change
steps.html: Reposition (RAMP/ear-to-sternal-notch in obesity), try a bougie with video laryngoscopy, try a hyperangulated blade — change something rather than repeating the identical attempt. No view at all? Come out and bag.

steps.title: Can you bag them? — the branch point that matters most
steps.html: Good BVM seal and ventilation present: you have time. Adjust variables, consider a flexible/rigid intubating scope or an intubating SGA. Cannot bag effectively: place a supraglottic airway immediately — SGA placement is the standard next rescue step before jumping to a surgical airway, and restores oxygenation faster than repeated laryngoscopy.

steps.title: SGA also fails to oxygenate → this is CICO, act now
steps.html: Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate. This is the true emergency pathway. Do not attempt to "wake the patient" — that option was deliberately removed from the 2022 ASA emergency pathway, since a non-patent airway isn't reliably reversible by simply stopping drugs.

steps.title: Surgical cricothyrotomy — the definitive adult rescue
steps.html: Scalpel cricothyrotomy is preferred over needle cricothyrotomy for adult CICO per ASA 2022 / current DAS guidance — needle cric with jet ventilation is temporizing only; CO₂ accumulates fast and it's easy to lose the airway again. Technique: palpate the cricothyroid membrane between thyroid and cricoid cartilage (ultrasound if landmarks are unclear); vertical stab incision, horizontal extension through the membrane, bougie-guided ETT placement — bougie-assisted open technique is fastest to teach and perform under pressure. Pediatrics: no surgical cric under age 8–12 — needle cric only until then.

steps.title: Watch elapsed time and saturation throughout — not just attempt count
steps.html: The 2022 ASA guidelines emphasize continuous oxygenation and time-awareness over a strict attempt-count rule. "Three attempts" isn't a protocol — it's an ego limit. Have your next move planned after attempt one, not after attempt three.

blocks.title: The surgical airway is not a failure — not doing it when you should is
blocks.html: CICO incidence is low (roughly 0.002–0.04% of general anesthetics) but accounts for a disproportionate share of anesthetic mortality when it happens. Hesitation, not the procedure itself, is what kills people in this scenario.

A difficult airway is any clinical situation where a trained provider experiences difficulty with face mask ventilation, supraglottic airway ventilation, laryngoscopy, intubation, or extubation — the 2022 ASA guidelines explicitly broadened the definition beyond just "hard to intubate" to include SGA and extubation problems as well.

The truly emergent version — Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate (CICO) — occurs in roughly 0.0019–0.04% of cases but represents close to 25% of anesthesia-related mortality, making it the most common lethal respiratory emergency in perioperative practice. The problem is almost never that the anatomy was impossible; it's that the failure to oxygenate wasn't recognized and acted on quickly enough.

rows: Look externally · Evaluate 3-3-2 (3 finger-breadths mouth opening, 3 chin-to-hyoid, 2 hyoid-to-thyroid notch) · Mallampati · Obstruction · Neck mobility — the core difficult-laryngoscopy screen.
Restricted mouth opening · Obstruction · Distorted airway · Stiff lungs/cervical spine — predicts difficult supraglottic airway ventilation specifically.
Surgery (prior neck surgery/radiation changes anatomy) · Hematoma · Obesity · Radiation · Tumor — predicts a difficult surgical airway, worth assessing even when you don't expect to need one.

Hypoxemia, hypotension, and metabolic acidosis predict a bad outcome on induction independent of anatomy — "the crash." A physiologically hostile patient can die on induction with a perfectly normal-looking airway.

blocks.html: The ugly airway is usually ugly before you touch it — look harder. Trauma-specific red flags: blood in the oropharynx, restricted mouth opening, an expanding neck hematoma (the airway you see now may not be the airway in 10 minutes — Zone II penetrating trauma with a growing hematoma means the surgical airway decision comes earlier than feels comfortable).

sections.title: Plan Before You Touch the Patient (In Place of "Room Setup")

blocks.html:
• Name your primary, backup, and bailout before induction — all three, every time. If you don't have a bailout, you don't have a plan. Know explicitly who performs the surgical airway and under what trigger.
  • Consider awake intubation when difficulty is anticipated plus any of: known/suspected difficult airway on exam, high aspiration risk, poor tolerance of an apneic period, or a predicted CICO scenario — awake technique carries far lower risk than inducing first and finding out.
  • Difficult airway cart immediately available and stocked: video laryngoscope, bougie, multiple SGA sizes, surgical airway kit, and the cricothyroid membrane marked/identified in advance (palpation, or ultrasound if landmarks are unclear) for any anticipated-difficult case.
  • Preoxygenate as treatment, not prep — see Numbers to Know below. A 100% SpO₂ on the monitor is a margin, not a guarantee; it reflects reservoir oxygen, not whether the airway is currently patent.
  • Use nasal cannula apneic oxygenation during laryngoscopy (15 L/min, Levitan's NODESAT technique) — low-cost, no-harm, use it routinely. Evidence for meaningful benefit is stronger in healthy well-preoxygenated patients than in critically ill ones (the FELLOW trial showed no benefit in ICU patients specifically) — treat it as a helpful adjunct, not a substitute for real preoxygenation.
  • State the difficult-airway status explicitly during time-out, and document the specific findings (grade of view, device that worked, number of attempts) in the chart for every future anesthetic.

rows: Tight-seal BVM at 15 L/min for 3–5 minutes replaces alveolar nitrogen with O₂ — roughly 3,000 mL of O₂ reservoir in the lungs vs. ~450 mL on room air. This is the actual intervention that extends safe apnea time, not the pulse ox reading.

Nasal cannula at 15 L/min left running through laryngoscopy. Extends safe apnea time in healthy, well-preoxygenated patients; benefit not demonstrated in critically ill ICU populations (FELLOW trial). Use it — it doesn't replace nitrogen washout.
~0.0019–0.04% of general anesthetics — rare per case, but accounts for a large share of airway-related mortality when it occurs.
Roughly 25% — the single most common lethal respiratory emergency in perioperative medicine.

No fixed number of attempts is "the rule" — the 2022 ASA guidance emphasizes continuous awareness of elapsed time and oxygen saturation over any specific attempt count. Most airway deaths occur after the third attempt because providers keep trying the same thing instead of escalating.
6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight, not actual weight — obese patients have the same lung, bigger body; dosing on actual weight risks volutrauma.

blocks.html:
Why "wake the patient" was removed from the emergency pathway: the option assumes that stopping drugs restores a patent airway and spontaneous ventilation quickly enough to prevent hypoxic injury. In a true CICO scenario the airway itself may not be patent regardless of anesthetic depth, so waiting for the patient to wake up wastes the exact time that oxygenation rescue needs. The non-emergency pathway (can ventilate, can't intubate) still reasonably includes waking the patient as an option — the distinction is whether oxygenation, not just intubation, has failed.

Why oxygenation is monitored separately from intubation success: pulse oximetry reflects the oxygen already bound to hemoglobin and stored in a preoxygenated lung — it can stay reassuring for a period of time after the airway has actually become non-patent. Treating SpO₂ as a real-time "is the airway open" signal is a common and dangerous misread; it's a lagging indicator, not a live one.

Why SGA rescue comes before surgical airway, but doesn't delay it if it fails: supraglottic airway placement restores oxygenation faster than repeated laryngoscopy attempts and is successful in the large majority of "can't intubate" scenarios, which is why it's the standard next step. But if it doesn't restore oxygenation, that failure defines true CICO — the moment SGA also fails, further attempts at anything other than a surgical airway are wasting the same limited oxygen reserve that killed the "wake the patient" option above.

Why scalpel cricothyrotomy is preferred over needle cric in adults: needle techniques with jet ventilation are genuinely temporizing — CO₂ clearance is poor, barotrauma risk is real, and the airway can be lost again quickly. A scalpel-bougie-tube approach delivers a cuffed, definitive airway in comparable or faster time in trained hands, which is why current guidelines designate it the preferred adult CICO rescue rather than a last resort.

Why nitrogen washout matters more than people give it credit for: a "100% SpO₂" on a patient who was only briefly preoxygenated with a loose mask seal still has a small functional oxygen reserve, because most of the reservoir gain comes from actually displacing alveolar nitrogen with oxygen over several minutes of tight-seal breathing — not from the number on the monitor at the moment of induction.

rows: IgE-mediated, fast onset (minutes), systemic — skin, cardiovascular, and airway together. Epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM (adult) is first-line and works well.
Slower onset than anaphylaxis but faster than HAE; airway edema without the full systemic pattern; responds to epinephrine/antihistamines similarly to anaphylaxis.

Bradykinin-mediated, not histamine-mediated. Slow onset over hours. Airway edema dominant, no hives, no hypotension. Epinephrine may slow it but does not reverse it — definitive treatment is C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, both hospital-level.

Bacterial (H. influenzae, S. aureus), onset over hours to days. Classic triad: drooling, dysphagia, distress ("tripod" positioning). Do not examine the throat or force the patient supine — either can trigger complete obstruction. Position of comfort, transport to a controlled airway setting (OR).
Trismus, muffled "hot potato" voice, unilateral tonsillar deviation (peritonsillar) — differentiate from diffuse angioedema by the asymmetric, localized exam finding.

Clear temporal link to a procedure or trauma mechanism; progressive, exam-visible swelling rather than diffuse edema — decompression (opening the wound at bedside if post-surgical) may be needed before any airway attempt.

blocks.html: The voice is an early warning most people miss. A muffled, "hot potato" voice quality in an ambulatory, normally-saturating patient reflects airway narrowing before saturation ever drops — by the time SpO₂ falls or stridor appears, the window to secure the airway electively may already be closing.

Confirmation: waveform capnography is the only reliable confirmation of correct tube placement — pulse oximetry and chest rise are not sufficient on their own. Loss of the waveform at any point should be treated as a displaced tube until proven otherwise, not an equipment glitch.

Depth and positioning: mark and document tube depth at the teeth/lips, confirm bilateral breath sounds — right mainstem intubation is a common and easy-to-miss complication, especially after a rushed attempt in a bloody or distorted airway.

Post-intubation sedation: a paralyzed, unsedated patient is a sentinel event — plan sedation before the paralytic wears off, not after. Reasonable options: ketamine infusion, midazolam plus fentanyl, or propofol if hemodynamically stable.

Disposition: ICU-level monitoring for any difficult or failed airway case, regardless of how the eventual airway was secured. Do not extubate a documented difficult airway in an uncontrolled setting — plan extubation as deliberately as the original intubation, ideally with the same difficult-airway equipment immediately available.

Documentation: record the specific difficulty encountered, what worked, what didn't, and grade of view — this becomes the single most valuable piece of information for every subsequent anesthetic this patient ever has.

protocols.title: Laryngospasm
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Airway
protocols.subtitle: A protective reflex turned airway emergency — the escalation ladder from jaw thrust to succinylcholine, why the low-dose route is usually the right one, and the complication that shows up after you've already broken the spasm.
protocols.description: Escalation ladder from jaw thrust to succinylcholine, WFSA-aligned dosing, negative pressure pulmonary edema as the delayed complication.

sections.title: Emergency Management — The Escalation Ladder
sections.tagline: Most laryngospasm resolves with the first two steps. Escalate quickly if it doesn't — hypoxia plus a paralytic is a dangerous combination if the airway still isn't secured.

steps.title: Stop the stimulus, call for help
steps.html: Remove the triggering stimulus if one is identifiable (suction catheter, surgical stimulation, extubation timing). Get another set of hands — this escalates fast if it doesn't break quickly.

steps.title: Jaw thrust / Larson's maneuver + CPAP with 100% O₂
steps.html: Firm jaw thrust at the "laryngospasm notch" — bilateral pressure behind the ramus of the mandible, anterior to the mastoid process. Simultaneously apply CPAP via tight-seal BVM with a PEEP valve. Avoid vigorous positive-pressure ventilation attempts — forceful bagging against a closed glottis risks gastric insufflation. Larson's maneuver has limited controlled evidence behind it, but it's low-risk and widely used as first response.

steps.title: Clear the airway, deepen anesthesia
steps.html: Suction the pharynx if blood or secretions are contributing. If not already breaking: propofol 0.5–0.8 mg/kg IV (subhypnotic doses as low as 0.25 mg/kg have been effective) — deepens anesthesia and relaxes upper airway tissue without the full apnea burden of a paralytic.

steps.title: Desaturating or no response — succinylcholine
steps.html: Low dose often sufficient to break the spasm: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV (full paralysis in 30–45 sec, breaks spasm in 45 sec–1 min). Severe/refractory: full dose 1–1.5 mg/kg IV and proceed to intubation. No IV access: succinylcholine 4 mg/kg IM (onset slower, roughly 3–4 minutes) or 2 mg/kg intralingual (IM into the tongue body — retains perfusion better than peripheral muscle during hypoxia, but carries a high rate of transient arrhythmia). Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg IV is a reasonable alternative if succinylcholine is contraindicated.

steps.title: Treat bradycardia if it develops
steps.html: Airway manipulation and succinylcholine can both provoke bradycardia/arrest in a hypoxic patient, especially children. Correct hypoxia urgently and give atropine 0.02 mg/kg for symptomatic bradycardia.

steps.title: Intubate if the spasm doesn't break
steps.html: Forced orotracheal intubation, even through partially closed cords if necessary, rescues the airway — some vocal cord trauma is an acceptable trade for hypoxic arrest. Laryngospasm is often followed by a brief gasp; that moment can be your window to pass the tube.

steps.title: Surgical airway — last resort
steps.html: Cricothyrotomy/tracheostomy only if intubation also fails and oxygenation cannot otherwise be restored — same CICO logic as any other failed airway.

blocks.title: Not always obvious
blocks.html: Roughly 23% of laryngospasm cases don't present with the classic high-pitched crowing sound — some present only as increasing work of breathing, paradoxical chest movement, or desaturation without any audible warning. Suspect it whenever airway obstruction appears without an obvious supraglottic cause.

Laryngospasm is an exaggeration of the normal protective glottic-closure reflex — sustained closure of the true (and often false) vocal cords that partially or completely obstructs the airway. Sensory input runs through the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; the motor response is mediated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve driving the intrinsic laryngeal muscles. It occurs most often during induction and emergence from general anesthesia, though it's also described during procedural sedation and, rarely, in the awake state.

It's a relatively common perioperative event, more frequent in children than adults — pediatric procedural sedation series report roughly 3.9 per 1,000 cases versus about 1.1 per 1,000 in adults, and the large majority of reported cases involve ketamine sedation specifically.

rows: Classic warning sign of partial laryngospasm — but absent in a meaningful minority of cases.
No audible sound at all once the cords fully close — the most dangerous presentation because it's easy to miss initially.
Chest and abdomen moving in opposite directions ("see-saw" breathing) against an obstructed airway.
Bradycardia in this setting is usually hypoxia-driven — correcting oxygenation is the primary fix, not atropine alone.
Airway obstruction unresponsive to an oral airway
Distinguishes true laryngospasm from simple supraglottic (tongue-based) obstruction, which typically resolves with an OPA and jaw thrust alone.

sections.title: Risk Factors & Prevention (In Place of "Room Setup")

blocks.html:
• Patient factors: young age (children, especially infants), airway hypersensitivity, recent upper respiratory tract infection, passive or active smoke exposure, obesity with obstructive sleep apnea, GERD, structural airway anomaly.
  • Anesthetic/procedural factors: light plane of anesthesia during airway manipulation, blood/secretions/gastric contents irritating the cords, laryngoscopy or suction catheter stimulation, extubation during a light ("stage 2") plane of anesthesia — a well-recognized higher-risk moment.
  • Prevention strategies: IV propofol induction rather than inhalational induction in children reduces risk; IV lidocaine or magnesium sulfate given prophylactically has supporting evidence in at-risk cases; extubating either fully awake or fully deep (not in between) avoids the highest-risk light plane; suctioning and clearing the airway thoroughly before extubation reduces stimulus load.
  • Have the ladder ready before extubating a higher-risk patient: propofol drawn up, succinylcholine dose calculated and available, difficult airway equipment nearby — treat any extubation in a known at-risk patient the way you'd treat a planned difficult airway.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: First pharmacologic step if positioning/CPAP alone doesn't break it; deepens anesthesia without full paralysis.
Often sufficient to break the spasm alone; full paralysis in 30–45 sec.
Use for severe/refractory spasm; proceed directly to intubation.
No IV access; onset markedly slower (~3–4 min) than IV routes.
Faster onset than peripheral IM since tongue retains perfusion better during hypoxia; high rate (>50%) of transient arrhythmia reported.
Alternative if succinylcholine contraindicated; longer duration of action.
Reported successful when no IV access and succinylcholine unavailable — not first-line, but a documented rescue option.
For symptomatic bradycardia during airway manipulation/succinylcholine administration.

blocks.html:
Why deepen anesthesia before reaching for a paralytic: laryngospasm is fundamentally a reflex problem — the cords are closing in response to a stimulus interpreted as threatening. Deepening anesthesia with propofol reduces the reflex arc's sensitivity directly, often resolving the spasm without the apnea and full recovery time a paralytic requires. It's the lower-risk intervention and is tried first whenever the patient isn't yet critically hypoxic.

Why low-dose succinylcholine is often enough: the goal isn't full surgical paralysis — it's relaxing the intrinsic laryngeal muscles enough to break the spasm. A fractional dose (0.1–0.2 mg/kg) frequently accomplishes this while preserving some respiratory drive and shortening total recovery time compared to a full RSI dose, which is why experienced anesthesia providers often reach for the low dose before escalating.

Why avoid vigorous bag-mask ventilation attempts: forcing positive pressure against a closed or partially closed glottis pushes air into the stomach instead of the lungs, distending it and increasing aspiration risk without improving oxygenation — CPAP (steady pressure, not forceful bagging) is the correct technique while waiting for pharmacologic treatment to work.

Why the tongue is used for IM injection when there's no IV: peripheral skeletal muscle perfusion drops significantly during hypoxia and shock, slowing drug uptake from a standard IM injection exactly when speed matters most. The tongue retains relatively better blood flow under those conditions, which is the physiologic basis for intralingual succinylcholine as a faster-acting alternative to a deltoid or thigh injection — at the cost of a higher reported arrhythmia rate.

Why Larson's maneuver persists in every algorithm despite weak evidence: the proposed mechanism is that firm, painful pressure at the laryngospasm notch triggers vocal cord relaxation via a pain-mediated autonomic reflex — plausible, widely taught, and low-risk to attempt, but it has never been validated in a controlled trial. It's kept in the sequence because it costs nothing to try while CPAP and repositioning are already underway, not because the evidence is strong.

rows: Resolves promptly with jaw thrust and an oral/nasal airway alone — true laryngospasm does not resolve with positioning adjuncts.
Expiratory wheeze rather than inspiratory stridor; obstruction is lower-airway, not glottic; treated with bronchodilators rather than the laryngospasm ladder.
Foreign body / secretions occluding the airway
Suctioning or removal resolves it directly; laryngospasm can co-occur if the material itself is the triggering stimulus.
Accompanied by hypotension, urticaria, or other systemic features; treated with epinephrine, not the airway-deepening ladder.
Hours-to-days onset, drooling/dysphagia/distress triad — an entirely different, infectious process; do not examine the throat.
Vocal cord dysfunction / paradoxical vocal fold motion
Can mimic laryngospasm in awake or lightly sedated patients; often has a psychogenic or irritant-triggered component and doesn't follow the anesthesia-induction/emergence timing pattern.

blocks.html:
Watch for negative pressure pulmonary edema: forceful inspiratory effort against a closed glottis generates markedly negative intrathoracic pressure, which can pull fluid into the alveoli once the obstruction clears — this can present minutes to a couple of hours after the laryngospasm itself resolves, so don't consider the episode "closed" the moment oxygenation normalizes.

Reintubation/airway support: once broken, support with 100% O₂ and reassess. If the patient was intubated to break the spasm, continued intubation may be appropriate if airway soiling or pulmonary edema occurred, allowing suctioning and lung recruitment before extubation is reattempted.

Disposition: extended PACU or ICU-level observation after any laryngospasm requiring pharmacologic intervention, specifically to catch delayed negative pressure pulmonary edema and confirm full recovery from any paralytic given.

Documentation and future anesthetics: record the trigger, the intervention that worked, and the total drug doses given. Recurrent laryngospasm (especially post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy patients) may warrant a modified extubation plan or subhypnotic propofol prophylaxis on future anesthetics; genuinely recurrent cases occasionally prompt consideration of superior laryngeal nerve block as an extreme preventive measure.

protocols.title: Acute Transfusion Reactions
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Perioperative
protocols.subtitle: AHTR, TRALI, and TACO can look nearly identical at the bedside within the first hour — and TACO's treatment (diuresis) is close to the opposite of what TRALI needs. Getting the differential right is the whole game.
protocols.description: AHTR vs. TRALI vs. TACO side-by-side, why TACO and TRALI need opposite fluid strategies, StatPearls/ASH-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Step 1 is universal. Steps after that diverge hard depending on which reaction you're actually looking at — misreading TACO as TRALI (or vice versa) means giving the wrong treatment entirely.

steps.title: Stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV open
steps.html: Universal first step regardless of which reaction is suspected. Maintain venous access with normal saline through a separate line/port — don't flush the suspect unit's tubing into the patient.

steps.title: Verify identity and notify the blood bank
steps.html: Recheck patient and unit ID for a clerical mismatch — the leading cause of ABO-incompatible AHTR is human error, not a lab failure. Send the remaining unit, tubing, and a fresh patient sample back to the blood bank for repeat type and crossmatch.

steps.title: Full ABCDE assessment, determine which reaction this actually is
steps.html: Fever + flank/back pain + hemoglobinuria points toward AHTR. Hypoxia + hypotension/normotension without hypertension points toward TRALI. Hypoxia + hypertension + rales + a positive fluid balance points toward TACO. These can overlap early — reassess as more information (BNP, imaging) comes in rather than committing to one diagnosis prematurely.

steps.title: Suspected AHTR
steps.html: Aggressive IV crystalloid to maintain urine output (targeting a diuresis around 500 mL/hr of 0.9% NaCl as tolerated) to protect the kidneys from hemoglobin-mediated injury. Anticipate hypotension, AKI, and DIC. If DIC with clinically significant bleeding develops, give FFP, cryoprecipitate (for fibrinogen), and platelets as indicated — don't wait for bleeding to become severe before treating the coagulopathy.

steps.title: Suspected TRALI
steps.html: Supportive oxygenation; escalate to mechanical ventilation with low tidal volume (ARDS-protective strategy) if needed. Diuretics are not indicated in the absence of clear concurrent volume overload — TRALI is permeability edema, not hydrostatic, and unnecessary diuresis can worsen an already hypotensive patient. No evidence supports steroids or antihistamines.

steps.title: Suspected TACO
steps.html: Sit the patient upright, give oxygen, and diurese — the most specific and effective treatment is stopping the transfusion and actively removing the excess volume. This is close to the opposite instinct from TRALI management, which is exactly why correctly distinguishing the two matters so much in the first few minutes.

steps.title: Allergic / anaphylactic reactions
steps.html: Urticaria alone: diphenhydramine, and the transfusion may be restarted after ~20 minutes if symptoms resolve. Multi-system involvement (hypotension, angioedema, respiratory compromise): treat as full anaphylaxis with epinephrine — see the Anaphylaxis crisis file. Fever is characteristically absent in allergic/anaphylactic reactions, which is one of the more useful bedside clues separating this from AHTR.

steps.title: Suspected septic/bacterial contamination reaction
steps.html: High fever is the hallmark. Start broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics immediately, with antipseudomonal coverage specifically if red cells were the product transfused. Culture the remaining unit and the patient.

blocks.title: In an anesthetized or unconscious patient, the usual warning signs are hidden
blocks.html: Fever, pain, and dyspnea — the symptoms that usually flag AHTR — are masked under general anesthesia. Unexplained hypotension, oozing in the surgical field, hemoglobinuria in the Foley bag, or an unexplained rise in temperature may be the only available clues. A high index of suspicion has to substitute for the symptoms the patient can't report.

Acute transfusion reactions occur within 24 hours of starting a transfusion (as opposed to delayed reactions, which occur 24 hours to 30 days out) and range from benign to fatal. The clinically important severe ones are acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR), transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), and transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) — together with anaphylaxis and septic/bacterial contamination reactions, these account for essentially all transfusion-related morbidity and mortality, even though the much more common reactions (febrile non-hemolytic, mild allergic) are far more frequently encountered day to day.

AHTR is antibody-mediated destruction of transfused red cells, most often from ABO incompatibility — usually the result of a clerical/identification error rather than a laboratory failure, and most severe when type A donor blood is given to a type O recipient. TRALI is noncardiogenic (permeability) pulmonary edema, historically the leading cause of transfusion-related death in FDA fatality data. TACO is cardiogenic (hydrostatic) pulmonary edema from volume or rate of transfusion exceeding the recipient's cardiac reserve — now recognized as one of the two leading causes of transfusion-related death alongside TRALI.

rows: During or within 6 hr of transfusion
During or within 6 hr of transfusion
Flank/back/chest pain, hemoglobinuria (or hematuria as the first sign under anesthesia), nausea, wheezing
No response to diuretics; BNP not typically elevated
Elevated BNP; positive fluid balance; improves with diuresis
Donor anti-HLA/anti-HNA antibodies (or biologically active lipids) activating recipient neutrophils in the pulmonary microvasculature
Recipient's cardiac/renal reserve can't handle the transfused volume/rate

blocks.html:
• Positive patient identification at every step — bedside verification against the unit tag by two providers, since clerical/ID error is the dominant cause of ABO-incompatible AHTR, not a lab typing failure.
  • TRALI mitigation is a donor-side strategy: using plasma from male donors, or from female donors who are nulliparous or have tested negative for HLA antibodies, meaningfully reduces TRALI incidence — this is a blood-bank-level intervention, not something adjusted at the bedside. Prophylactic antihistamine or acetaminophen before transfusion has no proven role in preventing TRALI specifically.
  • TACO prevention is rate- and volume-focused: decrease the transfusion rate, especially in patients with heart failure, renal dysfunction, hypoalbuminemia, or an already-positive fluid balance. Prophylactic diuretic co-administration can be considered in higher-risk patients.
  • Leukoreduction helps prevent febrile non-hemolytic reactions specifically, and is now standard for most blood products at many institutions.
  • Know your patient's risk factors before transfusing — pre-existing cardiac/renal disease and volume status change both the TACO risk calculus and the transfusion rate you should be using.
  • Monitor vital signs at defined intervals through and after transfusion (commonly hourly through several hours post-transfusion) — early detection shortens the interval between reaction onset and stopping the unit.

rows: TRALI incidence, historical vs. after male-donor-plasma mitigation
Fell from ~2.57 to 0.81 per 10,000 transfusions with reduced use of female-donor plasma
Share of transfusion-related deaths from TRALI (FDA data)
Share of transfusion-related deaths from ABO/non-ABO hemolytic reactions
PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 mmHg, or SpO₂ <90% on room air
~500 mL/hr 0.9% NaCl as tolerated, titrated to urine output
TRALI resolution window with supportive care
Typically 1–3 days after stopping the transfusion

blocks.html:
Why TACO and TRALI need opposite fluid strategies despite looking similar: TACO is fundamentally a volume problem — the recipient's heart can't handle the transfused load, so hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the lungs; removing volume (diuresis) directly treats the mechanism. TRALI is fundamentally a permeability problem — donor antibodies or lipid mediators activate recipient neutrophils, which damage the pulmonary capillary endothelium and let fluid leak out regardless of intravascular volume status; removing volume here doesn't address damaged capillaries and can push an already-hypotensive TRALI patient into worse shock. The "2-hit" model helps explain why the same transfused product can trigger either picture depending on the recipient's baseline condition (cardiac/renal reserve for TACO vs. an already-primed inflammatory state for TRALI).

Why aggressive fluids protect the kidney in AHTR specifically: free hemoglobin released from lysed red cells is directly nephrotoxic and can precipitate in renal tubules under low-flow, concentrated-urine conditions. Maintaining a brisk diuresis dilutes the free hemoglobin and keeps tubular flow high enough to reduce the risk of acute kidney injury — this is a mechanical flushing strategy, not a treatment aimed at the antibody-antigen reaction itself (there's no way to stop hemolysis that's already underway once incompatible cells have been transfused).

Why low tidal volume ventilation is used for TRALI even though it's not classic ARDS: TRALI's pathophysiology — neutrophil-mediated capillary endothelial injury leading to permeability edema — closely resembles ARDS mechanistically, so a lung-protective ventilation strategy (lower tidal volumes, avoiding additional stretch injury to already-damaged alveolar-capillary membranes) is extrapolated from ARDS management and applied here, even without TRALI-specific trial data proving the same mortality benefit.

Why donor-side mitigation, not bedside intervention, is the primary TRALI prevention lever: the antibodies responsible for immune-mediated TRALI come from the donor's plasma, most often a multiparous woman who developed anti-HLA antibodies through prior pregnancy exposure to fetal antigens. No amount of bedside premedication changes that donor-plasma risk factor, which is why restricting high-plasma-volume products to male or nulliparous donors produced a measurable, real-world drop in TRALI incidence, while prophylactic antihistamines/acetaminophen have not been shown to help.

Why hematuria can be the first sign of AHTR under anesthesia: the classic AHTR symptoms — fever, flank pain, chest discomfort — all depend on a conscious patient reporting subjective sensations, which general anesthesia eliminates entirely. Hemoglobinuria (visible as pink/red urine in the Foley bag) is one of the few objective findings that persists regardless of consciousness, which is why it functions as a critical, easily-missed warning sign in the anesthetized surgical patient specifically.

rows: Can present similarly to AHTR (fever, hypotension) — send blood cultures on both the patient and the remaining unit to help distinguish septic transfusion reaction from unrelated sepsis versus AHTR.

Can be difficult to differentiate from AHTR acutely, since AHTR doesn't always present with fever. Look for urticaria/angioedema and a faster, more purely allergic timeline; IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA antibodies are at particular risk and should receive washed red cells for future transfusions.
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema from a primary cardiac event (unrelated to transfusion)

Look for a temporal relationship to the transfusion itself and pre-existing cardiac risk factors; overlaps substantially with TACO by definition, so the distinction is sometimes more about attribution than a different clinical picture.
Pulmonary embolism or amniotic fluid embolism (if applicable clinical context)
No temporal link to the transfusion; different risk factor profile and typically a different mechanism of hypoxemia (obstructive vs. edema-driven).
Onset beyond 24 hours (up to several weeks), typically milder, from an alloantibody the recipient developed from a prior transfusion or pregnancy rather than the current unit.
Fever/chills without hemolysis, hypotension, or respiratory compromise — a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out AHTR, TRALI, and sepsis; benign and self-limited.

blocks.html:
Immediate labs: repeat ABO type and crossmatch on a fresh sample, direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, CBC, haptoglobin/LDH/indirect bilirubin (hemolysis markers), coagulation panel if DIC is a concern, BNP (helps favor TACO over TRALI when elevated), blood and unit cultures if a septic reaction is suspected.

Imaging: chest X-ray for both TRALI and TACO — the infiltrate pattern alone often can't distinguish the two, which is why BNP, fluid balance history, and blood pressure trend all get weighed together rather than relying on imaging in isolation.

Blood bank involvement: the remaining unit, attached tubing, and a post-reaction patient sample all get sent back for investigation — for AHTR/hemolytic workup and, for suspected TRALI, specifically to screen the donor unit for anti-HLA/anti-HNA antibodies.

Disposition: ICU-level monitoring for any severe reaction — AHTR with hemodynamic instability or DIC, TRALI requiring ventilatory support, or TACO requiring more than straightforward diuresis. Milder, rapidly-resolving reactions may be manageable with closer floor-level monitoring depending on institutional protocol.

Reporting: all significant transfusion reactions get reported through institutional hemovigilance processes (and nationally, e.g., CDC NHSN Biovigilance in the US) — this isn't optional paperwork, it's how donor-level risk factors (like the plasma-donor sex restriction that reduced TRALI incidence) get identified and acted on across the whole blood supply.

protocols.title: Awareness Under Anesthesia
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Perioperative
protocols.subtitle: Unintended intraoperative recall — why the benzodiazepine you give after the fact can't undo it, why BIS hasn't outperformed a well-run ETAC protocol, and what the postoperative interview actually needs to accomplish.
protocols.description: Why post-event benzos can't undo recall, BIS vs. ETAC trial evidence, ASA Practice Advisory-aligned prevention and postop workup.

sections.title: Emergency Management — When You Suspect It's Happening
sections.tagline: Unlike most crises in this series, the intervention window is often already closing by the time you notice — recognition itself is the hard part. Act on suspicion; don't wait for certainty.

steps.title: Deepen anesthesia immediately
steps.html: This is the single most important intervention — increase volatile agent concentration or bolus/increase IV hypnotic infusion the moment light anesthesia is suspected. Do this before troubleshooting why it happened.

steps.title: Give a benzodiazepine
steps.html: ASA guidelines suggest immediate benzodiazepine administration if awareness is suspected — but recognize its real limitation: midazolam and similar agents are unreliable at preventing retrograde recall. If pain, paralysis, or distress has already registered, a benzodiazepine given afterward may blunt further memory formation but won't erase what already happened.

steps.title: Check the delivery system while deepening
steps.html: Vaporizer level and function, IV line patency and connections, infusion pump function, circuit for leaks — a large share of intraoperative awareness traces back to an equipment or delivery error (empty vaporizer, disconnected IV, occluded line) rather than a dosing decision. Fix the actual cause in parallel with deepening the anesthetic.

steps.title: Note the time and clinical signs that triggered concern
steps.html: Document what was observed (movement, hemodynamic surge, BIS value if monitored) and what was done, in real time — this becomes essential for both the postoperative patient interview and the case review.

steps.title: Plan for a multidisciplinary, proactive postoperative response
steps.html: Once suspected or confirmed, a prompt, structured, multidisciplinary approach to follow-up is the standard of care — this isn't something to quietly note and move past.

blocks.title: Recognition is the actual bottleneck
blocks.html: Autonomic signs (tachycardia, hypertension, lacrimation, diaphoresis) are the classic teaching, but they're unreliable — especially in a paralyzed patient, on beta-blockers, or under high-dose opioids, where the usual physiologic tells are blunted or absent entirely.

Intraoperative awareness (also called accidental awareness during general anesthesia, AAGA) is explicit recall of sensory perceptions from a period intended to be unconsciousness under general anesthesia. It ranges from vague, non-distressing recollections to the most severe cases involving explicit memory of pain, paralysis, or a sense of impending death — the latter carrying real risk of subsequent anxiety, depression, and PTSD.

Incidence estimates vary substantially by study design and population: older literature cited roughly 0.1–0.9% in general surgical populations, while a large 2007 study of over 87,000 patients found a lower rate around 0.0068% (about 1 in 14,560). High-risk populations — cardiac surgery, cesarean delivery, trauma/emergency surgery, chronic high-dose opioid use, prior awareness history — see incidence approaching 1%, which is why risk stratification matters more than a single population-wide number.

sections.title: Signs of Light Anesthesia — And Why They're Unreliable

rows: Blunted or absent with beta-blockade, high-dose opioids, or autonomic dysfunction — a normal heart rate does not rule out awareness.
Nonspecific; can occur for reasons unrelated to anesthetic depth.
Absent entirely once a neuromuscular blocking agent is on board — movement as a warning sign disappears exactly in the population (paralyzed patients) where awareness risk and severity are highest.

A useful, low-cost threshold — the APSF specifically identifies potent inhaled agent at ≥0.7 MAC as the single best line of defense against awareness in a paralyzed patient — but MAC requirements vary by individual and by co-administered drugs.

Correlates with lighter anesthetic depth in general, but the ASA task force found a specific numerical value doesn't correlate uniformly with anesthetic depth across different drugs and patient populations — treat it as one data point, not a definitive readout.

blocks.html:
• Preoperative risk review: check for prior awareness history, substance use (opioids, benzodiazepines, cocaine, chronic alcohol use — all raise anesthetic requirement), history of difficult intubation, and case type — cardiac surgery, cesarean delivery, trauma/emergency surgery, and chronic high-dose-opioid patients are all recognized higher-risk categories.
  • Equipment checklist before every case: vaporizer level and function, IV line patency, infusion pump programming, backflow check valves — errors in anesthetic drug delivery systems are a well-documented, preventable cause of intraoperative awareness, not just a dosing-decision problem.
  • Maintain potent inhaled agent at ≥0.7 MAC whenever a neuromuscular blocking agent is used — the APSF-endorsed position is that this is the single best line of defense in a paralyzed patient specifically, since movement is no longer available as a backstop warning sign.
  • Balanced technique combining IV and inhalational agents, rather than relying on a single delivery pathway, reduces the risk that one system's failure (a disconnected line, an empty vaporizer) goes completely uncompensated.
  • Brain function (BIS) monitoring — use judiciously, not as a guarantee: two major randomized trials (BAG-RECALL and the Michigan Awareness Control Study) did not demonstrate BIS-guided protocols to be superior to a well-executed ETAC-alarm protocol for preventing awareness. Consider it on a case-by-case basis for higher-risk patients rather than treating it as a routine standard that eliminates risk on its own.
  • Discuss risk with substantially-increased-risk patients preoperatively when appropriate — informed patients who experience a milder awareness event tend to have better psychological outcomes than those who weren't warned at all.

rows: APSF-endorsed minimum potent agent level (with NMBA on board)
ETAC alert thresholds used in major prevention trials
~75% occur during the maintenance phase; the remainder cluster at induction or toward the end of the procedure, often from mistimed bridging between short- and long-acting agents

blocks.html:
Why the post-event benzodiazepine can't undo what's already happened: benzodiazepines act on future memory consolidation, not on memories already formed. If a patient has already experienced pain or distress with intact conscious perception, giving midazolam afterward may reduce further memory encoding going forward but cannot retroactively prevent recall of what already registered — this is precisely why prevention (adequate anesthetic depth in the first place) carries so much more weight than any rescue intervention.

Why movement disappears as a warning sign under paralysis: neuromuscular blockade doesn't affect consciousness or pain perception at all — it only removes the ability to move in response to it. This is exactly why the APSF frames adequate potent-agent dosing (≥0.7 MAC) as the primary defense specifically in paralyzed patients: the normal behavioral warning system has been deliberately disabled by the paralytic, so the anesthetic depth itself has to be trustworthy on its own.

Why BIS hasn't proven superior to a good ETAC protocol: BIS derives an index from processed EEG signal, but the ASA task force's own review found that a given numerical value doesn't correlate consistently with anesthetic depth across different drug combinations and patient populations — a ketamine- or nitrous-heavy technique, for instance, can produce a misleadingly reassuring BIS number. Two major randomized trials tested BIS-guided care against simple ETAC-based alerting and found no statistically demonstrated superiority for BIS, which is why current guidance treats BIS as a selective tool for specific higher-risk cases (e.g., TIVA where there's no volatile agent concentration to alarm on) rather than a universal solution.

Why most events cluster in the maintenance phase, not induction: induction is typically the most heavily and deliberately dosed part of an anesthetic, with close attention paid by the entire team. Maintenance is longer, more routine, and more vulnerable to a slow vaporizer drift, an undetected line occlusion, or attention shifting elsewhere — which is exactly why continuous, active monitoring of delivered concentration matters throughout the case, not just at the start.

rows: A recognized and generally benign phenomenon distinct from true intraoperative consciousness — the patient reports dream-like content without accurate recall of actual intraoperative events, conversations, or sensations. Not classified as awareness.

Memory of events after emergence but before full lucidity is not intraoperative awareness — clarify the exact timeline with the patient, since these events are managed differently (sedation practice in recovery, not anesthetic depth in the OR).
Postoperative delirium or confusion misattributed as intraoperative memory

Confabulated or confused recollections, often inconsistent on repeat questioning, without the specific, verifiable event detail (a particular phrase said in the room, a specific sensation tied to a specific surgical step) that characterizes genuine explicit recall.

Some patients recall auditory or tactile perceptions without pain, paralysis-awareness, or fear — still a true awareness event and worth taking seriously, but carries a different psychological risk profile than distressing awareness with paralysis or pain.

blocks.html:
Structured postoperative interview: patients with suspected awareness should be interviewed at multiple intervals (a same-day/early interview and a follow-up interview, commonly using a structured tool like the Brice questionnaire) to assess and characterize what was recalled — a single conversation right after surgery, when the patient may still be sedated or confused, is not sufficient.

Multidisciplinary, proactive response: once suspected or confirmed, engage the anesthesia team, surgical team, and — when distressing content is reported — psychological/psychiatric support promptly. This is described as the standard of care, not an optional escalation.

Screen for psychological sequelae: anxiety, depression, and PTSD are documented risks after a distressing awareness event; early identification and referral improves outcomes compared to a "wait and see" approach.

Documentation and incident review: record the case in as much detail as possible — equipment status, drug administration timeline, monitoring values, and the exact clinical trigger for suspicion — both for the patient's future anesthesia records and for institutional incident review and prevention.

Communicate directly with the patient: acknowledge the event, explain what's known about what happened, and discuss what will be different for any future anesthetic (increased monitoring, technique changes, explicit risk discussion) — patients who feel heard and informed generally have better psychological outcomes than those who feel dismissed.

protocols.title: Fat Embolism Syndrome
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Orthopedic Trauma / Critical Care
protocols.subtitle: Marrow fat entering the circulation after a long-bone fracture — a diagnosis of exclusion made by pattern recognition, treated entirely with support since nothing pharmacologic has proven itself.

badges.text: SUPPORTIVE CARE ONLY — NO PROVEN DRUG

protocols.description: Gurd and Wilson criteria, supportive-care-only management, cerebral fat embolism as the easy-to-miss isolated-neuro variant.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: There is no proven pharmacologic cure — management is early recognition plus aggressive, organ-by-organ support while the syndrome runs its course.

steps.title: Maintain a high index of suspicion
steps.html: In any patient with a long-bone or pelvic fracture developing new hypoxemia, altered mental status, or a petechial rash in the 24–72 hour post-injury (or post-fixation) window — FES is a clinical diagnosis, and no single test confirms it, so suspicion has to drive early action.

steps.title: Support oxygenation aggressively
steps.html: Supplemental O₂ titrated to maintain adequate saturation; escalate to mechanical ventilation early if hypoxemia is significant (PaO₂ <60 mmHg is a commonly cited threshold). High levels of PEEP are the recommended ventilatory approach for the acute pulmonary presentation, similar in principle to other causes of capillary-leak lung injury.

steps.title: Hemodynamic support and fluid management
steps.html: IV fluids and drugs to maintain adequate blood volume and perfusion — help support end-organ perfusion and may assist in diluting/removing circulating free fatty acids, though this specific mechanism isn't proven to change outcomes on its own.

steps.title: ICU-level monitoring
steps.html: Admit to a critical care environment for detailed physiological observation, with early institution of invasive support (ventilation, vasopressors) if the patient deteriorates — most series describe favorable outcomes when this escalation happens promptly rather than reactively.

steps.title: Neurologic monitoring and seizure management
steps.html: CNS involvement (agitation, confusion, progressing to stupor or seizures) is common and frequently doesn't improve simply by correcting hypoxia — treat seizures with standard anticonvulsant management and pursue neuroimaging (MRI is more sensitive than CT for cerebral fat embolism) if focal or persistent deficits are present.

steps.title: Definitive fracture fixation, timed thoughtfully
steps.html: Early stabilization of the fracture is generally beneficial and is the main prevention lever, but in a severely traumatized or already-deteriorating patient, damage control orthopedics (external fixation first, definitive fixation delayed) may be preferred over immediate intramedullary instrumentation, which itself can worsen embolic load.

steps.title: Consider corticosteroids on a case-by-case basis
steps.html: Some case series describe a short course of IV methylprednisolone; the evidence base is not conclusive, and steroids, heparin, and albumin have all been studied without demonstrating clear, reproducible benefit. Reasonable to consider in select cases, not a default reflex.

blocks.title: No definitive treatment exists
blocks.html: Despite decades of study, no pharmacologic therapy — steroids, heparin, albumin — has demonstrated conclusive efficacy for FES. Management is supportive care, done well and started early, not a specific rescue drug.

Fat embolism syndrome is a systemic condition caused by fat globules — most often bone marrow fat — entering the venous circulation, typically after a long bone or pelvic fracture, orthopedic instrumentation (intramedullary nailing, arthroplasty), or less commonly after severe burns, liposuction, pancreatitis, or CPR. Fat first embolizes to the pulmonary capillary bed, and can subsequently reach the systemic circulation via a patent foramen ovale, arteriovenous shunts, or passage through the pulmonary bed itself — producing the classic multi-organ pattern of pulmonary, neurologic, and dermatologic injury.

Two proposed mechanisms operate together: a mechanical theory (fat droplets physically obstructing small vessels) and a biochemical theory (free fatty acids triggering a profound inflammatory response that increases capillary permeability). Reported incidence varies enormously by diagnostic method and population — roughly 0.5–2% after an isolated long-bone fracture, rising to 5–10% with multiple long-bone or pelvic fractures, while fat globules are detectable in blood in the majority of orthopedic trauma patients if specifically looked for (a landmark study found clinical FES by Gurd's criteria in 19% of trauma patients). Reported mortality ranges widely (3–67% across older literature) but more consistent modern series cite roughly 5–15%.

rows: Respiratory insufficiency (hypoxemia, tachypnea, bilateral infiltrates), cerebral involvement unrelated to head trauma or other cause, petechial rash — classically axillary, conjunctival, over the upper body, appearing 24–36 hours after injury and resolving quickly.

Tachycardia, pyrexia (low-grade), retinal changes (fat globules/hemorrhages on fundoscopy), renal changes (fat in urine, oliguria), sudden unexplained drop in hemoglobin, thrombocytopenia, elevated ESR, fat globules in sputum.

1 major + 4 minor criteria (Gurd and Wilson), though other schemes (Lindeque, Schonfeld, modified Gurd) exist and none are fully validated — diagnosis remains clinical and is ultimately one of exclusion.
Symptoms usually appear 24–72 hours after trauma or intraoperatively during fracture repair; the classic teaching "24–72h window" is where most nursing/monitoring protocols concentrate observation.

blocks.html: Cerebral fat embolism (CFE) is an incomplete variant with isolated or predominant neurologic involvement, without the full respiratory/dermatologic picture — occurs in roughly 0.9–11% of long-bone fracture patients depending on the series, carries a mortality around 10%, and is easy to misattribute to a primary stroke or seizure disorder if the orthopedic context isn't kept in mind.

• Early fracture stabilization is the most consistently cited prevention strategy, though definitive comparative data proving it reduces FES incidence specifically (rather than just improving overall trauma outcomes) remains limited.
  • Minimize additional surgical trauma to the marrow cavity during fixation — technique matters, since more fat globule release corresponds to a higher embolic load.
  • Damage control orthopedics in severely traumatized or physiologically unstable patients: external fixation to control the injury acutely, with definitive intramedullary fixation delayed until the patient is more stable — reduces the additional embolic insult of reaming/instrumentation during an already-vulnerable window.
  • Vigilant monitoring in every at-risk patient regardless of whether fixation is delayed or immediate — FES can occur even after appropriate fixation, so prevention reduces but doesn't eliminate risk.
  • Standardized early-warning observation (e.g., pulse oximetry trends, structured early warning scoring) correlates well with catching unrecognized hypoxemia in these patients before it becomes a crisis.

rows: Incidence by strict clinical criteria in a landmark trauma cohort (Gurd)
Fat globules detectable in blood (asymptomatic subclinical fat embolism)
Up to 67% of orthopedic trauma patients in some studies
Reported mortality, more consistent modern series
Cerebral fat embolism incidence (long-bone fracture patients)

blocks.html:
Why treatment is purely supportive: the injury has two overlapping mechanisms — mechanical vessel obstruction by fat droplets, and a biochemical inflammatory cascade from free fatty acids damaging capillary membranes. No drug reverses either process once it's underway; the biology behaves more like a self-limited inflammatory insult than a condition with a specific antidote, which is why decades of trials on steroids, heparin, and albumin have failed to establish clear benefit.

Why high-PEEP ventilation is favored for the pulmonary presentation: the biochemical injury pattern in FES resembles other forms of capillary-leak-mediated lung injury (ARDS-like physiology) more than it resembles simple mechanical vascular obstruction — PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli and improves oxygenation in this pattern the same way it does in ARDS from other causes.

Why CNS symptoms often don't track cleanly with hypoxia correction: the systemic (biochemical) mechanism means that fat and inflammatory mediators can reach the brain independently through a shunt pathway or the pulmonary bed itself — correcting oxygenation addresses one input to cerebral dysfunction but not necessarily the direct embolic/inflammatory injury already present in cerebral vessels, which is why neurologic findings can persist or evolve even as respiratory status improves.

Why intramedullary reaming/instrumentation is handled cautiously in unstable patients: the fixation procedure itself pressurizes the marrow cavity and can push additional fat into the venous system — reasonable in a stable patient where the benefit of definitive fixation outweighs this added embolic load, but a real consideration for delaying definitive fixation (damage control orthopedics) in someone already physiologically compromised.

Why diagnosis stays clinical despite decades of proposed criteria systems: no imaging or lab test has proven sufficiently sensitive and specific on its own — fat globules in blood are common even in patients who never develop the syndrome, and radiographic/CT findings are often normal or nonspecific early on. This is why Gurd and Wilson (and its competitors) remain pattern-recognition tools rather than confirmatory tests, and why a high index of suspicion in the right clinical context still does most of the diagnostic work.

rows: Often the first thing considered in a post-fracture/post-op patient with new hypoxemia — CT angiography differentiates the two; FES lacks a discrete filling defect and instead shows diffuse, often ground-glass changes if imaging is abnormal at all.
ARDS from another cause (aspiration, sepsis, transfusion-related)
Look for a clear alternative trigger and the absence of the petechial rash/neurologic pattern; timing relative to fracture is a key clue for FES specifically.
Imaging (CT/MRI) findings consistent with direct trauma rather than the diffuse, small-vessel pattern seen on MRI in cerebral fat embolism; mechanism and head-strike history matter.
Vascular territory-specific findings on imaging rather than the diffuse pattern of cerebral fat embolism; FES-related neurologic findings are often more diffuse/global than focal.
Fever and hemodynamic instability with an identifiable infectious source; can coexist with FES in a trauma patient and complicate the picture.
Petechiae/purpura present in both, but DIC has a distinct coagulation panel derangement (prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen) not typical of FES alone.

blocks.html:
Supportive labs/imaging: ABG for hypoxemia severity, CBC (thrombocytopenia, sudden hemoglobin drop), coagulation panel to help exclude DIC, chest imaging (often normal early; CT may show bilateral ground-glass opacities), brain MRI if neurologic findings are present (more sensitive than CT for the diffuse "starfield" pattern of cerebral fat embolism).

Serial monitoring: continuous pulse oximetry with structured early-warning scoring, given how easily early hypoxemia is missed; serial neurologic exams given the sometimes-delayed or evolving nature of CNS involvement.

Disposition: ICU admission for any suspected or confirmed case — this is standard given the potential for rapid deterioration and the need for close observation and rapid escalation to mechanical ventilation if respiratory status worsens.

Course and recovery: most patients who survive the acute phase recover fully, though prolonged mechanical ventilation is common in severe cases; the petechial rash itself typically resolves within days regardless of overall trajectory.

Documentation: record which Gurd/Wilson (or alternative) criteria were met and when, imaging findings, and the clinical course — useful both for this admission's ongoing management and for future reference given how often FES remains a retrospective, pattern-based diagnosis.

protocols.title: Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Regional
protocols.subtitle: CNS and cardiovascular collapse from local anesthetic overdose or inadvertent intravascular injection — the lipid rescue protocol, why the code drugs change, and how to keep it from happening in the first place.
protocols.description: ASRA 2020 lipid emulsion protocol, modified ACLS, max doses by agent, prevention during regional blocks.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: You have roughly a 3-minute window from recognition to lipid emulsion running before hypoxia and acidosis make the cardiac blockade harder to reverse.

steps.title: Stop injecting local anesthetic, call for help
steps.html: Get the LAST rescue kit (lipid emulsion, syringes, checklist). Ask for a "designated reader" to run the ASRA checklist out loud — improves adherence under stress.

steps.title: Manage the airway
steps.html: 100% O₂, prevent hypoxia and acidosis — both potentiate LAST. Low threshold for intubation if seizing or obtunded.

steps.title: Suppress seizures with benzodiazepines
steps.html: First-line. If only propofol is available, use small 20 mg increments — larger doses worsen cardiovascular depression on top of the LA-induced depression already present. Propofol is not a substitute for lipid emulsion; its lipid content is far too low to act as one.

steps.title: Start 20% lipid emulsion — ASRA 2020 regimen
steps.html:
≥70 kg: bolus 100 mL over 2–3 min, then infuse 250 mL over 15–20 min.
<70 kg: bolus 1.5 mL/kg over 2–3 min, then infuse 0.25 mL/kg/min (consider a pump if <40 kg).
If unstable: repeat the bolus and double the infusion rate. Maximum total dose 12 mL/kg. Continue ≥15 minutes once stable. Order of bolus vs. infusion isn't critical — get it running.

steps.title: Modify ACLS — this is not a standard arrest
steps.html: Epinephrine, if needed for arrhythmia or hypotension, at a reduced dose <1 mcg/kg — standard 1 mg ACLS boluses can trigger lethal arrhythmias in an LA-poisoned heart. Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, and additional local anesthetic as antiarrhythmics — all worsen outcomes in this specific arrest physiology.

steps.title: If ACLS + lipid emulsion fail — alert for CPB/ECMO
steps.html: Call the nearest facility capable of cardiopulmonary bypass early; prolonged resuscitation has a track record of good outcomes in LAST specifically, so don't terminate on the usual arrest timeline.

steps.title: Monitor after stabilization
steps.html: Continue lipid infusion ≥15 minutes past hemodynamic stability. Watch for recurrence — LA redistribution can cause delayed relapse.

blocks.title: Standard code doses of epinephrine can kill this patient
blocks.html: 1 mg epinephrine boluses are appropriate for a normal arrest and dangerous in LAST. Reduced dosing (<1 mcg/kg) and avoidance of vasopressin/CCB/BB is a deliberate, LAST-specific deviation from standard ACLS — not an error.

LAST results from elevated plasma concentrations of local anesthetic — most often from inadvertent intravascular injection during a nerve block, less often from cumulative absorption after a large-volume block or infusion. Local anesthetics block sodium channels everywhere, not just at the injection site: at toxic plasma levels they disrupt CNS inhibitory/excitatory balance and cardiac conduction simultaneously.

Estimated incidence is roughly 1.8 per 1,000 peripheral nerve blocks by signs/symptoms, and closer to 1 in 384 surgeries with a block by lipid-emulsion-use as a surrogate marker in some populations — for a "rare" event, not actually rare. Lidocaine is the most commonly implicated agent overall (44% of reported cases, reflecting its frequency of use), but bupivacaine carries the narrowest safety margin and the greatest cardiotoxicity per dose; ropivacaine has a comparatively better safety profile.

rows: Circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, lightheadedness — often the first warning, easy to miss under drapes or in a sedated patient.
Visual disturbance, agitation, muscle twitching, progressing to generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
Drowsiness, obtundation — especially with bupivacaine, where cardiac and CNS toxicity can present nearly simultaneously.
Bradycardia, conduction block on ECG, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac arrest.

Occur — CNS and CV signs don't always appear in the "expected" order, and severe cardiotoxicity can be the presenting sign with no preceding CNS symptoms, particularly with bupivacaine or in a patient under general anesthesia who can't report prodromal symptoms.

Most cases begin within minutes of injection, but severe manifestations have been reported up to 6 hours later — keep suspicion up for delayed presentation, not just the immediate post-injection window.

blocks.html:
• Every site using LA at toxic-capable doses stocks 20% lipid emulsion and basic resuscitation equipment — not just the OR. Outpatient and procedural settings are exactly where delayed rescue kills.
  • Aspirate before injecting, use incremental dosing rather than a single large bolus, and use ultrasound guidance for regional blocks — ultrasound guidance measurably reduces LAST risk versus landmark/nerve-stimulator technique.
  • Calculate the maximum dose before you draw it up, using ideal body weight, not actual weight, in patients where the two diverge significantly.
  • Reduce dose at the extremes of age (under 4 months or over 70 years) and in patients with cardiac conduction defects, ischemic heart disease, or hepatic dysfunction — generally 10–20% dose reduction.
  • Have the LAST checklist physically posted or in the kit — a printed/electronic checklist and a designated reader measurably improves adherence during an actual event.
  • Toxicity is additive across agents — account for cumulative dose if more than one local anesthetic is used in the same case or within the same 4-hour window.

sections.title: Maximum Recommended Doses by Agent
sections.tagline: There's no lab that predicts LAST before it happens — the equivalent "numbers to know" here are the weight-based ceilings that keep you from causing it.

rows: ~3.5 mg/kg (less consistently increased by epi than others)
8 mg/kg (methemoglobinemia risk above ~8 mg/kg regardless of toxicity)

blocks.html: Relative cardiotoxicity, high to low: bupivacaine > levobupivacaine ≈ ropivacaine > lidocaine ≈ mepivacaine. Lidocaine and mepivacaine tend to reduce cardiac contractility more; bupivacaine and ropivacaine tend to cause more malignant arrhythmias — different failure modes, both dangerous.

Why lipid emulsion works — the "lipid sink/shuttle" mechanism: local anesthetics are lipophilic. Infused lipid emulsion was originally thought to simply sequester ("sink") free drug out of plasma, pulling it away from the heart and brain. Current understanding favors a "shuttle" model instead: lipid redistributes local anesthetic away from high-perfusion, high-toxicity-risk organs (heart, brain) toward storage/metabolism sites (muscle, liver). Lipid also has an independent cardiotonic effect — increased contractility and blood pressure support — separate from its sequestration role, which is part of why it works even before drug redistribution is complete.

Why epinephrine dosing is reduced, not eliminated: epinephrine is still used for hemodynamic support, but LA-blocked myocardium responds differently to catecholamine surges than a normal ischemic arrest — full ACLS doses have been linked to worsened arrhythmia and reduced effectiveness of lipid rescue in animal and case-report data, which is the basis for the <1 mcg/kg recommendation.

Why vasopressin, CCBs, and beta-blockers are avoided: the LA-poisoned heart is already profoundly depressed at the sodium-channel level. Vasopressin has been associated with worsened outcomes (including pulmonary hemorrhage) in this specific setting; CCBs and beta-blockers add further conduction/contractility depression on top of an already-blocked heart, risking irreversible asystole.

Why benzodiazepines over propofol for seizures: propofol causes independent cardiovascular depression, which compounds the LA-induced depression already present — exactly the wrong direction when the heart is the organ you're trying to protect. It also doesn't carry enough lipid to function as rescue therapy, despite superficially "being a lipid."

Why resuscitation is prolonged beyond a normal arrest timeline: case reports and registry data show good neurologic outcomes after unusually long resuscitations in LAST arrests when lipid emulsion and modified ACLS are used correctly — the pathophysiology is reversible in a way a primary cardiac arrest often isn't, which justifies escalating to CPB/ECMO rather than terminating on standard timelines.

rows: Vasovagal / syncopal reaction to the procedure itself
Bradycardia and hypotension without seizure or the classic LAST prodrome; resolves quickly with positioning and reassurance, not lipid emulsion.
Tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety — opposite hemodynamic direction from LAST cardiotoxicity; timing immediately post-injection, self-limited.
Anaphylaxis to the local anesthetic or a co-administered drug
True LA allergy is rare; look for urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm rather than the CNS-first LAST pattern. Co-administered antibiotics are a more common culprit than the LA itself.
High or total spinal (after neuraxial technique)

Rapidly ascending sensory/motor block, hypotension, bradycardia, potential respiratory arrest — mechanical spread of block rather than systemic toxicity; different treatment pathway (airway/hemodynamic support, not lipid emulsion).
No temporal relationship to LA administration; other eclampsia features (hypertension, proteinuria) present.
Cyanosis and low SpO₂ that doesn't correct with O₂, pulse ox reading in the high-80s/low-90s regardless of FiO₂ — different mechanism, different antidote (methylene blue), not lipid emulsion.

blocks.html:
Acute phase: LAST is a clinical diagnosis based on temporal relationship to LA administration plus the CNS/CV pattern above — there's no confirmatory point-of-care test. Serum LA levels can be sent but rarely change acute management.

Monitoring: continuous ECG, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry through resuscitation and recovery. Repeat neuro checks once sedation/seizure activity clears.

Disposition: admit for monitoring after any LAST event with cardiovascular involvement or seizure — recurrence after apparent stabilization has been reported due to LA redistribution. Isolated, rapidly resolved prodromal symptoms without seizure or arrhythmia may be observed for a shorter period per institutional protocol, but err toward longer observation with any cardiac involvement.

After the event: document the total LA dose given and route, report the event per institutional/departmental safety process, and review the case for a modifiable cause (dose, technique, ultrasound use) before the next block.
