protocols.title: Malignant Hyperthermia
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Perioperative
protocols.subtitle: Recognition, immediate treatment, and the physiology behind every step of an MH crisis — from room setup for the susceptible patient through disposition and family counseling.
protocols.description: RYR1-mediated hypermetabolic crisis. Dantrolene, room setup for the susceptible patient, genetics, recrudescence.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Sequence matters less than speed — get help, stop the trigger, and get dantrolene running. Steps below are typically executed in parallel by a full team, not strictly serially.

steps.title: Stop all triggering agents
steps.html: Turn off volatile agent, switch to TIVA (propofol), do not give further succinylcholine. Continue the case only if it must be finished; convert to IV anesthesia.

steps.title: Call for help and the MH cart
steps.html: Declare the emergency, get extra hands (dantrolene reconstitution is labor-intensive), and call the MHAUS Hotline 1-800-644-9737 for real-time consultation.

steps.title: Hyperventilate with 100% O₂
steps.html: Flows of 10 L/min, high minute ventilation to flush residual volatile agent and blow off CO₂. Change to a clean circuit or insert activated-charcoal filters on inspiratory and expiratory limbs if immediately available; replace filters hourly.

steps.title: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, rapid bolus
steps.html: Through the largest available IV. Repeat 2.5 mg/kg boluses every 5–10 minutes until ETCO₂, rigidity, and heart rate improve. No fixed ceiling — doses of 10–20+ mg/kg are occasionally required; reassess the diagnosis if no response at all after ~10 mg/kg.

steps.title: Cool the patient
steps.html: Cold IV crystalloid, surface ice packs to axillae/groin/neck, cold lavage of open cavities if surgical field allows. Stop active cooling around 38–38.5°C to avoid overshoot. Cooling is adjunctive — dantrolene is the priority.

steps.title: Treat hyperkalemia
steps.html: IV calcium chloride 10–30 mg/kg for membrane stabilization if arrhythmia/ECG changes; insulin 10 U regular in 50 mL D50, titrated; hyperventilation and bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg if no ABG available. Avoid calcium channel blockers — case reports describe fatal interaction with dantrolene.

steps.title: Treat arrhythmias with standard agents
steps.html: Most arrhythmias resolve as acidosis and hyperkalemia correct. Use standard antiarrhythmics for persistent/life-threatening rhythms; again, avoid CCBs.

steps.title: Protect the kidneys
steps.html: Target urine output >2 mL/kg/hr with hydration ± mannitol/furosemide — each dantrolene vial already contains 3 g mannitol, so track cumulative dose before adding more. Send urine for myoglobin.

steps.title: Monitor and reassess
steps.html: Arterial line, core temperature probe, Foley. Serial ABG, CK, K⁺, lactate, coagulation panel roughly every 15 minutes during the acute phase.

steps.title: Admit to ICU
steps.html: Minimum 24 hours of observation for recrudescence, with maintenance dantrolene continuing through that window (see Rationale, below).

blocks.title: Do not delay dantrolene for confirmation
blocks.html: MH is a clinical diagnosis made in real time. Waiting on labs before treating measurably worsens outcomes — treat first on the pattern of rising ETCO₂, rigidity, and tachycardia.

Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare, life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle. In susceptible individuals, exposure to a volatile anesthetic and/or succinylcholine triggers uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through a defective ryanodine receptor (RYR1), producing sustained muscle contraction, a hypermetabolic state, and progressive heat production.

Reported incidence of a clinical MH event ranges roughly from 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 50,000–100,000 general anesthetics using triggering agents, with wide variation by population and genetic background; the true prevalence of MH susceptibility (genotype) is higher than the rate of clinical events, since not every exposure in a susceptible patient produces a full crisis. Untreated, MH is fatal in the majority of cases; with early dantrolene, mortality drops to under 5%.

rows: Earliest and most sensitive sign — often >55 mmHg despite unchanged minute ventilation; reflects the hypermetabolic CO₂ load before temperature changes.
Trismus after succinylcholine; a subset of these patients go on to a full MH episode. Not universal, but a strong red flag when generalized rigidity follows.
Persists despite adequate neuromuscular blockade — a key discriminator from other causes of rigidity, which typically resolve with a nondepolarizer.
Early and nonspecific but frequently the first vital-sign change noted by the team.
Can climb 1–2°C every 5 minutes once established, sometimes exceeding 40°C — but temperature is often a late finding, not an early one.
CO₂ overproduction plus anaerobic metabolism from sustained contraction.
Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis; a marker of muscle breakdown severity and a driver of downstream renal injury.
ECG correlate of hyperkalemia released from breaking-down muscle.
Seen in a minority (~20%) — supportive but not required for diagnosis.

sections.title: Room Set-Up for the MH-Susceptible Patient

blocks.html:
• Non-triggering technique: total IV anesthesia (propofol-based), no volatile agents, no succinylcholine. Regional/neuraxial anesthesia is not a trigger and is a reasonable option when the case allows it.
  • Prepare the machine: either use a machine with no history of volatile agent, or flush thoroughly with high-flow O₂ per your machine's specific washout protocol, or place activated-charcoal filters (e.g. Vapor-Clean) on inspiratory and expiratory limbs — filters saturate after roughly an hour and need hourly replacement.
  • Dantrolene immediately available: confirm the MH cart is stocked and physically nearby before induction — MHAUS recommends a minimum of 36 vials of Dantrium/Revonto (20 mg each) or 3 vials of Ryanodex (250 mg each) on hand.
  • Monitoring: standard ASA monitors plus continuous core temperature from induction — temperature is not routinely monitored in every case, but is mandatory here.
  • Cooling supplies staged: cold IV fluids and ice readily accessible, not something to send for after a crisis starts.
  • Scheduling: first case of the day when possible, to minimize residual volatile agent contamination in the room and give the team maximum bandwidth if a crisis develops.
  • Team briefing: state the MH-susceptible status explicitly during the pre-induction time-out, not just in the chart.

rows: Rising, often >55 mmHg, disproportionate to ventilation settings
Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis, often with a significant base deficit
Elevated, sometimes rapidly and severely — the dominant early cardiac risk
Markedly elevated, rises over hours as rhabdomyolysis progresses — often the highest single lab value seen in medicine
Elevated, correlates with cola-colored urine and renal risk
Elevated from anaerobic metabolism in sustained contraction
Can progress to DIC in severe/delayed cases — check if the crisis is prolonged
Rate of rise (up to 1–2°C/5 min) is more diagnostic than any single value

sections.title: Rationale for MH Management Steps
sections.tagline: The "why" behind the protocol — the physiology that makes each step non-negotiable.

blocks.html:
Root cause: a defective RYR1 (or, less commonly, CACNA1S) channel allows uncontrolled calcium efflux from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the myoplasm. Free calcium drives continuous actin-myosin cross-bridging — this is what produces rigidity, and it is also what produces heat: sustained muscle work is enormously energy-inefficient, and essentially all of that energy dissipates as heat and CO₂.

Why dantrolene works when nothing else does: dantrolene binds RYR1 directly and reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, uncoupling excitation from contraction at the source. Cooling, hyperventilation, and hyperkalemia treatment all manage downstream consequences; dantrolene is the only intervention that turns off the underlying process.

Why cooling is secondary, not first: aggressive thermal management without adequate dantrolene and correction of hypercarbia/acidosis treats a symptom while the metabolic engine keeps running. Current expert opinion (echoed in MHAUS guidance) is to prioritize dantrolene and ventilation/acid-base correction before investing heavily in cooling logistics.

Why calcium channel blockers are avoided: case reports describe severe hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse when CCBs are combined with dantrolene, plausibly via interaction with calcium handling that dantrolene itself is trying to correct — the mechanism isn't fully settled, but the clinical signal is consistent enough that CCBs are avoided as a category.

Why maintenance dosing continues for 24 hours: recrudescence — recurrence of MH signs after apparent initial control — occurs in roughly 20% of treated patients. Median time to recrudescence is around 9 hours, with 80% occurring by 16 hours, which is why observation and maintenance dantrolene extend well past the point the crisis appears resolved.

rows: Develops over days on antipsychotics, not minutes-to-hours after a trigger agent; CK rise is slower; doesn't respond as rapidly to dantrolene as true MH.
Clonus and hyperreflexia more prominent than sustained rigidity; history of serotonergic drugs; rigidity itself is comparatively rare.
No temporal link to anesthetic trigger; look for known thyroid disease, exophthalmos, prior labs.
Slower onset, hemodynamics more distributive (warm, vasodilated) than the hypermetabolic picture of MH.
Extreme, labile hypertension is more dominant than in MH; catecholamine surge pattern.
Rigidity resolves promptly with deepening anesthesia or a nondepolarizing paralytic — true MH rigidity does not.
History/exposure driven, no relationship to volatile agent or succinylcholine administration.
Rare, but check warming devices, ambient temperature, and drapes before assuming MH if the rest of the picture doesn't fit.

blocks.html:
Acute phase: no lab confirms MH in real time — treatment is empiric. Once stabilized, definitive diagnosis requires referral to an MH testing center for the caffeine-halothane contracture test (CHCT), the current gold standard, performed on a fresh muscle biopsy.

Genetic testing: targeted RYR1 (and CACNA1S) panel testing can identify a causative variant in known MH families and spares relatives an invasive biopsy if a familial variant is confirmed; a negative genetic panel does not exclude susceptibility, since not all causative variants are known.

Disposition: ICU admission for a minimum of 24 hours with continuous monitoring; maintenance dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV every 4–6 hours (or infusion around 0.25 mg/kg/hr in fulminant cases) continued until the patient has been stable and improving for 24 hours.

Longitudinal care: patient and family education, referral for CHCT/genetic testing, MedicAlert bracelet, documentation in the anesthesia record and problem list, and cascade screening discussion for first-degree relatives.
MHAUS Hotline — 1-800-644-9737 (outside the U.S.: 001-209-417-3722). Available for real-time crisis consultation and post-event guidance; call during the event, not just after.

MH susceptibility is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable and incomplete penetrance — a positive family history matters even without a documented prior event, and a negative family history does not exclude risk (de novo variants occur).

  • RYR1 (ryanodine receptor 1, chromosome 19q13.1) accounts for the large majority of identified causative variants in MH-susceptible families.
  • CACNA1S (the skeletal muscle L-type calcium channel α1 subunit) accounts for a smaller minority of cases.
  • Over 200 RYR1 variants have been described; only a subset are considered functionally confirmed as causative, which is part of why genetic testing complements — but doesn't replace — the CHCT.
  • MH susceptibility overlaps genetically and clinically with certain congenital myopathies, most notably central core disease, which also maps to RYR1.
  • First-degree relatives of a confirmed or strongly suspected MH patient should be counseled as presumptively susceptible until tested, and managed with a non-triggering technique for any anesthetic in the meantime.

protocols.title: Negative Pressure Pulmonary Edema
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Airway
protocols.subtitle: Post-extubation laryngospasm's downstream complication — forceful inspiration against a closed airway pulls fluid into the lungs by pure hydrostatic mechanism, which is exactly why it resolves as fast as it appears once the obstruction is fixed.
protocols.description: Post-extubation laryngospasm's downstream complication, hydrostatic mechanism, why diuretics stay contested. Linked to the Laryngospasm file.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Fix the obstruction first — the edema is downstream of the airway problem, not a separate crisis to treat in parallel.

steps.title: Relieve the upper airway obstruction
steps.html: Reintubate or address laryngospasm directly (see the Laryngospasm crisis file for that escalation ladder). If intubation fails and the airway can't otherwise be secured, cricothyrotomy is the next step — same CICO logic as any other failed airway.

steps.title: 100% O₂, assess severity
steps.html: Mild cases: supplemental oxygen and noninvasive ventilation (CPAP/NIV) to maintain airway patency and oxygenation may be sufficient.

steps.title: Severe cases: intubate and ventilate with PEEP
steps.html: Lung-protective positive-pressure ventilation with PEEP is the mainstay for significant NPPE — recruits flooded alveoli and improves oxygenation while the edema clears.

steps.title: Diuretics — use judiciously, not reflexively
steps.html: Guidance here is genuinely mixed: some sources recommend diuresis unless the patient is in shock, while others explicitly advise against it since NPPE isn't caused by volume overload and diuresis can worsen a perioperative patient who may already be relatively volume-depleted. Reasonable default: reserve diuretics for cases with clear additional volume overload, not as a routine first-line step.

steps.title: Consider beta-agonist therapy
steps.html: Nebulized beta-agonists (e.g., albuterol) may accelerate alveolar fluid clearance independent of any bronchospastic component — a reasonable adjunct even though bronchospasm isn't the primary mechanism here.

steps.title: Refractory severe cases
steps.html: Prone positioning and advanced ventilatory strategies (e.g., airway pressure release ventilation) have been used successfully in unusually severe cases resembling ARDS. ECMO is a documented rescue option for refractory hypoxemia.

steps.title: Steroids — not currently recommended
steps.html: Historically used, but current understanding is that corticosteroids don't address the actual hydrostatic mechanism driving NPPE and aren't supported by current evidence.

blocks.title: Resolution is usually fast if the obstruction is fixed
blocks.html: Most NPPE resolves within 12–48 hours with appropriate supportive care, in part because alveolar fluid clearance mechanisms remain structurally intact — this is fundamentally different from ARDS, where the alveolar-capillary membrane itself is damaged.

Negative pressure pulmonary edema (also called postobstructive pulmonary edema, POPE) is non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema caused by intense inspiratory effort against an obstructed upper airway. Forceful attempts to breathe against a closed or nearly closed glottis generate markedly negative intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return and right ventricular preload while simultaneously lowering extramural alveolar pressure — the resulting pressure gradient pulls fluid out of the pulmonary capillaries into the interstitium and alveoli. Edema fluid collected from these patients is characteristically low in protein, supporting a hydrostatic (not permeability/inflammatory) mechanism.

NPPE is classified as Type I — occurring immediately after acute airway obstruction, most commonly post-extubation laryngospasm in adults or croup/epiglottitis in children — or Type II, developing after relief of a chronic obstruction (e.g., adenotonsillar hypertrophy). Reported overall incidence is roughly 0.1% of anesthetics; among cases specifically tied to post-extubation laryngospasm, estimates range from 0.1–3.0%.

rows: Type I develops within minutes of the obstructing event (e.g., post-extubation laryngospasm).
Can be severe and rapid — a well-documented cause of dramatic post-extubation desaturation.
Classic finding, identical in appearance to cardiogenic pulmonary edema — this overlap is exactly why the two are frequently confused initially.
Appear rapidly, again indistinguishable in appearance from cardiogenic edema on plain imaging alone.
Stridor, paradoxical chest/abdominal breathing before the edema develops — recognizing these early, before frank pulmonary edema sets in, is the actual prevention window.

blocks.html:
• Avoid premature extubation — this is the single highest-leverage prevention step, since post-extubation laryngospasm is the dominant adult cause.
  • Ensure at-risk patients are genuinely awake before extubation — an intermediate ("stage 2") depth of anesthesia is the highest-risk window for triggering laryngospasm.
  • Suction secretions before extubation and limit the number of laryngoscopy attempts if reintubation becomes necessary — both reduce airway irritation that can trigger or prolong spasm.
  • Use airway adjuncts (oral/nasopharyngeal airways) to help maintain patency through emergence.
  • Consider deep or fully-awake extubation deliberately in higher-risk patients rather than defaulting to routine timing; IV lidocaine can help blunt the reflex that triggers laryngospasm.
  • Recognize early signs of obstruction (stridor, paradoxical breathing) and intervene before the patient generates the sustained negative pressure that produces edema — CPAP or noninvasive ventilation applied at this stage, for partial obstruction, can prevent the excessive negative intrathoracic pressure from ever developing.
  • Staff education specifically on this syndrome improves recognition — NPPE is easy to misattribute to aspiration or cardiogenic edema if the preceding airway event isn't kept in mind.

rows: Incidence tied to post-extubation laryngospasm specifically
Type I incidence after acute post-extubation airway obstruction
Type II incidence after relief of chronic obstruction
Typical resolution window with appropriate treatment
12–48 hours (some sources cite up to 24–72 hours)
Low — supports hydrostatic rather than permeability mechanism

blocks.html:
Why NPPE looks cardiogenic on imaging despite being non-cardiogenic: the negative intrathoracic pressure increases right ventricular preload, causing RV dilation and a leftward septal shift that impairs left ventricular diastolic filling. This mimics the hemodynamic picture of heart failure closely enough that chest X-ray findings alone can't distinguish the two — but the low-protein character of the edema fluid, and the clear temporal link to an airway obstruction event, both point away from a primary cardiac cause.

Why it resolves so much faster than typical ARDS: the alveolar-capillary membrane itself isn't structurally damaged in NPPE the way it is in inflammatory/permeability-mediated lung injury — the problem is a transient hydrostatic pressure gradient, not membrane injury. Because the lung's normal alveolar fluid clearance machinery remains intact, resolution can happen within 12–48 hours once the obstruction is relieved, versus the much longer course typical of true ARDS.

Why diuretic use is genuinely contested rather than settled: the pathophysiology isn't fluid overload, so diuresis doesn't address the actual mechanism generating the edema. But a perioperative surgical patient may also carry some genuine volume load from intraoperative fluids, and clearing existing edema fluid faster has plausible benefit — this tension is exactly why recommendations diverge across sources, and why judgment based on the individual patient's volume status (not a blanket rule) is the more defensible approach.

Why beta-agonists can help despite bronchospasm not being the primary problem: beta-2 agonism upregulates active sodium transport across the alveolar epithelium, which drives alveolar fluid clearance independent of any bronchodilating effect — this is the same fluid-clearance mechanism exploited in other forms of pulmonary edema management, not a treatment aimed at a bronchospastic component that isn't actually present in most NPPE cases.

Why prevention concentrates so heavily on the extubation moment: because post-extubation laryngospasm is the dominant precipitant in adults, essentially every prevention strategy (avoiding light-plane extubation, suctioning first, considering deep or fully-awake extubation, lidocaine) is really laryngospasm prevention wearing NPPE's name — treat this file and the Laryngospasm crisis file as a linked pair rather than two unrelated problems.

rows: Echo typically shows preserved ejection fraction in NPPE versus reduced function in true cardiogenic edema; look for the preceding airway obstruction event as the key historical clue in NPPE.
Witnessed or suspected aspiration event, often with a more localized/dependent infiltrate pattern rather than the diffuse bilateral pattern of NPPE.
Accompanied by hypotension, skin findings, and a drug-administration trigger rather than an airway-obstruction trigger; treat as anaphylaxis if those features are present.
TRALI / TACO (if a transfusion was given)
Clear temporal link to transfusion rather than to an airway event; TACO specifically reflects genuine volume overload, unlike NPPE.
Review the fluid balance and administration timeline — genuine volume overload responds to diuresis in a way NPPE fundamentally does not.

Can also produce sudden hypoxemia perioperatively, but the mechanism (right heart air lock, Doppler/EtCO₂ changes) and clinical setting (open venous site above the heart) are distinct from an airway-obstruction trigger.

blocks.html:
Imaging and confirmation: chest X-ray to characterize the bilateral infiltrate pattern; echocardiography is useful specifically to help exclude a cardiogenic cause by demonstrating preserved cardiac function.

Monitoring: continuous pulse oximetry and close observation through the expected resolution window; most patients improve substantially within 12–48 hours with appropriate airway management and ventilatory support.

Disposition: extended PACU or ICU-level monitoring depending on severity — a mild, rapidly-improving case may not require ICU admission, while any case needing reintubation, PEEP-dependent ventilation, or advanced rescue therapy (prone positioning, ECMO) clearly does.

Documentation and future anesthetics: record the precipitating event (laryngospasm, extubation timing, any contributing factors) — this directly informs extubation planning for any future anesthetic in the same patient, given how strongly this syndrome clusters around the same precipitating pattern.

protocols.title: Perioperative Anaphylaxis
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Perioperative
protocols.subtitle: NMBA, latex, and chlorhexidine as the leading intraoperative triggers — epinephrine dosing by severity, why it's the only drug that matters acutely, and how to work up the trigger afterward.
protocols.description: NMBA/latex/chlorhexidine triggers, tryptase timing, epinephrine dosing by severity, risk-stratified observation.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Epinephrine is the only first-line drug. Everything else on this list is adjunct or supportive — delay in epinephrine, not lack of antihistamine, is what kills people.

steps.title: Stop the suspected trigger, call for help
steps.html: Discontinue the last agent given if a specific trigger is suspected (NMBA, antibiotic, colloid, chlorhexidine, latex). Continue the case only if hemodynamically safe to do so.

steps.title: Epinephrine — immediately, no absolute contraindication
steps.html: Awake/non-arrested, IM: 0.3–0.5 mg (0.3–0.5 mL of 1:1,000) adults, into the vastus lateralis; 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) children. Repeat q5–15min as needed. Intraoperative/IV access already present, hypotensive or arrested: small IV boluses 10–100 mcg titrated to effect, or an infusion 1–10 mcg/min for refractory hypotension — do not push a full IM-equivalent dose IV outside cardiac arrest (risk of malignant arrhythmia). There is no absolute contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, including in patients with coronary disease — anaphylaxis will kill first.

steps.title: Positioning and volume
steps.html: Supine with leg elevation unless respiratory distress prevents it. Large-bore IV access, 1–2 L crystalloid bolus for hypotension — distributive shock from massive vasodilation and capillary leak often needs aggressive volume on top of epinephrine.

steps.title: Airway and oxygen
steps.html: 100% O₂. Laryngeal edema/stridor is an airway emergency — secure early rather than waiting for complete obstruction; angioedema of the airway can progress fast and make later intubation difficult.

steps.title: Adjuncts — not first-line, don't substitute for epinephrine
steps.html: H1 antihistamine (diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV) for urticaria/pruritus only — doesn't stop the systemic reaction. H2 blocker as adjunct. Corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg IV) may reduce biphasic reaction risk (not proven) but has no acute effect — hours to work. Nebulized albuterol for bronchospasm refractory to epinephrine.

steps.title: Refractory anaphylaxis / vasoplegic shock
steps.html: Continues despite appropriate epinephrine dosing and fluids. Escalate to IV epinephrine infusion, add norepinephrine, consider methylene blue as a last-resort vasoplegia rescue (inhibits nitric oxide synthase), and involve ICU/consider ECMO if truly refractory.

steps.title: Glucagon if the patient is on a beta-blocker
steps.html: 1–5 mg IV — beta-blockade can blunt the response to epinephrine; glucagon works through a non-adrenergic pathway and bypasses the blocked beta-receptor.

blocks.title: Antihistamines and steroids do not abort anaphylaxis
blocks.html: They're adjuncts for symptom control and (unproven) biphasic-reaction reduction. Epinephrine is the only drug shown to reverse the acute reaction — delaying it to give diphenhydramine first is a preventable cause of death.

Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction — IgE-mediated (type I) in most cases, though some perioperative reactions (particularly to neuromuscular blocking agents) can occur via IgE-independent mast cell/basophil activation with a clinically identical presentation. Under anesthesia, the classic cutaneous warning signs are frequently hidden under drapes and surgical positioning, so cardiovascular collapse or a sudden rise in airway pressure may be the first thing anyone notices.

By NIAID/FAAN criteria, anaphylaxis is likely when any one of three patterns is met: (1) acute skin/mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise or hypotension; (2) two or more of skin/mucosal signs, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or GI symptoms occurring rapidly after a likely exposure; or (3) hypotension after exposure to a known allergen, even without skin signs — the third pattern is exactly the perioperative presentation, since drapes hide the skin findings that would otherwise make this obvious.

rows: Skin (~90% of cases, often absent/hidden intraop)
Urticaria, angioedema, flushing, pruritus — may be entirely absent or unseen under drapes in the OR, especially in rapid/severe reactions.
Bronchospasm (rising peak airway pressures on the vent), stridor, hoarseness from laryngeal edema, rhinorrhea.
Hypotension, tachycardia, dysrhythmia, syncope — often the first and only sign an anesthesia team sees under drapes.
Nausea, vomiting, cramping, diarrhea — not observable under general anesthesia but relevant if the reaction starts pre-induction.
Anxiety, sense of impending doom (awake patients), altered mental status.

Sudden hypotension refractory to usual pressor doses, unexplained rise in airway pressures, and unexplained tachycardia are frequently the presenting triad — treat as anaphylaxis until proven otherwise rather than waiting for skin signs that may never be visible.

sections.title: OR Triggers & Set-Up for the At-Risk Patient

blocks.html:
• Neuromuscular blocking agents are the most frequently implicated perioperative trigger in most large series, followed by latex and chlorhexidine (chlorhexidine allergy is increasingly recognized and easy to miss since it's used on skin, catheters, and mucosal antiseptic prep alike).
  • Antibiotics (especially beta-lactams given at induction) and blood products are also common triggers — timing relative to induction is a key clue: a reaction minutes after NMBA/induction agents points one direction, a reaction after the surgical antibiotic timeout points another.
  • Known latex allergy: latex-free room setup (gloves, catheters, tourniquets, drains), first case of the day if possible to reduce airborne latex particle load from prior cases.
  • Known chlorhexidine allergy: alternate skin prep (e.g., povidone-iodine), alternate central line/catheter coatings, flag on all vascular access supplies.
  • Prior perioperative anaphylaxis, unclear trigger: anesthesia record should specify exactly what was given and in what order at the time of the prior event — this timeline is the single most useful piece of information for the allergist who eventually works it up.
  • Epinephrine immediately available at the anesthesia workstation in a familiar concentration/dilution — under stress, drawing up and diluting epinephrine correctly is a common point of error.

rows: Peaks 1–2 hours post-reaction — draw a sample in this window if anaphylaxis is suspected intraoperatively; this is the single most useful confirmatory lab.

Draw >24 hours after the event (or at a routine follow-up visit) for comparison. An elevated baseline (not just peak) suggests mastocytosis, which raises future anaphylaxis severity risk and changes long-term management.
Not a lab, but the earliest and most actionable intraoperative signal — sudden, pressor-refractory hypotension is often the first data point available.

blocks.html: Baseline tryptase >8 ng/mL should prompt evaluation for hereditary alpha-tryptasemia or clonal mast cell disease — relevant for planning anesthesia in a patient with a history of severe or recurrent perioperative anaphylaxis.

Why epinephrine and only epinephrine reverses the acute reaction: anaphylaxis involves both alpha and beta receptor-mediated effects that need simultaneous correction — alpha-agonism reverses vasodilation and mucosal edema, beta-1 agonism supports cardiac output, and beta-2 agonism reverses bronchospasm and, critically, inhibits further mediator release from mast cells and basophils. No other single agent hits all three targets at once, which is why antihistamines and steroids can't substitute for it.

Why IM, not IV, is the default route: IM injection into the vastus lateralis achieves faster peak plasma concentration than IM deltoid or subcutaneous routes, and is dramatically safer than IV push outside of arrest — IV push epinephrine in a non-arrested patient risks precipitating malignant ventricular arrhythmia. IV infusion becomes appropriate specifically for refractory cases already under continuous monitoring, which describes the OR.

Why glucagon matters specifically in beta-blocked patients: beta-blockade can blunt or completely block the response to epinephrine, since epinephrine's mechanism runs through the same receptors the beta-blocker occupies. Glucagon raises cAMP through a separate, non-adrenergic receptor pathway, restoring some inotropic/chronotropic support even when beta-receptors are blocked.

Why the observation-period recommendation has moved away from a flat 4–6 hours: older guidance treated biphasic-reaction risk as roughly uniform across all anaphylaxis presentations. Current (2023 practice-parameter and subsequent) evidence shows biphasic reactions cluster heavily in patients with a severe initial presentation, more than one epinephrine dose required, or an unknown/non-food trigger — patients without those risk factors who are symptom-free after roughly 1 hour of observation have a very low subsequent biphasic-reaction rate. This matters directly for perioperative cases, since the patient is typically going to a monitored PACU/ICU setting regardless, which changes the calculus versus discharging someone from an ED.

rows: No urticaria (critical distinguisher), bradykinin-mediated, does not respond to epinephrine, antihistamines, or steroids. Treatment is C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate, icatibant, or ecallantide.
Bradykinin-mediated like HAE; no urticaria; face/tongue/larynx involvement; does not respond to epi/antihistamines/steroids; risk persists up to 3 months after stopping the ACEi.
CNS-first pattern (tinnitus, perioral numbness, seizure) rather than skin/respiratory/GI pattern; clear temporal link to LA administration rather than antibiotic/NMBA timing.
Bradycardia (not tachycardia) with hypotension, no bronchospasm or skin findings, resolves with positioning alone.
Simple bronchospasm (asthma exacerbation, light anesthesia, mechanical tube issue)
Isolated respiratory finding without the hypotension/skin/GI multi-system pattern; check tube position and depth of anesthesia before assuming anaphylaxis.
Scombroid poisoning (histamine toxicity from spoiled fish, pre-op context)
Flushing and urticaria without true IgE-mediated systemic involvement; tryptase stays normal.
Mast cell activation from direct drug effect (opioids, vancomycin "red man syndrome")

Cutaneous flushing/pruritus from direct, non-IgE mast cell degranulation — usually milder, tryptase typically not significantly elevated, doesn't require full anaphylaxis protocol though epinephrine is still appropriate if hemodynamically significant.

blocks.html:
Observation: risk-stratify rather than applying a blanket window. Low-risk (rapid, complete response to a single epinephrine dose; no hypotension/hypoxia; known/likely trigger) can reasonably be observed on the shorter end. Higher-risk (multiple epinephrine doses required, hypotension, hypoxia, unknown trigger, wide pulse pressure at presentation) warrants extended observation — commonly 4–6+ hours — or ICU admission. Given a perioperative patient is already headed to a monitored PACU/ICU setting, err toward the longer end of that range as a practical default.

Timed tryptase: draw during the 1–2 hour post-reaction window, plus a baseline sample >24 hours later for comparison — this pairing is what makes the diagnosis retrospectively confirmable and is frequently missed if not ordered proactively at the time of the event.

Allergy referral: every patient gets referred to allergy/immunology for trigger identification (skin testing, sometimes graded challenge) before their next anesthetic — the anesthesia record's exact timeline of what was given, in what order, is the single most useful document for that workup.

Documentation and future anesthetics: flag the chart, prescribe/discuss an epinephrine autoinjector if there's any risk of non-perioperative re-exposure to the trigger, and plan future anesthetics around a confirmed or presumed trigger (e.g., latex-free room, NMBA-avoidance technique) even before allergy workup is complete.

protocols.title: Severe Intraoperative Bronchospasm
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Perioperative
protocols.subtitle: Rule out the mechanical mimics first, deepen anesthesia, escalate through inhaled to IV bronchodilators — and watch for the dynamic hyperinflation that can quietly turn a respiratory problem into a hemodynamic one.
protocols.description: Mechanical-cause rule-out, stepwise inhaled-to-IV escalation, dynamic hyperinflation as the hidden hemodynamic threat.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Rule out the mimics before you commit to "bronchospasm" — treating a kinked tube with albuterol wastes the time you don't have.

steps.title: 100% O₂, disconnect from the ventilator, hand-ventilate
steps.html: Squeezing the bag yourself lets you feel resistance directly and assess whether this is truly high-resistance bronchospasm versus a mechanical problem.

steps.title: Rule out mechanical and other causes fast
steps.html: Check for ETT kink or mucus obstruction, endobronchial (mainstem) intubation, tension pneumothorax, aspiration, pulmonary edema, and pulmonary embolism — all can mimic bronchospasm and none respond to bronchodilators. Reposition/pull back the tube and confirm placement by auscultation if endobronchial intubation is possible. If anaphylaxis is on the differential, check for rash and BP and stop any newly-given agent.

steps.title: Deepen anesthesia
steps.html: The first pharmacologic step. Increase inhaled volatile concentration — sevoflurane is a potent direct bronchodilator and a good choice here — or bolus/increase an IV agent (propofol, or ketamine specifically for its bronchodilating properties).

steps.title: Inhaled beta-2 agonist
steps.html: Albuterol 8–10 puffs via an MDI adapter in the circuit (a larger-than-usual dose is needed because a large fraction deposits on the ETT and circuit rather than reaching the lungs) or nebulized 2.5 mg. Add ipratropium, especially if a recent viral URI is a likely contributor.

steps.title: Severe or unresponsive — IV epinephrine
steps.html: 1–2 mcg/kg IV, or titrated boluses of 10–100 mcg. Reach for this early rather than persisting with inhaled therapy alone if SpO₂ is critically low or the chest is silent — inhaled drug often can't reach the alveoli through a severely obstructed airway, while IV epinephrine works systemically regardless.

steps.title: Refractory — add multimodal adjuncts
steps.html: IV magnesium sulfate, ketamine bolus/infusion, IV lidocaine, or dexmedetomidine. Corticosteroids (methylprednisolone) help reduce recurrence/prolonged course but take 4–8 hours to act — give early anyway, but don't expect it to break the acute event.

steps.title: Watch for dynamic hyperinflation ("breath stacking")
steps.html: Severe obstruction can prevent full exhalation before the next breath is delivered, progressively raising intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return, and causing hypotension or even PEA. If hypotension develops during severe bronchospasm, briefly disconnect the circuit to allow full passive exhalation — both diagnostic and therapeutic. Reduce respiratory rate and extend expiratory time; permissive hypercapnia is an acceptable trade-off.

steps.title: If reversing neuromuscular blockade
steps.html: Use sugammadex rather than neostigmine if the patient is actively wheezing — neostigmine's muscarinic activity can worsen bronchoconstriction.

blocks.title: Small share of claims, disproportionate severity
blocks.html: Bronchospasm accounts for only about 2% of anesthesia closed-claims cases, but roughly 90% of those specific claims involve severe brain injury or death — this is a low-incidence, high-lethality event when it goes wrong.

Bronchospasm is smooth-muscle-mediated narrowing of the bronchioles, producing airflow obstruction concentrated in the expiratory phase. Perioperative causes include reactive airway disease (asthma), COPD, anaphylaxis, direct mechanical/chemical airway irritation (ETT stimulating the carina or a mainstem bronchus, aspiration of gastric acid), and drug-related histamine release.

A large retrospective review found combined intraoperative bronchospasm and laryngospasm incidence around 1.7%, more frequent in older patients and those with active asthma. Even though it's a fairly infrequent event overall, its severity profile in closed-claims data (above) makes rapid, correct management disproportionately important relative to its incidence.

rows: Classic finding — but a truly silent chest can mean the airways are so severely obstructed that no air movement is audible at all, which is a worse sign, not a reassuring one.
Reflects increasing airway resistance during mechanical ventilation.
An upsloping expiratory limb replacing the normal plateau reflects delayed, obstructed exhalation — a fast, readily-available clue even before auscultating.
From worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch as obstruction progresses.
High felt resistance when bagging manually — a direct, immediate way to assess severity once disconnected from the ventilator.
Suggests dynamic hyperinflation with impaired venous return rather than a primary cardiovascular event — treat by allowing exhalation, not just with fluids/pressors alone.

blocks.html:
• Preoperative optimization for known reactive airway disease: confirm the patient is on their routine inhaled beta-agonist/steroid regimen, consider having them use their inhaler the morning of surgery, and postpone elective cases with poorly-controlled asthma when feasible.
  • Risk history matters more than exam findings the day of surgery — a history of frequent exacerbations, hospital visits, or prior intubation/mechanical ventilation for a severe asthma attack signals real risk even in a patient who looks and sounds fine at preop assessment.
  • Consider a supraglottic airway instead of an ETT when the case allows it, to reduce direct tracheal/carinal stimulation in a hyperreactive airway.
  • Ensure an adequate depth of anesthesia before airway manipulation — laryngoscopy and intubation performed too lightly are a well-recognized trigger.
  • Be cautious with histamine-releasing drugs (e.g., older-generation neuromuscular blockers like atracurium, morphine) in higher-risk patients.
  • Plan extubation deliberately — either fully awake or under a genuinely deep plane, avoiding the intermediate ("stage 2") depth that raises airway reactivity risk; IV lidocaine before extubation can help blunt reflex bronchoconstriction.
  • Reoccurrence on emergence is common once volatile anesthetic is turned off — keep an albuterol nebulizer and IV bronchodilator options accessible through emergence and early recovery, not just during the case itself.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: Larger than the outpatient dose — most deposits on the ETT/circuit before reaching the lung.
Alternative delivery if in-line MDI adapter isn't available.
For severe/refractory bronchospasm not responding to inhaled therapy.
Titrate to response; keep separate from any sodium bicarbonate line (incompatible).
Useful multimodal adjunct in refractory cases; watch for muscle weakness/CNS depression at higher doses.
Onset 4–8 hours — give early for the recurrence-prevention benefit, not as acute rescue.
Higher in older patients and active asthmatics.
~2% of claims, ~90% of those involve severe brain injury or death
Low frequency, high stakes when it happens.

blocks.html:
Why ruling out mechanical causes comes before treating "bronchospasm": a kinked tube, mainstem intubation, or tension pneumothorax can produce an identical clinical picture — high airway pressure, desaturation, difficulty ventilating — without any bronchodilator having a chance of helping. Time spent nebulizing albuterol into a mechanically obstructed circuit is time not spent fixing the actual problem.

Why deepening anesthesia is the first pharmacologic step: a light anesthetic plane during airway stimulation is one of the most common precipitants of reflex bronchoconstriction, and volatile agents (sevoflurane in particular) are themselves direct bronchodilators — this single intervention can address both the trigger and the treatment simultaneously.

Why IV epinephrine gets used even though inhaled therapy is first-line in outpatient asthma care: inhaled drug delivery depends on the drug actually reaching distal airways, which becomes progressively less reliable as obstruction worsens — in a genuinely severe or "silent chest" presentation, systemic (IV) epinephrine bypasses that delivery problem entirely and acts through the same beta-2 mechanism regardless of how obstructed the airways are.

Why neostigmine is avoided when the patient is wheezing: neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase non-selectively, increasing muscarinic as well as nicotinic cholinergic tone — the muscarinic effect promotes bronchoconstriction, directly working against what you're trying to treat. Sugammadex reverses rocuronium/vecuronium by direct encapsulation rather than through the cholinergic system, so it doesn't carry this risk.

Why dynamic hyperinflation causes hypotension that looks cardiac but isn't: when expiratory time is inadequate relative to the degree of obstruction, each subsequent breath adds volume on top of air that hasn't fully left the lungs. The resulting rise in intrathoracic pressure compresses the great veins and reduces venous return to the heart — a mechanical, not a primary cardiac, cause of hypotension. This is exactly why briefly disconnecting the circuit (allowing full passive exhalation) is both the diagnostic test and the treatment, rather than reaching first for fluids or vasopressors.

rows: ETT obstruction (kink, mucus plug, cuff herniation)
Passing a suction catheter fails to advance freely, or direct visualization/fiberoptic check reveals the obstruction — doesn't respond to bronchodilators.
Unilateral breath sounds, asymmetric chest rise; resolves immediately with pulling the tube back to correct depth.
Unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, hypotension, distended neck veins — a distinct mechanical emergency, not bronchospasm.

Often a known event (witnessed regurgitation) or occurs in a high-risk patient; gastric acid causes irritant-mediated bronchoconstriction that responds less reliably to epinephrine than immune-mediated bronchospasm — focus on suctioning and supportive care alongside bronchodilator therapy.
Pink frothy secretions, diffuse crackles rather than wheeze predominating, different hemodynamic picture (often volume-overloaded rather than obstructed).
Sudden desaturation and hypotension without a clear airway-pressure/wheeze pattern; consider especially with new hypotension out of proportion to apparent respiratory findings.

Bronchospasm can be a component of anaphylaxis itself — check for rash, angioedema, and hypotension out of proportion to a pure airway problem, and treat as anaphylaxis (epinephrine, stop the trigger) if those features are present.

blocks.html:
Confirm resolution before proceeding: reassess airway pressures, breath sounds, and capnography waveform once treatment is given — don't assume resolution just because the immediate crisis feels over.

Chest imaging if there's any residual concern: a chest X-ray can rule out a missed pneumothorax or confirm tube position if endobronchial intubation was in the differential.

Emergence and extubation planning: anticipate recurrence as volatile anesthetic is discontinued; have bronchodilator therapy immediately available through extubation and early recovery, and plan a deep or fully-awake extubation deliberately rather than defaulting to routine timing.

Disposition: a severe or refractory episode — especially one involving dynamic hyperinflation with hemodynamic compromise, or requiring IV epinephrine/multimodal rescue — warrants postoperative ICU-level monitoring rather than routine PACU-to-floor progression.

Documentation and future planning: record the trigger if identifiable, treatments given and response, and flag the chart for anesthesia technique adjustments (SGA over ETT, avoidance of a specific drug, more aggressive preoperative optimization) on future anesthetics.

protocols.title: Total & High Spinal
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Neuraxial & Obstetric
protocols.subtitle: Local anesthetic spreading above the intended level after a neuraxial technique — the four-stage ascending pattern, why "spinal after epidural" is the classic setup, and the airway/hemodynamic support that carries the patient through.
protocols.description: Four-stage ascending recognition, "spinal after epidural" as the classic setup, airway/hemodynamic support, NYSORA/WFSA-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: This is supportive care, not a reversible-agent scenario — there's no antidote. Airway, breathing, circulation, and time are what carry the patient through until the block regresses.

steps.title: Stop any further epidural/spinal dosing, call for help
steps.html: Stop the infusion or bolus immediately. Get a second anesthesia provider — this can escalate from numb hands to loss of consciousness in minutes.

steps.title: If obstetric: left lateral tilt, monitor fetal heart rate
steps.html: Aortocaval compression compounds the hypotension already in play. Maintain uterine displacement throughout resuscitation.

steps.title: Airway and breathing — support before it's an emergency
steps.html: 100% O₂ by mask early. Stage 3–4 (shoulder weakness, respiratory failure, or loss of consciousness): secure the airway with RSI and ventilate — don't wait for frank apnea. A patient who is awake but rapidly ascending toward respiratory failure still needs a controlled, deliberate intubation rather than a crash one.

steps.title: Treat hypotension aggressively
steps.html: Rapid crystalloid or colloid bolus 500–1,000 mL. Vasopressor boluses: metaraminol 0.5 mg or ephedrine 6 mg, repeated as needed. Persistent hypotension: start a metaraminol or norepinephrine infusion; place an arterial line for beat-to-beat monitoring if inotropes are needed.

steps.title: Treat bradycardia
steps.html: Atropine 0.6 mg boluses. If bradycardia persists despite atropine and vasopressors, add an epinephrine infusion — profound bradycardia from high sympathetic blockade can be resistant to atropine alone.

steps.title: Sedation and reassurance if the patient is conscious but distressed
steps.html: A patient who can't move or feel their hands but remains fully conscious is a frightening experience — communicate constantly, and use judicious sedation once the airway is secured or clearly not at immediate risk. Awareness during emergency intubation for this indication has been reported and is a recognized source of later psychological distress; explain what's happening as you go.

steps.title: Central line if inotropes are required, arrange ICU-capable monitoring
steps.html: Ongoing pressor/inotrope support and ventilation typically require a higher level of monitoring than routine PACU once the acute phase is controlled.

blocks.title: This resolves — the job is to get the patient there safely
blocks.html: Total spinal anesthesia has a good outcome when treated promptly; poor outcomes are consistently associated with delayed recognition and inadequate resuscitation, not with the block itself. The local anesthetic wears off — your job is airway, breathing, and circulation until it does.

High spinal is spread of local anesthetic affecting spinal nerves above T4. Total spinal goes further — intracranial spread causing loss of consciousness, and is distinguished clinically from a high-but-not-total block by worsening respiratory function. Both are recognized complications of any neuraxial technique: spinal, epidural, caudal, and even paravertebral or interscalene blocks performed near the vertebral column.

Incidence estimates vary widely by definition and technique — obstetric high neuraxial block is reported around 1 in 4,336 anesthetics in one large complication repository (the single highest incidence among serious anesthesia complications tracked), while strict total spinal is much rarer, historically cited around 1 in 16,000–27,000 obstetric epidurals. "Spinal after epidural" — giving a spinal dose in a patient with an existing, possibly partially-functioning epidural — is the most frequently reported precipitant in recent obstetric series.

rows: Hypotension and bradycardia from sympathetic blockade of the cardioaccelerator fibers.
Numb or tingling hands, shortness of breath as intercostal muscle function is affected.
Shoulder weakness, progressive respiratory failure as the diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) becomes involved.
Sedation, loss of consciousness, fixed and dilated pupils, apnea — this is total spinal.

blocks.html: Onset timing is not always fast. Classic teaching describes onset within 3 minutes of injection, but reported cases range from 1 to 180 minutes — insidious, delayed presentations happen, especially with catheter migration rather than a direct large-volume injection. Hypotension is not invariable either (present in only about half of reported cases), so don't rule out a high/total spinal just because the blood pressure looks reasonable early on.

• Test dose and incremental dosing: treat every epidural bolus as a test dose — incremental 5 mL increments rather than one large volume, with reassessment between doses.
  • Aspirate before every bolus to check for blood or CSF, confirming the catheter hasn't migrated intrathecally or intravascularly since placement.
  • High suspicion during epidural top-up in labor or theater — a rapid onset of dense sensory and motor block from what should be a low-dose infusion is abnormal and should prompt immediate reassessment, not reassurance.
  • Reduce spinal dose if a functioning (or possibly still-functioning) epidural is in place — giving a standard spinal dose on top of residual epidural effect is the leading modern precipitant; reductions to roughly 1–1.5 mL of local anesthetic have been suggested for a spinal following a failed epidural top-up, though there's no firm consensus on the exact reduction.
  • Avoid injecting during a contraction, cough, or Valsalva — transiently raised intra-abdominal/intrathecal pressure increases cephalad spread.
  • Position awareness: block height with hyperbaric ("heavy") solutions can still be manipulated for up to 30 minutes after injection — if using a head-down position to establish the block, remove it as soon as the desired level is reached, and use an Oxford wedge to help limit cephalad spread while also optimizing positioning for airway access if general anesthesia becomes necessary.
  • Dose reduction in short-stature or morbidly obese patients — smaller CSF volume and altered anatomy both increase the risk of a given dose spreading higher than intended.

rows: Intracranial spread with loss of consciousness; distinguished from high-but-not-total by worsening respiratory function
~1 in 4,336 anesthetics (highest incidence among serious anesthesia-related complications tracked in the SOAP complication repository)
~1 in 16,000–27,000 obstetric epidurals depending on source and era
Present in roughly half of reported cases — its absence doesn't exclude the diagnosis
Median bupivacaine dose in de novo spinal TSA case reports
~12.75 mg (range 10–15 mg) — well within a routine spinal dose, underscoring that this can happen at normal doses

blocks.html:
Why there's no drug that reverses it: unlike LAST or anaphylaxis, there's no antidote or rescue agent that reverses neuraxial local anesthetic action — the block resolves as the drug redistributes and metabolizes on its own timeline. This is why management is entirely supportive: keep oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion adequate until that happens.

Why the ascending stage pattern predicts what's coming: the anatomic progression (thoracic sympathetics → cervical dermatomes → phrenic nerve → intracranial structures) is a direct map of ascending local anesthetic concentration in the CSF or epidural space. Recognizing which stage the patient is in tells you what's about to happen next — numb hands with dyspnea (stage 2) is a warning that phrenic involvement and respiratory failure may be minutes away, which is why controlled, early airway management beats waiting for frank apnea.

Why "spinal after epidural" is uniquely dangerous: a partially functioning epidural has already primed the epidural space and altered local anesthetic distribution; giving a standard spinal dose on top of that unpredictable baseline can produce far higher effective spread than the same dose would in a naive patient, which is the physiologic basis for reducing spinal dose in this specific situation.

Why left lateral tilt matters specifically in the obstetric case: the gravid uterus compresses the aorta and inferior vena cava in the supine position, independently reducing venous return and cardiac output. Stacking that on top of high-block-induced sympathectomy and vasodilation compounds the hypotension — correcting one without the other leaves a preventable component of the collapse untreated.

Why atropine sometimes isn't enough for the bradycardia: the bradycardia in a high thoracic block comes from blockade of the cardioaccelerator sympathetic fibers (T1–T4), not primarily from vagal tone — atropine addresses the vagal component but doesn't restore the lost sympathetic drive, which is why refractory bradycardia sometimes needs an epinephrine infusion rather than repeated atropine dosing.

rows: CNS excitation (seizure) rather than a clean ascending sensory/motor block; occurs from systemic absorption/intravascular injection rather than intrathecal/epidural spread.
Bradycardia and hypotension without an ascending sensory or motor block; resolves with positioning and reassurance.

Sudden collapse with cardiovascular and coagulopathic features, typically without the characteristic ascending numbness/weakness pattern; often has a preceding event (rupture of membranes, uterine manipulation).
Intracranial event (stroke, seizure) — can be genuinely difficult to distinguish acutely

Case reports describe a fixed, dilated pupil high-spinal presentation mimicking a catastrophic neurologic or embolic event, fully reversible once recognized. Stable hemodynamics and spontaneous ventilation despite altered consciousness should raise suspicion for high spinal over a primary CNS catastrophe in a patient with a recent neuraxial technique.
No ascending sensory/motor findings; responds to volume alone without the neurologic component.
Opioid-related respiratory depression (if intrathecal/epidural opioid was co-administered)
Depressed respiratory rate without the ascending numbness/motor block pattern; responds to naloxone, which a true high spinal will not.

blocks.html:
Confirm the mechanism once stable: aspirate and check the catheter for CSF or blood, and consider imaging or catheter-tip review if intrathecal migration is suspected — this matters both for the current case and for documenting exactly what happened.

Monitoring: continue ventilatory and hemodynamic support until the block clearly regresses — motor and sensory function returning to normal levels, hemodynamics stable without pressor support. This can take one to several hours depending on the agent and dose involved.

Disposition: ICU or equivalent high-acuity monitoring for any case requiring intubation, pressor support, or prolonged ventilatory support; less severe cases that never required airway intervention can often be managed in a well-monitored PACU/labor-and-delivery setting with continuous observation until the block resolves.

Documentation and debrief: record the technique, dose, catheter status, and timeline in detail — this is exactly the kind of event where structured documentation prevents recurrence in that patient's future anesthetics and contributes to institutional learning. Address the patient's experience directly afterward, including counseling about intraoperative awareness if it occurred during emergency airway management.

protocols.title: TURP Syndrome
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Urologic
protocols.subtitle: Hypotonic irrigant absorbed through open prostatic venous sinuses — acute dilutional hyponatremia that gets treated aggressively precisely because it's acute, plus the newer saline-irrigant variant that trades one problem for a different one.

badges.text: <1% INCIDENCE, UP TO 25% MORTALITY IF SEVERE

protocols.description: Acute hyponatremia treated fast on purpose, glycine CNS toxicity, hypertonic saline dosing, TURis/saline hyperchloremic acidosis variant.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: This is acute, not chronic, hyponatremia — that distinction changes the correction-rate rules and is the single most important thing to get right.

steps.title: Alert the surgeon, finish the resection quickly
steps.html: Every additional minute of open prostatic venous sinuses is more irrigant absorption. If TURP syndrome is suspected mid-case, the surgeon should complete resection and achieve hemostasis as efficiently as possible.

steps.title: 100% O₂, support airway/breathing/circulation
steps.html: Secure the airway if consciousness is impaired. Treat hypotension and bradycardia as they arise — standard supportive measures while the diagnosis is confirmed.

steps.title: Send serum sodium and electrolytes STAT
steps.html: Check intraoperatively for any prolonged case (>90 minutes) or when clinical suspicion is raised — don't wait for symptoms to develop before checking if the resection has run long.

steps.title: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia — 3% hypertonic saline
steps.html: For seizures, coma, or marked mental status change: 100–150 mL IV bolus or continuous infusion, targeting a 6 mmol/L rise in the first 6 hours. Transfer immediately to ICU with continuous monitoring. Treat active seizures with benzodiazepines in parallel.

steps.title: Cap total correction — don't overshoot
steps.html: After the initial 6 mmol/L in 6 hours, limit further correction to roughly 2 mmol/L over the next 18 hours; total correction should not exceed 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Rapid correction targeting >1 mmol/L/hour is appropriate specifically because this is acute (developing over hours), not chronic, hyponatremia — but the 24-hour cap still applies to avoid overshoot.

steps.title: Loop diuretic — only if hemodynamically stable
steps.html: Furosemide can help eliminate excess absorbed fluid in a volume-overloaded but stable patient. Avoid diuretic therapy in a hemodynamically unstable patient — it removes volume from a circulation that may already be compromised.

steps.title: Refractory/severe cases — consider hemodialysis
steps.html: Particularly when there's a large osmolal gap (significant hyperglycinemia/hyperammonemia from glycine irrigant) or renal impairment limiting other correction strategies — hemodialysis can rapidly correct both the sodium and remove the glycine metabolites simultaneously.

steps.title: If a saline-based irrigant (TURis/bipolar) was used and the picture doesn't fit classic hyponatremia
steps.html: Check an ABG/chemistry for hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis — large-volume normal saline absorption can cause this distinct picture, which responds to bicarbonate rather than vasopressors when hypotension is present.

blocks.title: Acute hyponatremia gets treated differently than chronic
blocks.html: The traditional "correct hyponatremia slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination" rule applies to chronic hyponatremia, where the brain has already adapted. TURP syndrome develops over hours during a single procedure — there's been no time for that adaptation, so rapid initial correction of severe symptoms is appropriate and the real risk being managed is cerebral edema, not overly-fast correction.

TURP syndrome is a systemic complication from excessive absorption of electrolyte-free irrigation fluid through open prostatic venous sinuses during transurethral resection of the prostate (also described with transurethral bladder resection, ureteroscopy, and hysteroscopy). It produces a combination of acute hypervolemia, dilutional hyponatremia, and — with glycine-based irrigants specifically — direct CNS toxicity from the glycine itself, which acts as an inhibitory GABA agonist while paradoxically potentiating NMDA receptors.

Reported incidence is under 1% (roughly 0.78–1.4% in recent series), reflecting the shift toward bipolar resectoscopes using saline irrigant, which have made the classic glycine-mediated syndrome less common than it once was. Despite the low incidence, mortality in severe cases has been reported as high as 25%, and onset can occur as early as 15 minutes into resection or be delayed up to 24 hours postoperatively.

rows: An early hemodynamic pattern from acute hypervolemia — hypertension may be masked or absent if there's concurrent significant surgical bleeding.
Develops as the syndrome advances, sometimes with a confounding contribution from surgical blood loss.
Early neurologic signs — easy to miss or attribute to sedation/anxiety in an awake patient under neuraxial anesthesia.
A relatively specific clue pointing toward glycine toxicity specifically (glycine is a retinal inhibitory neurotransmitter) — worth asking about directly in an awake regional-anesthesia patient.
T-wave depression or inversion, sometimes persisting up to 24 hours; troponin can rise even without a primary cardiac event.
Severe end of the spectrum — reflects cerebral edema from acute hyponatremia and/or direct glycine CNS toxicity.
From acute volume overload; can occur with any irrigant type, not just glycine-based ones.

blocks.html:
• Limit resection time to under 90 minutes where possible — the single most direct lever, since absorption is time-dependent on open venous sinuses.
  • Prefer bipolar resectoscope with isotonic saline irrigant (TURis) over monopolar with glycine when available — eliminates the classic hyponatremic/glycine-toxic syndrome, though large-volume saline absorption can still cause volume overload and, less commonly, hyperchloremic acidosis.
  • Control irrigation bag height/pressure — lower hydrostatic pressure reduces the driving force for absorption through open sinuses.
  • Prophylactic furosemide has trial-level evidence for reducing hyponatremia incidence in monopolar TURP specifically — worth considering as an institutional protocol element for higher-risk cases, though it's not yet universal practice.
  • Consider neuraxial rather than general anesthesia for TURP when feasible — an awake patient can report early neurologic symptoms (confusion, visual changes, restlessness) that would otherwise go unnoticed under general anesthesia.
  • Intraoperative monitoring options for higher-risk or prolonged cases: transesophageal Doppler to detect acute hypervolemia, ethanol-tagged irrigant with breath testing as an absorption marker, or intraoperative voiding score assessment — useful adjuncts, though not universally deployed.
  • Check serum sodium intraoperatively for any case running long or with a large resected gland, rather than waiting for symptoms.

rows: As early as 15 minutes into resection; can be delayed up to 24 hours postop
Resection time threshold to limit absorption
Prophylactic irrigant absorption reduction (standard saline 6 mL/kg/hr, cited comparator)
Still produces TURP syndrome in ~25% of patients without additional prophylaxis in some series — underscoring why irrigant choice and resection time matter more than co-fluid alone

sections.title: Rationale for TURP Syndrome Management Steps

blocks.html:
Why rapid correction is appropriate here, unlike most hyponatremia teaching: the standard "correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome" rule exists because in chronic hyponatremia, brain cells have already adapted by extruding intracellular osmoles to match the low extracellular sodium — correcting too fast reverses that adaptation faster than the cells can respond, causing demyelination. TURP syndrome develops over the course of a single procedure; there's been no time for that cellular adaptation, so the actual immediate risk is cerebral edema from the acute drop, not overcorrection. This is why severely symptomatic acute hyponatremia is treated with deliberately faster initial correction than the classic chronic-hyponatremia teaching would suggest.

Why glycine causes symptoms out of proportion to the sodium number alone: glycine is itself an inhibitory neurotransmitter at GABA receptors and also potentiates NMDA receptors — it has direct CNS effects independent of the sodium level. This is why some patients with only moderately low sodium can present with severe neurologic findings (visual disturbance, coma): the glycine toxicity and the hyponatremia are compounding, not the same problem measured twice. It's also why measured serum osmolality often looks less deranged than the sodium alone would predict — glycine is an osmotically active nonsodium solute, partially explaining the "pseudohyponatremia" component of the picture.

Why furosemide is avoided in the unstable patient specifically: a volume-overloaded but hemodynamically stable patient benefits from diuresis to offload the absorbed fluid. A patient who is already hypotensive or in cardiovascular collapse from the same syndrome doesn't have volume to spare — removing more preload in that setting worsens the hemodynamic problem you're simultaneously trying to fix.

Why the saline-irrigant (TURis) variant needs a different antidote entirely: switching to isotonic saline solves the hyponatremia/glycine-toxicity problem, but large-volume saline absorption introduces a new mechanism — dilutional hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis — that doesn't respond to the usual vasoactive-agent approach to hypotension. Recognizing which irrigant was used changes what "correcting" the picture actually requires.

rows: No temporal link to irrigant absorption or resection time; diagnosis of exclusion based on urine studies once TURP syndrome has been ruled out by timeline.
No correlation with irrigant volume/resection duration; imaging findings would support a structural cause rather than a metabolic one.
Fever and a more gradually evolving hemodynamic picture rather than the acute, procedure-timed presentation of TURP syndrome — though the two can coexist.
Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (if regional block used)
CNS excitation/seizure pattern tied to LA administration timing rather than resection duration/irrigant volume.

Preexisting cardiac history and a hemodynamic profile consistent with pump failure rather than acute volume absorption — though TURP-associated volume overload can also produce pulmonary edema directly.
Rapid point-of-care glucose check rules this in or out quickly and should be part of the initial altered-mental-status workup regardless of TURP suspicion.

blocks.html:
Serial labs during correction: recheck serum sodium every 2–4 hours during active correction to confirm you're tracking the target rate, not over- or under-correcting. Check osmolality, and consider ammonia level if a large volume of glycine irrigant was used, since hyperammonemia can independently contribute to altered mental status.

Cardiac monitoring: continuous ECG given the described T-wave changes and troponin elevation pattern with glycine absorption — these findings can persist up to 24 hours and don't necessarily indicate a primary cardiac event.

Ophthalmology follow-up if visual disturbance or transient blindness occurred and doesn't resolve promptly with correction.

Disposition: ICU admission for any symptomatic case, particularly one requiring hypertonic saline or presenting with seizure/altered consciousness — this is not a routine PACU-to-floor recovery.

Documentation and future planning: record the irrigant type, total volume used, resection duration, and the patient's clinical course — this directly informs whether future procedures should use a saline-based bipolar system, shorter staged resections, or neuraxial rather than general anesthesia for earlier symptom detection.
