protocols.title: Venous Air Embolism
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Anesthesiology / Neurosurgical & Positioning
protocols.subtitle: Sitting craniotomy is the classic setting, but any surgical site above the heart can entrain air — the Durant maneuver, why the precordial Doppler beats you to it, and the paradoxical embolism trap hiding behind PEEP.
protocols.description: Durant maneuver, precordial Doppler detection, PEEP's paradoxical-embolism trade-off, UpToDate/StatPearls-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Stop more air from getting in, trap and evacuate what's already there, then support the circulation while the right heart clears the air lock.

steps.title: Alert the surgeon, stop further air entry
steps.html: Flood the surgical field with saline and have the surgeon seal/pack any open venous sinuses or bone edges immediately — this is the single highest-yield action to stop the bleeding-air-into-the-circulation problem at its source.

steps.title: Lower the surgical site below the heart if feasible
steps.html: Reduces the pressure gradient that's entraining air in the first place. In sitting craniotomy this may mean repositioning; do this in coordination with the surgical team, not unilaterally.

steps.title: Bilateral jugular venous compression
steps.html: Raises venous pressure at the surgical site, further reducing the gradient favoring air entrainment while the field is being sealed.

steps.title: Position — left lateral decubitus + Trendelenburg (the Durant maneuver)
steps.html: Traps air in the apex of the right ventricle, away from the right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary artery — preventing the "air lock" that obstructs forward flow. This is the classic rescue position once VAE is suspected.

steps.title: Aspirate air if a multiorificed central venous catheter is in place
steps.html: A catheter tip positioned about 1 cm past the SVC–right atrial junction gives the best chance of aspirating entrained air and breaking up an air lock — this is why high-risk sitting-position cases are set up with this specific catheter placement in advance.

steps.title: 100% O₂, discontinue nitrous oxide
steps.html: Nitrous oxide diffuses into air bubbles faster than nitrogen diffuses out, expanding bubble volume — turn it off immediately if it's running. Secure the airway with intubation if not already done.

steps.title: Hemodynamic support
steps.html: Volume expansion, vasopressors, and inotropic support as needed — ephedrine has been reported to rapidly reverse the cardiopulmonary picture in case reports, and early right-ventricular inotropic support is a reasonable default when VAE is suspected. Mechanical ventilation support as needed for the ventilation-perfusion mismatch VAE creates.

steps.title: Cardiac arrest — closed-chest cardiac massage
steps.html: Standard chest compressions can mechanically break up a large air lock in the right ventricle in addition to their usual circulatory function — don't withhold CPR because you suspect an "obstructive," not primarily cardiac, cause.

steps.title: Hyperbaric oxygen for severe or arterial (paradoxical) involvement
steps.html: Indicated for severe VAE and is the definitive treatment for arterial gas embolism specifically — reduces bubble size and improves tissue oxygenation. Arrange transfer/consultation once the patient is stable enough to move.

blocks.title: The mill-wheel murmur is a late sign
blocks.html: By the time a mill-wheel murmur is audible, a substantial volume of air has already entered the heart chambers. Doppler tone changes and a sudden EtCO₂ drop come first — don't wait for the murmur to start treating.

Venous air embolism is a predominantly iatrogenic complication in which atmospheric gas enters the systemic venous circulation, most classically when a surgical site sits above the level of the right atrium — creating a pressure gradient that draws air into an open venous structure rather than blood flowing out. Sufficient entrained air can obstruct right ventricular outflow ("air lock"), causing acute right heart strain, increased pulmonary dead space, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and — if enough enters — cardiovascular collapse.

Sitting-position neurosurgery (craniotomy, posterior fossa, cervical spine) carries the highest classically-cited risk, with reported clinically significant VAE incidence around 0.13–0.61% in that setting, though asymptomatic air entrainment detected by sensitive monitoring is far more common than clinically significant events. VAE has also been well described during laparoscopic surgery, central line placement, cesarean section, and any other procedure with an open venous structure above heart level.

sections.title: Signs — Order of Appearance (Most to Least Sensitive)

rows: Most sensitive noninvasive monitor — detects volumes as small as roughly 0.02–0.05 mL/kg, often before any other sign appears. Correct probe position (right parasternal, 3rd–6th intercostal space) matters — misplacement gives false negatives.

A fall of more than about 5 mmHg, especially with concurrent hypotension or desaturation, is highly suggestive — reflects increased dead space as air obstructs pulmonary capillary flow. Widely available, so it's often the first alarm a whole team notices even without dedicated Doppler monitoring.
Reflects the developing right-heart outflow obstruction.
The degree of hemodynamic change does not reliably correlate with clinical severity — a hemodynamically unimpressive picture doesn't rule out a significant VAE.
Right heart strain/ischemia pattern — right bundle branch block, ST-segment changes — can progress to arrhythmia.
From the same V/Q mismatch driving the EtCO₂ drop.
Late sign — churning, machinery-like sound from air/blood mixing in the right ventricle. By the time it's audible, a substantial air volume has already entered.

The single most sensitive and specific modality overall, directly visualizing air in the right atrium/ventricle/pulmonary artery — but invasive, expensive, and not used routinely outside high-risk cases.

sections.title: Room Set-Up & Monitoring for High-Risk Cases

blocks.html:
• Preoperative PFO screening for any planned sitting-position case — a patient with an intracardiac shunt is at risk for paradoxical (arterial) embolism if venous air crosses to the left side, which changes the risk calculus for choosing that position at all.
  • Precordial Doppler placed correctly before positioning — right parasternal border, 3rd–6th intercostal space; combine with continuous EtCO₂ monitoring for the best readily-available sensitivity/affordability combination. TEE for the highest-risk cases where the resource and expertise are available.
  • Multiorificed central venous catheter with the tip positioned roughly 1 cm past the SVC–right atrial junction, placed specifically to allow air aspiration if VAE occurs — set this up before, not during, an event.
  • Minimize the vertical distance between the operative site and the right atrium wherever the surgery allows; consider alternative positioning (prone, "park bench") instead of sitting when feasible.
  • Maintain adequate hydration rather than running the patient dry — hypovolemia lowers venous pressure and increases the gradient favoring air entrainment.
  • PEEP is a genuinely debated prevention strategy — raising CVP with PEEP (commonly cited around 10 cmH₂O) can reduce entrainment, but it also raises right atrial pressure and can promote paradoxical embolism across a PFO by reversing the normal left-to-right pressure gradient. Weigh this specifically in any patient with a known or unexcluded shunt.

rows: Clinically significant VAE incidence, sitting neurosurgery
Detects as little as ~0.02–0.05 mL/kg of entrained air
~1 cm past the SVC–right atrial junction
PEEP level sometimes used for prevention
~10 cmH₂O — weigh against paradoxical embolism risk in unexcluded PFO

blocks.html:
Why the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus + Trendelenburg) works: the right ventricular outflow tract sits anteriorly and superiorly relative to the RV apex. Positioning the heart so entrained air rises toward the apex, away from the outflow tract, prevents the air from forming a discrete "lock" that mechanically blocks forward flow into the pulmonary artery — buying time for the air to be aspirated or gradually absorbed rather than causing acute obstructive shock.

Why nitrous oxide is stopped immediately: N₂O is far more soluble in blood than nitrogen and diffuses into any existing gas bubble faster than nitrogen diffuses out, physically enlarging the embolus at exactly the moment you're trying to shrink the problem, not grow it.

Why the catheter tip location matters so specifically: air rising through the venous system tends to collect near the SVC-right atrial junction before it disperses further into the right heart — positioning the aspiration port right at that anatomic collection point gives the best chance of pulling out a meaningful volume of air rather than blood alone.

Why PEEP is a genuine double-edged sword: raising intrathoracic and right atrial pressure reduces the pressure gradient that draws air in at the surgical site — helpful for prevention. But if a patient has an unrecognized PFO, that same elevated right atrial pressure can exceed left atrial pressure and drive venous air directly into the systemic (arterial) circulation — a paradoxical embolism with stroke-level consequences. This is exactly why preoperative shunt screening changes the calculus before, not after, choosing PEEP as a prevention strategy.

Why chest compressions help even though this isn't a primary cardiac arrest: VAE causes obstructive shock — the heart itself is often mechanically fine, but forward flow is blocked by the air lock. Compressions provide mechanical agitation that can help disperse a discrete air lock in addition to their usual role generating forward circulation, which is why CPR remains appropriate even when the underlying problem is obstruction rather than a primary rhythm or pump failure.

rows: No positional/surgical-site risk pattern tied to timing; Doppler tone change and correlation with a specific surgical maneuver (bone drilling, sinus opening) point toward VAE instead.
Skin/systemic features and a temporal link to a drug administration rather than a surgical positioning/site event; VAE has no allergic component.
ECG changes are ischemic-pattern rather than the right-heart-strain pattern (RBBB, ST changes) seen in VAE; troponin rises, unlike VAE.
Unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, rising peak airway pressures — a distinct mechanical picture from the Doppler/EtCO₂ pattern of VAE.
Tachycardia and hypotension without the characteristic EtCO₂ drop or Doppler changes; visible surgical field blood loss usually points the diagnosis the right direction.

Coagulopathy and DIC-driven features develop; VAE during cesarean section is actually more common than historically appreciated and can look similar early on — Doppler/EtCO₂ monitoring, when used, helps distinguish the two.

Same obstructive-shock mechanism as VAE, but CO₂ is far more soluble and typically better tolerated in smaller volumes — management overlaps heavily (stop insufflation, position, support), so distinguishing the exact gas matters less acutely than recognizing the obstructive picture itself.

blocks.html:
After stabilization: echocardiography (TTE or TEE) to look for residual intracardiac air and to evaluate for a previously unrecognized PFO, especially if there was any neurologic deficit suggesting a paradoxical arterial component.

Watch for delayed pulmonary edema: case reports describe non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema developing after an otherwise well-managed VAE, in some cases resolving only after roughly a week of supportive care — don't consider the event fully closed once initial hemodynamics normalize.

Neurologic evaluation: if there's any suspicion of paradoxical (arterial) embolism — new focal deficit, altered consciousness disproportionate to the hemodynamic picture, visual symptoms — imaging (CT/MRI) and consideration of hyperbaric oxygen referral.

Disposition: ICU-level monitoring for any clinically significant VAE, given the risk of delayed pulmonary edema, ongoing hemodynamic instability, and the need to complete a shunt/paradoxical-embolism workup.

Documentation and future planning: record the surgical maneuver associated with onset, monitoring modality that detected it, and interventions used — this directly informs whether the same patient can safely undergo the same position/approach again, and whether PFO screening changes the plan.

badges.text: COMPRESSIONS AND SHOCKS ARE THE HIGHEST-VALUE ACTIONS

sections.title: The Circular Algorithm
sections.tagline: Compressions and defibrillation are the highest-value actions in the whole algorithm — everything else is built around minimizing interruptions to them.

steps.title: Start high-quality CPR immediately, attach the monitor/defibrillator
steps.html: Begin compressions before the monitor is even on. Check rhythm as soon as available.

steps.title: Shockable (VF/pVT) — shock immediately, then resume CPR with minimal pause
steps.html: Single-shock approach preferred over stacked shocks. Prefer biphasic waveform. Use the device's recommended energy, escalating for later shocks if the defibrillator supports it. CPR for 2 minutes, then recheck rhythm.

steps.title: Non-shockable (asystole/PEA) — epinephrine as soon as feasible
steps.html: Give the first dose of epinephrine as early as possible in non-shockable rhythms — this is a specific 2025 emphasis point, distinct from the shockable pathway.

steps.title: Shockable — give epinephrine after initial defibrillation attempts fail
steps.html: The updated 2025 sequencing: prioritize rapid defibrillation over medication for shockable rhythms — epinephrine follows once shocks alone haven't converted the rhythm, commonly after the second shock.

steps.title: Continue epinephrine every 3–5 minutes throughout
steps.html: 1 mg IV/IO, regardless of rhythm, once the pathway-specific timing above has been triggered.

steps.title: Refractory VF/pVT after the third shock — add an antiarrhythmic
steps.html: Amiodarone or lidocaine — see Numbers to Know for dosing. Neither is clearly favored over the other in current guidance; choose based on availability and institutional protocol.

steps.title: Actively search for and treat reversible causes throughout — don't wait for a lull
steps.html: The H's and T's aren't a checklist to run once things stall; they're a live differential to be working through continuously, especially in PEA and asystole where there's no shockable rhythm to anchor on. See the dedicated table below with links to full crisis files.

steps.title: Consider advanced airway and capnography without delaying compressions
steps.html: Airway placement should never come at the cost of compression quality or timing. Waveform capnography helps confirm placement, monitor CPR quality, and detect ROSC (a sustained PETCO₂ jump >25 mmHg, or >40 mmHg, suggests ROSC).

blocks.title: The "don't give this routinely" list — 2025 emphasis
blocks.html: Do not substitute or add vasopressin to epinephrine (no benefit). Do not use high-dose epinephrine routinely. Do not give calcium, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium, or steroids routinely during undifferentiated arrest — each has a role, but only for a specific indication (see Numbers to Know), not as a default add-on.

ACLS is the general-purpose algorithm for adult cardiac arrest — a cycle-based approach combining high-quality CPR, timely defibrillation for shockable rhythms, epinephrine, and a continuous search for reversible causes. The 2025 AHA update kept the overall structure stable while sharpening specifics: earlier epinephrine in non-shockable rhythms, epinephrine deliberately delayed until after initial defibrillation in shockable rhythms, and a clearer "don't add extras without a specific indication" stance on calcium, bicarbonate, magnesium, and steroids.

This file is the algorithm skeleton the rest of this crisis series plugs into. Where a trigger-specific pathway diverges meaningfully from standard ACLS — LAST, MH, hyperkalemia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, PE, traumatic arrest, refractory VF/ECPR — that divergence is covered in its own dedicated file, cross-linked from the H's and T's table below rather than duplicated here.

sections.title: Shockable vs. Non-Shockable — The First Branch Point

rows: Shockable — immediate defibrillation, epinephrine after initial shocks fail, antiarrhythmic after 3 shocks if still refractory.
Non-shockable — no defibrillation; epinephrine as early as possible; CPR and reversible-cause search are the entire treatment.
Non-shockable — organized rhythm without a pulse; treatment is entirely dependent on identifying and fixing the underlying cause (see H's and T's below) — echo is invaluable here.
See the dedicated Refractory VF/pVT & ECPR crisis file for vector-change defibrillation, DSED, and early ECPR candidacy assessment.
A distinct entity from flatline asystole — consider emergency transcutaneous/transvenous pacing rather than the standard non-shockable pathway alone.

sections.title: CPR Quality Standards (In Place of "Room Setup")

blocks.html:
• Rate: 100–120 compressions per minute.
  • Depth: at least 2 inches (5 cm), up to 2.4 inches (6 cm).
  • Full chest recoil between compressions — leaning on the chest between compressions measurably reduces effectiveness.
  • Minimize interruptions — every pause reduces coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure, which then takes multiple subsequent compressions to rebuild.
  • Change compressor every 2 minutes, or sooner if fatigued — compression quality degrades with fatigue well before the compressor consciously feels tired.
  • Ventilation ratio: 30:2 without an advanced airway; 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) with continuous compressions once an advanced airway is placed. Avoid excessive ventilation — hyperventilation raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return.
  • IV access preferred over IO for drug delivery, though IO is reasonable if IV can't be obtained quickly without delaying other key interventions.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: The only vasopressor used in the algorithm; timing differs by pathway (see Treatment above).
300 mg IV/IO first dose; 150 mg second dose if VF/pVT persists
For refractory VF/pVT after 3 shocks. Do not use for torsades (worsens QT prolongation — see the Torsades crisis file).
1–1.5 mg/kg first dose; 0.5–0.75 mg/kg subsequent doses; max 3 mg/kg or 3 doses total
Reasonable alternative to amiodarone for refractory VF/pVT.
Hyperkalemia, CCB overdose, hypocalcemia, hypermagnesemia — see the Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest crisis file.
TCA overdose, severe hyperkalemia with documented acidosis. Not for presumed acidosis from arrest duration alone.
Torsades de pointes / suspected hypomagnesemia — see the Torsades crisis file for full dosing.
Only if opioid overdose is suspected as the cause of arrest.

blocks.html:
Why epinephrine timing now diverges by rhythm: in non-shockable rhythms, there's no competing intervention (no shock to prioritize) — early epinephrine gives the best chance of restoring perfusion, and pediatric data specifically shows shorter time-to-first-dose correlates with better outcomes. In shockable rhythms, the highest-value action is defibrillation itself; giving epinephrine first (or simultaneously) doesn't improve on rapid, uninterrupted shock delivery, and current evidence supports letting defibrillation attempts run their course first before adding the drug.

Why vasopressin was formally dropped: multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses consistently found no survival advantage for vasopressin alone or in combination with epinephrine — a rare case of a once-common ACLS drug being explicitly removed rather than just deprioritized, based on accumulated null results rather than new harm data.

Why calcium, bicarbonate, magnesium, and steroids are "not routine" rather than "never": each has a real, evidence-supported role in a specific reversible-cause scenario (hyperkalemia for calcium, TCA toxicity for bicarbonate, torsades for magnesium) but no demonstrated benefit — and some plausible harm — when given reflexively in undifferentiated arrest. This is the clearest expression of the "diagnosis-driven resuscitation" theme running through this whole crisis series: the same drug is right or wrong depending entirely on whether the specific indication is actually present.

Why the H's and T's search happens continuously, not as a fallback: in PEA and asystole specifically, there's no rhythm-based intervention (no shock) doing any of the work — the entire treatment is finding and fixing the actual cause. Treating the differential search as something to start only after "standard measures fail" wastes the exact window where a reversible cause is still reversible.

sections.title: The H's and T's — Linked to Full Crisis Files

headers: Where to go for the full workup
rows: See the Massive Transfusion Protocol and Traumatic Cardiac Arrest crisis files.
Airway-focused — see the Difficult/Failed Airway and Laryngospasm crisis files.
Rarely treated directly (see bicarbonate note above); address the underlying driver of the acidosis instead.
See the dedicated Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest crisis file.
Changes resuscitation duration and ECPR thresholds entirely — see the Refractory VF/pVT & ECPR crisis file for the hypothermia-specific exception.
See the dedicated Tension Pneumothorax crisis file.
See the dedicated Pericardial Tamponade crisis file.
LAST, MH, and specific overdose syndromes each have or will have their own crisis file — see LAST and Malignant Hyperthermia for the two currently live.
See the dedicated Peri-Arrest Pulmonary Embolism crisis file.
Treat as ACS once ROSC achieved; urgent coronary angiography per post-ROSC care below.

blocks.html:
Immediate targets: MAP ≥65 mmHg (fluids first, then vasopressor infusion if needed), PaCO₂ 35–40 mmHg avoiding both hyper- and hypoventilation, SpO₂ 90–98% using the lowest FiO₂ that achieves it.

12-lead ECG and continuous monitoring to assess for STEMI; urgent coronary angiography with transfer to a cath-capable facility if indicated.

Continue searching for and treating reversible causes in the post-ROSC window — hypovolemia, hypoxia, acidosis, electrolyte derangement, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, and thrombosis all remain relevant after circulation returns, not just during the arrest.

Targeted temperature management per standard post-arrest protocol.

Disposition: ICU admission is standard for any resuscitated arrest, with close coordination between the resuscitation team and ICU on ongoing management. Institutions should have a standard of care in place to evaluate cardiac arrest survivors — including those unlikely to have a favorable outcome — for organ donation potential, per the 2025 update's new Class 1 recommendation, and to provide ongoing disability support for survivors.

protocols.title: Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Electrolyte
protocols.subtitle: Calcium doesn't lower potassium — it buys the 20–30 minutes the shifting therapies need to work. ROSC here comes from correcting the potassium, not from more epinephrine.

badges.text: DON'T WAIT FOR THE LAB VALUE

protocols.description: Calcium-shift-eliminate sequence, why arrest duration should be longer here, insulin-before-albuterol ordering. ILCOR 2025/AHA-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Standard ACLS runs in parallel, but the actual path to ROSC here is stabilizing the membrane and correcting the potassium — plan for a longer resuscitation than usual.

steps.title: Calcium chloride immediately — don't wait for lab confirmation
steps.html: 1 g IV (10 mL of 10% solution) through a well-running peripheral line or central line. If hyperkalemia is clinically suspected (dialysis patient, renal failure, crush injury, known history) with arrest or malignant ECG findings, give it on suspicion — repeat every 5 minutes until the QRS narrows or ECG changes resolve.

steps.title: Insulin plus dextrose — the most reliable shifting agent
steps.html: Regular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose 25 g (50 mL of D50W) if the patient isn't already hyperglycemic. This is the single most potent, most evidence-supported intervention for actually lowering serum potassium acutely — expect a drop of roughly 0.5–1.5 mEq/L over 15–60 minutes.

steps.title: Nebulized albuterol — after insulin/glucose, not before
steps.html: 10–20 mg nebulized (far above a standard bronchodilator dose) as an additive shifting agent. Give it after insulin/glucose — a beta-agonist given first, before the insulin effect is underway, can transiently worsen serum potassium in some patients.

steps.title: Sodium bicarbonate — situational, not routine
steps.html: 50–100 mEq IV if concurrent metabolic acidosis is documented or strongly suspected. Do not give bicarbonate reflexively just because an arrest has been prolonged and acidosis is presumed — that specific practice has no proven benefit and can worsen intracellular acidosis.

steps.title: Continue standard ACLS in parallel — but expect a longer code
steps.html: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes per standard protocol, defibrillation for shockable rhythms. Continue high-quality CPR until the hyperkalemia is actually corrected — this may take considerably longer than a typical resuscitation, and ROSC when it occurs will be driven primarily by calcium's membrane-stabilizing effect and the shifting agents, not by additional epinephrine.

steps.title: Activate emergency dialysis
steps.html: The only intervention that actually removes potassium from the body rather than shifting or buffering it. Involve nephrology immediately in any known or suspected renal failure patient — this is the definitive fix everything else is bridging toward.

steps.title: Reassess and redose calcium as needed
steps.html: Calcium's stabilizing effect wears off in roughly 20–30 minutes (up to an hour by some estimates) — if ECG changes recur or the QRS re-widens, redose rather than assuming a single dose was sufficient for the duration of the resuscitation.

steps.title: Suspected digoxin toxicity — avoid calcium
steps.html: If digitalis toxicity is a concern, avoid calcium (historically linked to a "stone heart" phenomenon in this specific combination) and use magnesium sulfate 2 g over 5 minutes instead for arrhythmias in this setting.

blocks.title: Treat the ECG and the clinical picture, not just a lab number
blocks.html: A prior blood gas, known dialysis status, or crush injury mechanism is enough to start treatment before a confirmatory potassium level returns. Waiting for lab confirmation in a patient with malignant ECG changes or arrest wastes the exact minutes the myocardium doesn't have.

Hyperkalemia is defined as serum potassium above roughly 5.0–5.5 mEq/L, present in about 2% of hospitalized patients. Mild elevation is usually asymptomatic; severe elevation (commonly cited around 6.5–7 mEq/L or higher, especially with an acute rate of rise) narrows the gap between resting and threshold membrane potential in cardiac myocytes, slowing conduction and predisposing to life-threatening arrhythmias, including cardiac arrest.

Common causes include chronic kidney disease or acute kidney injury with impaired excretion, medications (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics), cellular potassium release (burns, hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis), acidosis-driven extracellular shift, and endocrine causes such as adrenal insufficiency. Cardiac arrest from hyperkalemia is one of the few arrest etiologies where the underlying cause is both rapidly identifiable and directly, pharmacologically reversible — which is exactly why it gets its own dedicated management pathway distinct from standard ACLS.

sections.title: ECG Progression (In Place of "Signs and Symptoms")

rows: Peaked, narrow-based T waves — often the first visible change.
PR interval prolongation, flattened or absent P waves.
QRS widening — a key treatment target; calcium redosing is often guided by watching this narrow back down.
Sine wave pattern — QRS and T wave merging into a smooth, undulating waveform. A harbinger of imminent VF or asystole.
Weakness, paresthesias, areflexia, ascending paralysis — can precede cardiac findings and is easy to miss if the presentation is mistaken for another neurologic process.

blocks.html: ECG severity doesn't track cleanly with the absolute potassium number. Some patients with dramatic lab values show minimal ECG change, while others decompensate at more moderate levels — treat the ECG and clinical trajectory in front of you, not a number in isolation.

• Point-of-care potassium testing availability for dialysis patients, renal failure patients, or anyone with a mechanism (crush injury, burns, rhabdomyolysis) that predisposes to rapid hyperkalemia.
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring for any patient with known or suspected hyperkalemia, even before ECG changes are visible.
  • Avoid succinylcholine in patients with renal failure, burns, prolonged immobility, or other conditions predisposing to an exaggerated hyperkalemic response — see the Difficult/Failed Airway and general anesthesia-specific crisis files for related detail.
  • Medication review in at-risk patients (ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, potassium supplements) — identifying and holding contributing medications is part of both prevention and ongoing management.
  • Have calcium chloride, insulin, dextrose, and albuterol immediately accessible in any unit managing dialysis or renal failure patients regularly, rather than treating this as a rare-event kit to be located under pressure.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: ~6.5–7 mEq/L or higher, especially with acute rise
1 g IV (10 mL of 10%), repeat q5min as needed
10 units IV + 25 g dextrose (50 mL D50W)
50–100 mEq IV, only with documented/suspected concurrent acidosis
Every 30–60 minutes for at least 4–6 hours (delayed hypoglycemia risk)

blocks.html:
Why calcium is given first despite not lowering potassium at all: hyperkalemia narrows the gap between a myocyte's resting membrane potential and its threshold potential, making the cell dangerously easy to depolarize inappropriately. Calcium raises that threshold back toward normal, directly counteracting the arrhythmogenic mechanism within minutes — independent of, and much faster than, anything that actually changes the serum potassium level. It's cardiac membrane protection, not potassium treatment, which is exactly why it has to be paired with a shifting agent rather than used alone.

Why the COCA trial's findings on calcium don't overturn this specific indication: recent evidence (including a 2021 trial and a 2025 systematic review) has questioned routine calcium administration in undifferentiated cardiac arrest, with some data suggesting possible harm. That evidence base is about calcium given empirically in arrests of unknown cause — the hyperkalemia-specific indication, where a clear mechanistic rationale and consistent clinical experience support rapid ECG improvement, remains distinct and is why expert guidance continues to favor calcium specifically when hyperkalemia is the suspected or confirmed driver.

Why insulin/glucose is the preferred shifting agent over albuterol alone: insulin directly stimulates the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, driving potassium into cells through the same mechanism the body normally uses — it's more potent and more predictable than beta-agonism alone. Albuterol works through a related but weaker pathway and requires a much larger-than-bronchodilator dose to have a meaningful potassium-shifting effect, which is why it's used as an addition to, not a substitute for, insulin/glucose.

Why albuterol specifically follows insulin rather than preceding it: beta-agonist stimulation can transiently increase serum potassium before its shifting effect takes hold, related to an initial catecholamine-driven potassium efflux. Giving it after insulin/glucose is already underway avoids stacking a transient worsening on top of a still-elevated potassium level during the most dangerous part of the timeline.

Why the resuscitation should run longer than a typical arrest: in most cardiac arrests, prolonged CPR without ROSC signals a poor trajectory. In hyperkalemic arrest specifically, the underlying cause is actively being corrected in real time by calcium, insulin/glucose, and (if activated) dialysis — ROSC is expected to follow correction of the potassium, not simply more time or more epinephrine. This is the clearest example in this crisis series of why "diagnosis-driven" resuscitation (see the Perioperative Cardiac Arrest file) changes not just the drugs given but the entire decision about how long to continue.

rows: Sodium channel blocker toxicity (TCA, cocaine, other)

Also produces QRS widening, but the mechanism and treatment differ — sodium bicarbonate is central to management here (not just situational), and calcium's role is different; history of ingestion/exposure is the key clue.
Can independently prolong QT and predispose to arrhythmia; check ionized calcium directly rather than assuming hyperkalemia explains all ECG changes.
Can cause bradyarrhythmias and conduction delay; often coexists with renal failure and hyperkalemia, so consider checking magnesium in the same patient population.
Can present with hyperkalemia (in acute toxicity) but changes the treatment approach — avoid calcium, treat arrhythmias with magnesium, and consider digoxin-specific antibody fragments.

Artificially elevated lab value from a hemolyzed sample or severe leukocytosis/thrombocytosis — send a repeat, non-hemolyzed sample once treatment is underway, but don't delay treatment for confirmation if the ECG and clinical picture already support true hyperkalemia.
Hyperacute T waves from early STEMI
Can superficially resemble the peaked T waves of hyperkalemia; look for reciprocal changes, regional distribution, and clinical context (chest pain, risk factors) to distinguish.

blocks.html:
Confirm and trend: a repeat, non-hemolyzed potassium level, along with glucose, renal function, and an ABG/VBG for acid-base status. Recheck potassium at defined intervals (commonly around 1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 hours) after treatment to confirm the trajectory and catch rebound as insulin's effect wears off (typically 2–4 hours).

Glucose monitoring: finger-stick glucose every 30–60 minutes for at least 4–6 hours post-insulin, given the well-documented risk of delayed hypoglycemia.

Identify and treat the underlying cause: renal function assessment, medication reconciliation (hold ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, potassium supplements), and workup for rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, or endocrine causes as clinically indicated.

Definitive potassium removal: dialysis remains the definitive treatment for refractory or renal-failure-associated hyperkalemia; potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) or diuretics may have a role in less acute management but shouldn't be relied on for the acute, arrest-level presentation.

Disposition: ICU admission for any patient who arrested or had malignant ECG changes from hyperkalemia, with continuous cardiac monitoring until the potassium is clearly trending down and stable.

protocols.title: Peri-Arrest Pulmonary Embolism
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Obstructive Shock
protocols.subtitle: Full-dose thrombolysis in arrest, half-dose otherwise — why ongoing CPR isn't a contraindication to lysis, and why the evidence supporting this is honestly weaker than the confidence with which it's practiced.

badges.text: ONGOING CPR IS NOT A LYSIS CONTRAINDICATION

protocols.description: Full-dose lysis in arrest vs. half-dose peri-arrest, echo-guided redosing, why CPR isn't a contraindication. 2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: The dosing calculus flips between peri-arrest and true arrest — know which one you're in before you draw up the drug.

steps.title: Cardiac arrest with suspected/known PE as the cause — full-dose systemic thrombolysis
steps.html: Continue high-quality CPR and give thrombolytics without delay. The most consistently applied regimen is alteplase (tPA) 50 mg IV bolus. Ongoing CPR is not a contraindication — international resuscitation guidance is explicit that compressions should continue through and after administration.

steps.title: Peri-arrest (not yet arrested), high-risk PE with cardiogenic shock — half-dose thrombolysis preferred when no absolute contraindication
steps.html: Half-dose alteplase: 0.5 mg/kg (max 50 mg) — 10–20 mg bolus, remainder infused over 2 hours. Half-dose tenecteplase: 0.25 mg/kg single bolus (max 25 mg). Systemic thrombolytics are favored over catheter-based options specifically in the peri-arrest patient with no absolute contraindication, given the time-critical nature.

steps.title: Guide redosing with bedside echocardiography
steps.html: If ROSC is achieved but right ventricular dysfunction persists on echo, a second bolus (case reports describe a repeat 50 mg alteplase dose roughly 20 minutes after the first) has been used successfully to address ongoing clot burden — let the echo, not a fixed protocol alone, guide whether more is needed.

steps.title: Continue CPR for an extended period after thrombolysis
steps.html: The drug needs time to work — hemodynamic improvement may not be immediate. There's no firm consensus duration in the literature, but extending resuscitation efforts well beyond a typical arrest timeline (commonly practiced in the 60–90 minute range post-lytic) before considering termination is standard practice specifically because of this delayed-effect pharmacology.

steps.title: Consider nebulized pulmonary vasodilators as an adjunct
steps.html: Nebulized nitroglycerin (50 mg/50 mL, 5 mL nebulized over 15 min) or nebulized milrinone (10 mg/mL, 5 mL over 15 min) have been used in cardiac arrest and peri-arrest PE based on limited data — reasonable adjuncts, not a substitute for thrombolysis or definitive therapy.

steps.title: Escalate to mechanical/surgical options if thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated
steps.html: Aspiration/mechanical thrombectomy, surgical embolectomy, or VA-ECMO as a bridge — all documented rescue options in refractory cases, particularly when a contraindication (e.g., recent major surgery, active bleeding) rules out lysis.

steps.title: Activate a Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) if available
steps.html: Now a Class 1 recommendation in the 2026 AHA/ACC guideline specifically to improve timeliness of care — involve them early rather than after initial stabilization attempts have already run their course.

blocks.title: The evidence is honestly weaker than the confidence it's given
blocks.html: ILCOR's 2020 consensus lists thrombolysis for suspected PE-caused arrest as a weak recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. A large blinded RCT of rescue thrombolysis in undifferentiated PEA arrest showed no benefit — but PE-specific registries and case series suggest real benefit when the diagnosis is genuinely likely. The practice is followed because the alternative, in a patient who is otherwise going to die, carries little additional downside — not because the evidence is strong.

Acute pulmonary embolism causes a sudden rise in pulmonary vascular resistance, producing right ventricular pressure overload, dilation, and impaired systolic function. The failing right ventricle reduces left ventricular filling (via septal shift and reduced venous return through the pulmonary circuit), causing a fall in cardiac output that can progress to cardiogenic/obstructive shock and cardiac arrest — most commonly presenting as pulseless electrical activity.

The first dedicated AHA/ACC clinical practice guideline for acute PE (2026) replaces the older, blunt "massive/submassive" terminology with a new A-through-E severity classification based on the most severe clinical, laboratory, and imaging finding — Category E1 (cardiopulmonary failure with recurrent or persistent hypotension/cardiogenic shock) corresponds roughly to the old "massive" category and carries a Class 2a recommendation for systemic thrombolysis; Category D represents incipient cardiopulmonary failure. PE is estimated to be a contributing cause in a meaningful share of cardiac arrests overall, alongside acute MI.

rows: Pulseless electrical activity as the initial rhythm
The dominant presentation in PE-caused arrest across multiple case series (roughly 78–83% of cases) — a strong pattern-recognition clue even before imaging.

Suggests massive PE specifically — with pulmonary blood flow obstructed, little CO₂ reaches the alveoli regardless of ventilation quality, producing a disproportionately low reading relative to compression quality.
A supportive finding, but its absence doesn't reliably exclude PE — one case series specifically noted the absence of RV dilation "argued against, but not conclusively" the diagnosis.
Classic but insensitive; useful when present, not reliable enough to exclude PE when absent.

Recent surgery, prolonged immobilization, active malignancy, known hypercoagulable state, or recent long-bone fracture (cross-reference the Fat Embolism differential) — all raise pretest probability significantly when arrest occurs in this context.
Sudden collapse with a preceding history of dyspnea, pleuritic pain, or leg swelling
When collateral history is available (family, EMS report), these are the classic pre-arrest PE symptoms.

blocks.html:
• Have a thrombolytic immediately accessible in any resuscitation area — the time to locate and reconstitute the drug is time the patient doesn't have once arrest occurs.
  • Bedside echo capability for real-time diagnostic support and to guide redosing decisions after an initial bolus.
  • Know your institution's PERT activation pathway before you need it — a Class 1 recommendation now, meaning this should be a routine reflex for high-risk PE, not a rare escalation.
  • Label thrombolytic doses clearly for indication — institutions using tenecteplase across stroke, STEMI, and PE indications benefit from clear dose labeling on the drug itself, since the correct dose varies meaningfully by indication and getting it wrong under pressure is a real risk.
  • Identify high-risk patients proactively — recent surgery, malignancy, prolonged immobilization — so that a sudden collapse in this population triggers PE-specific suspicion immediately rather than defaulting to a generic arrest workup.

rows: 50 mg IV bolus, most consistently applied regimen
0.5 mg/kg (max 50 mg): 10–20 mg bolus + remainder over 2 hours
Repeat-bolus interval described in case reports
~20 minutes after first dose, guided by persistent RV dysfunction on echo
PEA as initial rhythm in PE-caused arrest
Only ~1/3 of eligible high-risk PE patients actually receive systemic thrombolytics
Observational data — a real, documented care gap
2026 AHA/ACC classification for full-dose lysis recommendation (Class 2a)
Major bleeding rates in arrest-thrombolysis series
Roughly 10–25% across reported case series — real, but weighed against near-certain mortality without intervention

blocks.html:
Why the dose flips from half to full between peri-arrest and true arrest: half-dose regimens exist specifically to reduce bleeding risk in a patient who is still perfusing and has time for a more conservative approach. Once circulation has actually stopped, the calculus changes entirely — the patient is going to die imminently without rapid, maximal clot dissolution, and the marginal bleeding risk of a full dose becomes a secondary concern relative to the near-certainty of death without aggressive intervention.

Why ongoing CPR isn't a contraindication to giving the drug: a natural instinct is to worry that chest compressions during or after thrombolysis increase bleeding or trauma risk. Current resuscitation guidance explicitly rejects this concern for PE-suspected arrest — compressions may even mechanically help fragment and distribute the thrombus, and stopping CPR to "protect" against a theoretical bleeding risk guarantees the more immediate risk of death from ongoing circulatory arrest.

Why extended CPR duration after thrombolysis is standard practice despite no formal consensus number: thrombolytic drugs take time to actually dissolve the obstructing clot and restore pulmonary blood flow — a resuscitation that looks unsuccessful in the first several minutes after the bolus may simply not have had enough time yet. This is conceptually similar to hyperkalemic arrest (see that crisis file): the underlying cause is being actively treated in real time, which justifies continuing well past when a typical arrest would prompt termination.

Why the negative TROICA trial result doesn't overturn the PE-specific approach: TROICA tested rescue thrombolysis in undifferentiated PEA arrest of unknown cause — a population where the large majority didn't actually have PE, diluting any true PE-specific benefit into statistical noise. Subsequent registries and case series specifically selecting patients with known or strongly suspected PE (like the French National Cardiac Arrest Registry) show a real survival signal. The lesson isn't "thrombolysis doesn't work for arrest" — it's that diagnostic specificity is what determines whether the intervention actually helps, which is exactly the diagnosis-driven framing this whole crisis series is built around.

Why bedside echo drives redosing rather than a fixed protocol: a single 50 mg bolus dissolves a variable amount of thrombus depending on clot burden and time since embolization — persistent RV dysfunction after apparent ROSC is direct evidence that meaningful obstruction remains, which is a more physiologically grounded trigger for a second dose than an arbitrary fixed-protocol cutoff.

rows: Focal regional wall motion abnormality on echo rather than the global RV strain/dilation pattern of PE; troponin and ECG changes point toward coronary occlusion; treated with reperfusion (PCI/thrombolysis for STEMI) rather than PE-specific dosing.
Unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation — a mechanical rather than embolic obstructive process; see the dedicated Tension Pneumothorax crisis file.
Pericardial effusion with chamber compression on echo rather than isolated RV strain; see the dedicated Tamponade crisis file.
Collapsed, not distended, cardiac chambers on echo; look for an obvious bleeding source.
DIC-driven coagulopathy and a peripartum clinical context distinguish this from thrombotic PE, though both can present with sudden collapse and obstructive-shock physiology.
Skin findings and a clear temporal trigger (drug, exposure) point away from PE; treated with epinephrine, not thrombolysis.

blocks.html:
Confirm once stabilized: CT pulmonary angiography as soon as the patient is stable enough to transport, since thrombolysis in the acute setting is typically given on clinical/echo suspicion rather than confirmed imaging.

Anticoagulation after thrombolysis: transition to a heparin infusion for ongoing anticoagulation once the acute lytic phase is complete, per standard PE management principles.

Monitor for bleeding: close neurologic and hemodynamic monitoring for the bleeding complications inherent to thrombolytic therapy, particularly intracranial hemorrhage.

Escalation if incomplete response: catheter-directed therapy, mechanical thrombectomy, or surgical embolectomy for persistent right heart strain or hemodynamic compromise despite systemic lysis — increasingly available and structured under the 2026 guideline's risk-stratified framework.

Disposition: ICU admission for any patient post-arrest or post-thrombolysis for PE, with PERT/multidisciplinary involvement continuing through the acute and subacute phases, including decisions about IVC filter placement if anticoagulation is later contraindicated.

protocols.title: Pericardial Tamponade
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Obstructive Shock
protocols.subtitle: Beck's triad is present in a minority of real cases — echo, not the classic exam, is what actually catches this. The "last-drop" pressure-volume curve is why you can't wait for hypotension to act.
protocols.description: Beck's triad present in only 10–40% of cases, "last-drop" pressure-volume curve, needle vs. surgical drainage decision. StatPearls/AMBOSS-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Drainage is the treatment — everything else is a bridge to get there. Route (needle vs. surgical) depends heavily on cause.

steps.title: Confirm with bedside echo, don't wait for the full clinical picture
steps.html: POCUS for pericardial effusion is highly sensitive and specific (96–100% in ED series). Suspect tamponade with hemodynamic instability plus any supportive finding — don't require the complete classic triad, which is frequently absent.

steps.title: Avoid positive-pressure ventilation and heavy sedation if at all possible
steps.html: Both reduce cardiac output and can precipitate acute decompensation in a patient already dependent on preload to overcome external compression. If intubation is unavoidable, anticipate hemodynamic collapse at induction and have pressors/drainage ready.

steps.title: IV fluids as a temporizing bridge, not a treatment
steps.html: Volume can transiently improve filling pressures and cardiac output while preparing for drainage — it does not fix the underlying compression and should not delay definitive intervention.

steps.title: Non-traumatic tamponade — echo-guided pericardiocentesis
steps.html: Target the largest, shallowest fluid pocket with no intervening vital structures, using low-depth sonographic views for needle guidance. Confirm intrapericardial catheter placement with agitated saline injection before proceeding to full drainage.

steps.title: Drain slowly
steps.html: Rapid, large-volume decompression risks pericardial decompression syndrome — remove fluid incrementally rather than all at once, especially in a large chronic effusion.

steps.title: Traumatic hemopericardium (penetrating injury) — surgery is preferred over needle
steps.html: Definitive management is a pericardial window or thoracotomy, not needle aspiration — clotted traumatic hemopericardium is a well-recognized cause of a falsely negative pericardiocentesis. Reserve needle drainage as a temporizing measure only when surgery isn't immediately available.

steps.title: Cardiac arrest from tamponade
steps.html: Emergency pericardiocentesis (or resuscitative thoracotomy in the trauma setting) is indicated without delay — there is no absolute contraindication to pericardiocentesis when obstructive shock from tamponade is the acute life threat.

steps.title: Consider a drain over single aspiration for ongoing/recurrent effusions
steps.html: Serous effusions typically require multiple days of drainage; a Seldinger-placed pigtail catheter left in place can avoid recurrent tamponade and repeat procedures — decide with cardiology input based on volume and etiology.

blocks.title: Don't wait for hypotension
blocks.html: Tamponade is a "last-drop" phenomenon — the pericardium sits on a steep pressure-volume curve where the final increment of fluid produces a disproportionate rise in intrapericardial pressure. Early recognition with echocardiography in a patient with dyspnea and tachycardia alone, before Beck's triad ever develops, can be lifesaving.

Cardiac tamponade results from pericardial fluid accumulating under pressure, impairing diastolic filling of all four cardiac chambers roughly equally, reducing cardiac output and precipitating obstructive shock. How much fluid it takes depends entirely on the rate of accumulation: a slowly developing chronic effusion (inflammatory, malignant, uremic) can stretch the pericardium to accommodate up to 2 liters before compromising output, while rapid accumulation — as with traumatic hemorrhage — can cause tamponade with as little as 150 mL.

Causes span infection, uremia, malignancy, autoimmune disease, post-myocardial infarction (free wall rupture), aortic dissection, and trauma — more often penetrating than blunt, since blunt chamber rupture is typically fatal before the patient reaches care. Tamponade is fundamentally a clinical-plus-imaging diagnosis: clinical findings alone are notoriously insensitive, which is why bedside echocardiography has become the primary diagnostic tool rather than an adjunct.

rows: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds)

Classically taught as diagnostic — actually present in only about 10–40% of real cases. A 2017 retrospective series of 150 confirmed pericardial effusion patients found zero with all three elements present. Don't wait for this to act.
The more common actual presentation — nonspecific enough to be mistaken for heart failure if echo isn't obtained.
Inspiratory drop in systolic BP >10 mmHg during normal breathing — a genuinely useful supportive sign, though still not universally present or easy to elicit under time pressure.
ECG: tachycardia, low-voltage QRS, electrical alternans

Tachycardia is the single most common ECG finding. The combination of tachycardia + low voltage + electrical alternans has a reported 100% positive predictive value for tamponade specifically in patients with known malignant pericardial effusion.
Sensitive finding, often appears before RV collapse as compression worsens.
Sensitive — a collapsible IVC (>50% collapse with sniffing or throughout the respiratory cycle) effectively argues against tamponade.
Invasive hemodynamics: equalization of diastolic pressures
CVP ≈ PAOP ≈ RAP converging to a similar value is the hemodynamic hallmark when invasive monitoring is in place — all four chambers are being compressed equally by the surrounding fluid.

blocks.html:
• POCUS availability and low threshold to use it in any patient with unexplained dyspnea, tachycardia, or hypotension, especially post-cardiac surgery, post-central-line placement, or with known malignancy/uremia/pericarditis.
  • Echo guidance (or fluoroscopy) for essentially every non-emergent pericardiocentesis — blind pericardiocentesis carries meaningfully higher complication risk and is reserved for true crash situations where imaging isn't immediately available.
  • Have a pericardiocentesis kit with agitated saline available for placement confirmation, plus a Seldinger/pigtail drain setup for cases likely to need extended drainage.
  • Minimize inspiratory pressures in any intubated patient with a known or suspected pericardial effusion — this is a direct extension of avoiding positive-pressure ventilation's preload-reducing effect wherever feasible.
  • Correct coagulopathy and anemia proactively before an elective/semi-urgent procedure when time allows, since bleeding risk is a real consideration for pericardiocentesis specifically.
  • For penetrating chest trauma with suspected hemopericardium, have the surgical team and OR readiness in place from the start rather than defaulting to a needle-first approach.

rows: Chronic effusion volume tolerated before tamponade
Acute/traumatic volume that can cause tamponade
Beck's triad prevalence in real cases
~10–40%; often described as rare to see all three together
PPV of tachycardia + low voltage + electrical alternans (malignant effusion)
Effusion size typically visible as enlarged cardiac silhouette on CXR

blocks.html:
Why the classic exam is so unreliable: Beck's triad describes end-stage findings that only become apparent once compensatory mechanisms (tachycardia, increased systemic vascular resistance) have already failed. Most patients present earlier in that compensated phase — dyspneic and tachycardic, but not yet hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled sounds — which is exactly why relying on the full triad before acting misses the window where intervention is easiest and safest.

Why positive-pressure ventilation is specifically dangerous here: tamponade physiology depends on adequate venous pressure to force blood into a heart being externally compressed — it's a preload-dependent state. Positive intrathoracic pressure from PPV directly opposes venous return at the exact moment the patient needs it most, which is why intubation in an unstable tamponade patient can precipitate immediate cardiovascular collapse rather than simply supporting oxygenation.

Why drainage speed matters (pericardial decompression syndrome): a heart that has adapted to chronic external compression can respond paradoxically when that compression is suddenly and completely relieved — some patients develop acute pulmonary edema or even cardiogenic shock in the aftermath of rapid, complete drainage. The exact mechanism isn't fully settled, but the clinical pattern is well-documented enough that incremental, monitored drainage is the standard approach for larger or chronic effusions rather than removing the entire volume at once.

Why traumatic hemopericardium gets treated surgically rather than by needle: blood in the traumatic setting clots relatively quickly within the pericardial space, and a needle aspirating through a clotted, organized hemopericardium frequently comes back falsely negative — giving false reassurance while the underlying compression persists. A surgical window or thoracotomy directly visualizes and definitively addresses the source, which is why needle aspiration is relegated to a bridging measure specifically when surgery isn't immediately accessible.

Why the "last-drop" framing matters clinically: the pericardial pressure-volume relationship is markedly nonlinear — early fluid accumulation is well tolerated as the pericardium stretches, but once that compliance reserve is exhausted, small additional volume increments produce disproportionately large pressure rises. This is the physiologic basis for why a patient can look reasonably stable and then decompensate rapidly with what seems like a minor further accumulation — the curve, not the absolute volume, is what determines when things turn critical.

rows: Unilateral markedly decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side — tamponade compresses all chambers/lung fields symmetrically, so breath sounds are typically equal bilaterally.
Acute right heart strain on echo without a pericardial effusion; risk factor profile and D-dimer/imaging point toward thromboembolic disease rather than pericardial fluid.

A chronic process with a different hemodynamic signature (Kussmaul's sign — JVP rising with inspiration — is more characteristic here); echo shows pericardial thickening/calcification rather than a large free-flowing effusion.
Regional wall motion abnormalities and ischemic ECG changes rather than the global chamber compression pattern of tamponade; troponin markedly elevated.
Collapsible IVC on POCUS (opposite of the plethoric, non-collapsible IVC typical of tamponade); no pericardial effusion on the same scan.

blocks.html:
Immediately post-procedure: repeat point-of-care echocardiography to document resolution of tamponade physiology, and check for lung sliding to rule out an iatrogenic pneumothorax from the procedure itself.

Fluid analysis: send drained pericardial fluid for chemical analysis, cytology, and culture as clinically indicated to work up the underlying etiology.

Drain vs. single aspiration: decide with cardiology input based on total volume removed and suspected cause — serous/malignant effusions often benefit from an indwelling drain over several days rather than a single tap.

Disposition: ICU admission for any patient who required emergency pericardiocentesis, with cardiothoracic surgery involvement for any traumatic or recurrent case.

Address the underlying cause: definitive management ultimately depends on the etiology — malignancy, uremia, infection, autoimmune disease, or a surgical/traumatic source each need their own directed workup and treatment beyond the acute drainage itself.

protocols.title: Perioperative Cardiac Arrest
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Perioperative
protocols.subtitle: Witnessed, monitored, and usually reversible — why the PeRLS 2025 guideline treats this as a diagnosis-driven discipline rather than a straight ACLS algorithm, and why the OR-specific reversible-causes list looks nothing like the standard H's and T's.
protocols.description: PeRLS 2025-aligned, OR-specific reversible causes in place of the standard H's and T's, early ECMO escalation, rhythm-specific notes.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Start the ACLS backbone immediately, but pivot fast to the OR-specific cause — you likely already know, or can quickly find, why this patient just arrested.

steps.title: Declare the arrest, call for help, start CPR
steps.html: High-quality chest compressions immediately. Call for additional anesthesia/surgical/nursing help and the code cart. Note the exact time — OR arrests are almost always witnessed, which is an advantage over community arrest that should translate to faster intervention.

steps.title: Shockable rhythm — defibrillate immediately
steps.html: VF or pulseless VT: immediate defibrillation, no delay for further workup first. This is a strong recommendation independent of suspected cause.

steps.title: Asystole with P-waves — consider emergency pacing
steps.html: A distinct scenario from flatline asystole; temporary pacing is specifically indicated here rather than proceeding straight through the standard non-shockable pathway.

steps.title: Immediately consider what was happening in the room right before the arrest
steps.html: Recent drug given (NMBA, antibiotic, LA)? Blood product running? Position change or insufflation just started? Central line just placed? Succinylcholine given to a patient with occult neuromuscular disease? This context, unavailable in a community arrest, is the single biggest advantage the perioperative setting has — use it.

steps.title: Empirically treat for hyperkalemia early if the cause is unclear
steps.html: Calcium chloride/gluconate, insulin/dextrose, hyperventilation, bicarbonate — hyperkalemia is common enough and rapidly treatable enough in the OR (transfusion, succinylcholine, renal failure, crush injury) that empiric treatment while the workup continues is reasonable rather than waiting for a potassium level.

steps.title: Use echocardiography (TTE/TEE) to work up PEA
steps.html: Especially valuable for pulseless electrical activity — directly visualizing a distended right ventricle (PE, tension physiology), tamponade, hypovolemia, or a hypocontractile heart focuses resuscitation on the actual mechanism rather than working through a generic differential blindly.

steps.title: Match the antidote to the trigger — don't default to standard ACLS dosing
steps.html: LAST-triggered arrest: reduced epinephrine (≤1 mcg/kg, not standard 1 mg boluses) plus lipid emulsion — repeated full-dose epinephrine measurably worsens lipid emulsion's effectiveness. MH-triggered arrest: dantrolene is the priority alongside CPR. Anaphylaxis: epinephrine at anaphylaxis dosing. See each respective crisis file for full detail — the point here is recognizing that standard ACLS pharmacology can be actively wrong for several OR-specific triggers.

steps.title: Refractory arrest — escalate to ECMO/CPB early, not late
steps.html: If a reversible cause is identified or suspected and standard measures aren't working within several minutes, involve a cardiac surgery/ECMO team early. Perioperative ECPR series report survival to discharge around 57.6% — substantially better than traditional CPR outcomes — which supports earlier rather than later escalation when support is available. Intraoperative thrombolysis is a reasonable consideration specifically for suspected massive PE, weighed against surgical bleeding risk.

blocks.title: The reversible-causes list here isn't the standard H's and T's
blocks.html: Community/ward arrests draw on a generic differential. The OR has its own dominant causes — hemorrhage, gas embolism, hyperkalemia, LAST, MH, anaphylaxis, high spinal, vagal reflex from surgical stimulation — and the PeRLS 2025 guideline explicitly frames this as reason to move away from a one-size-fits-all ACLS protocol toward diagnosis-driven resuscitation.

Perioperative cardiac arrest has an incidence of roughly 2–13 per 10,000 anesthetics, with mortality before hospital discharge ranging from 32–75% depending on the population and cause. It differs fundamentally from out-of-hospital or ward cardiac arrest: OR arrests are almost always witnessed, occur under continuous invasive monitoring, involve trained anesthesia/surgical staff already at the bedside, and frequently have an identifiable, immediately treatable cause — because the team usually knows exactly what was happening in the room in the moments before the arrest.

The 2025 Perioperative Resuscitation and Life Support (PeRLS) guideline — the third iteration of this evolving guidance, published in Anesthesiology — explicitly reframes perioperative arrest as a diagnosis-driven discipline rather than a straightforward extension of community ACLS. Standard ACLS was developed primarily for out-of-hospital and general in-hospital arrest, and several of its default assumptions (standard epinephrine dosing, generic reversible-causes search) can be actively counterproductive for OR-specific triggers like LAST or MH.

sections.title: OR-Specific Reversible Causes (In Place of Generic H's and T's)

rows: Surgical bleeding, often the leading cause in OR arrests — activate MTP alongside resuscitation.
Rapid transfusion, succinylcholine (especially undiagnosed neuromuscular disease/burns/immobility), renal failure, crush injury, tumor lysis.
Sitting craniotomy, laparoscopic insufflation, any open venous site above heart level — see the dedicated VAE crisis file.
Recent regional block or large-volume LA administration — CNS prodrome may have preceded the arrest.
Recent volatile agent/succinylcholine exposure, rising ETCO₂ and temperature preceding collapse.
Recent NMBA, antibiotic, chlorhexidine, or blood product exposure; sudden pressor-refractory hypotension ± rising airway pressures.
Recent central line placement, positive-pressure ventilation, thoracic/upper abdominal surgery.
Recent cardiac/thoracic procedure, central line placement, or penetrating trauma.
Peritoneal insufflation, bowel/mesenteric traction, oculocardiac reflex during ophthalmic/strabismus surgery — often bradycardia-predominant and atropine-responsive.
Check delivered concentrations and pump function — profound bradycardia/hypotension from anesthetic depth is reversible by simply lightening the anesthetic.
Hypoxia, acidosis, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, pulmonary/coronary thrombosis remain relevant — the OR-specific list above is additive, not a replacement.

blocks.html:
• Continuous invasive monitoring is already the OR's built-in advantage — leverage it. A sudden EtCO₂ drop, arterial line waveform change, or arrhythmia on the monitor often gives earlier warning than a community arrest ever could.
  • Have a cognitive aid immediately accessible (e.g., Stanford Emergency Manual / Cognitive Aids for Perioperative Crisis) — under the stress of a real arrest, a structured checklist measurably improves adherence to the right sequence of steps.
  • Know your institution's ECMO/CPB activation pathway before you need it — who to call, how fast a team can mobilize, and what criteria trigger the call. This is not something to figure out mid-arrest.
  • Stock and know the location of trigger-specific rescue kits — MH cart with dantrolene, LAST lipid emulsion kit — matched to the case-specific risk profile before a high-risk case even starts.
  • For known higher-risk patients (severe cardiomyopathy, planned high-hemorrhage-risk surgery), pre-arrange blood availability, consider standby perfusion/ECMO readiness, and involve cardiac anesthesia/ICU early rather than reactively.
  • Debrief structurally after every event — immediate or delayed, either is better than none, and structured post-event reflection has been shown to improve team performance on the next event.

rows: Arrest persisting beyond 5–10 minutes is associated with a significantly worse prognosis and more complex management
Perioperative ECPR survival to discharge (single-center series)
~57.6%, with favorable neurologic outcomes reported — notably higher than traditional CPR outcome data

blocks.html:
Why standard ACLS isn't simply "good enough" here: ACLS was built primarily around common cardiac causes of arrhythmic arrest in the community and general hospital ward, with pharmacology (especially epinephrine dosing) optimized for that context. Several dominant OR-specific causes — LAST, MH, anaphylaxis, gas embolism, vagal reflex — either need different drugs entirely or need the same drugs at meaningfully different doses. Applying unmodified ACLS to a LAST-triggered arrest, for instance, can actively worsen outcomes through repeated full-dose epinephrine undermining lipid emulsion's effectiveness — which is exactly the gap PeRLS 2025 was written to close.

Why the team's situational knowledge matters as much as any algorithm: in a witnessed OR arrest, the team usually knows the drugs given, the procedure step underway, and the patient's baseline physiology in real time — information a code team responding to an unwitnessed ward or community arrest simply doesn't have. Building the resuscitation around "what was just happening" rather than working mechanically through a generic differential is what "diagnosis-driven" resuscitation actually means in practice.

Why echocardiography is weighted so heavily for PEA specifically: PEA is a description of the rhythm, not a diagnosis — it can result from tamponade, massive PE, severe hypovolemia, tension pneumothorax, or profound myocardial dysfunction, each needing a completely different immediate intervention. Bedside echo turns "PEA, differential unclear" into a specific, actionable finding (a collapsed, empty left ventricle vs. a distended, hypocontractile right ventricle vs. a pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology) far faster than working through the possibilities empirically.

Why earlier ECMO/CPB escalation is increasingly favored over waiting: traditional CPR outcome data for prolonged in-hospital arrest is poor — one large multicenter dataset found under 2.5% favorable outcomes after more than 40 minutes of CPR even in shockable-rhythm scenarios. Perioperative ECPR series showing survival to discharge above 50%, often with good neurologic outcomes, reflect a population where the underlying cause is frequently reversible and mechanical support can bridge the patient through it — the earlier that bridge starts relative to arrest duration, the better the odds, which is the basis for escalating early rather than only as a last resort.

rows: Immediate defibrillation regardless of suspected cause — a strong, unambiguous recommendation.
A distinct entity from flatline asystole — emergency temporary pacing is specifically indicated here rather than the standard non-shockable pathway alone.
Use echo aggressively to identify the mechanism — treatment is entirely dependent on the underlying cause found.
Often rapidly reversible with atropine and removal of the surgical stimulus (release traction, deflate insufflation) — recognize this pattern before escalating to a full arrest algorithm.
Consider the ECMO-CPR pathway specifically — see the dedicated Refractory VF/pVT crisis file for the detailed cannulation-decision framework.

blocks.html:
Immediate post-ROSC targets: MAP ≥65 mmHg (crystalloid boluses first, then vasopressor infusion if needed), PaCO₂ 35–40 mmHg avoiding both hyper- and hypoventilation, SpO₂ 90–98% using the lowest FiO₂ that achieves it, continuous cardiac monitoring with a 12-lead ECG to assess for STEMI.

Identify and treat reversible causes in the post-ROSC window too — hypovolemia, hypoxia, acidosis, electrolyte derangement, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, and pulmonary/coronary thrombosis all remain relevant after return of circulation, not just during the arrest itself.

Coronary evaluation: urgent coronary angiography with transfer to a cath-capable facility if STEMI or a strong suspicion of acute coronary occlusion is present.

Disposition: ICU-level care is standard for any perioperative arrest, with close coordination between the anesthesia/surgical team and ICU on medication adjustments, device optimization, and relevant subspecialty consultation.

Debrief: structured post-event debriefing — immediate or delayed — improves subsequent team performance and is worth doing after every event, not just the ones that go poorly.
