protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Refractory Arrest
protocols.subtitle: Vector change and double sequential defibrillation, why ERC still won't recommend DSED despite a positive trial, and why low-flow time — not a fixed clock — is the number that actually determines the ECPR decision.

badges.text: ASSESS FOR ECPR EARLY, NOT AFTER STANDARD CARE FAILS

protocols.description: Vector change vs. DSED, why ERC won't recommend DSED despite positive trial data, low-flow time as the real ECPR clock. ERC 2025/ELSO-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Escalate defibrillation strategy while simultaneously starting the ECPR candidacy clock — these run in parallel, not sequentially.

steps.title: Confirm refractory VF/pVT and continue standard care
steps.html: Defined as persistent VF/pVT after ≥3 full shocks with appropriate CPR, vasopressors, and antiarrhythmics. Continue epinephrine every 3–5 minutes; give amiodarone or lidocaine after the third failed shock per standard ACLS.

steps.title: Vector change (VC) defibrillation — the lower-barrier next step
steps.html: Reposition pads from anterolateral to anteroposterior using the same defibrillator. No additional equipment needed. The DOSE-VF pilot and subsequent trial showed higher termination-of-VF and ROSC rates with VC compared to standard defibrillation.

steps.title: Double sequential defibrillation (DSED) — consider, but know the guideline stance
steps.html: Two defibrillators, pads in combined anterolateral + anteroposterior positions, discharged in close succession. The pivotal DOSE-VF trial (NEJM 2022) showed improved survival with DSED and VC versus standard defibrillation — but ERC 2025 does not recommend routine use given the practical challenges of coordinating two defibrillators and residual uncertainty in the broader evidence base. Reasonable to use where your system has trained for it; not yet a default step everywhere.

steps.title: Start ECPR candidacy assessment immediately — don't wait to see if defibrillation strategy changes work
steps.html: Time to ECMO flow (low-flow duration) is the dominant prognostic variable — assess candidacy from the moment refractory VF/pVT is recognized, in parallel with ongoing resuscitation, not as a fallback after everything else has failed.

steps.title: Apply mechanical CPR if available
steps.html: Frees hands for defibrillator coordination and cannulation, and provides consistent compressions during transport or the cannulation process itself.

steps.title: Begin cannulation once ECPR candidacy criteria are met
steps.html: Reasonable to consider commencing cannulation after 10–20 minutes of failed resuscitation. Cannulation itself can be achieved in as little as 10 minutes with an experienced team, though it often takes longer. Continue high-quality CPR throughout.

steps.title: Target ECMO flow within 60 minutes of arrest onset
steps.html: The overall goal per current ELSO consensus. Some dedicated prehospital ECPR systems target roughly 45 minutes from collapse. Survival drops substantially with each additional interval of low-flow time — this is a genuine race against a continuous, not stepwise, decline in probability of good outcome.

steps.title: Recognize CPR-induced consciousness
steps.html: Signs of consciousness (eye opening, purposeful movement, resistance) during ongoing compressions reflect good cerebral perfusion and are a favorable sign — pause briefly for a pulse check when this occurs, but don't mistake it for ROSC without confirmation.

blocks.title: Hypothermic arrest is a genuine exception to normal time limits
blocks.html: In hypothermic cardiac arrest specifically, cold dramatically reduces metabolic demand — neurologically intact survival has been reported after more than 3 hours of mechanical CPR before ECPR in this population. The usual low-flow time thresholds simply don't apply the same way when the patient is cold; "not dead until warm and dead" reflects real physiology, not just a saying.

Refractory VF/pVT — persistent shockable rhythm despite three or more defibrillation attempts plus appropriate CPR, vasopressors, and antiarrhythmics — occurs in roughly 10–25% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests presenting with an initial shockable rhythm, with about 20% of all VF-presenting patients eventually going refractory. Survival to discharge with standard care alone is dismal, roughly 2–12%.

Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) — initiating veno-arterial ECMO during ongoing, refractory arrest — offers a mechanism to restore circulation and oxygen delivery when conventional resuscitation can't. The landmark ARREST trial (University of Minnesota) was stopped early after showing a clear survival benefit for ECPR over standard ACLS in appropriately selected refractory VF patients, and subsequent series report neurologically intact survival up to roughly 54% in selected refractory VF populations — a dramatic improvement over conventional outcomes when the system, patient selection, and timing all align.

rows: A core, near-universal selection criterion — reflects a shorter, more reliably known no-flow interval.
Also core — early compressions limit ischemic injury before EMS/ECPR team arrival.
Initial shockable rhythm (or PEA in some protocols)
The strongest single predictor across most published criteria; some centers additionally include PEA if other criteria are strongly met.
Younger patients with fewer comorbidities are consistently favored — reflects both baseline physiologic reserve and post-arrest recovery potential.
Some protocols specifically exclude candidates with no-flow (time to start of any CPR) exceeding 5 minutes.
ECPR is intended as a bridge to treating the underlying problem (coronary occlusion, PE, toxicological arrest, hypothermia) — not a rescue for an irreversible process.
Along with the above, factors directly into scoring tools like the SAVE score, used to predict survival for ECMO in refractory cardiogenic shock/arrest.

sections.title: Program Set-Up & Readiness (In Place of "Room Setup")

blocks.html:
• A well-defined, rapidly deployable ECPR protocol is essential — outcomes in the absence of a clear protocol have been shown to be highly unfavorable. Candidate selection criteria, cannulation approach, and post-cannulation management should all be pre-specified, not improvised.
  • Preprimed ECMO circuits meaningfully reduce time to initiation — a core operational lever for hitting the 60-minute (or tighter) flow target.
  • Choose a cannulation strategy model matched to your system's geography: on-site cannulation when significant transport time is expected; a "rendezvous at initiation hospital" (Minnesota model) approach in more remote areas, where the patient and a dedicated ECPR team converge at a pre-designated site.
  • Regionalization is now a 2025 AHA recommendation: concentrating ECPR capability at designated centers, with defined intra-arrest transport protocols to reach them, rather than every facility attempting to build independent capability.
  • Train specifically for VC and DSED techniques if your system plans to use them — pad placement, timing, and defibrillator coordination all need deliberate practice, not improvisation mid-code.
  • Build a standard of care spanning inpatient and outpatient domains for cardiac arrest survivors, including ECPR recipients — a new Class 1 recommendation area given the substantial disability burden even among survivors.

blocks.html:
Why ERC declines to recommend DSED despite a positive pivotal trial: the DOSE-VF trial showed a real survival benefit, but implementing it reliably requires coordinating two synchronized defibrillators under extreme time pressure, with genuine device-safety and equipment-damage considerations that a single trial hasn't fully resolved. Guideline bodies weigh not just "does it work in a trial" but "can it be implemented safely and consistently across diverse real-world systems" — DSED currently sits in the gap between promising trial data and guideline-level confidence in routine, widespread deployment.

Why vector change is a more accessible next step: it requires no additional equipment, only repositioning the pads already in use — this removes the logistical and safety barriers that keep DSED from being universally adopted, while still drawing on the same underlying evidence base (both interventions were tested together in DOSE-VF) suggesting altered current pathways through the myocardium can succeed where standard vectors fail.

Why low-flow time, not a fixed clock, drives the ECPR decision: even excellent manual CPR generates only a fraction of normal cardiac output, so ischemic injury to the brain and heart accrues continuously throughout the arrest, not just during pauses. This is why "early assessment for ECPR candidacy" is emphasized rather than waiting to exhaust standard measures first — every minute of low-flow time before ECMO flow is established is a minute of accumulating, largely irreversible injury, which is also why the operational target is expressed as total time from collapse (not time from arrival, or time from decision) to actual ECMO flow.

Why witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, and initial shockable rhythm dominate selection criteria: each is a proxy for the same underlying variable — a shorter effective interval of inadequate perfusion before meaningful intervention began. A witnessed arrest with immediate bystander CPR and a shockable rhythm signals a heart and brain that likely haven't yet sustained the degree of injury that makes ECPR futile, which is why these factors consistently outperform other candidate variables across different ECPR selection protocols.

Why hypothermia changes the entire calculus: metabolic demand — and therefore the rate of ischemic injury accumulation — falls steeply with core temperature. The same 90-minute low-flow duration that predicts poor outcomes in a normothermic arrest can be survived intact in a sufficiently cold patient, which is the direct physiologic basis for extending resuscitation efforts and ECPR consideration far beyond normal thresholds specifically in this population.

rows: The most common underlying driver — a strong argument for early coronary angiography/PCI once circulation is restored (including peri-ECMO in appropriate systems).

Hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, or hypomagnesemia can each sustain a shock-refractory rhythm — see the dedicated Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest crisis file; magnesium is specifically useful if torsades-type polymorphic VT is contributing.

Sodium channel blocker toxicity (TCA, cocaine), digoxin toxicity, and other cardiotoxic ingestions can all produce refractory arrhythmia — case reports describe ECPR permitting recovery even after prolonged low-flow time (up to 4 hours) in poisoning-induced arrest.
Both a cause of arrest and a reason to extend resuscitation duration — see above.
Tension pneumothorax or tamponade preventing effective defibrillation/perfusion — address per the dedicated crisis files for each; a shock can't fix a heart that can't fill or eject.
Recurrent/refibrillating VF (distinct from truly refractory VF)

Converts to an organized rhythm then reoccurs — may reflect ongoing ischemia or an unstable substrate rather than failure to convert in the first place; worth distinguishing from persistent, unresponsive VF when planning next steps.

blocks.html:
Identify and treat the precipitating cause immediately: coronary angiography for suspected ACS, CT for PE/other structural causes — ECPR buys time and circulation, but doesn't fix the underlying problem on its own.

Watch for differential hypoxia (North-South/Harlequin syndrome): in peripheral VA-ECMO, if native cardiac function recovers before native lung function, poorly oxygenated blood from the native heart can preferentially perfuse the upper body/coronary circulation while the ECMO circuit oxygenates the lower body — a recognized complication requiring specific monitoring (right upper extremity SpO₂) and, if present, circuit modification.

Monitor for cannulation-site vascular complications: limb ischemia is a real risk with femoral cannulation — a distal perfusion catheter is frequently placed proactively rather than reactively.

Targeted temperature management per standard post-arrest care protocols, adapted to the ECMO circuit's thermal management capability.

Disposition and trajectory planning: ICU-level, multidisciplinary care (critical care, cardiology, cardiac surgery, neurology) — the goal is full cardiac recovery where possible, with bridge-to-durable-device or transplant as a secondary pathway in select cases, and appropriately delayed neuroprognostication before any withdrawal-of-care discussion.

protocols.title: Tension Pneumothorax
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Trauma
protocols.subtitle: A clinical diagnosis, not a radiographic one — the site-selection debate between 2nd ICS midclavicular and 5th ICS midaxillary, why needle decompression alone is never the last step, and why nitrous oxide makes it worse.

badges.text: DECOMPRESS ON CLINICAL SUSPICION — DON'T WAIT FOR IMAGING

protocols.description: 2nd ICS-MCL vs 5th ICS-MAL site debate, finger thoracostomy vs needle, why nitrous oxide worsens it. StatPearls/NAEMSP-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Decompress based on the clinical picture. Waiting for a chest X-ray to confirm what the exam already told you is how this becomes a fatal delay.

steps.title: Recognize it clinically and act immediately
steps.html: Hemodynamic instability plus unilateral absent/diminished breath sounds and clinical suspicion is enough — do not delay decompression to obtain a chest X-ray in an unstable patient.

steps.title: Needle decompression — choose your site deliberately
steps.html: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (2nd ICS-MCL): the traditional, most widely taught site. 5th intercostal space, anterior/midaxillary line (5th ICS-MAL): increasingly favored when time and anatomy allow — chest wall is measurably thinner here across multiple studies, translating to a lower reported failure rate (~16.7% vs. ~42.5% for 2nd ICS-MCL with a short needle in one cadaveric comparison). Left-sided tension: the 2nd ICS-MCL is the safer choice given proximity of the heart to the 5th ICS-MAL on that side.

steps.title: Use an adequately long needle/catheter
steps.html: A catheter ≥7–8 cm is recommended to reliably reach the pleural space, especially in patients with a thicker chest wall — shorter needles (5 cm) have documented high failure rates on CT-based chest wall thickness studies.

steps.title: Consider finger (simple/open) thoracostomy instead, especially in trauma/peri-arrest
steps.html: Several EMS and trauma bodies now favor finger thoracostomy over needle decompression given needle decompression's high real-world failure rate (catheter kinking, inadequate length, clotting). Performed at the 4th–5th ICS, anterior axillary line — the same site used for the definitive chest tube that follows. Incise, blunt-dissect with forceps down to pleura, and sweep a finger through to confirm entry and break up adhesions.

steps.title: Discontinue nitrous oxide immediately if it's running
steps.html: N₂O diffuses into the gas-filled pleural space faster than nitrogen leaves, actively enlarging the pneumothorax and worsening tension physiology.

steps.title: Reassess immediately after decompression
steps.html: Expect a rush of air, improving breath sounds, and hemodynamic improvement. If there's no improvement, reconsider the diagnosis, check catheter position/patency, or escalate to finger thoracostomy.

steps.title: Always follow with definitive tube thoracostomy
steps.html: Needle or finger decompression is a temporizing bridge, not a cure — the lung remains collapsed and the air leak persists until a formal chest tube is placed and connected to a drainage/seal system.

steps.title: Cardiac arrest / peri-arrest with suspected tension
steps.html: Bilateral finger thoracostomy is reasonable in traumatic arrest with suspected bilateral tension physiology or when the affected side is uncertain — don't let uncertainty about laterality delay decompression in extremis.

blocks.title: Positive-pressure ventilation can create or worsen this
blocks.html: A ventilated patient who suddenly becomes hard to bag, desaturates, and develops rising peak airway pressures should be assumed to have tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise — barotrauma from positive-pressure ventilation is a well-recognized cause, not just a complication of trauma.

Tension pneumothorax results from a one-way valve mechanism: air enters the pleural space but cannot exit, progressively raising intrapleural pressure. The expanding air collapses the ipsilateral lung, shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side, and — critically — kinks the vena cava and reduces venous return, producing obstructive shock that progresses to PEA cardiac arrest if not decompressed.

Causes include blunt or penetrating chest trauma, iatrogenic injury (central line placement, thoracentesis, mechanical ventilation with barotrauma in a patient with an undetected simple pneumothorax or bronchopleural fistula), and rarely spontaneous pneumothorax progressing to tension physiology. Pneumothorax of some form is present in up to 20% of major trauma victims found alive; missed or delayed tension pneumothorax specifically is estimated to account for a meaningful share (roughly 5%) of preventable deaths from serious thoracic injury.

rows: Diminished or absent unilateral breath sounds
The single most-cited finding driving field decompression decisions.
Reflects the obstructive-shock mechanism — reduced venous return from vena caval compression.
From the collapsed lung and worsening V/Q mismatch.
A classic teaching point, but unreliable and often a late or absent finding — don't wait for it before acting.
Reflects elevated central venous pressure from impaired venous return — can be absent if the patient is also significantly hypovolemic from associated hemorrhage.
Supportive findings when present, though not always elicited reliably in the field or under time pressure.
Ventilated patient: rising peak airway pressures, difficulty bagging, desaturation
Often the first and most reliable clue in an intubated patient, where auscultation alone may be harder to interpret.

blocks.html: The "classic" exam is often incomplete. In one retrospective EMS series, diminished/absent breath sounds and hypoxia were the dominant documented indications for decompression — not the full textbook constellation of tracheal deviation and JVD. Build clinical suspicion from whatever combination of findings is actually present, not from waiting for every textbook sign to appear.

• Post-procedure imaging after central line placement — a chest X-ray specifically to rule out an iatrogenic pneumothorax before it has a chance to progress to tension physiology.
  • Point-of-care ultrasound for rapid bedside diagnosis (absence of lung sliding) in any patient with sudden desaturation or hemodynamic instability where pneumothorax is plausible — faster than waiting for a portable film.
  • Avoid unnecessarily high peak airway pressures during mechanical ventilation, and maintain a high index of suspicion for barotrauma in any ventilated patient with known or suspected lung pathology (COPD, asthma, prior pneumothorax).
  • Have decompression equipment immediately accessible in any setting where the risk is elevated (trauma bay, thoracic surgery, central line procedures) — long (≥8 cm) angiocatheters specifically, given the documented failure rate of shorter needles.
  • Individualize site selection to the patient rather than defaulting reflexively to one taught site — chest wall thickness varies significantly by age, sex, BMI, and COPD status, all of which affect which site is actually reachable with standard equipment.

blocks.html:
Why 5th ICS-MAL is gaining favor over the traditional 2nd ICS-MCL site: CT-based chest wall thickness measurements consistently show the 5th ICS-MAL is thinner across most body habitus categories, which is why real-world failure rates run lower there — a needle simply has a better chance of actually reaching the pleural space. The tradeoff is proximity to the heart on the left side, which is why left-sided tension pneumothorax still favors the 2nd ICS-MCL specifically, even though it has a documented higher overall failure rate.

Why needle decompression is inherently a temporary fix, not a treatment: the catheter is thin, can kink, clot, or become dislodged, and does nothing to address the underlying air leak causing the tension in the first place. Every successful needle decompression still needs a formal chest tube to follow — treating the needle as "done" rather than as a bridge is a recognized failure mode.

Why finger thoracostomy is increasingly preferred in trauma/peri-arrest settings specifically: it creates a large, direct opening into the pleural space that a provider can physically confirm with a finger sweep — bypassing the failure modes (wrong depth, kinked catheter, inadequate length) that plague needle decompression. It also happens to be performed at the exact site the definitive chest tube will go, so it doubles as the first step of definitive management rather than a separate procedure.

Why clinical diagnosis takes priority over imaging: the physiology driving deterioration — progressive vena caval compression reducing venous return — worsens continuously and can progress from hemodynamic compromise to full arrest within minutes. Waiting for a portable chest X-ray in a hemodynamically unstable patient converts a survivable, rapidly treatable condition into a resuscitation.

Why nitrous oxide is a specific, avoidable aggravating factor: N₂O's high blood:gas solubility means it diffuses into any closed gas space (a pneumothorax, an air embolus, a bowel loop) faster than the nitrogen already there can diffuse out — the same principle that makes it dangerous in venous air embolism. In a patient with any suspected or confirmed pneumothorax, this converts a background anesthetic gas into an active contributor to the emergency.

rows: Breath sounds typically symmetric bilaterally (unlike the unilateral finding in tension pneumothorax); JVD present in both, but percussion/auscultation of the chest is the key differentiator — echo confirms.
No unilateral breath sound change; look for a clear PE risk factor profile and, where available, echo findings of acute right heart strain rather than a mediastinal shift.
ECG ischemic changes, troponin elevation; breath sounds equal bilaterally, no hyperresonance.
Hemodynamically stable — the defining distinction. Doesn't require emergency decompression; managed with observation or elective chest tube depending on size and symptoms.
Dull, not hyperresonant, to percussion on the affected side — blood rather than air filling the pleural space; may coexist with pneumothorax as a hemopneumothorax.

Can present with chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and hemodynamic instability; history (recent instrumentation, forceful vomiting) and mediastinal air on imaging point toward this rather than a primary pleural process.

blocks.html:
Confirm and formalize: chest X-ray or point-of-care ultrasound after decompression to confirm re-expansion and correct chest tube position; watch specifically for reexpansion pulmonary edema after rapid decompression of a significantly collapsed lung.

Persistent air leak: if the chest tube continues bubbling well beyond the expected window, evaluate for bronchopleural fistula or ongoing parenchymal injury — this may need surgical or interventional pulmonology involvement rather than continued observation alone.

Disposition: ICU or trauma monitoring for any patient who required emergency decompression, given both the underlying injury severity and the need to confirm re-expansion and rule out recurrence.

Documentation: record which site was used, needle/catheter length, and the clinical response — useful for the immediate chest tube placement that follows and for any subsequent procedures in the same patient.

protocols.title: Torsades de Pointes
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Arrhythmia
protocols.subtitle: Magnesium works regardless of the serum level — because it's not correcting a deficiency, it's suppressing the afterdepolarizations. The QT interval is what tells you this is torsades and not just any polymorphic VT.

badges.text: MAGNESIUM ONLY WORKS IF QT IS PROLONGED

protocols.description: Magnesium works regardless of serum level, overdrive pacing/isoproterenol, why amiodarone is contraindicated here. 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Unstable or degenerating to VF: defibrillate without delay. Otherwise, magnesium first — and confirm the QT is actually prolonged before assuming magnesium will work.

steps.title: Unstable or pulseless — defibrillate immediately
steps.html: Torsades can degenerate into VF; treat with the same unsynchronized defibrillation strategy. Don't delay shock to give medications first if the patient is unstable or pulseless.

steps.title: IV magnesium sulfate — first-line, regardless of serum magnesium level
steps.html: 1–2 g IV over 1–2 minutes if unstable/in extremis (slow IV push is reasonable), or over 5–15 minutes if more stable. Give it even when a measured magnesium level is normal — magnesium suppresses the arrhythmia through a mechanism independent of correcting a deficiency.

steps.title: Withdraw all QT-prolonging drugs immediately
steps.html: A Class I recommendation — stop the offending agent(s) as soon as identified, don't wait until after the arrhythmia resolves.

steps.title: Correct electrolytes aggressively
steps.html: Replete potassium to a supratherapeutic 4.5–5.0 mmol/L target (not just the normal range) — this shortens the QT interval and reduces recurrence risk. Correct hypocalcemia if present.

steps.title: Recurrent despite magnesium and electrolyte correction — increase the heart rate
steps.html: Temporary transvenous overdrive pacing at 100–120 bpm (occasionally up to 140 bpm) is the therapy of choice for drug-refractory, recurrent torsades — increasing heart rate shortens the QT interval and eliminates the pauses that trigger the arrhythmia.

steps.title: Isoproterenol if pacing isn't immediately available
steps.html: 2–10 mcg/min infusion (or a 10–20 mcg IV push), titrated to a heart rate around 100 bpm. Use only for acquired (not congenital) long QT with clearly pause-dependent torsades — isoproterenol is contraindicated in congenital long QT syndrome and in patients with ischemic heart disease or hypertension.

steps.title: Avoid making it worse
steps.html: Do not use amiodarone, procainamide, sotalol, or other Class Ia/III antiarrhythmics — all further prolong the QT and can worsen torsades. Do not use calcium channel blockers to terminate a wide-complex tachycardia of unknown origin. Lidocaine is a reasonable alternative if an antiarrhythmic is needed, since it doesn't prolong the QT.

steps.title: Refractory cases — consider point-of-care ionized magnesium monitoring
steps.html: Total serum magnesium correlates poorly with the physiologically active ionized fraction in critically ill patients — case reports describe genuinely refractory torsades responding to further magnesium dosing once guided by ionized magnesium measurement rather than total magnesium alone.

blocks.title: Magnesium won't help if the QT is normal
blocks.html: If the rhythm is polymorphic VT with a normal QT interval, magnesium is not the treatment — this distinguishes true torsades from other forms of polymorphic VT and points toward conventional antiarrhythmic therapy instead. Confirm QT prolongation before assuming this is torsades.

Torsades de pointes ("twisting of the points") is a distinctive form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with a prolonged QT interval, characterized on ECG by gradually changing QRS amplitude that appears to twist around the isoelectric baseline. QT prolongation predisposes to early afterdepolarizations and spatial dispersion of ventricular refractoriness — the electrophysiologic substrate that allows this specific reentrant rhythm to develop. Episodes are often self-terminating but frequently recurrent, and can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

A QTc is considered prolonged above 450 ms in men and 460 ms in women; a QTc >500 ms carries a 2–3-fold increased risk of torsades. The long QT interval can be congenital or acquired — acquired prolongation is most often medication-related, with antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, antiemetics, antifungals, and certain antimicrobials among the most frequently implicated drug classes in real-world pharmacovigilance data.

rows: QTc >500 ms, or an increase ≥60 ms from baseline
The key quantitative warning sign — worth checking proactively whenever starting or adjusting a QT-prolonging medication.
Marked QT-U prolongation and distortion after a pause
A specific pre-torsades pattern, especially in bradycardic or recently-paused rhythms.
New-onset ventricular ectopy, couplets, or short runs of polymorphic VT
Especially when initiated by a short-long-short R-R cycle sequence — the classic "pause-dependent" initiating pattern.
Can precede torsades, described even in non-drug-related settings such as Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
A recognized higher-risk combination — bradycardia lengthens the QT further and increases pause-dependent risk.

blocks.html:
• Obtain a baseline ECG before starting a QT-prolonging drug in any patient with an existing electrolyte abnormality, already on another QT-prolonging agent, or starting a high-risk agent.
  • Identify higher-risk patients proactively: organic heart disease, low baseline potassium/magnesium, a prior torsades episode, bradycardia, or baseline QT prolongation all raise risk when a QT-prolonging drug is introduced.
  • Modify dosing thresholds: if QTc reaches 560–600 ms after starting a QT-prolonging therapy, reduce the dose; discontinue the drug and admit immediately if lightheadedness, syncope, or increasing ventricular ectopy develops.
  • Anesthesia-specific risk awareness: several commonly used anesthetic and sedative agents (propofol, dexmedetomidine, ketamine) have documented associations with QT prolongation and, rarely, drug-induced torsades — worth factoring into anesthetic planning for a patient with known QT risk.
  • Maintain potassium and magnesium in the normal-to-high range proactively in any patient on multiple QT-prolonging agents, rather than only correcting reactively after an event.
  • Provide a QT-prolonging drug list (e.g., crediblemeds.org/qtdrugs.org) to patients with a history of torsades or known long QT syndrome, and educate them to avoid unnecessary combinations.

rows: QTc associated with 2–3x increased torsades risk

100–120 bpm typically; occasionally up to 140 bpm
2–10 mcg/min infusion, or 10–20 mcg IV push; titrate to HR ~100 bpm
6–8 mEq/L serum concentration — rare at standard 1–2 g doses
Max 20 g/48 hours, with frequent serum monitoring
Dose threshold for pausing/reducing a QT-prolonging drug

blocks.html:
Why magnesium works even with a normal serum level: torsades arises from early afterdepolarizations triggered by prolonged repolarization — magnesium suppresses these afterdepolarizations directly at the cellular level, largely independent of whether the patient has a measurable magnesium deficiency. This is also why magnesium is considered safe to give even in diagnostic uncertainty: in true torsades it works, and in polymorphic VT with a normal QT (where magnesium won't help) it also won't make things worse, unlike a QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic given on the wrong assumption.

Why overdrive pacing and isoproterenol both work through the same underlying principle: faster heart rates shorten the QT interval and eliminate the pauses that create the short-long-short initiating sequence characteristic of torsades. Pacing does this mechanically and reliably; isoproterenol does it pharmacologically but carries real contraindications (ischemic disease, hypertension, and congenital — as opposed to acquired — long QT syndrome, where accelerating the heart doesn't address the underlying channelopathy the same way).

Why potassium gets repleted above the normal range specifically for this indication: standard "normal" potassium (3.5–5.0) is adequate for most cardiac purposes, but the QT-shortening effect specifically benefits from pushing potassium to the higher end (4.5–5.0) — this is a deliberate, indication-specific target rather than simply correcting a deficiency back to baseline.

Why amiodarone and other Class Ia/III agents are avoided despite being standard VT drugs elsewhere: these agents work by prolonging repolarization — exactly the mechanism that caused torsades in the first place. Using a QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic to treat a QT-prolongation-driven arrhythmia is directly counterproductive, which is why this is one of the clearest examples in resuscitation medicine of a "standard" drug being actively wrong for a specific rhythm.

Why the evidence base here is thinner than the confident-sounding guidance suggests: honest appraisal (First10EM among others) notes there are no randomized trials establishing pacing's efficacy for torsades, and the observational data supporting magnesium — while consistent and long-standing since the 1980s — earns only a modest evidence grade (Class IIb) in ACLS terms. The guidance is followed because decades of consistent clinical experience and a clear, plausible mechanism support it, and because the alternative (untreated pause-dependent recurrent torsades) is dangerous enough that acting on strong observational signal is the reasonable choice — not because the trials are definitive.

rows: Polymorphic VT with a normal QT (e.g., ischemic VT)
The critical distinction — magnesium is ineffective here; standard antiarrhythmic therapy (amiodarone, procainamide) is appropriate instead, the opposite of true torsades management.
Consistent QRS morphology beat-to-beat, unlike the twisting amplitude pattern of torsades; standard VT algorithm and antiarrhythmics apply.
Ventricular fibrillation (de novo, not degenerated from torsades)
No organized QRS complexes at all; treated with standard defibrillation and ACLS regardless of the distinction once truly fibrillating.

Occurs with a normal QT interval, classically triggered by exercise/catecholamine surge in younger patients — a distinct channelopathy from long QT syndrome, with different genetics and treatment (beta-blockade, flecainide) rather than magnesium.
A different ECG pattern (coved ST elevation in right precordial leads) and different arrhythmic mechanism — not QT-prolongation-driven.

blocks.html:
Confirm and characterize: a 12-lead ECG once the rhythm resolves to measure the QTc directly, basic metabolic panel with magnesium and calcium, and a careful medication reconciliation to identify every potential QT-prolonging agent — not just the most obvious one.

Continuous monitoring: torsades frequently recurs even after apparent resolution — continuous cardiac monitoring is essential, not optional, following any episode.

Distinguish acquired from congenital: for a first episode without an obvious drug or electrolyte trigger, or in a younger patient, consider a personal and family history screen for congenital long QT syndrome — this changes long-term management (beta-blockade, possible ICD, family screening) substantially from a purely acquired, reversible cause.

Disposition: ICU-level monitoring for any patient with a torsades episode until the QTc has normalized and the precipitating factor is clearly identified and corrected/removed.

Documentation and follow-up: flag the chart with the specific culprit medication(s) if drug-induced, and provide the patient with a QT-prolonging drug avoidance list before discharge — recurrence risk with re-exposure to the same or a similar agent is real and preventable.

protocols.description: HOTT framework, why REBOA's own trial was stopped for harm, the 10-minute thoracotomy window. ERC 2025-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management — The HOTT Framework
sections.tagline: Treat all reversible causes simultaneously, not sequentially — this is context-sensitive prioritization, not a fixed step order.

steps.title: Control catastrophic external hemorrhage first
steps.html: Tourniquet, hemostatic dressing, or direct pressure — before airway if the bleeding is severe enough. A patient exsanguinating dies faster than one with a compromised but still-functioning airway.

steps.title: Secure the airway and maximize oxygenation
steps.html: Address hypoxia — the "O" in HOTT — as a parallel priority alongside hemorrhage control, not strictly after it.

steps.title: Bilateral chest decompression
steps.html: Needle or finger thoracostomy bilaterally to exclude tension pneumothorax — see the dedicated Tension Pneumothorax crisis file for site selection and technique. Do this even without clear lateralizing signs in the traumatic arrest setting, since the affected side may not be obvious under time pressure.

steps.title: Restore circulating volume
steps.html: IV/IO fluid and blood product replacement — see the Massive Transfusion Protocol crisis file for ratio-based resuscitation once products are available.

steps.title: Suspected tamponade — resuscitative thoracotomy
steps.html: Primarily indicated for penetrating chest or abdominal trauma resulting in arrest, particularly when an organized rhythm is present or arrest duration has been short — even in asystole. Allows direct tamponade relief and, via clamping the descending aorta, proximal hemorrhage control for infradiaphragmatic bleeding. Requires appropriate Expertise, Equipment, Environment, and Elapsed time (the "4 E's").

steps.title: REBOA — consider selectively, not as a default
steps.html: May be reasonable for exsanguinating hemorrhage below the diaphragm, prior to full cardiovascular collapse, only by appropriately trained personnel. Contraindicated when penetrating chest trauma is the suspected cause. The evidence is genuinely mixed — see Rationale below before reaching for this reflexively.

steps.title: Run conventional CPR in parallel if resources allow
steps.html: Chest compressions, defibrillation, and epinephrine can run simultaneously with reversible-cause treatment when staffing allows — but they do not take priority over addressing the actual mechanical/volume problem, and shouldn't delay it.

steps.title: Reassess for a medical cause preceding the trauma
steps.html: If a medical event (arrhythmia, MI, seizure) is reasonably suspected to have caused the trauma (e.g., a single-vehicle crash with no clear mechanism), switch to standard medical cardiac arrest management (full ACLS) rather than the trauma-specific pathway.

blocks.title: Time-critical, not open-ended
blocks.html: A favorable outcome from resuscitative thoracotomy is rarely possible — even in penetrating trauma — if initiated more than 10 minutes after the onset of arrest. Prolonged CPR (>10 minutes) after reversible causes have been addressed is almost never associated with a good outcome. This isn't a reason to give up early; it's a reason to move fast on the causes that are actually reversible.

Traumatic cardiac arrest (TCA) results predominantly from severe hemorrhage, hypoxia, or a mechanical cause of obstructive shock (tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade) — mechanisms that are frequently, at least in principle, reversible if identified and treated fast enough. This distinguishes it from most out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, where a primary arrhythmic event is the dominant cause and standard ACLS pharmacology and compressions are the mainstay.

TCA predominantly affects young males and, globally, most commonly results from blunt mechanisms, though penetrating trauma carries meaningfully better resuscitative outcomes. Reported survival is dismal overall — global rates persistently below roughly 7.5% — though individual series range from 4% to 40% depending heavily on patient selection and how survival is measured. Despite the historically grim outlook, contemporary evidence indicates that survival with good or moderate neurological recovery is genuinely possible when reversible causes are treated fast and correctly.

sections.title: Decision Surrogates (In Place of "Signs and Symptoms")

rows: A practical stand-in for the likely cause of arrest when the true mechanism is uncertain — a chest or upper-abdominal wound raises suspicion for tamponade and points toward thoracotomy; a pelvic or lower-body injury pattern points toward exsanguination and favors transfusion/hemorrhage control over immediate thoracotomy.

A rapid marker of physiological viability when exact arrest duration is unclear — an organized rhythm supports proceeding with thoracotomy even when timing is uncertain; asystole with an unclear or prolonged down-time argues against it, though a genuinely short asystolic arrest can still warrant intervention.
Real-time identification of tamponade, pneumothorax, and hypovolemia directly guides which HOTT component to prioritize first rather than working through all four blindly.

Penetrating trauma has consistently better resuscitative outcomes than blunt — this shapes both the threshold for aggressive intervention (thoracotomy) and the honest conversation about expected outcome.

blocks.html:
• Tourniquets and hemostatic dressings immediately accessible and staff trained to apply them without hesitation for catastrophic external hemorrhage.
  • Bilateral thoracostomy as a default step in traumatic arrest protocols, not something reserved for confirmed lateralizing findings — adoption of this practice has increased significantly over time in systems that track it.
  • Pelvic binder immediately available for suspected pelvic fracture with hemorrhagic shock — in a patient with a stable airway, rapid binder application and transfer may be more valuable than airway intervention first.
  • Thoracotomy and REBOA capability matched to actual training level — these interventions should only be performed by teams with genuine expertise, not attempted opportunistically by providers without specific training and a system built to support the intervention.
  • Prehospital blood product availability where the system supports it — early blood, not just crystalloid, meaningfully changes outcomes in hemorrhagic traumatic arrest.
  • Clear futility and withdrawal criteria established in advance — resuscitation of TCA is not futile by default and should generally be attempted, but injuries obviously incompatible with life are a recognized exception worth having explicit protocol guidance on before the moment arrives.

blocks.html:
Why reversible causes are prioritized over conventional CPR here: chest compressions on a heart that's mechanically obstructed (tamponade, tension pneumothorax) or has nothing left to pump (severe hypovolemia) generate minimal or no meaningful cardiac output — the substrate compressions need to work simply isn't present. Treating the mechanical or volume problem restores that substrate; compressions alone on an unaddressed cause are largely futile, which is why the trauma-specific algorithm inverts the usual medical-arrest priority.

Why external hemorrhage control comes before airway: a patient actively exsanguinating from a compressible source dies from blood loss faster than from a still-functioning, if imperfect, airway. This mirrors the MARCH sequence used in prehospital/military trauma care (see the Crush Syndrome crisis file for a related discussion) — massive hemorrhage control is treated as the first, not the last, priority.

Why resuscitative thoracotomy is concentrated on penetrating chest/abdominal trauma: this is where the intervention has the clearest mechanistic match to the problem — direct tamponade relief and aortic cross-clamping for infradiaphragmatic hemorrhage control are specific, targeted fixes for specific injury patterns. Outcomes in blunt trauma are consistently worse; one series found tamponade on thoracotomy in 15% of blunt TCA cases, yet none of those specific patients survived, underscoring that finding a "reversible" cause doesn't guarantee reversibility once combined with the broader physiological insult of blunt trauma.

Why REBOA's own pivotal trial is a cautionary tale, not an endorsement: REBOA can raise proximal blood pressure by occluding the aorta, but that's a physiologic number, not a cure — if inflating the balloon delays the actual definitive hemorrhage control (surgery, embolization) that stops the bleeding, the net effect can be harm despite an improving monitor reading. The UK-REBOA trial's early termination for harm, with increased mortality and delayed time to definitive control, is exactly this mechanism playing out in a randomized trial — which is why REBOA is described here as selectively considered rather than a default escalation step.

Why injury location and rhythm are used as decision surrogates despite real uncertainty: in the field, the actual cause of arrest and the precise duration of no-flow time are frequently unknowable in real time. These two proxies are pragmatic, fast substitutes that let a team make a directionally reasonable decision under genuine uncertainty rather than waiting for information that isn't going to arrive in time to matter.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis — What Kind of Arrest Is This?

rows: Primary medical arrest preceding the trauma

No clear mechanism explaining the traumatic event itself (e.g., unexplained single-vehicle crash) — treat as standard medical cardiac arrest with full ACLS rather than the trauma-specific HOTT pathway.

Visible or highly suspected massive external/internal bleeding as the dominant driver — prioritize hemorrhage control and transfusion over thoracic intervention unless tamponade/tension physiology is also present.
Tension pneumothorax as the dominant cause
Confirmed or strongly suspected via exam/POCUS — bilateral decompression may resolve the arrest without needing thoracotomy at all.
Cardiac tamponade as the dominant cause
Penetrating chest wound, especially medial to the nipples/scapulae — the clearest indication for immediate thoracotomy; see the dedicated Tamponade crisis file.
Direct airway injury or obstruction as the primary driver — securing the airway may be the single decisive intervention rather than a thoracic procedure.
Prolonged exposure/cold-water immersion changes the resuscitation calculus entirely ("not dead until warm and dead") — see the Severe/Hypothermic Cardiac Arrest crisis file when this applies.

blocks.html:
Watch for new bleeding after thoracotomy: internal mammary and intercostal arteries severed by a clamshell incision can start bleeding once circulation is restored — be ready to clamp with small forceps as needed.

Facilitate rapid transfer without delay: every post-ROSC TCA patient needs prompt movement to the operating room, angiography suite, or definitive diagnostic imaging as appropriate — don't linger at the point of resuscitation once circulation returns.

Minimize REBOA inflation time if the balloon is in place, keeping occlusion as brief as feasible while facilitating transfer to definitive care — this directly addresses the "delayed definitive hemorrhage control" mechanism of harm identified in trial data.

Address metabolic derangement proactively: hyperkalemia and calcium imbalances are common in this population, particularly with massive transfusion or crush mechanism — see the Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest and Crush Syndrome crisis files for specific management.

Disposition: ICU/trauma team handoff with continued hemostatic resuscitation as needed. In austere or prolonged-evacuation settings, post-ROSC care of a TCA patient is recognized as extremely challenging and should prioritize evacuation to higher-level care whenever feasible rather than attempting extended stabilization in place.

protocols.title: Beta-Blocker & Calcium Channel Blocker Overdose
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Toxicologic
protocols.subtitle: Conventional therapy fails more often than it succeeds — high-dose insulin is the therapy that actually turns the tide, and it works by feeding a starving heart, not by reversing the drug directly.

badges.text: HDI IS NOT A SPECIFIC ANTIDOTE — IT'S METABOLIC SUPPORT

protocols.description: High-dose insulin as metabolic support not antidote, why it beats escalating vasopressors, lipid rescue for lipophilic agents. EXTRIP/HIET-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Start conventional therapy, but don't wait for it to fail before considering HDI — early initiation outperforms rescue-only use.

steps.title: IV fluid resuscitation first
steps.html: Corrects the vasodilation and low cardiac filling pressures both drug classes produce — the essential first step before layering on other therapies.

steps.title: Calcium salts
steps.html: Calcium gluconate or calcium chloride — can help hypotensive patients from either agent alone or in combination, more reliably in CCB toxicity than beta-blocker toxicity specifically. Reasonable as an early adjunct regardless of exact agent.

steps.title: Glucagon and atropine — reasonable first attempts, often disappointing
steps.html: Glucagon bypasses the blocked beta-receptor to activate the same downstream intracellular pathway directly. Atropine for bradycardia. Both are worth trying, but conventional therapies (fluids, atropine, calcium, glucagon) frequently fail to restore hemodynamics in a severely poisoned patient — don't persist with escalating doses of a failing therapy at the expense of moving to HDI.

steps.title: High-dose insulin euglycemic therapy (HDI/HIET) — start early, not as a last resort
steps.html: Bolus 1 U/kg regular insulin, followed by an infusion starting at 0.5–1 U/kg/hr, titrated upward as needed (case series document rates as high as 10 U/kg/hr or more). Give 1–2 ampules of D50W (50–100 mL) when starting, unless glucose is already >250 mg/dL, and run a continuous dextrose infusion alongside. Effect can be delayed 15–60 minutes, so continue vasopressor/glucagon support in parallel while HDI takes hold — don't stop other support the moment HDI starts.

steps.title: Monitor potassium and glucose closely once HDI is running
steps.html: Check potassium and glucose before starting, then glucose every 10 minutes initially (less frequently once stable), given the real risk of profound, predictable hypoglycemia and hypokalemia at high infusion rates.

steps.title: Vasopressors as needed, without a ceiling
steps.html: There is no maximal dose of catecholamine vasopressors in this setting — some patients genuinely require unusually high doses. That said, HDI is generally preferable to escalating vasopressors alone, since high-dose catecholamines increase myocardial oxygen demand and systemic vascular resistance in ways that can worsen perfusion. Consider isoproterenol specifically for beta-blocker-driven refractory bradycardia — as a pure beta-agonist it targets the blocked receptor directly without unintended alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, though it also causes hypokalemia and lactic acidosis.

steps.title: Lipid emulsion therapy for lipophilic agents (propranolol, verapamil, diltiazem)
steps.html: Same regimen used for LAST — see that crisis file for dosing. Case reports describe successful combined use with HDI in refractory, cardiovascular-collapse-level overdose, particularly with lipophilic agents that respond to the "lipid sink" mechanism.

steps.title: Refractory cases — methylene blue, ECMO, extracorporeal removal
steps.html: Methylene blue has case-report-level evidence for hemodynamic improvement in refractory CCB overdose (vasoplegia rescue, similar rationale to its use in refractory anaphylaxis). ECMO is a genuine bridge option in truly refractory poison-induced cardiogenic shock. The EXTRIP workgroup's systematic reviews provide agent-specific recommendations on extracorporeal treatment (hemodialysis) for both beta-blocker and CCB poisoning — consult these for agent-specific guidance rather than assuming all agents in either class behave identically.

blocks.title: Assess mechanism before choosing your next drug
blocks.html: Bedside echocardiography to distinguish vasodilatory shock (needs more vasopressor) from cardiogenic shock (needs inotropic support — HDI, lipid emulsion) changes which therapy is actually going to help. Escalating the wrong category of drug wastes time in a patient who doesn't have much to spare.

Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are among the most commonly prescribed cardiovascular drugs, and overdose of either is common and potentially fatal — the National Poison Data System logged over 11,000 beta-blocker and 6,000 calcium-channel-blocker overdoses in a single recent year. Both classes converge on a similar clinical picture: profound bradycardia, depressed myocardial contractility, and vasodilation, producing hemodynamic instability that is frequently refractory to standard first-line therapy — a combined syndrome often called poison-induced cardiogenic shock.

CCBs block the L-type calcium channel directly, preventing the calcium influx that normally triggers myocyte contraction and, in the pancreas, insulin release — meaning CCB toxicity itself produces relative hypoinsulinemia and hyperglycemia, shifting cardiac metabolism away from its preferred glucose substrate toward less efficient fatty acid metabolism. Beta-blockers act further upstream, blunting the entire adrenergic signaling cascade that would otherwise drive heart rate and contractility. Both pathways converge on the same downstream problem: a heart that can't generate adequate cardiac output.

rows: Common to both classes; can be profound and refractory to atropine.

From reduced cerebral perfusion in severe cases.

Reflects CCB-induced insulin release inhibition — a clue toward CCB rather than beta-blocker as the primary agent, and a caution that "normal" glucose in this setting may actually reflect relative hypoinsulinemia.
Beta-blockers can facilitate hypoglycemia through impaired glycogenolysis — an opposite metabolic signature from CCB toxicity, useful when the specific agent is unclear.
More characteristic of certain lipophilic beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) with CNS penetration and sodium-channel effects.

blocks.html:
• Have an institutional HDI guideline/protocol in place before it's needed — guideline-driven implementation (concentrated insulin infusions, structured monitoring, clear escalation criteria) has been shown to improve safety of this therapy relative to ad hoc dosing.
  • Stock concentrated insulin (e.g., 20 units/mL) specifically for this indication — standard insulin concentrations become impractical at the infusion rates HDI sometimes requires, risking dangerous volume overload if concentrated formulations aren't available.
  • Call your regional poison center early — 1-800-222-1222 (US) — for real-time guidance on HDI titration, lipid emulsion timing, and when to escalate to ECMO; this is exactly the kind of case where expert consultation changes outcomes.
  • Use bedside echocardiography to distinguish the cardiogenic-shock component from the vasodilatory component — this directly determines whether the next escalation should be inotropic support (HDI) or additional vasopressor.
  • Know that HDI initiated early, before full refractory collapse, outperforms rescue-only use — this should shift practice toward earlier consideration in a deteriorating patient rather than waiting to exhaust every conventional option first.

blocks.html:
Why HDI works despite not being a specific "antidote" to either drug class: the poisoned heart, whether from beta-blockade or calcium-channel blockade, is metabolically starved — it can't efficiently use glucose the way it normally would, and shifts toward less efficient fatty-acid metabolism under stress. Insulin at supraphysiologic doses forces glucose utilization back into the cardiac myocyte, restores lactate metabolism, and directly increases contractility through calcium-handling pathways independent of the adrenergic or calcium-channel receptors that are actually blocked. This is why HDI is described as metabolic support rather than a receptor-level reversal agent — it works around the blockade rather than displacing the offending drug.

Why HDI outperforms escalating vasopressors alone: catecholamine vasopressors raise blood pressure partly by increasing systemic vascular resistance, which increases the workload (and oxygen demand) of a heart that's already struggling to contract — potentially worsening perfusion even as the blood pressure number improves. HDI's vasodilatory and inotropic effects work in the opposite direction, improving cardiac output without the same afterload penalty, which is the physiologic basis for preferring it over simply pushing vasopressor doses higher.

Why the effect is delayed 15–60 minutes and other support must continue in parallel: insulin's inotropic mechanism involves several intracellular signaling steps (PI3-kinase activation, calcium-handling changes) rather than an immediate receptor-blocking reversal — it takes real time for those downstream effects to translate into measurable hemodynamic improvement. Stopping vasopressor or glucagon support the moment HDI starts, expecting instant benefit, risks a dangerous gap in support during that lag window.

Why hypoglycemia and hypokalemia are predictable, not incidental, complications: at the doses used in HDI — sometimes hundreds of units per hour — insulin's normal glucose- and potassium-lowering effects scale proportionally. This isn't a rare idiosyncratic reaction; it's the expected pharmacologic consequence of the dose being used, which is exactly why frequent glucose monitoring is built into every HDI protocol from the start rather than added reactively.

Why lipid emulsion specifically helps the more lipophilic agents: propranolol, verapamil, and diltiazem are more lipid-soluble than their hydrophilic counterparts (e.g., atenolol, which is largely renally cleared and less lipid-soluble) — the same "lipid sink/shuttle" mechanism used in LAST has a more plausible mechanistic basis for these specific agents, which is why lipid emulsion is considered more strongly for lipophilic BB/CCB overdose rather than applied uniformly across the entire drug class.

rows: Also causes bradycardia and can coexist as a co-ingestion — check a digoxin level and characteristic ECG findings (see the dedicated Digoxin Toxicity crisis file); avoid calcium if digoxin toxicity is a concern.
Sinus node dysfunction / primary cardiac conduction disease
No ingestion history; look for baseline ECG abnormalities predating the acute presentation.

Can independently cause bradycardia and conduction abnormalities — check a potassium level regardless of suspected ingestion, and see the dedicated Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest crisis file if confirmed.
Clonidine or other alpha-2 agonist overdose
Can mimic the bradycardia/hypotension picture; history and specific toxidrome features (miosis, sedation) help distinguish.

Sodium-channel blockade produces QRS widening rather than the primarily bradycardic picture of most BB/CCB overdoses — see the dedicated TCA Overdose crisis file; bicarbonate is central there in a way it isn't for typical BB/CCB toxicity.
Can independently produce profound bradycardia; check core temperature as part of the initial assessment.

blocks.html:
Labs and imaging: glucose and potassium before and throughout HDI, ECG (QRS/QTc, conduction abnormalities), specific drug level if available and clinically useful, digoxin level if co-ingestion is possible. Bedside echocardiography to characterize the shock mechanism (cardiogenic vs. vasodilatory) and guide ongoing therapy choice.

ICU-level monitoring is standard for any patient requiring HDI, vasopressors, or lipid emulsion — this is not a floor-level management scenario given the intensity of monitoring HDI alone requires.

Weaning: once hemodynamically stable, wean the HDI infusion gradually (commonly halving the dose and observing for 2 hours before further reduction) rather than stopping abruptly — watch specifically for rebound hyperkalemia once the infusion is fully discontinued.

Consult toxicology/poison control early and throughout — this is a genuinely high-acuity, evidence-limited area (most HDI data is case-series level, with no completed RCTs) where real-time expert input meaningfully changes decision-making around escalation thresholds and agent-specific nuances.

protocols.title: Cocaine & Sympathomimetic Toxicity
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Toxicologic
protocols.subtitle: Benzodiazepines first, beta-blockers avoided — but the "unopposed alpha" dogma behind that avoidance is more contested than most training implies. Cocaine's sodium-channel blockade means it plays by LAST's rules too, not just an adrenergic surge's.

badges.text: SODIUM-CHANNEL BLOCKER, NOT JUST A STIMULANT

protocols.description: Benzodiazepines first, the real nuance behind the beta-blocker rule, cocaine as a sodium-channel blocker. StatPearls/CorePendium-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Benzodiazepines address the CNS sympathetic outflow driving nearly everything else — start there before reaching for a cardiovascular-specific drug.

steps.title: Benzodiazepines first-line for agitation, tachycardia, and hypertension
steps.html: Lorazepam 2–3 mg IV or diazepam 5–10 mg IV, titrated every 5 minutes to effect — small, incremental doses that reduce central sympathetic outflow, treating the CNS driver rather than just the downstream vitals. High cumulative doses are often needed; don't hesitate to escalate.

steps.title: Add an antipsychotic for severe agitation refractory to benzodiazepines
steps.html: Haloperidol or olanzapine; combination benzodiazepine-plus-antipsychotic therapy has shown better efficacy than either alone in this population. Avoid phenothiazines specifically — they lower seizure threshold and their anticholinergic effect impairs heat dissipation, working against you in a hyperthermic patient.

steps.title: Persistent hypertension despite adequate benzodiazepine dosing
steps.html: Nitroglycerin or nitroprusside (both also help reverse cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction), or phentolamine 1–5 mg IV slowly. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) reliably lower BP but don't reliably help the tachycardia; avoid dihydropyridines (nifedipine) — reflex tachycardia can worsen the picture.

steps.title: Avoid beta-blockers during active intoxication
steps.html: Current guidance still recommends avoiding all beta-blockers (including labetalol) while a patient shows active signs of intoxication (euphoria, tachycardia, hypertension) — see Rationale below for the real nuance behind this rule and why it's more contested than it's often taught.

steps.title: Aggressive, immediate cooling for hyperthermia
steps.html: Evaporative cooling and ice packs — hyperthermia is a leading driver of mortality and must be treated emergently. Antipyretics don't work here (this isn't a hypothalamic-set-point fever) and shouldn't be relied on.

steps.title: Widened QRS / ventricular dysrhythmia — treat as sodium-channel blockade
steps.html: Sodium bicarbonate is first-line for QRS widening, the same logic used for TCA overdose (see that crisis file) — cocaine has genuine local-anesthetic, sodium-channel-blocking properties. Lidocaine is a reasonable option if bicarbonate fails, despite lidocaine itself being another sodium-channel blocker — used cautiously and specifically for refractory ventricular dysrhythmia.

steps.title: IV volume resuscitation and rhabdomyolysis prevention
steps.html: 20–30 mL/kg isotonic fluid bolus for dehydration and to reduce rhabdomyolysis risk — agitation, hyperthermia, and seizures all predispose to significant muscle breakdown.

steps.title: Chest pain — evaluate as any potential ACS, avoid beta-blockers, give aspirin and nitroglycerin
steps.html: Cocaine-associated MI risk is markedly elevated in the first hour after use (up to 24-fold) but can also present with delayed coronary vasoconstriction from active metabolites persisting up to 24 hours — a normal-appearing early presentation doesn't rule this out. Thrombolytics are contraindicated with severe hypertension, seizures, intracranial hemorrhage, or aortic dissection.

blocks.title: Naloxone can unmask sympathomimetic toxicity
blocks.html: If a mixed opioid-stimulant ingestion is reversed with naloxone, the opioid's sedating effect disappears and the underlying sympathomimetic toxicity can become suddenly apparent — don't be caught off guard by a patient who "wakes up agitated" after reversal.

Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin, producing prolonged, amplified postsynaptic stimulation across alpha, beta, and central adrenergic receptors — the sympathomimetic toxidrome shared with amphetamines, phencyclidine, synthetic cannabinoids, and ketamine. Cocaine has a second, distinct mechanism: at higher concentrations, it blocks voltage-gated sodium channels directly, the same property that makes it useful as a topical local anesthetic and that produces QRS widening and malignant ventricular arrhythmia in overdose.

Life-threatening complications span hyperthermia, hypertension, tachydysrhythmias, myocardial ischemia/infarction, seizures, intracranial hemorrhage, and aortic dissection. A dose above roughly 1 gram is potentially lethal, though individual tolerance varies enormously with chronic use — a dose non-toxic to a novice user can be fatal to a tolerant one due to sensitization, not tolerance in the usual protective direction.

rows: Tachycardia, hypertension, chest pain, dysrhythmia — including QRS widening from sodium-channel blockade.
Agitation, euphoria, paranoia, seizures; focal neurologic signs should raise concern for intracranial hemorrhage.
Hyperthermia — often severe, a major mortality driver, and unresponsive to antipyretics.
"Crack lung" (cocaine-induced acute lung injury) with hypoxemia; consider intubation if severe.
Rhabdomyolysis risk from agitation, hyperthermia, and seizures — check CK, protect renal function with fluids.

Chest pain, focal neurologic signs, cardiac conduction abnormalities, or headache in this setting should be treated as heralding a potentially catastrophic complication (ACS, ICH, dissection) until excluded, not as routine intoxication findings.

blocks.html:
• Consider cocaine use in any young-to-middle-aged patient with atypical chest pain — many patients won't volunteer recent use, making a low threshold for toxicology screening reasonable in this presentation.
  • Know that a negative screen doesn't exclude sympathomimetic exposure — numerous "designer" sympathomimetics aren't detected by standard immunoassay panels; treat the clinical toxidrome, not just the lab result.
  • If RSI is needed, use a non-depolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) rather than succinylcholine — hyperkalemia risk from hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis makes depolarizing blockade a real concern in this population.
  • Avoid physical restraints when possible — struggling against restraint worsens hyperthermia, acidosis, and rhabdomyolysis; adequate chemical sedation is both more humane and physiologically safer.
  • Perform pregnancy testing routinely in reproductive-age patients — cocaine can precipitate miscarriage, premature labor, or placental abruption, and unrecognized pregnancy prevalence in this ED population runs up to 6%.
  • Have cooling equipment (ice packs, evaporative cooling setup) staged and ready rather than assembled reactively once hyperthermia is already severe.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: First-line for agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia
Refractory hypertension after benzodiazepines; alpha-mediated component only, doesn't help tachycardia
Cocaine-associated chest pain/ACS, first-line alongside nitroglycerin
Peak MI risk window after use
First hour: ~24-fold increased risk; most cocaine-associated MI within 3 hours
Delayed presentation up to 18–24 hours also documented via active metabolites

blocks.html:
Why benzodiazepines are first-line rather than a cardiovascular-specific drug: the tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and agitation of cocaine toxicity all trace back to excessive central sympathetic outflow. Benzodiazepines reduce that outflow at the source rather than blocking one downstream receptor at a time — which is why a systematic review found benzodiazepine-first management effectively treats both the cardiovascular and CNS effects together, rather than requiring separate drugs for each symptom.

Why "unopposed alpha stimulation" is real physiology but has become an overapplied dogma: the classical concern is that beta-blockade removes beta-2-mediated vasodilation while leaving alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening coronary vasospasm and hypertension. This is a legitimate concern specific to active, ongoing sympathomimetic intoxication. But the rule has been applied far more broadly than the evidence supports — it does not mean beta-blockers are dangerous for all stimulant-related tachycardia in all contexts (e.g., mild caffeine-driven tachycardia in a hemodynamically stable patient), and some recent data on mixed alpha/beta agents (labetalol, carvedilol) suggests the absolute contraindication may not hold as strongly as historically taught. Current guidelines still recommend avoiding beta-blockers during active cocaine intoxication specifically — the point is understanding *why* (a real but narrower physiologic concern), not just following the rule reflexively in every stimulant-adjacent scenario.

Why cocaine gets treated like a sodium-channel blocker overdose when the QRS widens: cocaine's local-anesthetic mechanism — blocking voltage-gated sodium channels — is pharmacologically the same class of problem as TCA overdose, even though cocaine is conceptually filed under "stimulant." Sodium bicarbonate raises extracellular sodium concentration and alkalinizes serum, both of which help overcome sodium-channel blockade — the same physiologic logic applies regardless of which drug produced the blockade.

Why hyperthermia gets treated as an independent emergency, not just a vital sign to note: elevated core temperature in this setting reflects a hypermetabolic state driven by excess catecholamines and muscular hyperactivity — it is not a hypothalamic set-point fever, which is exactly why antipyretics (which work by resetting the hypothalamic set point) do nothing here. Only active, external cooling addresses the actual mechanism, and prompt correction matters because mortality rises sharply with degree and duration of hyperthermia.

Why dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are specifically avoided despite CCBs generally being reasonable: nifedipine and similar dihydropyridines cause peripheral vasodilation that can trigger reflex tachycardia — adding fuel to a fire in a patient whose primary problem may already include dangerous tachycardia. Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) don't share this reflex mechanism to the same degree, which is why they're the reasonable CCB choice here while dihydropyridines aren't.

rows: Nearly identical clinical picture and management — both fall under the broader sympathomimetic toxidrome; distinguishing the specific agent rarely changes acute management.

Clonus and hyperreflexia more prominent, history of serotonergic drug combination (SSRIs, MAOIs, other stimulants) — see the dedicated Serotonin Syndrome vs. NMS crisis file for the full differential.
No temporal link to drug use; look for known thyroid disease and characteristic labs (suppressed TSH, elevated free T4).
Tied to recent anesthetic exposure (volatile agent/succinylcholine), not drug ingestion — see the dedicated MH crisis file for the full differential comparison.

Can also produce agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, and hyperthermia — history of recent cessation rather than acute intoxication is the key distinguishing clue; treatment (benzodiazepines) actually overlaps substantially.

Dry, flushed skin and absent bowel sounds distinguish this from the diaphoretic, hyperactive-bowel-sounds picture more typical of sympathomimetic toxicity ("hot as a hare, dry as a bone" vs. a wet, agitated stimulant picture).

blocks.html:
Labs and imaging: ECG (QRS width, ischemic changes), troponin and serial ECGs for chest pain, CK for rhabdomyolysis, CBC/BMP, CXR if fever or hypoxemia raises concern for aspiration or "crack lung." CT head ± CT angiography for altered mental status, focal neurologic findings, or head trauma.

Monitor until clinically resolved: continue observation until the patient is no longer tachycardic or hypertensive and is calm and cooperative — cocaine's effects are generally short-lived, so mild intoxication often needs no specific treatment beyond monitoring.

Watch for medication interactions worsening the picture: some agents given for other indications can compound cocaine's adverse effects — review the full medication list rather than treating each new symptom with an additional drug in isolation.

Disposition: ICU-level care for hemodynamic instability, refractory hyperthermia, significant rhabdomyolysis, or any evidence of ACS, ICH, or aortic dissection. Stable patients who normalize with supportive care can often be managed on a general floor or observation unit and connected to substance use resources before discharge.
