protocols.title: Digoxin Toxicity
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Toxicologic
protocols.subtitle: Almost any arrhythmia except a rapid SVT — DigiFab dosing philosophy has shifted away from complete upfront neutralization, and the classic "never give calcium" rule is more contested than it's usually taught.

badges.text: HYPERKALEMIA IS A SEVERITY MARKER, NOT JUST A LAB

protocols.description: Nearly any arrhythmia except rapid SVT, why calcium avoidance is more contested than taught, hyperkalemia as a pump-poisoning severity marker.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: DigiFab is the definitive treatment — everything else is supportive while you get it, or a bridge if it's not immediately available.

steps.title: Continuous cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG immediately
steps.html: Digoxin toxicity can produce nearly any arrhythmia — the ECG drives every subsequent decision. Hold further digoxin dosing.

steps.title: Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia or high-degree AV block
steps.html: 0.5 mg IV (adults) or 0.02 mg/kg IV (children) — a reasonable first attempt, though often only partially effective given the underlying vagal-tone mechanism.

steps.title: Digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) — the definitive treatment
steps.html: Give without delay for life-threatening manifestations: severe ventricular arrhythmias, progressive bradycardia or high-degree AV block unresponsive to atropine, or significant hyperkalemia with rapidly progressive symptoms. Dosing depends on known ingested amount, serum level, or empiric estimation — see Numbers to Know below. Clinical response typically begins within ~20 minutes, arrhythmias often improve within 30–45 minutes, complete response by 1.5–3 hours.

steps.title: Hyperkalemia — treat, but know DigiFab is the actual fix
steps.html: Standard hyperkalemia measures (insulin/glucose, bicarbonate — see the dedicated Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest crisis file) can be used as a bridge, but often fail to fully resolve digoxin-driven hyperkalemia until DigiFab is given, since the potassium leak is coming directly from the poisoned Na/K-ATPase pump, not a separate process.

steps.title: Calcium — approach with real caution, not blanket avoidance
steps.html: Classic teaching holds calcium is absolutely contraindicated in digoxin toxicity (the "stone heart" concern). Current toxicology sources describe more nuance: slow IV calcium chloride or gluconate has been used cautiously, under continuous ECG monitoring, specifically for membrane stabilization in digoxin-associated hyperkalemia when needed — see Rationale below before reaching for this reflexively.

steps.title: Avoid electrical cardioversion where possible
steps.html: Even low-energy DC cardioversion carries elevated risk of triggering refractory ventricular arrhythmia in a digoxin-toxic heart. Reserve for truly unstable arrhythmia with no better option, at the lowest effective energy.

steps.title: Activated charcoal for acute overdose, regardless of time since ingestion
steps.html: Digoxin undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, so charcoal retains value well beyond the usual 1–2 hour window that applies to most other ingestions.

steps.title: Correct contributing electrolyte abnormalities
steps.html: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia both increase myocardial sensitivity to digoxin's toxic effects and should be corrected alongside — not instead of — the steps above.

blocks.title: Toxicity can occur at "therapeutic" serum levels
blocks.html: A documented case presented with severe digoxin toxicity — bradycardia, hyperkalemia, hemodynamic instability — at a serum level of only 1.4 ng/mL, within the standard therapeutic range. Treat the clinical picture, not just the number; DigiFab resolved the case despite the reassuring level.

Digoxin inhibits the myocardial Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump. Therapeutically, this raises intracellular sodium, which in turn increases intracellular calcium via the sodium-calcium exchanger — improving contractility. In toxicity, the same mechanism drives dangerous calcium overload, causing afterdepolarizations and enhanced automaticity, while digoxin simultaneously increases vagal tone, suppressing SA and AV nodal conduction. The combination of enhanced automaticity plus suppressed conduction is why digoxin toxicity can produce nearly any dysrhythmia — with the classic exception of a rapidly conducted supraventricular tachycardia, which requires exactly the intact rapid AV conduction that digoxin suppresses.

Toxicity presents in two distinct patterns: acute (typically a large, often intentional single ingestion, more common in younger patients) and chronic (gradual accumulation in older patients, usually with renal impairment, drug interactions, or dose creep — now the more common clinical presentation as digoxin's role in routine cardiology practice has narrowed). Risk factors include advanced age, renal dysfunction (digoxin is renally cleared largely unchanged), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, dehydration, hypoxemia, and myocardial ischemia.

rows: Often the earliest presenting symptom, easy to attribute to something else in an elderly patient.
Reflects the vagally-mediated conduction suppression component.
Virtually any arrhythmia except rapid SVT
Frequent ventricular ectopy and bigeminy, paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with AV block, junctional tachycardia, sinus arrest, varying-degree AV block, and — in severe cases — VT/VF.
A therapeutic ECG finding, not itself a sign of toxicity — don't mistake this for pathology in a patient without other toxic features.
Xanthopsia (yellow-green tinge to vision), halos around lights — classic teaching point, though not consistently present.
Especially in elderly patients, can be the dominant or only presenting feature.
A marker of acute toxicity severity and a formal indication criterion for DigiFab — see Rationale below.

blocks.html:
• Monitor renal function proactively in any patient on chronic digoxin therapy — declining renal clearance is the single most common driver of chronic toxicity, since digoxin is excreted largely unchanged.
  • Check drug interactions before adding a new medication to a digoxin regimen — amiodarone, verapamil, and certain macrolides (e.g., clarithromycin) are well-known to raise digoxin levels significantly.
  • Correct electrolytes proactively, not just reactively — potassium, magnesium, and calcium should be checked periodically in chronic digoxin patients, since abnormalities in any of them lower the toxicity threshold.
  • Stock DigiFab and know where it is — an expert consensus panel specifically recommends institutional stocking for immediate availability given how time-sensitive severe toxicity can become.
  • Draw levels at the right time — a serum digoxin level obtained less than 6 hours after an oral dose can be misleadingly high, since distribution into tissue isn't yet complete; interpret early levels with real caution.

sections.title: DigiFab Dosing — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: Most chronic-toxicity patients have levels <5 ng/mL, so 1–2 vials is often sufficient for full neutralization; some protocols suggest a broader initial range (e.g., 3–6 vials)
>15 ng/mL at any time, or >10 ng/mL at 6h post-ingestion; chronic steady-state >6 ng/mL (adults) / >4 ng/mL (children)
>5.5 mEq/L (adults) or >6 mEq/L (children) with rapidly progressive symptoms
~20 minutes; arrhythmia improvement 30–45 minutes; complete response 1.5–3 hours
Continuous ECG for at least 24 hours

blocks.html:
Why "any arrhythmia except rapid SVT" is a genuinely useful pattern-recognition rule: digoxin toxicity produces two opposing electrophysiologic effects simultaneously — enhanced automaticity/afterdepolarizations from intracellular calcium overload (driving ectopy and tachyarrhythmia) and suppressed AV nodal conduction from increased vagal tone (driving bradycardia and block). A rapidly conducted SVT specifically requires fast, intact AV conduction — exactly what digoxin is actively suppressing — which is why this one arrhythmia category is essentially excluded from the differential while nearly everything else is fair game.

Why hyperkalemia functions as a direct severity marker rather than an incidental electrolyte finding: the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump that digoxin poisons is the same pump responsible for maintaining the normal transmembrane potassium gradient. Severe pump inhibition causes potassium to leak out of cells into the serum — meaning the degree of hyperkalemia in acute digoxin toxicity is a direct readout of how completely the pump has been poisoned, which is exactly why it correlates so strongly with mortality and is written into DigiFab's formal dosing/indication criteria rather than treated as a separate problem to fix independently.

Why the "never give calcium" rule has become genuinely contested: the historical concern — a sudden, catastrophic hypercontractile "stone heart" from adding calcium on top of digoxin's calcium-overload mechanism — traces back to older, limited case reports and animal data that haven't been robustly reproduced in modern clinical experience. Current toxicology literature describes cautious, monitored calcium use specifically for membrane stabilization in digoxin-associated hyperkalemia, under close ECG observation. The honest position is that the absolute-avoidance teaching is being revisited, not that the theoretical risk has been fully dismissed — which is why this file frames it as "approach with caution" rather than either a hard rule or an endorsement.

Why DigiFab dosing philosophy has shifted away from complete, immediate neutralization: traditional practice aimed to bind all circulating and tissue-bound digoxin upfront. More recent analysis argues this can be counterproductive — a large upfront dose may be renally cleared before digoxin, which continues redistributing out of tissue over hours, has fully re-equilibrated into the vascular space, effectively wasting expensive antibody. Complete neutralization also isn't actually required for clinical resolution, since even partial sequestration of free digoxin is often enough to reverse life-threatening arrhythmia. This is why incremental, response-guided dosing — especially for chronic toxicity, where total body burden is typically much lower than acute massive ingestion — is increasingly favored over the older "give it all at once" approach.

Why activated charcoal retains value well past the usual window: digoxin is excreted into bile and reabsorbed from the intestine in a repeating cycle (enterohepatic recirculation), continuously returning drug to the vascular space hours after the original ingestion. Charcoal given later than the typical 1–2 hour cutoff for most overdoses can still interrupt that ongoing recirculation loop, which is the specific pharmacokinetic reason digoxin gets an exception to the usual charcoal-timing rule.

rows: Hyperkalemia from another cause (renal failure alone)
No digoxin exposure or dosing history; correlate potassium trend with digoxin dosing/level timing to distinguish.
Beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity

Can produce a similar bradycardia/AV-block picture and frequently co-occurs since these drugs are often prescribed alongside digoxin — see the dedicated Beta-Blocker/CCB Overdose crisis file; treatment approaches differ meaningfully (DigiFab is specific to digoxin).
Sick sinus syndrome / primary AV conduction disease
No temporal relationship to a dose change, level, or new interacting medication; baseline ECG may show pre-existing conduction abnormality.
Other cardiac glycoside exposure (oleander, foxglove, toad venom/bufadienolides)

Non-digoxin cardiac glycosides can produce an identical clinical picture and, notably, can cross-react on some digoxin immunoassays, giving a falsely detectable "digoxin level" — history of plant/substance exposure is the key clue; DigiFab has been used successfully for these as well.
Also produces bradycardia independent of digoxin; check core temperature as part of the initial assessment.

blocks.html:
Labs and monitoring: 12-lead ECG on all suspected cases, potassium, magnesium, calcium, creatinine/renal function, and a serum digoxin level — ideally drawn ≥6 hours post-dose for accuracy. Note that DigiFab interferes with standard digoxin immunoassays, causing falsely elevated readings afterward — a free digoxin level is needed if reassessment is required post-treatment.

Continuous cardiac monitoring for at least 24 hours after DigiFab administration, watching specifically for rebound hypokalemia as digoxin's pump-inhibiting effect is reversed, and for signs of decompensated heart failure if the patient's baseline cardiac function was relying on digoxin's inotropic support.

Cardiology involvement given the implications for underlying atrial fibrillation or heart failure management — withdrawing digoxin affects the treatment plan for whatever it was originally prescribed for, and re-digitalization (if appropriate at all) should be postponed until Fab fragments have cleared, which can take several days to over a week in patients with renal impairment.

Disposition: ICU-level monitoring for any patient requiring DigiFab, atropine, or presenting with significant arrhythmia or hyperkalemia; report to poison control/toxicology for case documentation and follow-up guidance.

protocols.title: Opioid Overdose
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Toxicologic
protocols.subtitle: The goal is restored breathing, not a fully awake patient — go low, go slow when the history allows, and remember naloxone's half-life is shorter than most of the opioids it's reversing.
protocols.description: Titrate to respiration not consciousness, buprenorphine's unique dosing, re-narcotization and monitoring duration. StatPearls/ACMT-AACT-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Ventilate first, reverse second — naloxone treats respiratory depression, not unconsciousness, and bag-mask ventilation buys time regardless of dose or route available.

steps.title: Support the airway and ventilation immediately
steps.html: 100% FiO₂ with bag-valve-mask ventilation before or alongside naloxone administration — this is the actual life-saving intervention while naloxone takes effect, and matters even if naloxone is delayed or unavailable.

steps.title: Opioid-naive or unknown history — standard dosing
steps.html: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV/IM/SC (or 2–4 mg intranasal), repeated every 2–3 minutes as needed. Higher intranasal formulations (8 mg) exist but aren't associated with better outcomes than 4 mg — only more severe withdrawal when it does occur.

steps.title: Known or suspected chronic opioid use — go low and slow
steps.html: 0.04–0.1 mg IV initial dose, titrated upward every 1–3 minutes only as needed to restore adequate respiration. The goal is reversing respiratory depression, not fully waking the patient — overshooting risks severe, distressing precipitated withdrawal without added clinical benefit.

steps.title: Cardiac arrest — standard resuscitation, naloxone if pulse status uncertain
steps.html: Follow standard ACLS for pulseless patients; give naloxone if there's genuine uncertainty about pulse presence, but don't let naloxone delay chest compressions in a confirmed arrest — see the ACLS Quick Reference crisis file.

steps.title: Suspected buprenorphine overdose — higher dose needed
steps.html: Buprenorphine's high mu-receptor affinity and slow dissociation resist standard reversal. Bolus 2–3 mg IV, followed by a continuous infusion of 4 mg/hr — expect complete reversal within 40–60 minutes with this approach, and expect delayed onset compared to a typical full-agonist overdose.

steps.title: Repeated re-sedation — start an infusion
steps.html: A continuous naloxone infusion at roughly two-thirds the bolus dose that achieved arousal, per hour, is appropriate for patients requiring repeated boluses — common with longer-acting opioids (methadone, fentanyl patches, buprenorphine) whose duration outlasts naloxone's own half-life.

steps.title: Manage precipitated withdrawal if it occurs
steps.html: Uncomfortable but not typically life-threatening — supportive care (IV fluids for nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, benzodiazepines for anxiety, alpha-2 agonists like clonidine or dexmedetomidine, antiemetics). Rare severe cases (stress cardiomyopathy, significant dehydration) may need higher-acuity monitoring.

steps.title: Watch for non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema
steps.html: A recognized, uncommon complication of naloxone administration, possibly related to a sympathetic surge/catecholamine release from abrupt reversal — supportive management (oxygen, positioning, diuresis if genuinely fluid-overloaded) rather than withholding further naloxone if respiratory depression recurs.

blocks.title: The goal is breathing, not a fully alert patient
blocks.html: Titrating naloxone until someone is wide awake and irritated overshoots the actual clinical target. Enough naloxone to restore adequate respiration and airway protection is the endpoint — additional dose beyond that only raises the risk and severity of precipitated withdrawal without added safety benefit.

Opioid overdose produces a classic triad of CNS depression, respiratory depression, and miosis (though some opioids — meperidine, propoxyphene — don't reliably cause pinpoint pupils). Death results from respiratory depression progressing to apnea and hypoxic arrest, not from a direct cardiotoxic effect in most cases. Naloxone is a competitive mu-, kappa-, and delta-opioid receptor antagonist with no intrinsic opioid activity of its own — it displaces the causative opioid from receptors rather than metabolically clearing it, which is why it can be overwhelmed by ongoing opioid presence once naloxone itself wears off.

Naloxone's own half-life (roughly 30–80 minutes in adults) is shorter than many of the opioids it's used to reverse — methadone, fentanyl (including transdermal formulations), and buprenorphine in particular can all outlast a single naloxone dose, producing re-sedation once the antagonist effect fades. This mismatch is the single most important pharmacokinetic fact governing post-reversal monitoring.

rows: The actual life-threatening finding, and the target naloxone is meant to reverse.
Classic but not universal — absent with meperidine, propoxyphene, and in mixed ingestions.
Ranges from sedation to unresponsiveness; unresponsive to sternal rub in severe cases.
Can accompany severe overdose; resuscitate as any other hypotensive patient in parallel with reversal.
Not universal but seen with some agents and severe overdose.
Physical exam clues supporting the diagnosis, especially in an unknown-history presentation.

blocks.html:
• Have naloxone immediately accessible in any setting where opioids are administered or where overdose presentations are plausible — IV, IM, and intranasal formulations all have a role depending on access and setting.
  • Default to low-dose titration when chronic opioid use is likely — a quick history (pain management, known OUD, visible fentanyl patch) should shift the starting dose before the first bolus, not after a bad reaction to a standard dose.
  • Nalmefene is not a routine substitute for naloxone — the American College of Medical Toxicology and American Academy of Clinical Toxicology have taken a position statement against replacing naloxone as the primary antidote given its longer half-life (4–8 hours) and less-established safety profile in synthetic-opioid overdose, despite recent post-marketing data suggesting the precipitated-withdrawal signal may be lower than initially feared.
  • Plan monitoring duration around the causative opioid's half-life, not naloxone's — a patient reversed after a long-acting opioid needs a substantially longer observation window than naloxone's own duration of action would suggest.
  • Offer buprenorphine initiation after reversal where systems support it (e.g., the "ODNaloxoneBup" protocol model) — early medication-assisted treatment engagement immediately post-overdose has shown promise for reducing recurrence, using a mixed-agonist transition strategy rather than waiting for a separate visit.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: 0.04–0.1 mg IV, repeat q1–3min to effect
0.01 mg/kg IV/IM/SC (neonates); 0.1 mg/kg starting dose in children
2–3 mg IV bolus, then 4 mg/hr infusion
~2/3 of the arousal-achieving bolus dose, per hour
30–80 minutes (adults) — shorter than methadone, fentanyl, buprenorphine
6–12 hours minimum, longer for long-acting opioids

blocks.html:
Why the endpoint is respiration, not consciousness: naloxone's job is displacing opioid from mu-receptors enough to restore adequate ventilatory drive — full reversal of all opioid binding isn't necessary and isn't the target. Pushing dose further than that specifically to "wake the patient up" only increases receptor displacement further, which is exactly what triggers precipitated withdrawal in someone physically dependent on opioids.

Why low-and-slow titration matters specifically in chronic users: a patient with ongoing physical dependence has receptor and downstream adaptations calibrated to continuous opioid exposure. Abrupt, complete receptor displacement removes that exposure instantly rather than gradually, producing an acute withdrawal syndrome the body hasn't had time to buffer — titrating slowly gives just enough antagonism to restore breathing while minimizing the abruptness of that displacement.

Why the naloxone-outlasted-by-the-opioid problem drives monitoring duration: because naloxone is a competitive antagonist with its own pharmacokinetic clearance, once naloxone's blood level falls below the causative opioid's, that opioid re-occupies receptors and respiratory depression can recur — a phenomenon called re-narcotization. This is a pharmacokinetic mismatch problem, not a treatment failure, and it's the entire basis for extended observation after reversal with long-acting agents.

Why buprenorphine needs a fundamentally different dosing strategy: buprenorphine binds mu-receptors with unusually high affinity and dissociates slowly — a standard naloxone dose simply can't out-compete it at the receptor the way it can displace a typical full agonist. The higher bolus-plus-infusion approach is specifically calibrated to overcome that binding characteristic rather than being an arbitrary "give more because it's a stronger drug" escalation.

Why higher-dose naloxone/nalmefene products aren't simply "better": real-world data comparing naloxone doses hasn't shown improved reversal outcomes with higher doses — what it has shown is more frequent and more severe precipitated withdrawal. This is why current expert consensus (reflected in "compassionate overdose response" guidance) favors the lowest effective dose rather than defaulting to the highest available formulation, even as synthetic opioids have grown more potent.

rows: Respiratory depression without reliable pupillary miosis; no response to naloxone since these act on different receptor systems — flumazenil is a distinct and higher-risk consideration for benzodiazepines specifically, not routinely recommended in undifferentiated overdose.
Characteristic odor, no pinpoint pupils typically, no response to naloxone alone — though co-ingestion with opioids is common and naloxone should still be given if opioid use is plausible.
Focal neurologic findings, unequal pupils, or a clear trauma mechanism should raise this alternative, especially if naloxone produces no response despite adequate dosing.
Check a point-of-care glucose in any depressed-consciousness presentation regardless of suspected opioid involvement — cheap, fast, and treatable.
Clonidine or other alpha-2 agonist overdose
Can mimic opioid toxicity closely (sedation, respiratory depression, sometimes miosis) — history and lack of full naloxone response are the distinguishing clues.
Altered mental status without the reliable respiratory-depression-plus-miosis pattern; check carboxyhemoglobin if suspected, especially with multiple simultaneous patients from the same environment.

blocks.html:
Confirm and characterize: point-of-care glucose, pulse oximetry/ABG for oxygenation status, ECG if a specific agent (e.g., methadone with QT effects) is suspected. Urine toxicology can support the diagnosis but shouldn't delay treatment and often doesn't change acute management.

Observation duration: minimum 6–12 hours post-reversal, extended further for known long-acting opioid exposure (methadone, fentanyl patches, buprenorphine) given the re-narcotization risk described above.

Harm reduction and treatment engagement: every reversed overdose is an opportunity — take-home naloxone kits, discussion of medication-assisted treatment (buprenorphine, methadone), and connection to substance use treatment resources meaningfully reduce future overdose risk and are increasingly considered standard of care at the point of reversal, not a separate referral to arrange later.

Disposition: ED/observation-level monitoring is standard for any reversed overdose; ICU-level care for those requiring a naloxone infusion, experiencing significant complications (aspiration, pulmonary edema), or with a co-ingestion complicating the picture.

protocols.title: Serotonin Syndrome vs. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Toxicologic
protocols.subtitle: Two toxidromes that look alike until you check the reflexes and the timeline — and cyproheptadine, the textbook answer for one of them, has a weaker evidence base than its "mainstay therapy" reputation suggests.

badges.text: BENZODIAZEPINES ARE SAFE REGARDLESS OF WHICH ONE THIS IS

protocols.description: Side-by-side signs table, why cyproheptadine's evidence is weaker than its reputation, the dual-track algorithm for undifferentiated cases. IAEM 2024-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Stop the drug, support the patient, and use benzodiazepines freely — the diagnosis-specific drugs come after that, and picking the wrong one before you're sure can genuinely make things worse.

steps.title: Stop the causative agent(s) immediately
steps.html: All serotonergic drugs if SS is suspected; all dopamine-blocking agents if NMS is suspected. If genuinely uncertain which syndrome this is, stop both drug classes rather than guessing.

steps.title: Aggressive supportive care
steps.html: IV fluids, active cooling for hyperthermia (external cooling; consider paralysis and intubation for refractory temperatures >41°C, similar logic to the MH crisis file), electrolyte correction, and airway protection if mental status or rigidity threatens it.

steps.title: Benzodiazepines — first-line regardless of which syndrome this turns out to be
steps.html: Safe and useful for agitation, rigidity, and autonomic instability in both conditions. Start here while the diagnosis is still being sorted out — this step never needs to wait for certainty.

steps.title: Picture most consistent with SS — cyproheptadine, with real caveats
steps.html: 12 mg load (PO/NG), then 2 mg every 2 hours if symptoms persist, up to roughly 32 mg/24h. Reasonable to try for moderate-severe SS, but see Rationale — the evidence supporting it is weaker than its textbook reputation implies, and it should never delay benzodiazepines or supportive care.

steps.title: Avoid dantrolene, propranolol, and bromocriptine for SS
steps.html: Current guidance explicitly does not recommend these for serotonin syndrome — they target the wrong mechanism.

steps.title: Picture most consistent with NMS — dantrolene and/or a dopamine agonist
steps.html: Dantrolene IV for moderate-to-severe rigidity with hyperthermia (initiate around 38–40°C with significant rigidity — same drug, different indication from the MH crisis file; monitor LFTs). Bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO/NG q8–12h (max 45 mg/day) or amantadine 100 mg initial, up to 200 mg q12h — reverses the underlying hypodopaminergic state. If NMS followed abrupt withdrawal of a dopaminergic medication (e.g., in Parkinson's disease), rapid re-institution of that drug can itself improve symptoms.

steps.title: Genuinely undifferentiated or mixed picture — a specific dual-track algorithm
steps.html: When both serotonergic and neuroleptic agents were on board and the picture doesn't clearly fit one syndrome: start cyproheptadine and consider dantrolene together, but hold both bromocriptine (contraindicated if this turns out to be SS) and chlorpromazine (contraindicated if this turns out to be NMS) until the clinical trajectory clarifies. Add bromocriptine once the presentation becomes clearly consistent with NMS.

steps.title: Avoid fentanyl in suspected SS
steps.html: Fentanyl has meaningful serotonin-reuptake-inhibiting activity beyond its opioid effect — an easy-to-miss risk in perioperative and ICU settings where it's used routinely. Choose an alternative analgesic if SS is active or strongly suspected.

blocks.title: Cyproheptadine's reputation outruns its evidence
blocks.html: A 2025 evidence appraisal found cyproheptadine has very little supporting evidence of effectiveness, despite being the reflexive "board exam answer" for SS. It's still reasonable to try given its low risk profile — just don't let it substitute for benzodiazepines and supportive care, and don't be surprised if it doesn't dramatically change the course.

Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity, most often from combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid, triptans, MDMA, St. John's wort, and — notably — fentanyl) or from an isolated overdose. The classic triad is neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, diarrhea), and altered mental status/agitation.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is an idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine-receptor-blocking medications (typical antipsychotics more than atypical, though any can cause it) or to abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy. The hallmark tetrad is hyperthermia, lead-pipe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability. NMS is rare — reasonable estimates put incidence under 1%, likely closer to 0.1%, of patients exposed to neuroleptics — but carries a real mortality risk (roughly 10–15% if untreated), which is why it stays on the differential for any fever-plus-altered-mental-status presentation in a patient on antipsychotics.

rows: Rapid — often within hours, typically <24h of a new/increased serotonergic agent or overdose
Slow — median 4 days after starting/increasing a neuroleptic, can occur up to 30 days out
Tremor, myoclonus more than sustained rigidity
Lead-pipe rigidity — uniform resistance throughout range of motion; can be cogwheel with intermittent release
Dopamine antagonists — antipsychotics (especially first-generation: haloperidol, fluphenazine), or abrupt dopaminergic withdrawal
Markedly elevated CK, leukocytosis, elevated transaminases, and characteristically low serum iron — a real distinguishing clue in an ambiguous case
Resolves 24–72h after stopping the causative agent, with supportive care
Median illness duration ~9 days; can be considerably longer, especially with depot antipsychotic formulations

blocks.html:
• Careful medication reconciliation before combining serotonergic agents — MAOI plus SSRI is the classic dangerous pairing; adding tramadol or linezolid to an existing SSRI/SNRI regimen is a common, easy-to-miss real-world trigger.
  • Avoid fentanyl in patients with known SS risk — a genuinely underappreciated crossover point with routine anesthesia and ICU sedation practice.
  • Titrate antipsychotics carefully, especially high-potency first-generation agents — rapid dose escalation, dehydration, agitation, and catatonia are all recognized NMS risk factors.
  • Never abruptly discontinue dopaminergic medication in Parkinson's disease or related conditions without a bridging plan — sudden withdrawal is itself a recognized NMS trigger.
  • Have cyproheptadine, dantrolene, and bromocriptine/amantadine accessible in any unit managing psychiatric medication complications, given how time-sensitive both syndromes can become.
  • Wait a minimum of 2 weeks before restarting any antipsychotic after resolved NMS, and use a low-dose second-generation agent with slow titration and close monitoring when restart is clinically necessary.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: 12 mg load, then 2 mg q2h prn, max ~32 mg/24h
Moderate-severe SS (weak evidence base — see Rationale)
Initiate at temp 38–40°C with moderate-severe rigidity; monitor LFTs
Moderate-severe NMS; also used in mixed/undifferentiated pictures
NMS — dopamine agonist, reverses hypodopaminergic state
100 mg initial, up to 200 mg q12h
<1%, likely closer to 0.1%, of neuroleptic-exposed patients
Median 4 days; up to 30 days post-exposure
Can be prolonged if the serotonergic agent has a long half-life

blocks.html:
Why benzodiazepines are safe to start before the diagnosis is confirmed: both syndromes involve excess neuromuscular and autonomic activation, and benzodiazepines calm that activation through GABA-A potentiation — a mechanism unrelated to either syndrome's specific underlying receptor pathology (serotonergic excess vs. dopaminergic blockade). This is why they can be given immediately, regardless of which diagnosis ultimately turns out to be correct, unlike the drugs further down the algorithm.

Why cyproheptadine's evidence base doesn't match its textbook reputation: a 2025 evidence appraisal found the data supporting cyproheptadine for SS is largely retrospective and case-series level, with real methodological limitations — not the robust evidence its "board exam mainstay" status implies. It remains reasonable to try given its low risk, but treating it as a proven, reliably effective therapy overstates what the literature actually shows, and it should never be allowed to substitute for benzodiazepines or supportive care while waiting to see if it works.

Why dantrolene, propranolol, and bromocriptine are explicitly avoided for SS: none of these target serotonergic receptor overactivation, the actual mechanism driving SS. Bromocriptine specifically reverses dopaminergic blockade — the opposite problem from SS — and using it in a patient who turns out to have SS doesn't just fail to help, it risks worsening an already agitated, hyperthermic state without addressing the real mechanism.

Why bromocriptine and chlorpromazine are both withheld in a genuinely undifferentiated mixed picture: bromocriptine is directionally correct for NMS but specifically contraindicated in SS; chlorpromazine (a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic) has historically been used for SS-related agitation but is directly contraindicated in NMS, since it's the same drug class causing the syndrome in the first place. Holding both until the clinical trajectory clarifies avoids confidently picking the wrong-direction drug while the diagnosis is still genuinely uncertain — this is the specific logic behind the dual-track algorithm described in step 7.

Why fentanyl gets a specific warning despite being a routine perioperative drug: fentanyl's serotonin-reuptake-inhibiting activity is a real pharmacologic property, not a theoretical one — it's just easy to overlook because fentanyl is used so routinely and isn't mentally filed alongside SSRIs and MAOIs as a "serotonergic drug." In a patient already at risk for or actively experiencing SS, this makes fentanyl a genuine contributor to worsening the picture rather than a neutral analgesic choice.

Why NMS's lab findings (markedly elevated CK, low serum iron) carry real diagnostic weight: sustained lead-pipe rigidity and dopaminergic blockade drive genuine muscle breakdown and a systemic stress response that SS, even with prominent agitation and hyperthermia, typically doesn't produce to the same degree. A starkly elevated CK and low serum iron in an ambiguous presentation is one of the more objective data points available to shift the differential toward NMS when the exam alone isn't conclusive.

rows: No characteristic rigidity/reflex pattern from either syndrome; environmental or exertional trigger rather than a specific drug class.

Temporal link to anesthetic exposure (volatile agent/succinylcholine), not a psychiatric medication — see the dedicated MH crisis file; genetic predisposition rather than an idiosyncratic drug reaction.
Can closely mimic NMS; psychiatric history often includes prior catatonic features; may respond to benzodiazepines or ECT specifically — genuinely difficult to distinguish from NMS in some cases.
Dry, flushed skin (not diaphoretic) and absent bowel sounds (not hyperactive) — a distinct toxidrome from either SS or NMS.

Overlapping hyperthermia, agitation, and autonomic instability — see the dedicated Cocaine/Sympathomimetic Toxicity crisis file; drug history and the absence of the specific rigidity/reflex patterns help distinguish.
Fever and altered mental status without the characteristic rigidity/reflex pattern of either syndrome; infectious workup (LP, cultures) confirms.
Temporal correlation with known thyroid disease rather than a recent psychiatric medication change; distinct lab pattern (suppressed TSH, elevated free T4).

blocks.html:
Labs: CK, LFTs, CBC with differential, serum iron, electrolytes, renal function, urine myoglobin if rhabdomyolysis is a concern. A detailed medication history — including recent starts, dose changes, and stops of both serotonergic and dopamine-blocking agents — is often more diagnostically useful than any single lab value.

ECG and cardiac monitoring: both syndromes, and several of the causative drug classes themselves (TCAs, certain antipsychotics), carry QT-prolongation and arrhythmia risk — continuous monitoring is appropriate for any moderate-severe presentation.

Disposition: ICU-level care is standard for moderate-to-severe presentations of either syndrome, given the potential for rapid deterioration, need for close temperature/hemodynamic monitoring, and airway risk from rigidity or altered mental status.

Future medication planning: for SS, avoid re-challenge with the same serotonergic combination and consider necessary washout periods (particularly relevant given fluoxetine's long half-life or when an MAOI is involved). For NMS, document the causative agent clearly, wait at least 2 weeks before any antipsychotic restart, and favor a low-dose second-generation agent with slow titration and close monitoring if restart becomes clinically necessary.

protocols.title: Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Toxicologic
protocols.subtitle: Sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone — and it works through two separate mechanisms at once. Most patients presenting with this exact pattern today aren't actually on a TCA anymore, which matters for how you think about the differential.
protocols.description: Sodium bicarbonate's dual mechanism, why phenytoin is specifically avoided, why respiratory acidosis is a second emergency. StatPearls/EMCrit-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Bicarbonate for QRS widening comes before charcoal, before a quantitative level, before almost anything else — treat the ECG in front of you.

steps.title: Secure the airway early if indicated, get an ECG immediately
steps.html: Intubate for respiratory depression, altered mental status, or inability to protect the airway — before giving activated charcoal. Get a 12-lead or rhythm strip on arrival; QRS duration drives the entire next several steps.

steps.title: Sodium bicarbonate for QRS >100 ms or any life-threatening cardiotoxicity
steps.html: 1–2 mEq/kg IV bolus (1–2 amps), repeated every 5–10 minutes as needed. Target arterial pH 7.45–7.55. If the QRS narrows and later widens again, repeat the bolus — this can happen multiple times over a prolonged course.

steps.title: Never let respiratory acidosis develop — even transiently
steps.html: If intubating, hyperventilate to help achieve alkalinization quickly, then reduce minute ventilation as serum bicarbonate rises to avoid excess alkalemia. A brief period of hypoventilation during a difficult intubation can measurably worsen an already unstable TCA-poisoned patient.

steps.title: Benzodiazepines for seizures — avoid phenytoin
steps.html: First-line for TCA-associated seizures, which tend to be single and short-lived. For refractory seizures: barbiturates, propofol, or general anesthesia. Avoid phenytoin — it's itself a sodium-channel blocker and will worsen the cardiotoxicity you're simultaneously trying to treat.

steps.title: Hypotension — fluids and bicarbonate first, then direct-acting vasopressors
steps.html: IV isotonic fluid boluses plus bicarbonate correct much early hypotension. Persistent hypotension: norepinephrine or phenylephrine (direct-acting agents) — avoid agents relying on indirect catecholamine release, since TCAs already deplete that mechanism through norepinephrine reuptake blockade.

steps.title: QRS still wide after 4 amps of bicarbonate — consider hypertonic saline
steps.html: 100 mL of 3% saline as a next step when bicarbonate alone has reached its practical/safe ceiling (pH already near 7.5) but the QRS remains wide. Human evidence is limited but supportive; monitor serum sodium (keep <155) alongside pH.

steps.title: Refractory ventricular arrhythmia — lidocaine
steps.html: Reasonable when arrhythmia persists despite adequate bicarbonate therapy, expected to produce QRS narrowing and hemodynamic improvement. Magnesium can also be considered for persistent arrhythmias.

steps.title: Refractory hemodynamic collapse or cardiac arrest — lipid emulsion, then ECMO
steps.html: 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg (or 100 mL adult) bolus over 1 minute, repeatable for cardiac arrest or recurrent toxicity, followed by an infusion if response is achieved — the "lipid sink" mechanism sequestering lipophilic TCA molecules, same principle as LAST. VA-ECMO for cardiac arrest or refractory cardiogenic shock unresponsive to vasopressors, bicarbonate, lidocaine, and lipid emulsion; early consultation, before prolonged arrest, improves outcomes.

blocks.title: Activated charcoal is not a resuscitation priority
blocks.html: Give activated charcoal (1 g/kg, max 50 g, PO or via NG) only after the airway is secured and resuscitation priorities are addressed — typically reserved for ingestions >10 mg/kg presenting early. Charcoal never takes priority over stabilizing an unstable patient.

TCAs act through multiple receptor mechanisms simultaneously: cardiac sodium-channel blockade (producing QRS widening and depressed contractility — the dominant life-threatening mechanism), potassium-channel blockade (QT prolongation), GABA-A receptor inhibition (contributing to seizures), peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic blockade (vasodilation/hypotension), muscarinic acetylcholine antagonism (the anticholinergic toxidrome), and H1 histamine blockade (sedation). TCAs have a narrow therapeutic index — single-tablet fatalities have been historically reported — and prescribing has declined significantly with the rise of SSRIs, though TCA overdose-associated hospitalization has been trending upward in some recent data.

Onset is usually within an hour, with most symptoms appearing within 6 hours, but absorption can be unpredictable and delayed due to the anticholinergic effect slowing GI transit — a deceptively reassuring early presentation doesn't rule out later deterioration. Ingestions above roughly 10 mg/kg can produce coma, hypotension, seizures, and dysrhythmias; above 30 mg/kg, severe pH-dependent cardiotoxicity and coma lasting more than 24 hours should be expected.

rows: Validated predictor of ventricular arrhythmia risk.
Terminal R wave in aVR ≥3 mm
An additional validated ECG predictor of both seizures and ventricular arrhythmias, useful alongside QRS duration.
From potassium-channel blockade, compounded by the QRS widening itself.
Dry, flushed skin; mydriasis; urinary retention; ileus; tachycardia; hyperthermia; delirium — may mask or be masked by coma in severe overdose.
From combined alpha-1 blockade (vasodilation) and direct myocardial depression.
Typically single and short-lived, though refractory seizures occur in severe overdose.
Can be prolonged (>24 hours) in severe (>30 mg/kg) ingestions.

blocks.html:
• Get an ECG immediately on arrival for any suspected TCA ingestion, regardless of how the patient currently looks — the ECG, not symptoms, drives the decision to start bicarbonate.
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring for a minimum of 6 hours from ingestion, even in an initially asymptomatic patient with a normal early ECG — delayed absorption from anticholinergic-slowed GI transit makes early reassurance unreliable.
  • Have sodium bicarbonate and a lipid emulsion kit immediately accessible wherever overdose patients are managed — this isn't a rare-event kit to locate under pressure.
  • Avoid other sodium-channel-blocking or QT-prolonging drugs in a patient with confirmed or suspected TCA overdose — this includes phenytoin (as noted above) and Class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics (procainamide, flecainide), which stack directly onto the existing blockade rather than treating it.
  • Call poison control early (1-800-222-1222 in the US) — TCA overdose management, especially around hypertonic saline timing and prolonged bicarbonate infusion duration, benefits from real-time toxicology input.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: 1–2 mEq/kg IV, repeat q5–10min as needed
Terminal R wave in aVR threshold
1.5 mL/kg (or 100 mL adult) bolus over 1 min, repeatable; infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min if response achieved
1 g/kg, max 50 g, PO/NG — only after airway secured, typically >10 mg/kg ingestion presenting early
>10 mg/kg: coma/hypotension/seizures/dysrhythmias possible; >30 mg/kg: severe pH-dependent cardiotoxicity, coma >24h expected
6 hours from ingestion before medical clearance

blocks.html:
Why sodium bicarbonate works through two mechanisms at once: the literature identifies both an increased extracellular sodium concentration (which can partially overcome the drug's competitive-like blockade at the sodium channel through simple mass action) and serum alkalinization (which reduces the ionized, protein-unbound fraction of TCA available to bind the channel in the first place) as contributing mechanisms — the exact proportional contribution of each remains debated, but current consensus is that both matter, which is why sodium loading and alkalinization are pursued together rather than treated as interchangeable.

Why even brief respiratory acidosis is treated as a genuine emergency within the emergency: acidemia increases the free, protein-unbound fraction of TCA in the blood, directly amplifying the drug's ability to bind and block cardiac sodium channels. This means a technically difficult intubation with even a short period of inadequate ventilation can measurably worsen cardiotoxicity in real time — the airway management itself becomes a moment of real cardiovascular risk, not just a routine procedural step.

Why phenytoin is specifically excluded from the seizure algorithm: phenytoin is itself a sodium-channel blocker, working through a mechanism that directly compounds the TCA's own channel blockade rather than treating the seizure through an unrelated pathway (as benzodiazepines, which act on GABA-A receptors, do instead). Reaching for a "standard" anticonvulsant reflexively here can make the primary cardiotoxicity worse while treating a secondary symptom.

Why direct-acting vasopressors are preferred over agents like dopamine: TCAs block presynaptic norepinephrine reuptake, which over time saturates and depletes the readily-releasable catecholamine pool at nerve terminals — conceptually similar to the catecholamine-depletion problem seen in chronic cocaine use (see that crisis file). Vasopressors that depend partly on triggering endogenous catecholamine release may be less effective against an already-depleted system, while direct alpha-agonists (norepinephrine, phenylephrine) act independent of that mechanism and remain reliably effective.

Why observation extends to a full 6 hours regardless of how the patient looks early on: the same anticholinergic properties driving the toxidrome also slow gastric emptying and GI transit, which can delay absorption of the ingested dose well beyond what a "typical" overdose timeline would predict. A patient with a reassuring ECG and no symptoms at 1–2 hours can still deteriorate later as delayed absorption catches up — which is why the discharge/medical-clearance criteria require the full 6-hour window with a normal ECG and mental status throughout, not just a single reassuring snapshot.

rows: Other sodium-channel blockers (diphenhydramine, propranolol, flecainide, bupropion, citalopram, quetiapine, trazodone, cocaine)

Given declining TCA prescribing, most patients presenting today with the classic sodium-channel-blocker ECG pattern are actually intoxicated with one of these other agents, not a true TCA — the bicarbonate-based management approach generalizes reasonably well across this category regardless of the specific culprit, but confirming the actual agent (or lack thereof) still matters for other aspects of care.
Also produces QRS widening — check a potassium level in any wide-QRS presentation regardless of suspected ingestion; see the dedicated Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest crisis file if confirmed.

Can produce an identical anticholinergic exam without the same degree of cardiotoxicity depending on the specific agent — history and ECG findings (QRS widening specifically) point toward a sodium-channel-blocking co-ingredient.
Clonus and hyperreflexia more prominent, often from a serotonergic co-ingestion — see the dedicated Serotonin Syndrome vs. NMS crisis file; can coexist with TCA toxicity in a mixed ingestion.
Brugada syndrome / primary cardiac conduction disease
No ingestion history; baseline ECG abnormality predates the acute presentation — TCAs are specifically contraindicated in patients with a Brugada type 1 pattern for exactly this reason.

blocks.html:
ECG immediately and serially — this is the primary monitoring tool throughout the course, tracked far more closely than any drug level.

Quantitative TCA level is not clinically useful acutely — turnaround time is too slow to guide real-time decisions. A qualitative urine screen can support the diagnosis, and in prolonged cases, tracking urine screen positivity alongside QRS duration has been used to help guide when to wean a bicarbonate infusion, given that TCA elimination kinetics can be markedly unpredictable (delayed, saturable, and enterohepatically recirculated) at toxic doses.

Continuous cardiac monitoring for a minimum of 6 hours post-ingestion; patients with a normal ECG, normal mental status, and no cardiovascular instability or seizures throughout that window are medically clear for discharge or psychiatric evaluation. Patients with any abnormality need prolonged observation, and those requiring inotropic/vasopressor support or intubation need ICU-level care.

Mental health evaluation for any intentional overdose, once medically stable.

Disposition: ICU admission for any hemodynamically significant, seizure-complicated, or ECG-abnormal presentation; general medical/observation unit for minor, resolving abnormalities under continued cardiac monitoring.

protocols.title: Amniotic Fluid Embolism
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Obstetric
protocols.subtitle: Sudden peripartum cardiorespiratory collapse and DIC — why "embolism" is a misleading name, why the cesarean can save the mother as much as the baby, and the massive-transfusion math behind the coagulopathy.
protocols.description: Peripartum collapse and DIC, SMFM checklist-aligned, 4-minute resuscitative hysterotomy, 1:1:1 massive transfusion.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: High-quality CPR and rapid delivery are the two interventions proven to matter most — everything else is supportive around those two pillars.

steps.title: Call for help, start high-quality CPR immediately if arrested
steps.html: Standard BLS/ACLS protocols apply — vasopressor and antiarrhythmic dosing, and defibrillation, are not different from the nonpregnant patient. Don't let fetal monitor leads delay defibrillation; remove them if convenient, but never at the cost of delaying the shock.

steps.title: Airway and 100% oxygen, intubate as needed
steps.html: Secure the airway early given the frequent, rapid progression to respiratory failure.

steps.title: Left lateral tilt / manual uterine displacement if undelivered
steps.html: Improves venous return and CPR effectiveness by relieving aortocaval compression — do this throughout resuscitation, not just as an afterthought.

steps.title: Resuscitative hysterotomy within 4 minutes of arrest
steps.html: "Resuscitative hysterotomy" is now the preferred term over "perimortem cesarean delivery," reflecting that this is a maternal resuscitation intervention, not just a fetal-rescue one. If undelivered and circulation isn't restored: begin within 4 minutes of arrest, performed wherever the patient is located — do not delay by moving to the OR. Transfer to the OR should be considered only if achievable within 1–2 minutes. Operative vaginal delivery is reasonable only if the cervix is fully dilated and the head is crowning; otherwise it will just delay delivery compared to immediate cesarean.

steps.title: Assess right ventricular function early
steps.html: Bedside TTE or TEE as soon as feasible — right ventricular dysfunction supports the diagnosis and directly changes treatment. If RV failure is present, treat with inotropes and pulmonary vasodilators rather than volume.

steps.title: Prefer vasopressors over fluid boluses for hypotension
steps.html: In the setting of significant right ventricular compromise, excess fluid over-distends an already-failing right ventricle and can precipitate right-sided ischemia — avoid excessive fluid administration and lean on pressor support instead.

steps.title: Anticipate and treat coagulopathy aggressively
steps.html: DIC accompanies more than 80% of AFE cases — its rapid appearance is usually the clinical finding that confirms the diagnosis. Activate massive transfusion protocol early, but favor cryoprecipitate over fresh/frozen plasma specifically in AFE, to address the coagulopathy while limiting volume-overload risk to an already-strained right heart — a deliberate departure from the standard 1:1:1 MTP ratio used elsewhere. Give tranexamic acid if hemorrhage or DIC develops. ROTEM/TEG-guided correction, where available, helps target the specific factor deficits rather than transfusing blindly. Assign a dedicated timekeeper and blood-product documentation role from the outset.

steps.title: Anticipate uterine atony after delivery
steps.html: Start IV oxytocin prophylaxis immediately once the infant is delivered; have a low threshold for methylergonovine, carboprost, or misoprostol — atony compounds the coagulopathy-driven hemorrhage risk that's already elevated in AFE.

steps.title: Escalate to ECMO if refractory — even with coagulopathy present
steps.html: VA-ECMO can be considered for hemodynamically refractory AFE even in the context of ongoing coagulopathy — a 2025 systematic review of 79 cases found 72% maternal survival with only 6% incidence of major neurologic sequelae. ROTEM-guided management has allowed some teams to forgo initial anticoagulation given the concurrent coagulopathy. Availability-limited, but worth involving a capable center early if the patient isn't responding.

blocks.title: The AOK regimen (atropine, ondansetron, ketorolac) is now actively recommended against
blocks.html: This isn't just "unproven" — as of the 2026 SMFM checklist update, both the AHA and a 2026 expert panel specifically recommend against routine AOK use. The AHA recommends against atropine in the absence of bradycardia, and potential harms of the regimen include worsening renal function, bleeding coagulopathy, cardiac arrhythmia, and myocardial injury. Evidence supporting it remains limited to case reports — don't reach for this reflexively.

Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare, often catastrophic syndrome of sudden cardiorespiratory collapse during labor or shortly after delivery. Despite its name, current understanding holds that it isn't primarily a mechanical obstructive process — amniotic fluid is fully soluble in blood and doesn't cause obstruction the way a thromboembolism or air embolism does. The prevailing model instead describes a complex proinflammatory and hemostatic cascade triggered by maternal intravasation of fetal/pregnancy material (trophoblast, thromboplastins, fetal cells), which is why some clinicians prefer the older alternate name "anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy," though that terminology hasn't been universally adopted.

Incidence is roughly 2–6 per 100,000 births. Classically reported maternal mortality exceeds 50%, though more recent series suggest improving outcomes — attributed to better critical care delivery, increased recognition of milder/atypical cases without full cardiorespiratory collapse, and likely some inclusion of misclassified conditions in older administrative-database series.

rows: Sudden hypoxia + hypotension, followed in many cases by coagulopathy — all occurring in temporal relation to labor and delivery.
Seizures, agitation, anxiety, a sense of impending death, confusion, fainting — can precede the full collapse in some cases.

(1) Sudden cardiac arrest, or hypotension with respiratory compromise; (2) overt DIC following the cardiovascular collapse; (3) clinical onset during labor or within ~30 minutes of placental delivery; (4) no fever during labor.
Right ventricular dysfunction on bedside echo favors the diagnosis and directly guides treatment (inotropes/pulmonary vasodilators vs. volume).

blocks.html: No lab test confirms or refutes the diagnosis. SMFM explicitly does not recommend relying on any specific diagnostic test — AFE remains a clinical diagnosis made by pattern and exclusion, in real time, under pressure.

• There is no true prevention — AFE isn't reliably predictable or avoidable, so readiness replaces prevention as the operative concept here.
  • Keep a printed or posted checklist on every labor and delivery unit — because of its rarity, most obstetric providers may go their entire career without seeing a case, making a cognitive aid genuinely useful rather than redundant. The SMFM sample checklist is designed as a single printable page, deliberately excluding steps unlikely to be forgotten (calling a code, initial O2, IV access) to keep it focused on the parts teams actually miss under pressure.
  • Have massive transfusion protocol immediately activatable from L&D, with the blood bank pre-alerted to the possibility given how quickly DIC develops.
  • Multidisciplinary team readiness: anesthesia, respiratory therapy, critical care, and maternal-fetal medicine should all be part of the response plan, not brought in only after things have already gone badly.
  • Run simulation/drills specifically for AFE — given how rarely any individual provider encounters a real case, simulation is one of the only ways to build genuine team fluency with the checklist and sequence before it's needed for real.
  • Know your institution's threshold and process for resuscitative hysterotomy in advance — deciding this in the moment costs time you don't have.

rows: Time to resuscitative hysterotomy after arrest
Gestational age threshold for delivery consideration

blocks.html:
Why "embolism" is a somewhat misleading name for what's actually happening: amniotic fluid dissolves fully in blood — there's no discrete embolus mechanically blocking a vessel the way a clot or air bubble does. The clinical picture instead reflects an inflammatory, anaphylactoid-like cascade triggered by fetal/pregnancy material reaching the maternal circulation, which better explains why DIC and multi-organ dysfunction develop so rapidly and diffusely rather than following a single-vessel obstructive pattern.

Why the cesarean helps the mother, not just the baby: in a pregnant patient at or beyond mid-gestation, the gravid uterus compresses the aorta and vena cava in the supine position, independently impairing venous return and cardiac output during CPR. Delivering the fetus removes that mechanical compression, which is why the 4-minute resuscitative hysterotomy timeline is framed as a maternal resuscitation intervention as much as a fetal-rescue one.

Why fluid is restricted and pressors preferred when RV failure is present: AFE frequently produces acute pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular strain early in its course. A failing right ventricle is exquisitely sensitive to volume — additional fluid over-distends it further, can shift the interventricular septum and compromise left ventricular filling, and risks right-sided ischemia. Vasopressor support addresses blood pressure without adding to that specific mechanical burden.

Why the 1:1:1 transfusion ratio matters here specifically: AFE-associated DIC consumes clotting factors and platelets essentially simultaneously with red cell loss from any associated hemorrhage. Transfusing red cells alone (without matched plasma and platelets) dilutes remaining clotting capacity further — the balanced ratio approach, borrowed from trauma and massive obstetric hemorrhage protocols, replaces what's actually being lost rather than correcting only the anemia.

Why no lab test is recommended for diagnosis: AFE's presentation overlaps substantially with several other causes of peripartum collapse (PE, LAST, cardiomyopathy, sepsis, hemorrhagic shock), and no biomarker or imaging finding has proven specific enough to rule the diagnosis in or out reliably. Treating it as a clinical, pattern-based diagnosis avoids the trap of waiting for a test result that isn't going to definitively answer the question anyway — time better spent on resuscitation than on diagnostic certainty.

SMFM's updated checklist names five core differentials — pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, air embolism, high spinal block, and sepsis — and notes that initial management of all of them converges on the same ABC (airway, breathing, circulation) approach regardless of which is ultimately confirmed. The rapid appearance of DIC is usually the clinical finding that confirms AFE over these alternatives.

rows: No coagulopathy typically develops as rapidly or as severely as in AFE; CT angiography, when time allows, can differentiate.
Collapse timing usually relates directly to LA injection; CNS excitation/seizure pattern often precedes cardiovascular findings.
Ascending sensory/motor block pattern following neuraxial dosing — a mechanical, not inflammatory, process; no DIC develops.
Clear temporal link to a specific drug/antigen exposure; skin findings (urticaria, angioedema) more prominent; no DIC as a defining feature.
Look for cardiac risk factors, troponin elevation, echo findings of dilated cardiomyopathy rather than isolated RV dysfunction; onset is typically less abrupt than AFE.
Fever is present (AFE's structured criteria specifically require its absence), more gradual hemodynamic decline, identifiable infectious source.
Preceding hypertension/proteinuria; seizure-predominant picture without the same DIC/RV-failure signature.
Hemorrhagic shock (e.g., undiagnosed placental abruption or uterine rupture)

Visible or suspected significant blood loss as the primary driver; coagulopathy here is typically dilutional/consumptive from massive hemorrhage rather than a primary inflammatory DIC process — though the two can be difficult to separate acutely.

blocks.html:
Once stabilized: transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography to characterize ongoing cardiac function, coagulation panel (with ROTEM/TEG if available) to guide continued factor replacement, CBC and renal/hepatic function to assess multi-organ involvement.

Disposition: ICU admission is essentially universal for any suspected AFE case, with continued multidisciplinary involvement (obstetrics, anesthesia, critical care, maternal-fetal medicine) through the acute phase.

Anticipate ongoing hemorrhage risk: uterine atony and continued coagulopathy remain active threats well past the initial collapse — maintain a low threshold for additional uterotonics and blood product support in the following hours, not just during the acute resuscitation.

Documentation and debrief: given the rarity of AFE and the intensity of the response, a structured debrief soon after ICU transfer (or as soon as feasible if the patient dies) supports both clinical learning and accurate documentation. Explicitly address the need for psychological/emotional support for the patient, family, and staff — clinicians can experience genuine "second victim" trauma after an event like this, and that needs to be recognized, not just the clinical debrief.

Submit the case to the AFE Foundation's international registry (afesupport.org) — registry data is what's actually generating the field's understanding of risk factors and outcomes, and comprehensive reporting (including poor-outcome cases) is what makes future management improvements possible.

protocols.title: Eclampsia & Severe Preeclampsia
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Obstetric
protocols.subtitle: Magnesium sulfate is neuroprotective, not an antihypertensive — the two goals need different drugs, and the toxicity monitoring is bedside clinical exam, not a lab value you wait on.

badges.text: SEVERE HTN IS TREATED AS ITS OWN EMERGENCY

protocols.description: Why magnesium and BP control are two separate tracks, clinical (not lab) toxicity monitoring, why delivery isn't delayed for magnesium. ACOG PB 222-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Two parallel tracks, not one: stop/prevent seizures with magnesium, and treat severe hypertension as its own time-critical emergency with a different drug entirely.

steps.title: Active seizure — magnesium sulfate first-line
steps.html: 4–6 g IV loading dose over 20–30 minutes (or 4 g over 5–10 minutes specifically for active seizure per some protocols), then maintenance infusion 1–2 g/hr. If IV access can't be obtained/maintained: 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock), then 5 g IM q4h. Magnesium is dramatically more effective than benzodiazepines or phenytoin for this specific indication — see Rationale.

steps.title: Protect the airway during the seizure itself
steps.html: Position to prevent aspiration, supplemental O₂. Most eclamptic seizures are self-limited — don't reach for a benzodiazepine reflexively if magnesium is already running and the seizure is resolving on its own.

steps.title: Severe hypertension (SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110) — treat as a separate, time-critical emergency
steps.html: This is not the same problem magnesium is solving. Labetalol 20 mg IV bolus, then 40 mg at 10 min if inadequate, then 80 mg q10min (max total 220 mg). Alternative: hydralazine 5–10 mg IV, repeated until target reached. Goal is prompt, controlled reduction — not a specific target number achieved instantly, and not overcorrection.

steps.title: Monitor for magnesium toxicity clinically, at the bedside
steps.html: Check deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output at regular intervals — this is a clinical exam, not something to wait on a lab level for. Absent patellar reflex, respiratory rate <12/min, or urine output <25–30 mL/hr are hold/toxicity criteria.

steps.title: Calcium gluconate immediately available as the magnesium antidote
steps.html: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV (1 g total) over 3 minutes if toxicity develops — have this drawn up and at the bedside for any patient on a magnesium infusion, not something to locate after signs appear.

steps.title: Do not delay delivery to "complete" magnesium administration
steps.html: Delivery is the only definitive treatment for preeclampsia/eclampsia. Continue the magnesium infusion through delivery — including cesarean, despite theoretical interactions with muscle relaxants used in general anesthesia — rather than pausing it to finish a course first.

steps.title: Foley catheter, strict input/output
steps.html: Hourly urine output monitoring is both a magnesium-toxicity safety check and a marker of renal perfusion/severity — place early rather than reactively.

steps.title: Continue magnesium 12–24 hours postpartum
steps.html: Most institutions continue for 24 hours after delivery or after the last seizure, though evidence suggests 12 hours performs comparably for seizure prevention, reflex depression, respiratory depression, and pulmonary edema — reasonable practice variation exists here.

blocks.title: Magnesium and antihypertensives are two different jobs
blocks.html: Magnesium sulfate does not reliably lower blood pressure and is not an antihypertensive agent. A patient can be appropriately loaded on magnesium and still be in a hypertensive emergency requiring a completely separate drug — treat both tracks in parallel, not sequentially.

Preeclampsia is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks' gestation with proteinuria, or — in the absence of proteinuria — new-onset thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function with right-upper-quadrant/epigastric pain, pulmonary edema, new headache unresponsive to treatment, or visual disturbance. Severe features (SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 mmHg on two occasions ≥4 hours apart, thrombocytopenia <100,000/mm³, impaired LFTs, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, or new cerebral/visual symptoms) mark a meaningfully higher-risk category. Eclampsia is a new-onset generalized seizure in this setting not attributable to another cause — one of preeclampsia's most severe manifestations.

Magnesium sulfate is the first-line agent for both preventing and treating eclamptic seizures — a Cochrane review found it reduces eclampsia risk by roughly 92% compared to phenytoin (relative risk 0.08), with significantly reduced pneumonia, mechanical ventilation, and ICU admission compared to that alternative. ACOG restricts routine magnesium use to preeclampsia with severe features or eclampsia; use in milder disease remains a genuine area of practice variation, discussed further below.

rows: On two occasions at least 4 hours apart (unless antihypertensive therapy is started before that interval) — defines severe-range hypertension.
A severe feature; also raises concern for evolving HELLP syndrome.
Transaminases ≥2× normal, or RUQ/epigastric pain unresponsive to medication and not otherwise explained.
Creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline.
A severe feature in its own right.
Not attributable to another cause — a warning symptom that shouldn't be dismissed as routine.
Scotomata, blurred vision — another warning symptom preceding seizure in some patients.
Defines eclampsia once other causes (epilepsy, other structural/metabolic cause) are excluded.

blocks.html:
• Magnesium sulfate is recommended for preeclampsia with severe features or eclampsia — for milder disease (gestational hypertension or preeclampsia without severe features), the decision is genuinely unsettled. An estimated 100–129 women need treatment to prevent one eclampsia case in this lower-risk group, and ACOG explicitly leaves the decision to physician/institution judgment and patient preference rather than mandating it.
  • Have calcium gluconate immediately at the bedside for any patient on a magnesium infusion — not something to send for once toxicity signs appear.
  • Antihypertensive threshold for treatment varies by society — ACOG initiates treatment at severe-range hypertension, while NICE, SOGC, ISSHP, and SOMANZ recommend treating milder hypertension, several targeting 135/85 mmHg. Know your institution's specific threshold rather than assuming a single universal number.
  • Don't withhold or interrupt magnesium for operative delivery — continuing through cesarean, including with general anesthesia, is the current recommendation despite interaction considerations with neuromuscular blocking agents.
  • Place a Foley early in any patient started on magnesium — hourly urine output is both a safety monitor and a severity marker.
  • Contraindications to magnesium: myasthenia gravis, hypocalcemia, moderate-to-severe renal failure, cardiac ischemia, heart block, myocarditis — know these before reflexively loading every hypertensive obstetric patient.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: 4–6 g IV over 20–30 min (4 g over 5–10 min for active seizure)
Magnesium sulfate IM regimen (no IV access)
10 g IM (5 g each buttock) loading, then 5 g IM q4h
Continue until 24h after delivery or last seizure (12h shown comparably effective in meta-analysis)
20 mg IV bolus → 40 mg at 10 min → 80 mg q10min, max total 220 mg
5–10 mg IV, repeat until response achieved
10 mL of 10% solution (1 g) IV over 3 min
Absent patellar reflex; RR <12/min; urine output <25–30 mL/hr
>13 mEq/L (cardiac arrest at higher levels still)
NNT to prevent 1 eclampsia case (mild disease)

blocks.html:
Why magnesium outperforms benzodiazepines and phenytoin for this specific indication: unlike phenytoin or diazepam, which act as general anticonvulsants via unrelated mechanisms, magnesium's benefit in eclampsia is thought to work through NMDA receptor blockade, calcium channel modulation, and — based on animal model data — protection of the blood-brain barrier against the neuroinflammation that lowers seizure threshold in preeclampsia specifically. This mechanistic specificity is likely why a Cochrane review found such a dramatic relative risk reduction (0.08) against phenytoin, alongside significantly less respiratory depression, pneumonia, and ICU admission — benzodiazepines and phenytoin work reasonably well for generic seizures but aren't targeting the actual pathophysiology at play here.

Why magnesium and antihypertensive therapy are treated as two separate problems, not one: magnesium's mechanism (NMDA/calcium channel modulation, primarily central) doesn't reliably or predictably lower systemic blood pressure — it's not pharmacologically built to be an antihypertensive, despite both being given in the same patient for the same underlying disease. Severe hypertension carries its own acute stroke/hemorrhage risk independent of seizure risk, which is why it gets a dedicated, parallel treatment track (labetalol or hydralazine) rather than being assumed to resolve once magnesium is running.

Why toxicity monitoring is clinical, not lab-based, in real time: serum magnesium levels take time to result, and the toxicity progression (areflexia at lower levels, respiratory paralysis at higher levels, cardiac arrest beyond that) is well-characterized enough that bedside deep tendon reflex, respiratory rate, and urine output checks catch impending toxicity faster and more practically than waiting on a lab draw. This is why the standard protocol is built around a physical exam checklist rather than serial magnesium levels as the primary safety mechanism.

Why calcium gluconate works as the specific antidote: magnesium's toxic effects are largely mediated through its action at the same neuromuscular junction and calcium-channel-related pathways that produce its therapeutic anticonvulsant effect — calcium directly competes with and antagonizes magnesium's physiologic action at these sites, which is why it reverses toxicity relatively quickly when given, rather than simply providing generic supportive correction.

Why delivery isn't delayed to "finish" a magnesium course: magnesium is neuroprotective and seizure-preventive, but it doesn't address the underlying placental/vascular pathophysiology driving preeclampsia — delivery is the only intervention that does. Treating magnesium administration as a prerequisite to complete before proceeding to delivery inverts the actual priority; the drug is meant to support the patient safely through the process of delivery, not to be finished before delivery can happen.

rows: Known seizure history predating pregnancy, or a seizure pattern/EEG inconsistent with eclampsia; eclampsia is specifically a diagnosis of exclusion once other causes are ruled out.
Overlaps substantially with eclampsia's presentation and imaging findings; may coexist, and management principles (BP control, magnesium, delivery) largely overlap regardless of the exact label.
Focal neurologic deficits, severe headache with a different character; imaging is warranted for atypical presentation, focal findings, or failure to improve as expected.
Can present with seizure and headache in the peripartum period; consider particularly with a prothrombotic history or atypical imaging.
Thrombocytopenia and hemolysis overlap with HELLP syndrome (itself a preeclampsia variant); distinguishing features include the degree of schistocytosis and organ involvement pattern.
Check basic metabolic panel and glucose as part of the standard seizure workup regardless of obstetric context.

blocks.html:
Labs: CBC with platelets, LFTs, creatinine/renal function, uric acid, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection, coagulation panel if HELLP is a concern. Fetal monitoring (NST, growth assessment) as clinically indicated.

Neuroimaging for atypical presentation — focal deficits, failure to improve as expected, or diagnostic uncertainty about the seizure etiology.

Delivery planning: delivery is recommended at or beyond 34 0/7 weeks for preeclampsia with severe features, after maternal stabilization; delivery should not be delayed for steroid administration in the late preterm period given the acuity. Expectant management before 34 weeks is reserved for carefully selected candidates under close monitoring.

Postpartum continuation: continue magnesium 12–24 hours postpartum per institutional protocol; monitor for late-postpartum severe hypertension, which can present up to several days after delivery and warrants its own evaluation rather than being assumed resolved once delivery has occurred.

Disposition: ICU or high-acuity obstetric monitoring for any patient with eclampsia or severe-feature preeclampsia requiring magnesium and/or IV antihypertensive therapy; continued close monitoring through the postpartum window given ongoing seizure and hypertensive risk.
