protocols.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Obstetric
protocols.subtitle: The 4 T's as a working differential, why quantitative blood loss measurement changed outcomes at the population level, and why tamponade works best before shock — not as a last resort once it's already set in.
protocols.description: 4 T's differential, why tamponade works best before shock, why quantitative blood loss measurement changed outcomes. ACOG/FIGO-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Escalate uterotonics in rapid succession while working the 4 T's in parallel — atony is the most common cause, but don't stop looking once you've treated it.

steps.title: Activate the hemorrhage protocol, call for help
steps.html: Start quantitative blood loss measurement (calibrated drapes/canisters) rather than relying on visual estimation — this single change, bundled with structured protocol response, has been shown to meaningfully reduce severe hemorrhage and death.

steps.title: Uterine massage and bimanual compression
steps.html: First mechanical step for atony — the most common cause of PPH by a wide margin. Bimanual compression is also a reasonable temporizing measure while other therapies are mobilized.

steps.title: Oxytocin — first-line uterotonic
steps.html: 10–40 units in 500–1,000 mL IV as a continuous infusion, or 10 units IM if IV access isn't yet established.

steps.title: Add a second-line uterotonic in rapid succession if bleeding continues
steps.html: No evidence favors one over another — choice is driven by contraindication profile. Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM q2–4h (avoid with hypertension). Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α) 0.25 mg IM or intramyometrial q15min, up to 8 doses (avoid with asthma). Misoprostol — reserve for patients with both asthma and hypertension, given inconsistent efficacy and higher side-effect burden compared to the others.

steps.title: Tranexamic acid — within 3 hours of birth
steps.html: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, second dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours of the first dose. Give when initial uterotonic therapy fails to control bleeding — associated with roughly a 30% reduction in bleeding-related mortality when given within this window.

steps.title: Work the 4 T's in parallel, not just after atony treatment fails
steps.html: Examine for retained placental tissue, genital tract lacerations, and uterine rupture while uterotonics are being given — treating atony alone in a patient actually bleeding from trauma or retained tissue wastes critical time. See the dedicated differential table below.

steps.title: Uterine tamponade for bleeding refractory to uterotonics
steps.html: Balloon device (Bakri, Foley, condom catheter, or commercial system) filled with 250–500 mL saline, or gauze packing (often thrombin- or TXA-soaked). Placed before advanced shock develops, tamponade controls the large majority of otherwise-refractory bleeding with near-zero mortality — this is not a last-resort measure, it's most effective used early.

steps.title: Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol and escalate surgically as needed
steps.html: See the dedicated MTP crisis file for ratio-based resuscitation. Surgical escalation — compression sutures (B-Lynch), uterine artery ligation, uterine artery embolization (interventional radiology), and hysterectomy as a last resort — should not be delayed while waiting to correct coagulopathy if there's an ongoing surgical bleeding source.

blocks.title: Normal vital signs can be deceptively reassuring
blocks.html: Pregnancy's expanded blood volume and cardiac reserve let patients compensate for substantial blood loss while heart rate and blood pressure still look normal. By the time vitals clearly deteriorate, a dangerous volume may already be lost — track quantitative blood loss and escalate on that number, not just on the monitor.

Postpartum hemorrhage is traditionally defined as blood loss exceeding 500 mL after vaginal delivery or 1,000 mL after cesarean delivery; ACOG's 2017 redefinition instead uses cumulative blood loss ≥1,000 mL with signs/symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of birth, regardless of delivery mode — reflecting how consistently blood loss at delivery is underestimated visually. PPH remains the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide, though it's substantially preventable with timely recognition and a coordinated, protocolized response.

The most common cause by far is uterine atony (roughly 70–80% of cases), followed by genital tract trauma, retained placental tissue, and coagulopathy — commonly organized under the "4 T's" mnemonic (Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin). A second uterotonic beyond oxytocin is required in an estimated 3–25% of PPH cases, underscoring that atony frequently doesn't resolve with a single intervention.

rows: Quantitative measurement (calibrated drapes/canisters) is significantly more accurate than visual estimation, which reliably underestimates true loss.
Boggy, poorly contracted uterus on exam
Classic finding for atony — the most common underlying cause.
Points toward trauma as the cause; genital tract inspection is part of the initial workup, not an afterthought.
Diffuse oozing without a clear focal source
Raises concern for coagulopathy (the "Thrombin" T) — consider DIC from an underlying cause like amniotic fluid embolism, severe preeclampsia, or placental abruption.
Often a late finding given pregnancy's expanded blood volume and compensatory reserve — don't wait for these to appear before escalating based on measured blood loss.

blocks.html:
• Active management of the third stage of labor (AMTSL) — prophylactic uterotonic administration, controlled cord traction, and fundal massage — is the primary prevention strategy for every delivery, not just high-risk ones.
  • Identify risk factors in advance: prior PPH, multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, prolonged labor, chorioamnionitis, and macrosomia all raise risk and should prompt heightened readiness, though PPH also occurs unpredictably in low-risk patients.
  • Have organized, systematic hospital-wide response processes in place — ACOG specifically recommends this rather than leaving PPH response to individual provider judgment in the moment.
  • Stock uterine balloon tamponade and vacuum-induced hemorrhage-control devices and keep them immediately accessible to the delivery team, per ACOG clinical guidance.
  • Adopt calibrated, quantitative blood loss measurement as standard practice — the evidence supporting this as a bundle-level intervention (not just a documentation nicety) is strong enough that it's now considered a core prevention/early-detection strategy in its own right.
  • Ensure MTP readiness — see the dedicated Massive Transfusion Protocol crisis file for blood bank activation pathways and ratio-based resuscitation.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: ≥1,000 mL cumulative blood loss + hypovolemia signs, any delivery mode
10–40 units in 500–1,000 mL IV infusion, or 10 units IM
0.25 mg IM or intramyometrial q15min, max 8 doses (avoid with asthma)
1 g IV over 10 min; repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min or restarts within 24h; give within 3h of birth
Typically 6–48 hours with periodic reassessment/progressive deflation

blocks.html:
Why quantitative blood loss measurement changed outcomes at a population level: the E-MOTIVE trial demonstrated that calibrated, objective blood-loss detection combined with a structured response bundle substantially reduces severe hemorrhage, laparotomy, and bleeding-related death after vaginal birth. Visual estimation is notoriously inaccurate — blood mixes with amniotic fluid and other fluids, and providers systematically underestimate loss — meaning a purely visual approach delays the exact moment escalation should happen. This is why quantitative measurement is treated as a core intervention in its own right, not just better documentation.

Why TXA's benefit is time-locked to a 3-hour window: this mirrors the same time-dependent antifibrinolytic principle seen in trauma resuscitation (see the MTP crisis file) — TXA works by inhibiting an actively occurring fibrinolytic process. The WOMAN trial's mortality benefit was specifically demonstrated within this window; later administration hasn't shown the same benefit, which is why "within 3 hours of birth" is written directly into the dosing guidance rather than treated as a soft suggestion.

Why no single second-line uterotonic is preferred over another: methylergonovine, carboprost, and misoprostol all work toward the same end (myometrial contraction) through different receptor pathways, and head-to-head trial data hasn't established clear superiority among them. This is why the actual decision is driven by each patient's specific contraindications (hypertension ruling out methylergonovine, asthma ruling out carboprost) rather than by any presumed efficacy ranking.

Why tamponade is framed as an early intervention, not a last resort: mechanical compression works best before the coagulopathy and vascular collapse of advanced shock have set in — placing a balloon while the patient is still physiologically stable gives it the best chance to actually control bleeding, which is exactly why the evidence shows such strong outcomes (near-zero mortality, over 80% success) specifically when it's used before shock develops rather than after exhausting every other option first.

Why pregnancy's physiologic reserve makes vital signs a lagging indicator here specifically: the roughly 30–50% expansion in blood volume during pregnancy, combined with a young, otherwise healthy patient population, means compensatory mechanisms can maintain a normal-looking heart rate and blood pressure well into what would be a dangerous blood loss in a non-pregnant patient. This is the same physiologic principle that makes quantitative blood loss tracking more valuable than vital-sign trending as the primary escalation trigger — by the time the vitals clearly show trouble, the patient has already used up much of the reserve that was masking the problem.

rows: ~70–80% of cases — by far the most common; treated with the uterotonic escalation and tamponade sequence above.
Requires direct visualization/exam and surgical repair rather than uterotonic therapy alone. See the dedicated Uterine Rupture crisis file for that specific etiology.
Manual removal of retained tissue; placenta accreta spectrum may require surgical/interventional management planned in advance when suspected antenatally.

Consider DIC from amniotic fluid embolism, severe preeclampsia/HELLP, or placental abruption; also consider inherited bleeding disorders or anticoagulant use — see the dedicated AFE crisis file for the DIC-driving mechanism overlap.

blocks.html:
Labs: CBC, coagulation panel with fibrinogen, type and crossmatch, and quantitative blood loss tracking throughout. Bedside ultrasound can help assess for retained products of conception or an evolving hematoma.

Escalation pathway: interventional radiology consultation for uterine artery embolization when hemodynamically feasible; surgical team involvement early rather than as a delayed last resort, since delaying definitive surgical control while attempting to first correct coagulopathy can itself worsen outcomes in an ongoing surgical bleed.

Disposition: high-acuity labor-and-delivery or ICU-level monitoring for any patient requiring more than first-line uterotonic therapy; continue close observation for delayed bleeding (uterotonic effect wearing off, retained tissue becoming apparent later) even after apparent initial control.

Debrief and documentation: given how rapidly PPH can escalate and how much depends on early, coordinated response, structured post-event debrief helps both the immediate care team and institutional protocol refinement — treat this the same way any other high-stakes, relatively infrequent crisis in this series gets reviewed afterward.

protocols.title: Shoulder Dystocia
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Obstetric
protocols.subtitle: The HELPERR sequence starts with McRoberts because it's simple and fast — but posterior arm delivery has the higher success rate in the data, which is worth knowing even while following the standard escalation order.

badges.text: UNPREDICTABLE AND UNPREVENTABLE — BE READY EVERY DELIVERY

protocols.description: HELPERR sequence, why posterior arm delivery has the highest success rate despite not being first-line, why "unpredictable and unpreventable" shapes the whole prevention section. ACOG/RCOG-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management — The HELPERR Sequence
sections.tagline: Try each maneuver for 30–60 seconds before moving to the next. Never apply excessive downward traction, fundal pressure, or twisting at any step.

steps.title: H — Call for Help
steps.html: Additional obstetric staff, anesthesia, neonatal team, and a dedicated timekeeper/documenter. Do this the moment the "turtle sign" is recognized (fetal head retracting tightly against the perineum after delivery) — not after the first maneuver has already failed.

steps.title: E — Evaluate for Episiotomy
steps.html: Not routinely needed, since the obstruction is bony (shoulder against pubic symphysis or sacral promontory), not soft tissue — but can be performed to create room for internal maneuvers if needed.

steps.title: L — Legs: McRoberts Maneuver
steps.html: Hyperflex the maternal hips, bringing both knees toward the chest — rotates the symphysis pubis cephalad and flattens the sacral promontory, widening the effective pelvic outlet. Attempted first because it's simple, fast, and effective as a sole maneuver in up to 42% of cases (some series report success rates above 70% for McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure combined).

steps.title: P — Suprapubic Pressure
steps.html: Applied while maintaining McRoberts positioning — firm pressure just above the symphysis, directed to adduct and rotate the anterior shoulder out from behind the pubic bone. Combine with gentle, steady head traction only — never jerky or excessive force.

steps.title: E — Enter: Internal Rotational Maneuvers
steps.html: Wood's screw or Rubin maneuvers — internal manipulation to rotate the fetal shoulders out of the anterior-posterior alignment causing the impaction, moving them into an oblique plane that fits the pelvic diameters.

steps.title: R — Remove the Posterior Arm
steps.html: Sweep the posterior fetal arm across the chest and deliver it, effectively reducing the shoulder diameter and allowing the anterior shoulder to follow. Retrospective data shows this maneuver carries the highest success rate of any single technique (~86%) — worth knowing even while following the standard escalation order, since some clinicians move to it sooner in a severe or prolonged case.

steps.title: R — Roll the Patient (Gaskin Maneuver)
steps.html: Reposition to hands-and-knees ("all fours") — changes pelvic dimensions and uses gravity differently; effective as a later-stage option, and specifically useful when only a single birth attendant is present, since it can be combined with routine axial traction without needing multiple assistants for positioning.

steps.title: If all maneuvers fail — rescue options
steps.html: Cleidotomy (deliberate fracture of the fetal clavicle), Zavanelli maneuver (cephalic replacement followed by cesarean delivery), or symphysiotomy — reserved for genuinely refractory cases where standard maneuvers haven't worked. If still unresolved, return to the beginning and repeat the full sequence rather than abandoning the algorithm.

blocks.title: Avoid these specific actions at every step
blocks.html: Never apply excessive, downward, or jerky traction on the fetal head/neck, and never apply fundal pressure — both directly increase brachial plexus injury risk without improving the chance of delivery. Time each maneuver for roughly 30–60 seconds before moving to the next; urgency matters, but panic-driven force does not help.

Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when gentle downward guidance of the fetal head fails to accomplish delivery of the anterior shoulder after the head has already delivered, requiring additional obstetric maneuvers. It complicates roughly 0.5–1% of vaginal births, with the underlying mechanism being persistent anterior-posterior alignment of the fetal shoulders as they attempt to enter the pelvic inlet — driven by increased resistance between the vaginal walls and fetus (e.g., macrosomia), a large fetal chest relative to head size (e.g., infants of diabetic mothers), or rapid descent preventing normal rotation of the shoulder diameter.

ACOG and RCOG are both explicit and consistent on a central point: shoulder dystocia is largely unpredictable and unpreventable. Known risk factors (macrosomia, maternal diabetes, prior shoulder dystocia, operative vaginal delivery, labor dystocia) have poor individual and combined predictive value — most cases occur in patients without major identifiable risk factors, and clinical pelvimetry and imaging haven't proven useful for identifying at-risk deliveries in advance. This is why every delivery, not just "high-risk" ones, needs a team prepared to execute this sequence.

rows: The fetal head retracts tightly against the perineum immediately after delivery — the classic, most recognizable presenting sign.
The fetal head fails to rotate to its normal post-delivery position.
Slow, difficult delivery of the face and chin
An early clue preceding full presentation of the dystocia.
Failure of gentle downward guidance to deliver the anterior shoulder
The actual diagnostic criterion — this is what distinguishes shoulder dystocia from a routine, if slightly effortful, delivery.

There's no universally agreed objective threshold (e.g., a specific head-to-body delivery interval) — failure of the head-shoulder maneuver and the turtle sign remain the primary diagnostic criteria in practice, with the number of maneuvers required and any resulting injury serving as the better severity indicators after the fact.

blocks.html:
• Treat every vaginal delivery as a potential shoulder dystocia — given the poor predictive value of risk factors, readiness has to be the default posture, not something activated only for anticipated high-risk deliveries.
  • Consider elective cesarean delivery for specific macrosomia thresholds: estimated fetal weight ≥5,000 g in non-diabetic patients, or ≥4,500 g in patients with diabetes — a reasonable, evidence-based threshold for shifting delivery mode, even though macrosomia alone remains a poor individual predictor.
  • Simulation training and structured protocols measurably improve outcomes — regular obstetric emergency drills (PROMPT-style training, HELPERR-specific simulation) have been shown to improve team communication, maneuver execution, and documentation quality, and are explicitly recommended by ACOG as a way to reduce brachial plexus injury incidence.
  • Have a clear plan for team roles before the emergency, not during it — who calls for help, who times maneuvers, who documents in real time — this coordination is exactly what simulation training is designed to build.
  • Control maternal blood glucose and body weight where modifiable — the primary evidence-supported strategy for genuinely reducing shoulder dystocia risk at the population level, since direct prediction/prevention at the individual delivery level remains elusive.

rows: McRoberts maneuver success rate (as sole maneuver)
Up to 42%; combined with suprapubic pressure, >70% in some series
~86.1% — the highest of any single technique in retrospective comparison
External maneuver success rate (McRoberts + suprapubic alone)
Fetal pH <7.00 in a large case series (n=134), all delivered <8 min
<2% — reinforces that urgency matters, but true crisis timelines are usually measured in single-digit minutes, not seconds
~3.6%, with no permanent brachial plexus injury in that cohort

blocks.html:
Why McRoberts comes first despite not having the highest success rate: it requires no special equipment, no repositioning of the patient beyond leg flexion, and can be performed by the existing bedside team within seconds — the sequencing is optimized for speed-to-attempt and simplicity, not purely for probability-of-success. This is explicitly why ACOG and RCOG recommend it as the first maneuver: a fast, low-complexity intervention that resolves a meaningful share of cases immediately is worth trying before escalating to something that requires more coordination or carries more theoretical risk.

Why posterior arm delivery's higher success rate matters even though it's not first-line: a 2023 critical evaluation found the traditional external-then-internal sequencing "is not based on scientific evidence of its success rates, technical simplicity, or complication rates" — it's a reasonable, historically-derived escalation order, not one validated by head-to-head trials. Knowing that posterior arm delivery outperforms both McRoberts alone and rotational maneuvers is useful context for a clinician managing a severe or rapidly escalating case, even while the standard teaching (and most institutional protocols) still default to the traditional order.

Why excessive traction and fundal pressure are avoided at every single step, not just early on: the brachial plexus stretches when the fetal head and neck are pulled away from an already-fixed, impacted shoulder — force applied in this direction doesn't free the impaction, it just stretches the nerve roots further. Fundal pressure has a similar problem: it can drive the anterior shoulder further into the pubic bone rather than helping deliver it, worsening rather than resolving the impaction.

Why the "unpredictable and unpreventable" framing shapes the entire prevention section: because prepregnancy, antepartum, and intrapartum risk factors all have poor predictive value individually and in combination, focusing preparation on "identify the high-risk patient and prepare only for them" would systematically miss most actual cases. This is exactly why ACOG's practice bulletin frames universal team readiness and simulation training — not risk stratification — as the primary actionable prevention strategy.

Why documentation gets its own dedicated emphasis in every major guideline: the head-to-body delivery interval, the specific sequence and duration of maneuvers attempted, and the team members involved are all medicolegally and clinically significant after the fact — both for understanding what happened if a complication occurred and for informing counseling about future deliveries. This is why ACOG has a specific documentation checklist for this diagnosis rather than leaving it to general delivery note conventions.

sections.title: Complications — Not a Differential, a Watch List

rows: The most frequent neonatal complication — results from overstretching of the C5–6 nerve roots. Most cases are transient; permanent injury is uncommon with prompt, appropriately-executed maneuvers.
Can occur from the impaction itself or from maneuver-related force; generally heals well in neonates.
From the delay in delivery itself — the primary driver behind the urgency of the HELPERR sequence, though most cases still resolve within minutes with low rates of significant acidemia.
One of the most common serious maternal complications — see the dedicated PPH crisis file.
From the maneuvers themselves or the underlying obstruction; the other most common serious maternal complication alongside PPH.

blocks.html:
Immediate neonatal assessment: full exam for brachial plexus function, clavicle/humerus integrity, and standard newborn assessment including cord gas if there's any concern for hypoxic injury during the dystocia.

Maternal assessment: inspect for perineal/vaginal lacerations and assess for postpartum hemorrhage — both recognized complications requiring their own management pathways (see the dedicated PPH crisis file).

Documentation, immediately and in detail: head-to-body delivery interval, sequence and duration of maneuvers attempted, personnel present, and any complications — dictated or entered as a formal operative-style note right after delivery, not deferred. ACOG provides a specific documentation checklist for this purpose.

Institutional notification: notify hospital risk management for any case with infant complications, and use the case (regardless of outcome) as part of ongoing simulation/drill review given how much documented evidence supports simulation training's impact on real-world outcomes.

Future pregnancy counseling: prior shoulder dystocia is itself a risk factor for recurrence — this should be discussed in counseling for subsequent pregnancies, alongside the broader caveat that risk factors (including this one) still carry limited absolute predictive power.

protocols.title: Uterine Rupture
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Obstetric
protocols.subtitle: No reliable predictor and no unequivocal sign — abnormal fetal heart tracing plus abdominal pain is the pattern to catch, and emergency laparotomy is the only definitive treatment once it's suspected.

badges.text: ABNORMAL CTG IS THE MOST CONSISTENT FINDING

protocols.description: No reliable predictor, abnormal CTG as the most consistent finding, why surgery is the only treatment. RCOG/ACOG-aligned — Continuum case cited only as illustrative.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: There is no medical treatment for uterine rupture — this is a surgical emergency from the moment it's suspected, and resuscitation runs in parallel with getting to the OR, not before it.

steps.title: Recognize the pattern and act on suspicion — don't wait for confirmation
steps.html: Abnormal fetal heart tracing (present in roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of cases) combined with new abdominal pain, loss of station, cessation of previously effective contractions, or vaginal bleeding in a patient with a uterine scar or other risk factor should trigger emergency response immediately. There is no reliable single predictor or unequivocal sign — the diagnosis is often made only at emergency laparotomy itself.

steps.title: Call for immediate emergency cesarean delivery / laparotomy
steps.html: This is the only definitive treatment. Every minute of delay worsens both maternal hemorrhage and fetal hypoxic injury — activate the full emergency obstetric team (obstetrics, anesthesia, neonatal) without waiting for further confirmatory findings.

steps.title: Resuscitate in parallel with mobilizing to the OR, not before it
steps.html: Large-bore IV access, type and crossmatch, activate the Massive Transfusion Protocol early given the potential for rapid, severe hemorrhage — see the dedicated MTP crisis file. Do not delay surgical delivery to "finish" resuscitation first; the bleeding source needs surgical control.

steps.title: Damage control resuscitation principles apply
steps.html: Favor blood products over crystalloid, accept permissive hypotension until surgical hemostasis is achieved, and avoid over-resuscitating with fluid — particularly if the patient has any concurrent respiratory compromise, where aggressive volume can precipitate transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO — see the dedicated Transfusion Reactions crisis file).

steps.title: Surgical decision: repair vs. hysterectomy
steps.html: Made intraoperatively based on the extent of the rupture, ongoing hemorrhage control, and the patient's desire for future fertility where feasible — hysterectomy may be necessary for extensive rupture or uncontrollable hemorrhage.

steps.title: Neonatal resuscitation team should be present at delivery
steps.html: Given the fetal hypoxic risk from placental separation/rupture, the newborn frequently requires immediate resuscitation and NICU-level care.

steps.title: In an incidental, asymptomatic dehiscence found after successful VBAC
steps.html: Routine uterine exploration after an uncomplicated VBAC is not recommended in a hemodynamically stable patient with no abnormal bleeding. If dehiscence is identified incidentally and the patient is stable, blood analysis to exclude intraperitoneal bleeding is reasonable; surgical repair of an asymptomatic dehiscence found this way is not recommended, since it hasn't been shown to improve outcomes. This is a genuinely different clinical scenario from a symptomatic, actively bleeding rupture — don't conflate the two.

blocks.title: This isn't the version of the emergency that always happens in a hospital
blocks.html: A 2026 case report described catastrophic hemorrhage from uterine rupture managed entirely by a critical care transport team — simultaneously hypotensive and hypoxemic, with damage control resuscitation principles applied en route and REBOA considered (though not deployed) as a bridge option. That single case doesn't establish transport-specific standard of care, but it's a useful reminder that the same principles above — hemorrhage control priority, permissive hypotension, TACO vigilance — apply even when the OR isn't thirty seconds away.

Uterine rupture is a complete separation through all three layers of the uterine wall (endometrium, myometrium, serosa), most often occurring during labor in a patient with a prior cesarean scar attempting trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC). It's distinct from uterine dehiscence — an incomplete separation with intact serosa that may be found incidentally and doesn't carry the same acute hemorrhagic risk. The two are frequently conflated in older literature, which is worth knowing when interpreting historical rupture-rate statistics.

Two risk populations exist with different mechanisms: those with a prior myometrial scar (from cesarean delivery or other uterine surgery — the dominant modern population, given roughly 90% of ruptures occur in a scarred uterus) and those with an unscarred uterus (much rarer, associated with obstructed labor, uterine overdistension, grand multiparity, or trauma). Uterine rupture carries genuine mortality risk — maternal mortality under 1% and perinatal mortality in the range of 3–6% of cases in the TOLAC population specifically.

rows: The single most consistent finding, present in roughly 66–76% of confirmed cases — variable or late decelerations, bradycardia, or loss of previously reassuring tracing.
Often occurs alongside abnormal CTG rather than in isolation — over half of cases present with a combination of findings, most commonly abnormal CTG plus abdominal pain.
Loss of fetal station / presenting part
The fetus receding from a previously engaged position on exam.
Cessation of previously effective uterine contractions
A labor that was progressing suddenly stalling or the contraction pattern changing abnormally.
Can be present or notably absent — bleeding may be entirely intraperitoneal, which is part of why this diagnosis is so easy to miss until frank hemodynamic instability develops.
Can be a late finding — don't wait for hemodynamic collapse to act on the CTG and pain pattern above.
More than 90% of ruptures occur during labor, with peak incidence around 4–5 cm cervical dilation; roughly 18% occur in the second stage, and about 8% are identified only after vaginal delivery.

blocks.html: There are no reliable predictors and no unequivocal clinical sign. Physicians must maintain a high index of suspicion in any at-risk patient — particularly with fetal bradycardia or other fetal distress — because the diagnosis is frequently confirmed only at emergency laparotomy itself, not established beforehand by any specific test or finding.

• TOLAC should only be offered where immediate emergency cesarean and blood transfusion capability exist — ACOG specifically recommends Level 1 obstetric centers with a clinician capable of performing emergency cesarean immediately available throughout active labor, along with anesthesia support.
  • Careful patient selection and counseling before TOLAC: prior uterine incision type matters enormously — classical (vertical) and T-shaped incisions carry meaningfully higher rupture risk than the standard low-transverse incision, and a prior classical incision is generally a contraindication to TOLAC altogether.
  • Induction and augmentation raise risk further: studies show three to five times more ruptures among induced TOLAC patients compared to spontaneous labor onset; prostaglandin agents (misoprostol, dinoprostone) carry additional risk and require particular caution in this population.
  • Continuous fetal monitoring throughout TOLAC labor — given that abnormal CTG is the most consistent early warning finding, continuous rather than intermittent monitoring is standard practice.
  • Know the modifying risk factors: interpregnancy interval <12–18 months, unknown previous uterine incision type, poor healing of a prior scar, prior preterm cesarean, and multiple previous cesareans all raise risk further and should factor into the TOLAC counseling conversation.
  • Ensure MTP and hemorrhage protocol readiness on any unit offering TOLAC — see the dedicated MTP and Postpartum Hemorrhage crisis files for the resuscitation infrastructure this diagnosis can suddenly demand.

~0.87% vs. ~0.09% (meaningfully elevated odds, though absolute risk remains low in both groups)

blocks.html:
Why there's no medical treatment and surgery is the entire answer: a complete separation through all three uterine layers is a mechanical, structural problem — no drug closes the defect or stops the hemorrhage it produces. This is fundamentally different from most obstetric hemorrhage causes (atony, for instance) that respond to pharmacologic escalation before surgery becomes necessary; here, surgical control is the first-line and only definitive treatment from the moment the diagnosis is seriously entertained.

Why abnormal CTG is weighted so heavily despite not being universally present: fetal heart rate directly reflects placental perfusion, which is immediately compromised when the uterine wall separates and disrupts the maternal-fetal interface. This makes CTG change one of the fastest available signals of a process that otherwise has no reliable external sign — which is exactly why continuous monitoring during TOLAC labor is standard practice rather than an optional add-on.

Why vaginal bleeding can be absent even in a severe rupture: if the rupture communicates primarily with the peritoneal cavity rather than the vaginal canal, blood accumulates intra-abdominally rather than presenting externally — meaning the absence of visible bleeding provides false reassurance rather than ruling out a severe, ongoing hemorrhage. This is part of why the diagnosis leans so heavily on the CTG-plus-pain pattern rather than waiting for visible blood loss.

Why induction/augmentation and prior classical incisions both raise risk through a related mechanism: a classical (vertical) incision crosses the more actively contractile upper uterine segment, while induction/augmentation increases the force and frequency of contractions across the entire uterine wall — both increase mechanical stress specifically at the weakest point (the scar, or an already more vulnerable upper-segment incision), which is the direct physical basis for why these are the dominant modifiable and structural risk factors identified across every major society's guidance.

Why the dehiscence-vs-rupture distinction genuinely changes management, not just terminology: a dehiscence with intact serosa doesn't carry the same acute hemorrhage risk as a full-thickness rupture, since the outer layer is still containing the uterine contents. This is why an incidentally found, asymptomatic dehiscence in a stable patient doesn't need surgical repair — the intervention wouldn't improve an outcome that's already benign, whereas the same finding with active bleeding or hemodynamic instability represents a genuinely different, surgical emergency.

rows: Can produce a similar picture of abdominal pain and abnormal CTG; ultrasound and the absence of a prior uterine scar/TOLAC context can help distinguish, though the two can be difficult to separate acutely and both may require emergency delivery regardless.
The key distinguishing feature is a change from the patient's baseline pattern — new, different, or unusually severe pain, or contractions abruptly stopping, rather than expected labor discomfort.
See Rationale above — a fundamentally lower-acuity finding when asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable, though the distinction is sometimes only made at surgical exploration.
Painless vaginal bleeding with fetal heart rate abnormality, typically at rupture of membranes — a different mechanism (fetal, not maternal, hemorrhage) but a similarly acute fetal emergency.

Sudden collapse with DIC-driven coagulopathy rather than a mechanical uterine wall defect — see the dedicated AFE crisis file; can be difficult to distinguish acutely from a severely hemorrhaging rupture.
Postpartum hemorrhage from atony/trauma/retained tissue (after vaginal delivery)
See the dedicated PPH crisis file and its 4 T's framework — uterine rupture identified after vaginal delivery specifically falls under the "Trauma" category there.

blocks.html:
Confirmation is intraoperative: there is no reliable preoperative test that confirms the diagnosis with certainty — emergency laparotomy serves as both the diagnostic and therapeutic step simultaneously.

Postoperative monitoring: ICU-level care for significant hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability; ongoing hemoglobin/coagulation monitoring given the massive transfusion potential.

Neonatal disposition: NICU admission is common given the hypoxic risk from acute placental separation; the neonatal team's presence at delivery should be anticipated, not arranged reactively.

Future pregnancy counseling: a history of uterine rupture significantly changes counseling for future pregnancies — repeat cesarean delivery before labor onset is generally recommended rather than attempting TOLAC again, given the elevated recurrence risk in a uterus that has already ruptured once.

Debrief: given how rapidly this diagnosis can move from subtle CTG change to major hemorrhage, structured post-event review helps refine institutional TOLAC monitoring protocols and reinforces the recognition pattern for the next case.

protocols.title: Croup vs. Epiglottitis
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Pediatric / Neonatal
protocols.subtitle: Dexamethasone goes to nearly every croup case regardless of severity — but the moment the picture looks like epiglottitis, the entire approach to the airway exam flips, since the wrong kind of look can trigger the obstruction you're trying to avoid.

badges.text: DON'T EXAMINE THE THROAT IF EPIGLOTTITIS IS SUSPECTED

protocols.description: Why the airway exam itself is dangerous in suspected epiglottitis, why dexamethasone goes to nearly all croup regardless of severity, epi's rebound explained. AAP/CPS-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Croup gets treated at the bedside. Suspected epiglottitis gets managed by keeping the child calm and untouched until the airway can be secured in a controlled setting.

steps.title: If epiglottitis is suspected — do not examine the throat or agitate the child
steps.html: No tongue depressor, no forced supine positioning, no IV attempts that provoke crying. Keep the child calm, upright, and with a caregiver. Any of these can precipitate sudden, complete airway obstruction in a critically swollen epiglottis — this is the single most important branch point in the entire algorithm.

steps.title: Suspected epiglottitis — secure the airway in a controlled setting
steps.html: Move immediately toward controlled intubation in the OR with anesthesia and ENT/surgical airway backup immediately available — direct visualization and intubation should happen where a surgical airway (cricothyrotomy/tracheostomy) can be performed instantly if intubation fails, not at the bedside.

steps.title: Confirmed/suspected epiglottitis — IV antibiotics after the airway is secured
steps.html: Broad-spectrum coverage (e.g., ceftriaxone) targeting the historically dominant pathogen, Haemophilus influenzae type B, along with other possible bacterial causes. Blood cultures before antibiotics if it doesn't delay airway management.

steps.title: Croup — dexamethasone for essentially all patients, regardless of severity
steps.html: 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM/IV (max 10–12 mg), single dose — given the least invasive way possible, preferably oral. Lower doses (0.15–0.3 mg/kg) have also shown effectiveness in mild-moderate disease. Nebulized budesonide is a reasonable alternative if the child is vomiting, in severe distress, or the family declines systemic steroid.

steps.title: Croup — nebulized racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest or moderate-severe distress
steps.html: Racemic epinephrine 2.25%, 0.05 mL/kg (max 0.5 mL), or L-epinephrine 1:1,000 at 0.5 mL/kg if racemic isn't available. Clinical effect apparent within 10–30 minutes, sustained roughly 1–2 hours before dissipating.

steps.title: Croup — observe 2–4 hours after epinephrine before discharge
steps.html: Watching specifically for symptoms returning to their pre-treatment baseline as the epinephrine effect wanes — not a distinct "rebound" phenomenon, but a return to baseline severity while waiting for the slower-acting steroid to take over (see Rationale).

steps.title: Croup — hypoxia is a red flag, not an expected finding
steps.html: Hypoxemia is uncommon in croup — its presence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis (bacterial tracheitis, foreign body, lower respiratory tract process) rather than being treated as simply severe croup.

steps.title: Croup — mist therapy and heliox are not routinely recommended
steps.html: Both have been studied without demonstrating a clear added benefit over standard therapy — don't substitute either for dexamethasone and epinephrine when indicated.

blocks.title: The exam itself is the danger in suspected epiglottitis
blocks.html: A brief, gentle look with a tongue depressor is routine and safe in croup. In suspected epiglottitis, that same maneuver — or crying from an unwanted IV attempt, or lying the child flat — can trigger sudden complete obstruction of an airway that was tenuously patent seconds before. When epiglottitis is on the differential, the safest exam is often no exam at all until the airway team is ready.

Croup (viral laryngotracheitis) is inflammation of the subglottic larynx, trachea, and bronchi — most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus — producing the characteristic barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor, typically in children 6 months to 6 years, with peak incidence in October–November. Most cases are mild and self-limited; a small proportion progress to significant respiratory distress requiring more aggressive intervention.

Epiglottitis is inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures, historically caused predominantly by Haemophilus influenzae type B and carrying high mortality before the Hib vaccine era. Widespread Hib vaccination has dramatically reduced incidence and produced a notable epidemiologic shift — the disease now presents more often in older children and adults, and other pathogens (Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus) have become relatively more prominent among the remaining cases.

rows: Gradual, over 1–2 days, often preceded by a viral prodrome (rhinorrhea, low-grade fever, sore throat)
Notably absent — this contrast is one of the more useful bedside clues
Muffled, "hot potato" quality; may have dysphonia or aphonia
Tripod/sniffing position, drooling, refusal to lie flat
Dysphagia, drooling from inability/refusal to swallow secretions
Comfortable between coughing episodes in mild-moderate disease
Historically young children; now shifted toward older children and adults post-Hib vaccination

blocks.html:
• Croup is a clinical diagnosis — radiography and laboratory testing are not routinely needed and should be reserved for atypical presentations or when an alternate diagnosis is suspected.
  • Have both racemic and L-epinephrine nebulizer setups available — L-epinephrine 1:1,000 is a reasonable substitute where racemic isn't stocked (e.g., some EMS settings), though its duration of action may run somewhat longer.
  • If epiglottitis is even moderately suspected, alert anesthesia/ENT/OR before attempting any exam — the entire safety strategy depends on having a controlled airway setup ready before the child is examined or manipulated, not assembled reactively after a bedside look goes badly.
  • Hib vaccination remains the single most effective prevention strategy for classic pediatric epiglottitis — confirm vaccination status as part of the history, recognizing that under-immunized children remain at meaningfully higher risk.
  • Recognize atypical/adult presentations — given the epidemiologic shift, don't anchor exclusively on the classic toxic-appearing young child picture; epiglottitis in an adult or partially-vaccinated older child can be easy to miss if it isn't actively considered.

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM/IV, max 10–12 mg (0.15–0.3 mg/kg also shown effective in mild-moderate disease)
Effect apparent 10–30 min; sustained ~1–2 hours before dissipating
~6 hours — bridges the gap after epinephrine's effect fades
Toxic appearance, high fever, poor response to racemic epinephrine, rapid deterioration

blocks.html:
Why dexamethasone goes to essentially every croup patient regardless of severity: trial evidence consistently shows reduced return visits, hospitalization, and intubation rates even in mild croup — and a single dose of a well-tolerated steroid carries minimal downside compared to the chronic-exposure concerns that make clinicians reserve steroids more selectively in other conditions. The favorable risk-benefit ratio at a single low dose, combined with a consistent benefit signal even in mild disease, is why universal treatment (rather than a severity-based threshold) became the standard rather than the exception.

Why oral, IM, and IV dexamethasone are considered roughly equivalent despite different pharmacokinetics: all three routes achieve adequate systemic drug levels to produce the anti-inflammatory effect that matters clinically — the route choice is driven by practical tolerability (a child who can swallow gets oral; one who's vomiting or can't tolerate PO gets IM) rather than by a meaningful efficacy difference between routes.

Why the return of symptoms after epinephrine wears off isn't a distinct "rebound" phenomenon: nebulized epinephrine works through adrenergic vasoconstriction of the precapillary arterioles, reducing capillary hydrostatic pressure and pulling fluid out of the edematous laryngeal mucosa — a mechanical, physiologic effect that lasts only as long as the drug is active. It doesn't touch the underlying inflammatory process driving the edema in the first place; once the vasoconstriction fades, the mucosa simply returns to whatever degree of swelling the ongoing inflammation still supports. This is why the observation period exists — to catch a return to baseline severity, not to watch for a novel worsening — and it's also exactly why epinephrine and dexamethasone are given together: epinephrine buys the first hour or two, and dexamethasone (acting over the following several hours) is what actually resolves the underlying inflammation during that window.

Why the entire airway approach flips for suspected epiglottitis: a croup exam — even a brief, mildly uncomfortable look with a tongue depressor — poses minimal risk to an airway with a wide margin before complete obstruction. A critically swollen epiglottis has essentially no such margin: agitation, forced positioning, or direct manipulation can trigger laryngospasm or mechanical obstruction of an already critically narrowed airway with almost no warning. This is why the entire management strategy for suspected epiglottitis is built around avoiding any exam or manipulation until the airway team, OR, and surgical airway backup are all ready — the diagnostic exam itself is treated as a controlled procedure, not a bedside assessment.

Why the epidemiologic shift in epiglottitis matters clinically, not just historically: Hib vaccination has made the classic toxic-appearing young child with epiglottitis a genuinely rare presentation compared to the pre-vaccine era — but this means clinicians today have less frequent exposure to the diagnosis and may be more likely to encounter it in an atypical population (older children, adults, under-immunized patients) where it isn't the first thing that comes to mind. Lower baseline familiarity combined with a shifted age distribution is exactly the kind of situation where genuine diagnostic vigilance matters more, not less, even though the disease itself has become considerably rarer.

rows: Toxic appearance, high fever, and poor response to racemic epinephrine in a patient who otherwise looked like croup — suspect this specifically when croup-directed treatment fails or the patient deteriorates rapidly.
Sudden onset without a viral prodrome, often with a choking history; may have asymmetric breath sounds. Consider especially in a toddler with no preceding illness.
Fever, drooling, neck stiffness, lymphadenopathy, and variable toxicity — but the characteristic barking cough of croup is usually absent.
Congenital airway anomalies (laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, vascular ring)
Consider with recurrent croup-like episodes, especially without a clear viral trigger, or stridor present from early infancy rather than an acute new onset.

Rapid onset following an exposure/trigger, often with urticaria, hypotension, or other systemic findings — treated per the dedicated Anaphylaxis crisis file rather than the croup/epiglottitis pathway.
Pseudomembrane formation, distinct systemic toxicity — consider specifically in under-vaccinated populations or travel history to endemic regions.

blocks.html:
Croup — diagnostic testing: generally unnecessary; reserve radiography (lateral neck X-ray showing the classic "steeple sign") for cases with an atypical presentation or incomplete/poor response to racemic epinephrine after 2–3 doses.

Croup — discharge criteria: no stridor at rest, normal pulse oximetry, normal color and alertness, demonstrated ability to tolerate oral fluids, and reliable caregivers with clear return precautions. Admit patients requiring ≥3 racemic epinephrine doses, those with persistent stridor at rest, poor oral tolerance, significant dehydration, or an unreliable home situation.

Epiglottitis — confirmation: made under controlled, direct visualization during the airway-securing procedure itself — not established beforehand through bedside exam, given the risks described above. Blood cultures once the airway is secure.

Epiglottitis — disposition: ICU admission is standard once the airway is secured, given the ongoing need for close monitoring, continued antibiotics, and staged extubation planning once swelling resolves.

Both conditions: reassess severity at regular intervals (every 1–4 hours depending on acuity) throughout the observation period, since croup severity can fluctuate meaningfully within a single encounter.

protocols.title: Neonatal Resuscitation (NRP)
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Pediatric / Neonatal
protocols.subtitle: Ventilation is the single most important intervention — heart rate is the readout, not a separate problem. Real delivery-room data shows epinephrine timing lags guideline targets by minutes, which is exactly why anticipation and pre-drawn doses matter.

badges.text: PPV BEFORE COMPRESSIONS, COMPRESSIONS BEFORE EPINEPHRINE

protocols.description: Why ventilation, not epinephrine, is the core intervention; real-world epi timing lags guideline targets by minutes. AHA/AAP 9th edition (Oct 2025)-aligned.

sections.title: The NRP Algorithm
sections.tagline: Ventilation, then compressions, then epinephrine — in that order, and never skip ahead. Reassess heart rate at every step before escalating.

steps.title: Ask three questions at birth
steps.html: Term gestation? Good tone? Breathing or crying? If yes to all — routine care, skin-to-skin, deferred cord clamping ≥60 seconds. If no to any — move to the warmer and begin initial steps.

steps.title: Initial steps, within the Golden Minute
steps.html: Warm, dry, stimulate, position the airway, suction only if needed. Complete this within the first 60 seconds of life. If apneic, gasping, or heart rate <100 bpm — begin positive pressure ventilation (PPV) immediately, without waiting for the full minute to elapse if the baby clearly needs it sooner.

steps.title: PPV — the single most important intervention
steps.html: 40–60 breaths/min, reassess heart rate and chest movement after 30 seconds. If the chest isn't moving, work through the MR SOPA corrective steps: Mask adjustment, Reposition airway, Suction mouth/nose, Open mouth, Pressure increase, Alternate airway — in that order, before assuming ventilation has failed.

steps.title: Chest compressions if HR <60 after 30 seconds of effective PPV
steps.html: Secure an alternate airway (ETT or laryngeal mask) first if not already in place. Compressions at a 3:1 ratio with ventilation (90 compressions : 30 breaths per minute — 120 total events/min), 100% oxygen. Continue for a full 60 seconds of coordinated compressions and ventilation before reassessing.

steps.title: Epinephrine if HR remains <60 after 60 seconds of coordinated compressions + PPV
steps.html: IV/IO 0.01–0.03 mg/kg of 1:10,000 solution (a simplified 0.02 mg/kg starting dose is commonly taught for speed and consistency), preferably via umbilical venous catheter. Repeat every 3–5 minutes if heart rate remains <60. If IV/IO access isn't yet available, endotracheal epinephrine at a higher dose (0.05–0.1 mg/kg) is reasonable as a bridge — less reliably absorbed, so don't treat it as equivalent to the IV route once access is achieved.

steps.title: Anticipate epinephrine need before you reach the threshold
steps.html: If the trajectory suggests epinephrine may be needed, one team member should begin placing a UVC while others continue PPV and compressions — don't wait until the 60-second mark to start line placement.

steps.title: Volume expansion for suspected blood loss unresponsive to epinephrine
steps.html: Normal saline 10 mL/kg IV/IO when there's a history or exam consistent with blood loss (placental abruption, cord accident, twin-twin transfusion) and no response to epinephrine.

steps.title: No heart rate response by 20 minutes — discuss redirection of care
steps.html: A specific, evidence-anchored threshold for having the conversation with the team and family about continuing versus redirecting care, once every step above has been executed effectively.

blocks.title: Guideline timing and real-world timing don't match — plan for that gap
blocks.html: A retrospective delivery-room study found endotracheal epinephrine given at a mean of nearly 4 minutes, and IV epinephrine at a mean of nearly 11 minutes, after chest compressions began — far beyond the roughly 90-second target implied by the algorithm. This isn't a reason to abandon the timing targets; it's the specific reason anticipatory UVC placement and pre-calculated dosing are built into current guidance.

The Neonatal Resuscitation Program, first developed in 1987 and now in its 9th edition (jointly released by the AHA and AAP in October 2025), provides a standardized, sequential approach to supporting newborns transitioning from intrauterine to extrauterine life. Roughly 85% of term newborns transition spontaneously with little or no assistance; about 10% require some form of assistance (typically PPV); and only about 1% require intensive measures — intubation, chest compressions, or epinephrine.

The physiology here is fundamentally different from adult cardiac arrest: neonatal bradycardia is almost always a downstream consequence of inadequate lung aeration or hypoxemia, not a primary cardiac electrical or structural problem. This is why the entire algorithm is built around establishing effective ventilation first — heart rate serves as the readout of whether ventilation is working, not a separate parameter to be fixed independently with drugs.

rows: The single most important indicator of adequate resuscitation response — assessed by auscultation, with ECG monitoring placed early for any resuscitation beyond routine care, since it's faster and more reliable than pulse oximetry for rapid heart rate assessment.
Preductal SpO₂ targets by minute of life
1 min: 60–65% · 2 min: 65–70% · 3 min: 70–75% · 4 min: 75–80% · 5 min: 80–85% · 10 min: 85–95% — placed on the right hand/wrist specifically to reflect preductal saturation.
Assessed alongside gestational age at the initial "three questions" step — poor tone or absent/gasping respiration triggers immediate movement to the warmer.
The direct sign that ventilation is actually effective — absence of chest movement triggers the MR SOPA corrective sequence rather than simply continuing an ineffective technique.

No longer used to determine whether to begin resuscitation, since resuscitation often starts before the 1-minute mark — it remains useful as a structured post-hoc description of status and response to resuscitation, not a decision-making trigger.

blocks.html:
• Antenatal risk factor review and team briefing before every delivery — not just anticipated high-risk ones, given how quickly an apparently low-risk delivery can change trajectory.
  • Equipment check every time: preheated warmer, functioning suction, appropriately sized masks/airway equipment, pulse oximeter, ECG leads, and a UVC kit immediately accessible.
  • Identify the most qualified team member to lead and to perform intubation before delivery, not in the moment.
  • Pre-calculate and, when anticipated, pre-draw the epinephrine dose for the specific estimated newborn weight — this directly targets the real-world timing delay described above rather than leaving dose calculation to happen under pressure at the 60-second mark.
  • Consider laryngeal mask airway as an alternative secondary device for infants >34 weeks gestation when intubation isn't immediately successful — a validated, less invasive option increasingly incorporated into national guidelines.
  • Deferred cord clamping (≥60 seconds) for infants transitioning normally — this applies specifically to the population not requiring immediate resuscitation; don't let it delay initiating resuscitative steps in an infant who does need them.
  • Meconium-stained fluid: no routine endotracheal suctioning of non-vigorous infants — proceed directly to PPV per the standard algorithm rather than performing tracheal suctioning first, a practice reversed since 2016 and reaffirmed by more recent outcome data (see Rationale).

sections.title: Drug Doses — Numbers to Know (In Place of "Labs")

rows: Duration of coordinated compressions + PPV before epinephrine
0.01–0.03 mg/kg of 1:10,000 (0.02 mg/kg often taught as a simplified starting dose)
0.05–0.1 mg/kg — less reliably absorbed than IV/IO
10 mL/kg IV/IO for suspected blood loss unresponsive to epinephrine
Real-world mean time to endotracheal epinephrine (from start of compressions)
Real-world mean time to IV epinephrine (from start of compressions)
Increased death/morbidity risk per 30-second delay in initiating PPV
No-response threshold for discussing redirection of care

blocks.html:
Why ventilation, not epinephrine or compressions, is the single most important intervention: neonatal bradycardia at birth is overwhelmingly a consequence of inadequate lung aeration and resulting hypoxemia, not a primary cardiac rhythm or structural problem. Once effective ventilation is established, heart rate typically responds quickly on its own — which is exactly why heart rate is described as "the most important indicator that effective ventilation is occurring" rather than a separate target requiring its own independent fix. This is the core physiologic reason the entire algorithm is sequenced the way it is, and it's fundamentally different from adult cardiac arrest logic, where compressions and defibrillation take priority.

Why the real-world epinephrine timing gap matters as much as the guideline number itself: the algorithm calls for epinephrine at roughly 60–90 seconds after compressions begin if there's no response — but delivery-room data shows actual administration often lags this by many minutes, largely because umbilical line placement and weight-based dose calculation both take genuine time under pressure, especially in a low-frequency, high-stakes event that individual teams may not perform often. This is precisely why current guidance specifically recommends anticipatory UVC placement and pre-calculating the dose the moment the resuscitation trajectory suggests epinephrine may become necessary — the guideline isn't naive about this gap, it's built with the gap in mind.

Why the meconium-suctioning reversal is a genuinely instructive example, not just a historical footnote: the older practice of routine endotracheal suctioning in non-vigorous meconium-stained infants was based on a plausible mechanistic theory — removing meconium below the cords should prevent aspiration syndrome. Subsequent evidence, including more recent outcome data, found suctioned infants were actually more likely to be diagnosed with meconium aspiration syndrome and persistent pulmonary hypertension, and more likely to need surfactant — suggesting the suctioning procedure itself (via delayed PPV initiation and vagally-mediated bradycardia/trauma risk) caused net harm despite its intuitive rationale. This reinforces a theme running through the whole NRP algorithm: delaying PPV to perform an additional procedure is very rarely the right trade, even when that procedure sounds reasonable in isolation.

Why 20 minutes is named specifically rather than left to open-ended judgment: this reflects accumulated outcomes data showing extremely poor neurologic survival beyond this duration of fully-optimized, unresponsive resuscitation. Naming a concrete, evidence-anchored number gives teams and families a specific point to have the redirection-of-care conversation, rather than leaving an inherently difficult decision to be improvised in the moment with no anchor.

Why deferred cord clamping is scoped specifically to the "transitioning normally" population: continued placental blood flow during deferred clamping improves iron stores and reduces certain complications, but this benefit is only relevant to an infant who doesn't need immediate resuscitative steps. The guideline draws this line deliberately — prioritizing prompt initiation of resuscitation for infants who need it, rather than universally deferring clamping regardless of the infant's condition at birth.

sections.title: Reversible Causes of Persistent Bradycardia (In Place of Differentials)

rows: Reassess chest movement and airway position — work back through MR SOPA rather than assuming the airway/technique is adequate just because PPV has "been started."
Consider if chest movement is asymmetric or ventilation remains ineffective despite corrective steps — needle decompression per the same principles in the dedicated Tension Pneumothorax crisis file.
Placental abruption, cord accident, twin-twin transfusion — treat with volume expansion as above.
Congenital heart disease or other structural anomaly
Consider if the infant remains unresponsive to a well-executed resuscitation with no other identifiable cause.
Reflects prolonged, severe hypoxic-ischemic insult rather than a distinct primary cause — responds to continued effective ventilation and perfusion rather than a specific separate treatment.
From significant fetomaternal hemorrhage or similar — overlaps with the hypovolemia category above and responds to the same volume expansion approach.

blocks.html:
Glucose monitoring: hypoglycemia is a real risk after any significant resuscitation — check and correct proactively.

Temperature management: avoid hyperthermia specifically, which worsens outcomes after a hypoxic-ischemic insult; therapeutic hypothermia should be considered per a separate dedicated protocol for infants meeting criteria for moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.

Cord gas analysis to characterize the degree of acidosis at delivery, informing both immediate management and later neurologic prognostication discussions.

Disposition: NICU admission for any infant requiring PPV beyond the initial steps, chest compressions, or epinephrine — this is not a routine well-baby-nursery trajectory once significant resuscitation has occurred.

Debrief: team debriefing after every significant resuscitation is explicitly part of current guidance — given how infrequently individual teams perform the more advanced steps (compressions, epinephrine, UVC placement), structured post-event review is one of the few realistic ways to keep real-world execution closer to guideline-target timing.

protocols.title: Pediatric Septic Shock
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Pediatric / Neonatal
protocols.subtitle: The fluid recommendation genuinely depends on which hospital you're in — the FEAST trial's early-stopped-for-harm result reshaped resource-limited guidance in a way high-resource protocols never had to reckon with.

badges.text: FLUID STRATEGY DIVERGES BY RESOURCE SETTING

protocols.description: Why fluid strategy genuinely diverges by resource setting, the FEAST trial's early-stopped-for-harm result, why hypotension is a late warning sign. 2026 SSC pediatric guidelines-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Fluid dosing depends heavily on whether ICU-level support is actually available — reassess after every bolus rather than pushing volume reflexively.

steps.title: Recognize using the Phoenix Sepsis Score
steps.html: A score ≥2 in a child with suspected infection defines sepsis; septic shock requires that plus cardiovascular dysfunction (cardiovascular sub-score ≥1). This 2024 SCCM-developed criterion replaced older, less data-driven definitions.

steps.title: Empiric antimicrobial therapy — within 1 hour for septic shock
steps.html: A strong recommendation despite very-low-certainty evidence, reflecting the severity of delay in this population. For probable sepsis without shock: a time-limited period of rapid evaluation is reasonable, with antimicrobials ideally within 3 hours once concern is substantiated — balancing urgency against the real risk of unnecessary antibiotics in a population with substantial symptom overlap with other conditions.

steps.title: Fluid resuscitation — ICU-available setting
steps.html: Up to 40–60 mL/kg in bolus fluid (10–20 mL/kg per bolus) over the first hour, titrated to clinical markers of cardiac output, and discontinued if signs of fluid overload develop. Reassess hemodynamic status after every single bolus rather than running a fixed total volume on autopilot.

steps.title: Fluid resuscitation — no ICU availability, no hypotension
steps.html: A strong recommendation against fluid bolus therapy (high certainty) — start maintenance fluids instead. This is a direct consequence of the FEAST trial (see Rationale) and represents a genuine, evidence-driven divergence from high-resource practice, not an oversight.

steps.title: Fluid resuscitation — no ICU availability, with hypotension
steps.html: Up to 40 mL/kg in bolus fluid (10–20 mL/kg per bolus) over the first hour is suggested over no bolus therapy — a more permissive threshold than the "no hypotension" scenario above, but still more conservative than the ICU-available pathway.

steps.title: Fluid choice
steps.html: Balanced/buffered crystalloids (lactated Ringer's, Hartmann's) preferred over 0.9% saline, though saline is a suitable alternative if balanced solutions aren't available. Prefer saline specifically for hyponatremia or concern for elevated intracranial pressure (e.g., CNS infection). Crystalloid preferred over albumin for initial resuscitation.

steps.title: Vasoactive support if shock persists despite fluids
steps.html: Epinephrine or norepinephrine are both reasonable first-line choices — current evidence doesn't clearly favor one over the other, and this remains an active area of ongoing trial investigation. Titrate to clinical perfusion endpoints and blood pressure targets rather than a fixed dose.

steps.title: Hydrocortisone — situational, not routine
steps.html: Suggested against if fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy have already restored hemodynamic stability. Either hydrocortisone or no hydrocortisone is reasonable specifically when fluids and vasopressors have not restored stability — both options carry low-quality evidence, reflecting genuine clinical equipoise rather than a clear answer.

blocks.title: Glucose control: avoid tight targets
blocks.html: A moderate-certainty recommendation exists against targeting blood glucose ≤140 mg/dL in pediatric septic shock — the guideline panel was unable to specify an alternative target range given insufficient evidence, but is clear that tight glycemic control specifically is not the answer here.

Pediatric sepsis and septic shock account for an estimated 3 million+ child deaths annually worldwide, with the highest burden falling on children under 5 and disproportionately in low-resource settings. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign pediatric guidelines — 61 recommendation statements, 20 new and 13 updated from the 2020 edition — adopt the Phoenix Sepsis Score as the current data-driven definition, replacing prior consensus-based criteria, and explicitly acknowledge that most aspects of pediatric sepsis care still rest on relatively low-quality evidence despite meaningful expansion of the evidence base since 2020.

A defining feature of this guideline cycle is that fluid resuscitation recommendations diverge by healthcare system resource level — a distinction rarely made this explicitly in other resuscitation guidelines in this series. This isn't hedging; it reflects a genuine, trial-demonstrated difference in the risk-benefit calculus between settings with and without intensive care and mechanical ventilation capability.

rows: Delayed capillary refill (>3 sec), weak/thready pulses, cool mottled extremities, narrow pulse pressure — reflects predominant vasoconstriction with reduced cardiac output. More common in younger children.
Flash capillary refill, bounding pulses, warm extremities, wide pulse pressure — reflects predominant vasodilation, more closely resembling the classic adult septic shock picture.

A late finding in pediatric shock — children compensate remarkably well via tachycardia and vasoconstriction, meaning normal blood pressure does not rule out significant, ongoing shock. "Compensated shock" (severely impaired perfusion without hypotension) is the more clinically relevant early category.
Lethargy, irritability, poor interaction — an important and sometimes earlier clue than hemodynamic numbers alone.

A 0-hour score performed better than conventional vital signs at predicting need for vasoactive support/mechanical ventilation and early mortality in one observational study — though evidence certainty was judged too low to formally recommend for routine monitoring.

blocks.html:
• Have a clear institutional threshold for ICU/mechanical ventilation availability — the entire fluid strategy above depends on knowing which resource category your setting falls into, not defaulting to the higher-resource protocol regardless of actual capability.
  • Empiric antibiotic protocols pre-identified by likely source — given the 1-hour target for septic shock, having a standing broad-spectrum regimen ready to start immediately (rather than deliberating in the moment) directly supports meeting that timeline.
  • POCUS availability — a new conditional 2026 recommendation supports cardiac and lung point-of-care ultrasound to guide resuscitation where resources allow, though its clinical-outcome impact is still being evaluated.
  • Blood culture collection technique matters — attention to proper collection limits contamination and unnecessary downstream diagnostic/therapeutic cascades; in low-resource settings, a single culture set has shown similar yield to multiple sets per recent evidence.
  • Plan for post-sepsis follow-up before discharge — 30–40% of children surviving PICU-level sepsis treatment may face lasting health issues, a newly emphasized focus area in the current guideline cycle.

sections.title: Rationale for Pediatric Septic Shock Management

blocks.html:
Why fluid strategy genuinely diverges by resource setting rather than being a single universal recommendation: the FEAST trial, conducted specifically in resource-poor African hospitals without routine access to mechanical ventilation or inotropic support, was stopped early after finding significantly excess mortality in children randomized to a fluid bolus compared to controls (relative risk 1.45) — a result consistent across sepsis, malaria, coma, acidosis, and severe anemia subgroups. This is a genuinely different finding from the higher-resource-setting trials (Santhanam, Sankar, Inwald) that found no mortality difference between restrictive and liberal fluid strategies when ICU-level rescue was available. The guideline's resource-stratified recommendations reflect this real trial evidence, not institutional hedging — a child who develops fluid-overload-related respiratory failure from aggressive bolusing has a fundamentally different prognosis in a setting with mechanical ventilation available versus one without it.

Why the FEAST result still generates methodological debate: some critics have argued incorrect statistical methods were used in the original analysis, and the study's applicability outside its specific low-resource context has been questioned. This tension is worth holding honestly — the trial's core message (fluid boluses aren't automatically safe, especially without rescue capability) has been broadly influential, even as some of its specific statistical conclusions remain debated in the literature.

Why "discontinue if signs of fluid overload develop" is written directly into the ICU-available recommendation: even in a resource-rich setting where FEAST's harm signal doesn't directly apply, fluid boluses aren't free of downstream risk — pulmonary edema, worsening oxygenation, and tissue edema are recognized complications of aggressive volume therapy. This is why reassessment after every bolus, rather than a fixed total volume delivered regardless of response, is built into current guidance — the goal is titrated, monitored resuscitation, not a protocol-driven volume target pursued mechanically.

Why hypotension is treated as a late, unreliable early warning sign: children have robust compensatory mechanisms (tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction) that maintain blood pressure well into a state of significantly impaired perfusion — this is exactly why "compensated shock" is the more clinically emphasized pediatric category, and why relying on blood pressure alone as a trigger for escalation systematically identifies sepsis later than perfusion-based assessment would.

Why the antibiotic timing recommendation explicitly names the tension with overuse: the guideline is unusually direct that the urgency to treat septic shock quickly has to be balanced against the real risk of unnecessary antimicrobial therapy in children whose presentation overlaps substantially with numerous non-infectious or less severe conditions. Naming this tension explicitly, rather than simply stating "treat fast," reflects an honest acknowledgment that pediatric sepsis recognition is genuinely harder than the urgency of the 1-hour target might suggest in isolation.

rows: Look for a cardiac history, murmur, or hepatomegaly; POCUS can help distinguish poor cardiac contractility from a primarily vasodilated/septic picture.

Clear volume-loss history (vomiting/diarrhea, trauma, GI bleed) without the same degree of systemic inflammatory response; still responds to fluid resuscitation, but without the parallel antimicrobial urgency.
Clear exposure history, skin findings, rapid onset — treated with epinephrine per the dedicated Anaphylaxis crisis file rather than the sepsis pathway.
Can present with tachycardia, altered mental status, and dehydration; point-of-care glucose and ketones distinguish quickly.

Known adrenal insufficiency or recent steroid withdrawal; profound hypotension refractory to fluids and vasopressors should raise this consideration alongside the situational hydrocortisone guidance above.
See the relevant Toxicologic crisis files (BB/CCB overdose, TCA overdose) — can mimic shock physiology without an infectious source; history and specific toxidrome features distinguish.

blocks.html:
Labs and cultures: blood cultures (aerobic bottles alone are generally sufficient given similar yield to combined aerobic/anaerobic sets in most cases, unless anaerobic infection is specifically suspected), CBC, lactate, coagulation panel, renal/hepatic function, glucose. Don't let culture collection delay antimicrobial administration in septic shock.

Reassessment cadence: hemodynamic status after every fluid bolus, ongoing perfusion assessment (capillary refill, mental status, urine output) throughout resuscitation rather than a single initial assessment driving the whole course.

POCUS where available: cardiac and lung ultrasound can help distinguish cardiogenic from distributive shock and guide ongoing fluid/vasopressor decisions, per the new conditional 2026 recommendation.

Disposition: PICU admission is standard for confirmed septic shock, given the need for continuous monitoring, potential vasopressor titration, and reassessment cadence described above.

Follow-up planning: given that 30–40% of PICU sepsis survivors face lasting health issues, arrange structured post-discharge follow-up rather than treating survival to discharge as the endpoint of care.
