protocols.title: Crush Syndrome
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Environmental / Prehospital
protocols.subtitle: The crushing itself isn't what kills — it's what happens systemically the moment the crushing force is released. Standard TCCC permissive hypotension does not apply here, and that exception is easy to miss under pressure.
protocols.description: Why standard TCCC permissive hypotension doesn't apply here, MARCH-first sequencing, why calcium is given despite hypocalcemia. JTS/TCCC-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management — MARCH First, Then the Crush-Specific Cascade
sections.tagline: The casualty has to survive the primary survey before crush syndrome itself becomes the problem. Fluid resuscitation belongs before and during extrication, not after.

steps.title: MARCH — trauma primary survey, in this exact order
steps.html: Massive hemorrhage control (direct pressure, packing, tourniquets) before airway — over 90% of potentially survivable combat deaths involve hemorrhage. Airway. Respiration (tension pneumothorax, open chest wounds). Circulation (shock recognition, IV/IO access, blood products/fluids, TXA per protocol). Hypothermia/Head injury (active warming, TBI assessment) — hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy form the lethal triad.

steps.title: Begin fluid resuscitation before and during extrication — don't wait for release
steps.html: Isotonic saline 1–2 L/hour during extrication is the single most important field intervention. Avoid potassium-containing fluids (lactated Ringer's) given the hyperkalemia already accumulating behind the compressed tissue.

steps.title: Standard TCCC permissive hypotension does NOT apply here
steps.html: This is a genuine, important exception to typical damage-control-resuscitation teaching — see Rationale. Crush injury requiring extrication needs earlier, more aggressive fluid than the hypotensive-resuscitation approach used for straightforward hemorrhagic shock.

steps.title: Entrapment >2 hours with no fluid/monitoring available — consider proximal tourniquet before extrication
steps.html: Two tourniquets side by side, placed proximal to the injury immediately before release, if fluid resuscitation and cardiac monitoring genuinely aren't available. If not feasible before extrication, apply immediately after. This is a doctrine specifically about timing, not a routine step for every entrapment — see Set-Up below.

steps.title: ECG monitoring from the moment of extrication
steps.html: Capture serial 12-leads and continuous rhythm monitoring — peaked T waves are the earliest hyperkalemia sign, progressing toward a sine-wave pattern at severe elevation (commonly cited above ~9 mmol/L). Any ECG evidence of hyperkalemia warrants immediate treatment, not a wait for a lab-confirmed level.

steps.title: Treat ECG-evident hyperkalemia immediately
steps.html: Calcium chloride 10% 5 mL or calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilization — this doesn't lower potassium, it protects the heart while other measures work (see Rationale for why this drug is given even when hypocalcemia, not hyperkalemia, might be the primary derangement). Then shift potassium intracellularly: regular insulin 5–10 units with D50 1–2 amps IV, and/or nebulized albuterol. Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg slow IV push helps shift potassium and treat concurrent acidosis.

steps.title: Continue aggressive fluid resuscitation once extricated
steps.html: Target urine output 200–300 mL/hour (or roughly 2.5 mL/kg/hr) with isotonic saline, monitoring closely for fluid overload in patients with cardiac comorbidity. Delaying fluid resuscitation beyond 12 hours is associated with renal failure incidence approaching 100% — this is not an intervention that can wait for a calmer moment.

steps.title: Mannitol and bicarbonate for renal protection — know the evidence is genuinely mixed
steps.html: Multiple comparative studies have failed to show a consistent benefit over saline alone for preventing acute kidney injury, dialysis, or mortality. Reasonable under specialist/nephrology guidance in select cases, but current best evidence doesn't support routine, protocolized use — don't treat this as a mandatory step.

blocks.title: Decompression without preparation can convert a stable patient into cardiac arrest in minutes
blocks.html: A trapped limb sequesters enormous volume and toxic metabolic load behind the crush before extrication ever happens. The patient can look reasonably stable while entrapped and then crash within minutes of release — think about the moment of extrication itself as a distinct, high-risk event, not just the moment of original injury.

Crush syndrome was first described by Bywaters in patients trapped under rubble during the 1941 Blitz bombing of London. It is fundamentally a reperfusion injury: the danger isn't the crush itself, but what happens systemically the moment the crushing force is released and ischemic muscle reperfuses. It can develop after as little as one hour of entrapment with a large muscle mass involved.

The insult is biphasic. In Phase 1 (ischemia), sustained compression collapses capillary flow — myocytes shift to anaerobic metabolism, ATP depletes, and the sarcolemmal membrane begins to fail, with calcium and sodium accumulating intracellularly while potassium, myoglobin, creatine kinase, phosphate, and uric acid build up behind a still-intact barrier. In Phase 2 (reperfusion), releasing the crushing force restores flow and sweeps the entire toxic load into systemic circulation at once — leukocytes migrate into damaged muscle, generating cytokines, prostaglandins, and free radicals that cause further myolysis on top of the original injury.

rows: Up to several liters can sequester into a single severely crushed extremity — injured muscle takes up fluid like a sponge, and this volume was never actually available to the central circulation while entrapped.
Compensated hypovolemia can mask the true deficit while the patient is still entrapped — this is the single most dangerous feature of the whole syndrome for a first-arriving provider.
Sudden combined distributive + hypovolemic collapse on release
Reperfusion unmasks the hidden hypovolemia while simultaneously releasing vasodilatory and toxic mediators — the deficit and the vasodilation hit at the same moment.
Hyperkalemia-induced arrhythmia is the second most common cause of death immediately after extrication or reperfusion, after hemorrhage.
Peaked T waves → sine wave pattern
The ECG progression of worsening hyperkalemia; sine-wave morphology reflects severe, immediately life-threatening elevation.
The classic rhabdomyolysis triad — present in only a minority of patients, so its absence doesn't rule out significant muscle injury.

sections.title: Set-Up & Tourniquet/Chemical Isolation Doctrine (In Place of "Room Setup")

blocks.html:
• Entrapment under 2 hours: extricate and resuscitate per standard crush protocol — early fluid resuscitation before and during extrication is the priority intervention, not tourniquet placement.
  • Entrapment over 2 hours, fluid resuscitation/monitoring not immediately available: consider tourniquet placement proximal to the injury before extrication — two tourniquets side by side is the preferred technique; apply immediately after extrication if placement before isn't feasible. This recommendation is specifically about reperfusion timing changing the clinical calculus, not a default step for every entrapment.
  • Tourniquet placement before extrication remains genuinely controversial — some international disaster-response guidance (Renal Disaster Relief Task Force, International Search and Rescue Advisory Group) recommends reserving tourniquet use for life-threatening hemorrhage only, rather than routine crush-syndrome prevention. Know that reasonable guidance bodies disagree here.
  • Establish telemedicine/specialist consultation as early as possible — management of crush syndrome in an austere or prolonged-field-care setting is genuinely complex, and Joint Trauma System guidance specifically recommends early consult rather than managing this in isolation.
  • MARCH PAWS extension for prolonged field care — adds Pain, Antibiotics, Wounds, and Splinting; a 2017 performance-improvement review of US Air Force pararescue found it functioned effectively as a treatment checklist across a full deployment cycle.
  • Have calcium, insulin/D50, and sodium bicarbonate immediately accessible wherever entrapped patients are likely to be managed — the hyperkalemia cascade can move fast enough that these shouldn't need to be located reactively.

rows: Minimum entrapment time for syndrome to develop
~1 hour, with large muscle mass involved
Entrapment >2 hours without fluid resuscitation/monitoring available
Renal failure risk with fluid delay
Up to 50% increased incidence; approaching 100% if delayed >12 hours
5–10 units insulin with 1–2 amps D50 IV
Crush syndrome incidence among earthquake survivors
Crush syndrome patients developing acute renal failure

blocks.html:
Why standard TCCC permissive hypotension does NOT apply to extremity crush injury requiring extrication: hypotensive resuscitation in typical hemorrhagic shock accepts a lower blood pressure target to avoid disrupting clot formation at an active bleeding site. Crush injury is a fundamentally different physiologic problem — the danger isn't ongoing external hemorrhage but a hidden, massive volume deficit sequestered in the crushed tissue, about to be combined with a toxic metabolic load and vasodilatory mediators the instant the crush is released. Permissive hypotension in this specific setting doesn't protect a clot; it just leaves the patient under-resuscitated for the deficit that reperfusion is about to unmask all at once. This is exactly why Joint Trauma System guidance explicitly states the principles of hypotensive resuscitation according to TCCC do not apply in the setting of extremity crush injury requiring extrication.

Why the patient can look stable while entrapped and then crash within minutes of release: third-spaced fluid sequestered in the crushed compartment was never part of the effective circulating volume, even though it's technically still "in the body" — compensatory mechanisms can maintain acceptable vital signs against this hidden deficit right up until the crush is released. Reperfusion does two things simultaneously: it unmasks the true hypovolemic deficit (since compressed capillaries can no longer hide it) and releases vasodilatory/toxic mediators that further drop vascular resistance — a combined hypovolemic-and-distributive collapse landing at the same moment, which is why field providers are told to think about the moment of extrication itself as a distinct, high-risk event.

Why calcium is given even when hypocalcemia (not hyperkalemia) might technically be the more prominent derangement: injured muscle actively takes up calcium, which can produce genuine hypocalcemia in crush syndrome. But the calcium given acutely for ECG-evident hyperkalemia isn't primarily correcting that hypocalcemia — it's stabilizing the cardiac cell membrane against the arrhythmogenic effect of elevated extracellular potassium. This is why current guidance (e.g., AMBOSS) recommends a cautious, situational approach to calcium replacement generally, while still recommending calcium specifically and promptly for symptomatic hyperkalemia — two different indications for the same drug, aimed at two different problems.

Why mannitol and bicarbonate for renal protection remain controversial despite intuitive appeal: the theoretical rationale (forced diuresis and urinary alkalinization to reduce myoglobin/uric acid deposition in renal tubules) is mechanistically plausible and supported by some animal data — but repeated human comparative studies (several summarized directly against saline-alone controls) have failed to show a consistent, reproducible benefit for preventing acute kidney injury, need for dialysis, or mortality. This is a genuine area where intuitive pathophysiology and clinical trial evidence haven't lined up, which is why current best evidence treats these as situational/specialist-guided adjuncts rather than routine, protocolized therapy.

Why fluid delay carries such a steep, almost binary-sounding renal failure risk: the relationship between resuscitation timing and outcome in crush-associated AKI isn't gradual — multiple studies specifically link delayed initiation (particularly beyond roughly 12 hours) to renal failure incidence approaching universal, while early, vigorous fluid resuscitation begun before or during extrication substantially prevents progression to needing dialysis. This steep time-dependence is exactly why early fluid administration is framed as the single most important field intervention, ahead of any of the more specific pharmacologic hyperkalemia treatments that follow it.

rows: Can coexist with or follow crush injury independently — pain out of proportion, tense compartment, and the classic 5 P's; requires its own surgical decompression regardless of systemic crush-syndrome management.
Prolonged tourniquet application (>2 hours) or extremity compartment syndrome without external crush
Can independently produce reperfusion-driven rhabdomyolysis by the same mechanism as true crush syndrome — management principles are the same even though the mechanism of the original injury differs.
No entrapment/compression mechanism; still shares the hyperkalemia and AKI management principles described here once rhabdomyolysis is established, regardless of cause.
Standard TCCC permissive hypotension principles DO apply here — this is precisely the distinction that makes recognizing true crush physiology clinically important rather than academic.
Hyperkalemia from another primary cause (renal failure, DKA, medication)
No entrapment history; see the dedicated Hyperkalemic Cardiac Arrest crisis file for the broader hyperkalemia management framework that overlaps substantially with the acute treatment steps here.

blocks.html:
Labs: potassium, creatine kinase (CK), creatinine/renal function, calcium, phosphate, uric acid, coagulation panel, and urinalysis for myoglobinuria. Trend CK and renal function serially rather than relying on a single value — both continue to evolve over the following 24–72 hours.

Continuous cardiac monitoring from extrication through resolution of hyperkalemia, given how rapidly the ECG picture can change.

Fasciotomy evaluation for any limb with clinical concern for compartment syndrome — over half of severe crush syndrome cases ultimately require it; don't let systemic management alone substitute for the local surgical decision.

Renal replacement therapy planning — nephrology consultation early given how common progression to dialysis-requiring AKI is in this population; don't wait for frank renal failure to involve them.

Disposition: ICU-level care is standard for any confirmed or strongly suspected crush syndrome given the combination of hemodynamic instability, arrhythmia risk, and evolving renal injury — this is not a population managed on a general floor in the acute phase.

protocols.title: Heat Stroke
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Environmental / Prehospital
protocols.subtitle: Cold-water immersion beats every alternative by 6-10x on cooling rate — the 2025 SCCM guideline turns "cool fast" into a specific number: ≥0.155°C/min, target reached within 30 minutes.
protocols.description: Why immersion is 6-10x faster than any alternative, the specific ≥0.155°C/min target, why no drug (including dantrolene) helps. 2025 SCCM guideline-aligned.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Cooling is the treatment — not a supportive measure alongside the treatment. Cool first, transport second.

steps.title: Confirm the diagnosis and get a core temperature immediately
steps.html: Rectal temperature is the most accurate field/ED measurement. Heat stroke = core temperature elevation (commonly >40°C) plus CNS dysfunction (altered mental status, irrational behavior, seizure, coma). If rectal temperature isn't available in a collapsed athlete, use time-based immersion protocols rather than waiting for a monitoring device.

steps.title: Begin active cooling immediately — cold- or ice-water immersion first-line
steps.html: Ice-water immersion (1–5°C) or cold-water immersion (9–12°C) achieves the fastest cooling rate of any method and should be prioritized where available. Active cooling is recommended over passive methods across the board — this is a strong recommendation, not a preference.

steps.title: Target: core temperature <39°C within 30 minutes of recognition
steps.html: Prioritize any cooling method that achieves a rate ≥0.155°C/min. Similar cooling strategies apply to both classic (nonexertional) and exertional heat stroke — the underlying urgency is the same regardless of cause.

steps.title: Cool first, transport second
steps.html: Begin cooling on-site before transport whenever feasible — delays in initiating cooling are directly associated with worse outcomes. Activate EMS simultaneously with starting cooling, not sequentially after.

steps.title: If immersion isn't feasible, use the fastest available alternative
steps.html: Rotating ice-water-soaked towels, tarp-assisted cooling (TACO), or continuous cold-water dousing are reasonable alternatives — all clearly inferior to immersion in laboratory cooling-rate comparisons, but studied in real-world use with good outcomes when immersion genuinely isn't practical (mass-casualty settings, limited equipment).

steps.title: Monitor core temperature continuously during cooling
steps.html: Cease active cooling once rectal temperature reaches roughly 38.3–39°C to avoid overshooting into iatrogenic hypothermia — continue monitoring afterward since temperature can drift after cooling stops.

steps.title: Avoid pharmacologic temperature-control agents entirely
steps.html: No evidence supports acetaminophen, NSAIDs, salicylates, or dantrolene for heat stroke — avoid all of them. This isn't a fever responding to a hypothalamic-set-point drug; none of these have a mechanism that addresses the actual problem.

steps.title: Supportive care in parallel
steps.html: Cold IV fluids as an adjunct to cooling, airway protection for depressed mental status, and treatment of seizures if they occur — but prophylactic antiseizure medication or prophylactic antibiotics should be used only in a research context, not routinely.

blocks.title: The Currie response is a real but transient phenomenon — don't let it stop cooling
blocks.html: Cold-water immersion can cause a brief initial rise or plateau in core temperature (peripheral vasoconstriction trapping heat centrally) before the expected drop begins. This effect is minor (roughly 0.1–0.2°C) and short-lived — it is not a reason to abandon or delay immersion, which remains the fastest and most effective cooling method despite this transient response.

Heat stroke is severe hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction, subclassified as classic (nonexertional — typically elderly, chronically ill, or those with impaired thermoregulation during ambient heat exposure) or exertional (typically young, healthy individuals engaged in strenuous activity, often in heat). Both are true medical emergencies: ICU mortality can approach 60% in severe cases, and roughly 30% of survivors experience long-term cognitive or motor dysfunction. Cell death in the CNS increases exponentially with both temperature and duration of exposure — the entire treatment paradigm exists to interrupt that exponential curve as fast as possible.

The 2025 Society of Critical Care Medicine guideline — the current definitive reference — issued two strong recommendations, five good practice statements, and one research-only statement. The overall message is unusually unambiguous for a critical care guideline: active cooling, as fast as possible, using the best available method, started immediately, with essentially no role for pharmacologic temperature control.

rows: Elderly, chronically ill, infants, those with impaired thermoregulation or limited mobility during a heat wave
Young, healthy — athletes, military personnel, outdoor workers (firefighters, construction, landscaping)
Gradual, over days of heat exposure
Rapid, over minutes to hours during exertion
Core temperature elevation with CNS dysfunction
Rectal temperature >105°F (40.5°C) immediately post-collapse plus CNS dysfunction — though collapse is not required to consider the diagnosis
Irrational behavior, irritability, emotional instability, altered consciousness, collapse, coma, dizziness
Often absent (impaired sweat response is part of the mechanism)
May still be present — absence of sweating is not required for either diagnosis
Similar strategies to exertional per current guidance; evaporative/convective cooling reasonable in-hospital, though inferior cooling rates to conductive methods
Cold-water immersion strongly preferred; evaporative/convective cooling not indicated as primary treatment

blocks.html:
• Have an immersion cooling setup ready before it's needed — at any event, facility, or unit where heat stroke risk is plausible (athletic events, military training, high-heat occupational settings), not assembled reactively after a collapse.
  • Set up cooling capability during the first weeks of a heat-exposure season and whenever wet-bulb globe temperature crosses a defined threshold — this is standard athletic emergency action plan guidance, not something to improvise mid-season.
  • Know your fastest available alternative if immersion isn't feasible — rotating ice-water towels and TACO both have real supporting outcome data and should be part of the plan, not a last-minute improvisation.
  • Recognize medication-related risk factors: drugs that increase heat production (amphetamines, thyroid agonists, weight-loss supplements) or impair thermoregulation (anticholinergics, phenothiazines, diuretics, beta-blockers, antipsychotics, SSRIs) all raise individual risk and are worth knowing in a patient's history.
  • Have EMS activation and cooling happen simultaneously, not sequentially — "cool first, transport second" needs to be a rehearsed protocol, not a judgment call made under pressure.

rows: Exertional heat stroke survival with cooling <10 minutes of collapse
Water immersion duration if rectal temp unavailable (≤9°C water)
Water immersion duration if rectal temp unavailable (10–26°C water)
Reported exertional heat stroke mortality range across settings

blocks.html:
Why cold-water immersion isn't just "preferred" but categorically faster: immersion couples the body's entire surface area to a cold conductive medium simultaneously, while every alternative (fanning, misting, ice packs at discrete sites) relies on evaporation or localized conduction across a much smaller effective contact area. This is a physics difference, not a marginal clinical preference — laboratory and field data consistently show immersion cooling 6 to 10 times faster than the next-best widely available alternatives, which is why guideline language doesn't hedge on this point the way it does on many other critical care interventions.

Why the guideline expresses urgency as a specific numeric cooling rate rather than just "cool quickly": CNS cell death increases exponentially with both temperature and duration of exposure — meaning the actual physiologic damage isn't linear with time, and a vague "cool as fast as reasonably possible" instruction doesn't capture how much a delay of even a few extra minutes can matter. Anchoring to ≥0.155°C/min and a 30-minute target temperature gives providers something concrete to plan equipment and staffing around, rather than a qualitative goal that's easy to underachieve without realizing it.

Why no pharmacologic agent is recommended, including drugs that seem intuitively related: antipyretics like acetaminophen work by resetting the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point — but heat stroke isn't a set-point fever, it's a failure of the body's ability to dissipate heat faster than it's being generated or absorbed. There's no elevated set point to reset. Dantrolene, despite its unrelated but conceptually adjacent role in malignant hyperthermia (see that crisis file), specifically showed no benefit in reducing mortality or cooling time in heat stroke trials — different mechanism of heat generation entirely (excessive skeletal muscle metabolic heat production from a triggering anesthetic, versus environmental/exertional heat exceeding dissipation capacity), so a drug effective for one doesn't transfer to the other.

Why "cool first, transport second" is stated as a specific operational principle rather than assumed: transport time, even short transport time, is dead time with respect to the exponential CNS injury curve described above unless active cooling is already underway during that transport. Making this an explicit, named principle — rather than trusting individual judgment in the moment — pushes teams toward starting cooling on-site by default, which the outcome data (including reported 100% survival when cooling began within 10 minutes of collapse) directly supports.

Why the transient initial temperature rise on immersion (the Currie response) doesn't change the recommendation: peripheral vasoconstriction from sudden cold exposure can briefly trap heat centrally, producing a small, short-lived uptick or plateau before the expected drop. This is a normal, minor physiologic response (roughly 0.1–0.2°C) rather than a sign the intervention is failing — understanding this mechanism prevents a provider from second-guessing or discontinuing the single most effective treatment available based on a brief, expected, and clinically insignificant reading.

rows: A critical distinction in a collapsed endurance athlete — history of hyperhydration combined with exercise duration >4 hours is typical for EAH, while neurologic signs plus elevated rectal temperature point to exertional heat stroke instead; treatment differs substantially (fluid restriction/hypertonic saline for EAH vs. immediate cooling for heat stroke).
Sudden cardiac arrest in an athlete

Must be actively considered and ruled out in any collapsed endurance athlete alongside EHS and EAH — pulse check and standard ACLS take priority if arrest is present; see the ACLS Quick Reference crisis file.

Temporal link to volatile anesthetic/succinylcholine exposure rather than environmental or exertional heat — see the dedicated MH crisis file; dantrolene is specifically effective there and specifically not effective in heat stroke.
Temporal link to a serotonergic or dopamine-blocking medication rather than heat exposure — see the dedicated Serotonin Syndrome vs. NMS crisis file for the distinguishing exam findings.

Drug exposure history (cocaine, amphetamines) rather than environmental heat — see the dedicated Cocaine/Sympathomimetic Toxicity crisis file; hyperthermia management principles overlap substantially.
No clear heat-exposure or exertional trigger; consider particularly in classic (nonexertional) heat stroke presentations in elderly patients where infection can coexist or mimic the picture.
Known thyroid disease history and distinct lab pattern (suppressed TSH, elevated free T4) rather than a heat-exposure trigger.

blocks.html:
Labs: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, liver function tests, coagulation panel (DIC risk in severe cases), creatine kinase (concurrent rhabdomyolysis is common — see the dedicated Crush Syndrome crisis file for the broader hyperkalemia/AKI management framework that applies here too), and lactate. Continuous core temperature monitoring throughout the ED/ICU course, not just during active cooling.

CT imaging for altered mental status not clearly explained by heat stroke alone, or that fails to improve as expected with cooling — don't delay active cooling to obtain imaging first.

Monitor for multi-organ involvement: acute kidney injury, hepatic injury, coagulopathy/DIC, and rhabdomyolysis can all develop or worsen over the following 24–72 hours even after successful initial cooling — this is not a single-intervention-and-done presentation.

Disposition: ICU admission is standard for any confirmed heat stroke given the mortality and long-term morbidity data above, plus the need for continued monitoring of the multi-organ complications described.

Consider burn evaluation in classic heat stroke specifically — direct contact with surfaces like pavement, which can exceed 71°C, can produce concurrent burn injury that's easy to overlook amid the systemic presentation.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Standard ACLS pharmacology gets deliberately modified below 30°C — the drugs aren't wrong, they're just held until the body can actually metabolize them.

steps.title: Handle gently — avoid triggering rescue collapse
steps.html: A severely hypothermic myocardium is electrically unstable and can be provoked into VF by rough handling, sudden postural change, or a catecholamine surge during extraction/rescue. Move horizontally, minimize jostling, and avoid abrupt movement even in an apparently stable patient.

steps.title: Begin high-quality CPR immediately, prolonged if needed
steps.html: Mechanical compression devices are preferred, especially for extended transport. Intermittent or delayed CPR is an acceptable compromise specifically in difficult rescue settings (avalanche, technical terrain) when continuous CPR truly isn't feasible — not a routine substitute for continuous compressions.

steps.title: Defibrillation — attempt once, then hold further shocks below 30°C
steps.html: Reasonable to attempt defibrillation at any temperature for a shockable rhythm — there's no known harm in trying. But success is unlikely below 30°C given the hypothermic myocardium's altered electrophysiology; delay further shock attempts until core temperature exceeds 30°C rather than repeating shocks that aren't going to work.

steps.title: Hold or space standard ACLS drugs below 30°C
steps.html: Give epinephrine 1 mg IV once core temperature reaches 30°C, unless imminent ECPR is planned. Between 30–35°C, extend the dosing interval to 6–10 minutes (roughly double the normal interval). A 300 mg amiodarone load is reasonable if a shockable rhythm is present, but delay further doses until >30°C.

steps.title: Assess for ECPR/VA-ECMO candidacy immediately, in parallel with CPR
steps.html: There is no absolute contraindication to ECLS rewarming for core temperature <30°C. Between 30–32°C, or when the HOPE score estimates survival probability <10%, ECLS may still be considered but only on an exceptional basis. An unwitnessed arrest with asystole as the presenting rhythm is not, by itself, a contraindication to ECLS rewarming.

steps.title: Transport directly to an ECMO-capable center
steps.html: Even if it means bypassing a closer non-ECMO hospital, as long as travel time is reasonable (commonly cited threshold ~6 hours). Beyond that window, initiate conventional (non-extracorporeal) rewarming instead rather than pursuing a transport that will take too long to matter.

steps.title: If securing an advanced airway, use a non-depolarizing paralytic
steps.html: Avoid succinylcholine specifically to prevent an additional, avoidable rise in serum potassium on top of whatever the hypothermic insult itself has already produced.

steps.title: Once on ECMO, rewarm at a deliberate, not maximal, rate
steps.html: The circuit can technically warm at 7–10°C/hour, but some evidence favors a slower rate (closer to 2°C/hour) for better neurologic outcomes — see Rationale for the genuine, unresolved tension here.

blocks.title: Warmed fluids only — always
blocks.html: Room-temperature IV fluids actively worsen hypothermia. Use warmed isotonic crystalloid (38–42°C) through a rapid infuser, anticipating significant hypotension as rewarming-associated vasodilation and fluid shifts develop — often requiring large volumes.

Accidental hypothermia is an unintentional drop in core body temperature below 35°C. It causes progressive cardiovascular instability, myocardial irritability, and — at severe degrees — cardiac arrest. Critically, hypothermia developing before the arrest (primary hypothermia) suppresses cerebral metabolic demand ahead of any oxygen deprivation, providing genuine neuroprotection that allows for prolonged resuscitation with real potential for good neurologic outcome — the physiologic basis for "not dead until warm and dead."

This is fundamentally different from secondary hypothermia, where cardiac arrest or severe injury occurs first (trauma, drowning-related asphyxia before cooling, or another primary arrest cause) and hypothermia develops afterward as a consequence. In secondary hypothermia, the brain has already sustained a normothermic-duration ischemic insult before any protective cooling took effect — this population does not share the same favorable prognosis, and distinguishing the two is one of the most consequential early judgment calls in this entire crisis.

sections.title: Staging — Swiss System (In Place of "Signs and Symptoms")

rows: Cardiac arrest or unmeasurable vital signs — clinical staging emphasizes presence/absence of vital signs over an exact temperature threshold, since field temperature measurement is often imprecise
A retrospective, pathological determination — not something made prospectively in the field or ED

blocks.html: Fixed dilated pupils, apparent rigor mortis, and dependent lividity do not, by themselves, constitute contraindications to resuscitation in a severely hypothermic patient — these findings can occur in profound hypothermia without indicating true, irreversible death.

• Measure core temperature with the right device for the situation: esophageal probe (lower third) is most accurate once the airway is secured; an epitympanic (ear) thermometer with an isolating ear cap is the recommended field alternative when the airway isn't yet secured.
  • Prevent further heat loss actively during rescue and transport — insulation, vapor barrier, warm environment where possible — rather than treating rewarming as something that only starts on arrival.
  • Pre-identify a regional ECMO-capable receiving center and build direct-transport protocols — bypassing a closer non-ECMO hospital is a system-level decision that needs to be made and rehearsed in advance, not improvised mid-transport.
  • Have a mechanical CPR device available for any anticipated prolonged transport, given how much longer hypothermic-arrest resuscitation efforts may need to run compared to normothermic arrest.
  • Calculate the HOPE score where feasible to formally estimate survival probability and support the ECLS decision, rather than relying purely on bedside gestalt (see Rationale for why this specifically matters).

blocks.html:
Why "not dead until warm and dead" reflects real physiology: hypothermia suppresses cerebral metabolic rate substantially with each degree of core temperature drop — meaning the brain can tolerate a much longer period of reduced or absent perfusion without the degree of injury that the same duration would cause at normal temperature. This is the entire physiologic basis for prolonged resuscitation efforts and the genuinely excellent neurologic outcomes reported even after multiple hours of CPR in this population specifically.

Why the primary-vs-secondary hypothermia distinction is the single most important early judgment call: in primary hypothermia, cooling occurs before any hypoxic insult, meaning the neuroprotective mechanism is already in place before the brain is ever deprived of oxygen. In secondary hypothermia, the arrest or injury happened first at normal temperature — the brain has already sustained ischemic injury on a normothermic timeline before cooling developed afterward as a consequence, not a protection. This is why the same "keep resuscitating for hours" approach that's appropriate for primary hypothermia doesn't carry the same favorable prognosis in secondary hypothermia, and why making this distinction early genuinely changes the entire trajectory of the resuscitation.

Why drugs are held or spaced below 30°C: hepatic and renal drug metabolism slow substantially as core temperature drops, meaning standard-interval dosing (epinephrine every 3–5 minutes, as in normothermic ACLS) risks progressive drug accumulation that becomes toxic once the patient eventually rewarms and normal clearance resumes. Extending the interval and limiting total doses until a temperature threshold is crossed avoids stacking a large, delayed-release drug burden onto a patient who is about to regain the metabolic capacity to be affected by all of it at once.

Why ECMO is preferred specifically over cardiopulmonary bypass and over conventional rewarming: a patient in hypothermic arrest needs circulatory support, oxygenation, and rewarming simultaneously — ECMO provides all three through a single modality, while conventional methods address rewarming without solving the underlying perfusion failure, and CPB requires more anticoagulation and is less readily sustainable over the hours a hypothermic-arrest resuscitation may require.

Why the rewarming-rate question remains genuinely unresolved: ECMO can technically rewarm as fast as 7–10°C/hour, but some evidence suggests a slower rate (closer to 2°C/hour) may produce better neurologic outcomes — plausibly because very rapid rewarming creates a mismatch between quickly rising metabolic demand and still-recovering circulatory/oxygen-delivery capacity, alongside hemodynamic instability from rapid vasodilation. Current practice hasn't fully resolved this tension, which is why a team might reasonably choose a more conservative rewarming rate even when the circuit is technically capable of going faster — this is an honest area of ongoing clinical judgment, not a settled protocol.

Why the documented gap between guideline criteria and real-world stop-resuscitation decisions matters: a retrospective multi-center study found only about a third of decisions not to pursue ECLS rewarming were actually compliant with international guideline criteria when checked against admission serum potassium — while applying the validated HOPE score's probability threshold would have supported roughly two-thirds of those same decisions. This suggests a structured, validated tool outperforms ad hoc bedside judgment specifically for this consequential, hard-to-reverse decision — a parallel to the documented gap between guideline-target and real-world epinephrine timing described in the NRP crisis file, and a reminder that even well-intentioned clinical judgment benefits from a formal decision aid in exactly the highest-stakes moments.

rows: Secondary hypothermia from trauma or another primary arrest cause
The most clinically important distinction to make — see Rationale above; changes prognosis and the appropriateness of prolonged resuscitation/ECLS pursuit substantially.

Severe hypothyroidism can independently cause profound hypothermia with altered mental status; check TSH/free T4 if the picture seems disproportionate to a plausible cold-exposure history — treated with levothyroxine, a completely different intervention.

Can rarely present with hypothermia rather than fever, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients — a different underlying etiology requiring antimicrobial therapy rather than rewarming alone.

A common contributing factor in urban/exposure-related hypothermia — impairs shivering thermogenesis and judgment about seeking shelter; doesn't change acute management but is relevant to disposition and harm-reduction planning.
Can accompany or mimic a hypothermic presentation — check glucose as part of the standard altered-mental-status workup regardless of exposure history.
Can contribute to hemodynamic instability disproportionate to the degree of hypothermia alone — consider in a refractory or unusually unstable presentation.

blocks.html:
Labs on arrival: serum potassium (interpret with caution given hemolysis risk on a difficult draw), ABG, glucose, coagulation panel — hypothermia itself impairs coagulation, which is directly relevant to anticoagulation decisions once on ECMO (some protocols minimize or omit anticoagulation initially given this baseline impairment).

HOPE score calculation to formally estimate survival probability and support the ECLS decision, particularly in the 30–32°C exceptional-basis range described above.

Continue rewarming in-hospital to normothermia even after ROSC, with close monitoring for reperfusion complications — arrhythmia, coagulopathy, and rewarming-associated hypotension from vasodilation, often requiring substantial warmed fluid volumes.

Disposition: ICU admission is standard for any patient requiring active rewarming beyond mild cases; ECMO-treated patients need cardiothoracic/critical care co-management through decannulation.

Address the underlying and any secondary contributing cause once stable — toxicology screening, trauma workup, or endocrine evaluation as clinically indicated, rather than treating rewarming alone as the complete course of care.

protocols.title: Massive Transfusion Protocol
protocols.kicker: The Critical Vector · Crisis Management · Resuscitation / Hemorrhage
protocols.subtitle: Ratio-based resuscitation built to mimic whole blood, the lethal triad it's designed to break, and why TEG/ROTEM complements the protocol instead of replacing it.

badges.text: TXA WITHIN 3 HOURS OR NOT AT ALL

protocols.description: 1:1:1 ratio-based resuscitation, TXA's 3-hour window, calcium/lethal-triad management, TEG/ROTEM as complement not replacement.

sections.title: Emergency Management & Immediate Actions
sections.tagline: Transfusion buys time — it doesn't stop the bleeding. Activate the protocol and pursue source control in parallel, not sequentially.

steps.title: Activate the MTP, call for help
steps.html: Notify the blood bank immediately once criteria are met (see Activation Criteria below) — don't wait for confirmatory labs. Activation itself triggers pre-packaged, ratio-matched coolers to start moving.

steps.title: Start with universal products, transition to type-specific
steps.html: O-negative PRBCs with AB plasma (or low-titer group A plasma if AB is unavailable) until type-specific or crossmatched products are ready.

steps.title: Give products in a balanced ratio
steps.html: Empiric 1:1:1 (PRBC : FFP : platelets), extending to 1:1:1:1 with cryoprecipitate for prolonged/repeated rounds. Platelets ideally run through a separate IV, not through a rapid infuser — infuser shear can damage platelet function. RBCs and plasma can run simultaneously through the same line.

steps.title: Tranexamic acid — early, or not at all
steps.html: 1 g IV bolus over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours. Give within 3 hours of injury — CRASH-2 data shows benefit specifically in this window; later administration hasn't shown the same mortality benefit and isn't the default move.

steps.title: Replace calcium proactively
steps.html: Citrate in stored blood products chelates ionized calcium — check it and replace early and often rather than waiting for it to become critically low; hypocalcemia independently worsens coagulopathy on top of dilution.

steps.title: Actively prevent hypothermia and acidosis
steps.html: Warm fluids/blood, use active external warming, minimize exposure. Avoid excess crystalloid — it dilutes clotting factors and doesn't carry oxygen. Permissive hypotension (accepting a lower-than-normal blood pressure target) is appropriate in the actively hemorrhaging trauma patient before definitive hemostasis, to avoid disrupting early clot formation.

steps.title: Reassess with labs and, where available, viscoelastic testing
steps.html: Check CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen after every ~5 units of PRBCs. TEG/ROTEM, when available, helps target specific deficiencies — hyperfibrinolysis needing more TXA, or a low fibrinogen needing cryoprecipitate — rather than continuing to transfuse blindly on ratio alone.

steps.title: Pursue source control in parallel, not after
steps.html: Surgery, interventional radiology, or endoscopic hemostasis — whatever stops the bleeding definitively. REBOA or resuscitative thoracotomy are options in extremis. No transfusion ratio substitutes for actually stopping the hemorrhage.

blocks.title: Hemoglobin is a lagging indicator
blocks.html: Hemoglobin concentration doesn't fall immediately with acute blood loss — relying on it as an early marker of severity underestimates how much blood has actually been lost. Treat the clinical picture and activation criteria, not a normal-looking hemoglobin on an early sample.

Massive transfusion protocols exist to deliver blood components rapidly, in a pre-determined balanced ratio, to a patient in life-threatening hemorrhage — replacing the older practice of resuscitating primarily with crystalloid and PRBCs alone, which produces a dilutional coagulopathy that makes bleeding worse, not better. Modern MTPs grew out of military damage control resuscitation: rapid hemorrhage control, permissive hypotension, minimized crystalloid, and early balanced blood product use, rather than treating bleeding and coagulopathy as separate, sequential problems.

The classic definition of massive transfusion — 10 or more units of PRBCs in 24 hours — is arbitrary (chosen because it approximates one blood volume) and often too slow to guide real-time decisions. More clinically useful dynamic definitions include ≥4 units of PRBCs in 1 hour with ongoing need, ≥3 units in any 1-hour period in the first 24 hours, or replacing ≥50% of blood volume within 3 hours. Ultra-massive transfusion — more than 20 units of PRBCs within 24–48 hours — represents an even more extreme resuscitation tier with its own outcomes literature.

sections.title: Activation Criteria (In Place of "Signs and Symptoms")

rows: One point each for: penetrating mechanism, positive FAST exam, systolic BP ≤90 mmHg, heart rate ≥120 bpm. A score ≥2 suggests likely need for massive transfusion — a simple, fast bedside tool usable before labs return.
≥4 units PRBC in 1 hour with ongoing need, or ≥3 units in any 1-hour period — more responsive to real-time deterioration than the classic 10-units-in-24-hours definition.
Rapid, pattern-based recognition by the treating team remains a legitimate and commonly used activation trigger — don't wait for a formal score to confirm what's clinically obvious.
Persistent hypotension, tachycardia, rising lactate, and worsening base deficit despite initial resuscitation all support activation, independent of any single scoring tool.

sections.title: Set-Up & Institutional Readiness (In Place of "Room Setup")

blocks.html:
• Pre-packaged, ratio-matched coolers ready for immediate release on activation — most level 1 trauma centers maintain these specifically to avoid the delay of assembling individual components under pressure.
  • Rapid infuser and large-bore access ready — but keep platelets off the rapid infuser specifically, running them through a separate line to preserve platelet function.
  • Clear communication pathway with the blood bank established in advance — who calls, what's said, how products get delivered — this is exactly the kind of process that fails under stress if it hasn't been rehearsed.
  • Whole blood availability where possible — increasingly preferred over reconstructed component ratios where logistics allow, since it more closely mimics what was actually lost; over 80% of surveyed level 1 trauma centers currently still approximate this with component ratios rather than true whole blood.
  • Viscoelastic testing capability (TEG/ROTEM) available within the first hour of admission where resources allow, to complement — not replace — the initial empiric ratio-based approach.
  • Regular MTP simulation/drills for the full team (trauma, anesthesia, blood bank, nursing) — activation is rare enough at most institutions that unpracticed teams lose critical time on process alone.

rows: ≥4 units in 1 hour with ongoing need, or ≥3 units in any 1-hour period
1 g bolus over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 hours — within 3 hours of injury
10 units raises fibrinogen by roughly 75 mg/dL
After every ~5 units of PRBCs: CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen
Increased odds (OR ~2.65) — factor into timing of VTE prophylaxis once bleeding is controlled

blocks.html:
Why the 1:1:1 ratio replaced RBC-heavy resuscitation: transfusing PRBCs alone (or with disproportionate crystalloid) restores oxygen-carrying capacity but dilutes clotting factors and platelets that were never replaced — actively worsening the coagulopathy driving ongoing hemorrhage. A balanced ratio approximates whole blood's composition, treating the anemia and the coagulopathy simultaneously rather than sequentially.

Why TXA's benefit is time-locked to the first 3 hours: TXA works by inhibiting fibrinolysis at a point in the injury response when hyperfibrinolysis is actively contributing to bleeding. Given later, after the coagulation system has shifted toward a more prothrombotic state, the same antifibrinolytic effect no longer targets an active problem and instead just adds thrombotic risk without the offsetting hemostatic benefit — which is exactly what CRASH-2's time-stratified results showed.

Why calcium replacement is proactive, not reactive: citrate — the anticoagulant in stored blood products — binds ionized calcium, and large-volume transfusion delivers citrate faster than the liver can metabolize it. Since calcium is a required cofactor in the coagulation cascade, citrate-induced hypocalcemia directly impairs clot formation on top of dilutional coagulopathy — checking and replacing it early prevents a second, iatrogenic driver of the same bleeding problem you're trying to treat.

Why permissive hypotension and minimized crystalloid matter before definitive hemostasis: a higher blood pressure target can disrupt a fragile early clot before surgical or interventional control is achieved, effectively "popping the clot" and restarting hemorrhage. Excess crystalloid compounds the dilutional coagulopathy problem the balanced-ratio strategy is specifically designed to avoid — both practices exist to protect the clot you're trying to help the body form, not just to raise a number on the monitor.

Why TEG/ROTEM complements rather than replaces the empiric protocol: trial evidence (iTACTIC) found no significant outcome difference between viscoelastic-guided and conventional-coagulation-test-guided transfusion when both used immediate empiric transfusion up front — meaning the real value of viscoelastic testing shows up in identifying specific deficits (hyperfibrinolysis needing more TXA, isolated fibrinogen depletion needing cryoprecipitate) in a patient who continues bleeding despite standard MTP, not in replacing the initial ratio-based approach entirely.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis — Why Isn't This Working?

rows: Ongoing surgical/anatomic bleeding source not yet controlled
Persistent transfusion requirement despite adequate ratio and normalizing labs — this is a source-control problem, not a transfusion-ratio problem; escalate to OR/IR rather than transfusing further.

History of warfarin, DOACs, or antiplatelet therapy — needs specific reversal (vitamin K/PCC for warfarin, agent-specific reversal for DOACs) on top of the standard MTP, since balanced-ratio products don't reverse a pharmacologic anticoagulant.
Underlying hemophilia or von Willebrand disease
Disproportionate bleeding relative to injury severity, prior bleeding history — needs factor-specific replacement, not just ratio-based component transfusion.
DIC from a non-traumatic cause (sepsis, AFE, malignancy)

Bleeding out of proportion to a mechanical injury, with a clinical context (infection, peripartum collapse) pointing toward a primary consumptive coagulopathy rather than dilutional trauma-induced coagulopathy.
Isolated severe thrombocytopenia from another cause
Platelet count disproportionately low relative to the degree of hemodilution — consider immune thrombocytopenia or another primary hematologic process if the pattern doesn't fit simple dilution.

blocks.html:
Ongoing labs: continue serial CBC, coagulation panel, fibrinogen, ionized calcium, blood gas/lactate/base deficit roughly every 30–60 minutes through active resuscitation, and after every ~5 units of PRBCs specifically.

Stand-down criteria: deactivate the MTP once bleeding is controlled and the patient is hemodynamically stable — continuing ratio-based transfusion past the point of active hemorrhage risks unnecessary product use and volume overload (see the Transfusion Reactions crisis file for TACO specifically).

VTE prophylaxis timing: massive transfusion independently raises VTE risk, but prophylaxis has to be balanced against ongoing bleeding risk — this is a genuine timing judgment call made once hemostasis is achieved, not a fixed protocol step.

Disposition: ICU admission is standard for any patient who required massive transfusion, given the need for continued monitoring of coagulation status, electrolytes, and end-organ function.

Documentation and debrief: record total products given, ratio achieved, TXA timing, and viscoelastic results if obtained — both for this patient's ongoing care and for institutional review of MTP performance and blood product stewardship.
